events.title: Australian AI data centre operator NextDC shares shed 44% on revenue delay
events.summary: NextDC shares fell 44% and wiped about A$3.1 billion from its market value in early trade. NextDC shares fell 44% after it cut revenue and earnings forecasts, saying delays to power upgrades at its M3 Melbourne site will defer about A$140 million in contracted revenue. The company will pause all new development projects and land buys for now, and it may sell selected sites as it reviews capital recycling options. Jemena’s delayed network works pushed the next power increase for M3 to 2028, showing how community opposition and power limits can threaten data centre growth. SYDNEY – Australian data centre operator NextDC shed nearly half of its market capitalisation on Oct 21 after sharply cutting revenue forecasts for the year ahead and putting future developments on hold, extending the burst of negative sentiment towards global artificial intelligence stocks. The company said delays to electricity network upgrades at one of its major Melbourne assets would mean about A$140 million (S$125 million) worth of contracted customer revenue this financial year would be deferred. It would shelve all new development projects and land acquisitions for the foreseeable future and would evaluate capital recycling opportunities, including potential sales of selected development sites. The news sent NextDC shares down 44% and wiped about A$3.1 billion from its market value in early trade. The stock, now at its lowest since Jan 18, was also the biggest loser on the broader ASX200 benchmark index. Investments for data centre operators continue to pour in on expectations that surging demand for AI will drive a new wave of spending on digital infrastructure. However, sentiment has weakened in recent weeks as investors question whether massive AI spending can justify soaring computing, land and power costs. Signs of strain are emerging in some of those bets, with a data centre IPO withdrawn in Australia last week and credit investors becoming increasingly selective toward AI-linked companies. NextDC now expects net revenue of A$475 million to A$500 million in 2027, down from its prior outlook of A$615 million to A$640 million, excluding the affected M3 contracts. The company also cut its 2027 underlying earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) forecast to A$245 million to A$265 million, from A$385 million to A$410 million, excluding the affected M3 contracts. Delays to works by Jemena Electricity Networks meant the next increase in supply to its M3 Melbourne data centre was now expected in 2028, it said. Jemena had suspended parts of the electricity network works needed to increase power supply to M3 due to opposition from the community and stakeholders and does not expect to recommence them before February 2027. “Whilst out of the company’s control, delays to power supply and development applications relating to NXT’s M3 data centre is evidence that community concerns around data centre developments present a real risk to the timing of delivery of contracted capacity for data centre owners,” said Tom Beadle, RBC Capital Markets analyst. Separately, NextDC lowered its 2027 capital expenditure outlook to A$4.5 billion to A$5 billion from A$5.25 billion to A$5.75 billion and said it had begun a detailed review of its spending programme. REUTERS

events.title: The Secret Terms of Trump’s Venezuelan Oil Deal
events.summary: Alejandro Betancourt, a 46-year-old Venezuelan energy baron, is the key figure in a historic oil deal with the Trump administration. Venezuelan opposition leaders and U.S. congressional Democrats have criticized the agreement because Betancourt has been the target of investigations of alleged corruption. Antonio Heredia/El Mundo In late August, President Donald Trump announced what he called the “biggest oil deal in world history.” Since then, the full text of the accord — which grants the U.S. sweeping access to Venezuela’s oil reserves — has been one of the most sought-after secrets in Washington, D.C.  ProPublica has reviewed a copy of the 18-page strategic partnership agreement signed for the United States by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The document reveals carefully constructed terms that favor U.S. interests at every turn and cements the power of a small group of people handpicked by the Trump administration to govern and profit from the deal. The role of the Venezuelan government and the potential benefits to its people are largely absent from the text. One of the most criticized aspects of Trump’s announcement has been his choice of a partner: Alejandro Betancourt, a globe-trotting Venezuelan oligarch who has faced money-laundering investigations in three countries.  The Trump administration is taking a 35% stake in Betancourt’s firm, North American Blue Energy Partners, by acquiring shares in a Barbados-registered parent company. The deal document provides little information about the owners and investors behind the parent company, who could receive enormous wealth from the arrangement.  The agreement also safeguards Betancourt’s position as chief executive of NABEP and says the U.S. government will work with the parent company to appoint a powerful seven-member board to govern the venture for an initial 15-year term. Those aspects of the deal, according to people with knowledge of how it came together, were designed to prevent future U.S. and Venezuelan leaders from dismantling the enterprise.  Orlando Alvarado, a name not disclosed by the Trump administration as a party to the accord, signed the agreement on behalf of the parent company, alongside Betancourt, Hegseth and Rubio. Alvarado has held senior roles in multiple Betancourt businesses, including as chief financial officer of an energy firm that became embroiled in scandals a decade ago. According to the Miami Herald , federal prosecutors identified Alvarado as an unindicted co-conspirator in a scheme to embezzle money from Venezuela’s national oil company. NABEP spokesperson Terry Wade said that “neither Mr. Betancourt nor Mr. Alvarado has ever been charged with any crime in any country, and any claims against them are baseless.”  Do You Know More About This Topic? We’re still reporting. If you know more about this topic, please contact our reporting team. Cate Brown I’m interested in talking to people who understand how members of the Trump administration, or their family members, are doing business, at home or abroad. Contact Me Key aspects of the plan differ from the Trump administration’s public pronouncements. Trump has said the deal will secure America’s energy dominance for the next century. But the text indicates that U.S. purchasing rights expire in half that time and that the underlying operating rights appear to run afoul of Venezuelan laws limiting oil concessions to 25 years. The agreement does ensure the United States a deep discount from fair-market value on 20% of NABEP’s oil, as Trump has said. It does not, however, explicitly guarantee that Betancourt’s company is obligated to pay the estimated $200 billion in royalties and tax payments to Venezuela that the White House has said would benefit the country .  There are also significant caveats related to Trump’s central selling point to Americans — that the deal will bring a gusher of low-cost oil imports.  The agreement gives the U.S. the right to purchase 20% of NABEP’s oil at a discounted rate of $30 a barrel, or less than a third of what oil has sold for in recent months, according to one of three supporting documents reviewed by ProPublica.  But this fee does not account for the cost of getting Venezuela’s oil out of the country. Much of Venezuela’s raw crude is so thick that it won’t flow through pipelines unless it is first blended with 20% or more of oil thinner products. Under the deal, the potentially significant cost of importing millions of barrels of those blending materials is not included in the price. The White House, the State Department, the Pentagon and the energy company NABEP all defended the agreement, saying in statements that their new public-private venture will provide meaningful and lasting economic benefits to both countries that cannot be captured in a legal document. “This historic deal marks a major step toward stabilizing Venezuela’s economy after years of hyperinflation and almost no new investment, while more than doubling the United States’ oil reserves,” said White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers. Wade emphasized that NABEP was chosen because of its track record of expanding oil production in Venezuela in recent years and that the agreement was between the company and the U.S. government, not Venezuela. “Thanks in large part to the agreement,” Wade said, “there is a surge in confidence about the future of Venezuela’s oil industry and, as a direct result, substantial new investments are flowing into the country.” He added that much of NABEP’s oil comes from fields that require little or no blending materials and that blending costs would not meaningfully impact the price of production. “Our barrel economics are strong.” The newly revealed details of the agreement are nonetheless likely to raise more questions about whether the unorthodox marriage of the United States and a foreign energy baron can bring lasting benefits to either country — and which private parties might benefit along the way. Trump’s oil deal is likely to face scrutiny in both the United States and Venezuela, especially if Democrats win one or both chambers in the midterm elections, according to former U.S. diplomats and congressional staff. “Question number one in a new U.S. Congress will be: Why Betancourt?” said former Ambassador James Story, who served as the top U.S. diplomat in Caracas from 2018 to 2023, in an interview. “Why did he get this deal? And was he involved in criminality? events.title: US sanctions Chinese venture firm in Google AI secrets case
events.summary: The case centres on Ding Linwei, a former Google software engineer convicted in 2026 of stealing Google AI trade secrets. The US sanctioned Shanghai Zhisuan Technology and MiraclePlus-linked firms over alleged ties to a startup accused of stealing Google AI trade secrets. MiraclePlus denied investing in Zhisuan and said the sanctions came without warning; it is seeking to have them lifted through “candid communication”. The case centres on Ding Linwei, a former Google engineer convicted of stealing more than 2,000 pages of secrets, highlighting tougher US action on AI trade-secret theft. The US government has blacklisted a Chinese venture firm established by ex-Microsoft AI scientist Lu Qi for alleged ties to a start-up accused of stealing technology from Alphabet’s Google. The US State Department announced on Oct 20 measures against Shanghai Zhisuan Technology , founded by Ding Linwei, a former Google software engineer convicted in 2026 of stealing Google AI trade secrets. Lu’s MiraclePlus, the successor to a Chinese programme run by Silicon Valley’s Y Combinator, and three affiliates drew sanctions for providing seed financing to Zhisuan. The measures may include freezing their US assets and banking restrictions. MiraclePlus denied investing in Zhisuan and said the US sanctions were imposed without any prior communication, according to a company statement on Oct 21 . The firm said it is in talks with relevant parties to have the sanctions lifted and expects the matter to be resolved through “candid communication”. Established in 2023, Zhisuan developed a software platform designed to help train AI models. Ding applied on behalf of Zhisuan to MiraclePlus’s start-up incubation programme, touting his knowledge of Google’s technology, according to the State Department. The agency said it imposed the penalties under a law enacted in early 2023 aimed at curbing the theft of US trade secrets. Lu, a former Microsoft executive, was recruited in 2017 by Baidu to oversee the Chinese search leader’s AI efforts, only to quit a year later citing personal reasons. In 2018, Lu – recruited by then-Y Combinator President Sam Altman – joined the US firm to help create YC China. When Y Combinator abandoned the expansion a year later, Lu and his team continued operations under the MiraclePlus brand. It has since backed some of China’s most promising start-ups, including AI inference platform SiliconFlow and robotics maker AgiBot, both of which are considering Hong Kong listings. Ding secretly affiliated himself with two China-based AI companies while still working as a Google employee, the US Justice Department said following his conviction in January – one of the more closely watched AI IP cases between the world’s two largest economies. He allegedly siphoned more than 2,000 pages of trade secrets to his personal cloud account, and downloaded files to his computer less than two weeks before resigning in December 2023. Ding’s defence at the time hinged in large part on arguments that the documents he took do not meet the legal definition of a trade secret. His attorneys said prosecutors failed to show he had any intent to use the documents to benefit his company or China. He was sentenced to a year’s jail time in September. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Australian data center operator NextDC's shares plunge 40% after it slashes earnings forecast
events.summary: Australian data center operator NextDC slashed its fiscal year 2027 revenue and earnings guidance due to power supply delays at its Melbourne facility. Citi said in a note that the earnings impact could extend beyond 2027 due to delays in expansion approvals and transformer upgrades. The company lowered its fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to between $475 million Australian dollars and A$500 million, from A$615 million to A$640 million forecast earlier, while cutting its underlying earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or EBITDA, forecast to A$245 million to A$265 million from A$385 million to A$410 million. The delays to power stem from the suspension of infrastructure upgrades at the company's M3 Melbourne data center amid community opposition, with electricity distributor Jemena not expecting to resume work before February 2027, according to NextDC. Jemena cited safety concerns and restricted access to work sites due to community opposition, as well as a lack of consent from the local council pending further community consultation. Citi said in a note that NextDC's power delays could affect earnings beyond fiscal 2027, citing delays to approvals for the M3 expansion and a longer-than-expected timeline for transformer upgrades. The dispute reflects growing opposition to data center buildouts worldwide , amid concerns over their impact on local communities and the environment. NextDC shares have declined for seven straight weeks, and are on course to end lower for the eighth week.

events.title: UN experts call on India to stop using ‘excessive force’ against protesters
events.summary: UN experts have called on the Indian government to stop the use of “excessive force” in the wake of the crackdown on opposition and student protests in India. In a statement on Tuesday, the two dozen independent experts pressed for an impartial investigation into Indian authorities’ conduct, saying that demonstrators had sustained injuries and some reported being subjected to ill-treatment. list 1 of 3 At least 19 killed in stampede at religious gathering in India list 2 of 3 AI tool helps stranded protesters find their way home in the Indian capital list 3 of 3 Indian court extends detention of ‘Cockroach’ leaders “Protesters have sustained injuries, with some reporting being subjected to ill-treatment. The experts expressed particular concern about reports of sexual violence and other forms of gender-based abuse in the protests and related detentions,” according to the statement. UN experts are appointed by the UN Human Rights Council to monitor and document specific human rights crises but are independent of the organisation itself. India’s Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), along with other opposition parties and student organisations, has led protests this month demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation, after 130 million names were removed from voter lists. The protesting groups said the removal disproportionately affected poor and homeless people as well as ethnic minorities including Muslims, who are unlikely to vote for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The BJP and India’s Election Commission deny the accusations. The Election Commission said it was removing duplicate, deceased, shifted and otherwise ineligible voters and that anyone excluded in error can pursue appeals. “Despite the non-violent nature of the assemblies, law enforcement agencies have reportedly deployed force against unarmed students including by means of police so-called lathi charges, and have prevented thousands from joining the protests,” the UN experts said. Lathi charges are coordinated movements by a policing force using sticks to disperse crowds. “We call on the authorities to immediately cease the use of excessive force, rescind blanket assembly bans, and refrain from the misuse of digital surveillance, including through biometrics, and internet disruptions,” they added. India has repeatedly dismissed such criticism and cast it as interference in the country’s internal affairs, including when the UN human rights office earlier this month expressed concerns over mass detentions in relation to the latest protests.

events.title: Japan shifting to wage-driven inflation phase, finance minister says
events.summary: Satsuki Katayama, Japan's finance minister, during the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, on Oct 15. Japan says prices are rising from import costs, and Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama says the economy is near a shift to wage-driven inflation. The government plans a consumption tax cut and payouts to ease household costs, while Katayama says there is “no gap” with the Bank of Japan. The BOJ raised rates to 1.25% in September, and analysts warn tax cuts and spending could lift demand and clash with efforts to control inflation. TOKYO – Japan’s economy is seeing price rises driven by higher import costs and on the cusp of shifting to a period of sustained inflation driven by rising wages, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said on Oct 21. The government’s scheduled consumption tax cut and payouts are aimed at cushioning the blow to households from rising living costs, Katayama told Parliament. “We are exchanging views with the Bank of Japan on various fronts. I see no gap between the view of the government and that of the BOJ,” Katayama said when asked by a lawmaker whether the government’s tax cut plan could conflict with the central bank’s efforts to combat inflation with interest rate hikes. The BOJ raised interest rates to a 31-year high of 1.25% in September, as the Iran war-induced energy shock, strong global artificial intelligence demand and higher import costs from a weak yen heighten the risk of underlying inflation overshooting its 2% target. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s administration plans to cut by two years an 8% consumption tax rate on food items from April 2027. Analysts warn the tax cut and the administration’s big spending plans could boost demand and contradict the BOJ’s efforts to rein in inflation. Katayama said it was true that tax cuts generally work to push up inflation by stimulating demand. “But we will ensure that our responsible and proactive fiscal policy boosts Japan’s supply capacity in a way that does not accelerate inflation,” she said. events.title: South Korea’s export boom stays strong ahead of central bank rate decision
events.summary: On an unadjusted basis, shipments gained 105.4%, while imports rose 42.8%, resulting in a trade surplus of US$14.5 billion (S$18.5 billion). South Korea’s exports stayed very strong in early October, rising 65.9% on a working-day adjusted basis, led by booming AI-driven semiconductor demand. Chip exports jumped 222.5% to US$27.5 billion, while trade showed a US$14.5 billion surplus and gains also came from petroleum products and cars. The data support the Bank of Korea’s likely decision to keep rates unchanged on Oct 22, as inflation stays above target and policymakers watch wider economic effects. SEOUL – South Korea’s exports maintained strong growth in early October as booming global demand for artificial intelligence fuelled semiconductor shipments, underscoring the economy’s resilience on the eve of the central bank’s interest-rate decision. Exports adjusted for working-day differences rose 65.9% from a year earlier in the first 20 days of October, according to customs office data released on Oct 21 . That compared with an 89.8% increase during the same period in September. On an unadjusted basis, shipments gained 105.4%, while imports rose 42.8%, resulting in a trade surplus of US$14.5 billion (S$18.5 billion). Exports totalled US$61.6 billion in the first 20 days of October , extending momentum after shipments reached US$71.4 billion during the same period in September. Year-on-year comparisons have been distorted by the timing of the Chuseok holidays, which fell in September 2026 and October 2025 , making the working-day-adjusted figures a better gauge of the underlying trend. Semiconductors remained the main engine of growth, with chip exports surging 222.5% from a year earlier to US$27.5 billion. Shipments of petroleum products increased 68.3%, while automobile exports gained almost 41%. The figures reinforce a picture of an economy powered by a booming semiconductor sector that is also keeping inflation elevated. The data will also provide the Bank of Korea (BOK) a key economic input ahead of the Oct 22 rate decision, where it is widely expected to keep policy unchanged as it weighs the impact of its recent rate hikes. The BOK raised its benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point to 3% in August, its second straight hike, as stronger-than-expected growth and sticky inflation prompted policymakers to act preemptively. Governor Shin Hyun Song said the bank will keep a restrictive stance until it is confident inflation will converge to its 2% target. Headline inflation eased to 2.9% in September from 3.1% a month earlier but remains well above the central bank’s target. Shin has said the Middle East war and the AI boom are both adding to inflationary pressure. Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, was 2.8% in September . The strength of the chip cycle has boosted corporate earnings and investment, though policymakers are still assessing how widely those gains are spreading to household consumption and the broader domestic economy. events.title: Australian central banker says inflation outlook worse, unsure about November rate hike
events.summary: The central bank meets on Nov 2 and 3 to decide whether to raise its 4.60% cash rate for a fifth time in 2026. SYDNEY – A top Australian central banker on Oct 21 said tighter monetary policy was working to slow the economy, but the inflation outlook had still worsened, leaving him unsure whether interest rates would need to rise further in November. Speaking at a Citi investment conference, Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser said the bank’s economists were still finalising their quarterly forecasts, but the inflation outlook did look “materially worse”, in part due to even higher oil prices. Brent last traded at US$108 a barrel, up from US$102 a barrel when the central bank last met three weeks ago and lifted interest rates for a fourth time in 2026. It was a third higher than what the RBA had forecast in August. “The monetary policy is working, labour market is easing, consumption growth is quite tepid, but there are still pockets of growth and the inflation outlook has deteriorated, so that’s a pretty tricky balance,” said Hauser. “The challenge that’s facing the board is, do you do more to tackle high inflation?... Or do we hold our horses to protect the labour market?” he added. “We’re in a world of hard choices, and I think that’s the reality here.” Hauser said monetary policy could not deal with an oil shock directly, but it did need to make sure that higher costs did not feed through to rising inflation expectations. Markets now imply around a 40% chance rates will rise to 4.85% in November, up from 30% at the start of the week, and another rate rise is fully priced by May 2027. Consumer price data due next week could show headline inflation climbing to 4.0% in the third quarter as the Gulf war stokes fuel costs. Crucially, core inflation is seen holding around 3.5% and uncomfortably far above the RBA’s long-term target band of 2% to 3%. Hauser said it was “pretty clear” that the inflation outcome would likely be higher than the RBA had forecast. “Yes, we will study it carefully when we get the final number,” he added. “And at the moment, certainly those numbers are causing us to ask whether there’s less capacity in the economy than we previously thought.” Minutes of the RBA’s last meeting showed the board was still concerned inflation risks lay to the upside, even after lifting rates for a fourth time in 2026. Since then, labour data have shown unemployment unexpectedly hit a five-year peak of 4.7% in September, while house prices have fallen faster than policymakers foresaw. Hauser noted the labour market had eased more than expected, and there had been some softening in household demand and the housing market, but still, the unemployment rate was among the lowest in G-20 countries. events.title: Japan’s September exports rise 16.7%, helped by chip demand
events.summary: Solid global investment in artificial intelligence continued to support exports of semiconductors and related equipment. Japan’s exports rose 16.7% in September, the 13th monthly gain, driven by strong demand for semiconductors and AI-related products, according to the Ministry of Finance. Exports to the US rose 22.9% and to China 8.6%. Imports rose 18.9%, but slower crude oil arrivals cut the trade deficit to 536.6 billion yen. The figures show external demand still supports Japan’s economy, though global uncertainty remains. Markets now watch the Bank of Japan’s October meeting for rate hike clues. TOKYO – Japan’s exports in September rose 16.7% from a year earlier, government data showed on Oct 21, as strong demand for semiconductors and AI-related products offset weakness in other sectors. The increase marked the 13th consecutive month of gains, following a 19.3% rise in August and falling short of a median market forecast for a 20.1% increase, Ministry of Finance data showed. Exports have also been supported by corporate efforts to pass on higher costs through prices. By destination, exports to the United States rose 22.9% in September from a year earlier, while shipments to China increased 8.6%. Imports in September rose 18.9% from a year earlier, compared with economists’ median forecast for a 19.6% expansion. Growth in imports slowed from 28% in August due to lower crude oil arrivals after tankers rerouted away from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait when Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi militia declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia, delaying deliveries into Japan. For October, crude oil procurement is expected to recover to around 100% of the level seen in the same month a year earlier, as tankers travelling via the Suez Canal are expected to arrive, the government has said. Slower imports helped narrow Japan’s trade deficit to 536.6 billion yen (S$4.33 billion) in September from 1.1 trillion yen in the previous month. It compared with a forecast for a 181 billion yen deficit. The data suggests external demand remains supportive of Japan’s economy, although uncertainty over the global outlook continues to cloud prospects for exporters. The Bank of Japan holds a key policy meeting later in October where it will release fresh quarterly growth and inflation forecasts that markets will scrutinise for clues on the timing of the next interest rate hike. events.title: Elice's huge stock swings show AI's spending boom is getting more investor scrutiny
events.summary: Elice's bruising IPO debut and next-day recovery highlights growing investor scrutiny over whether AI infrastructure spending can deliver sustainable profits. Rising borrowing costs are exposing debt-heavy neocloud providers to financing risks. Analysts expect a widening divide between AI companies generating sustainable returns and those reliant on external financing. The artificial intelligence boom may be entering a more unforgiving phase, as investors increasingly question whether the billions poured into data centers will translate into sustainable profits. A bruising stock market debut by South Korean AI infrastructure provider Elice has become the latest warning sign that investors may be more closely scrutinizing ambitious expansion plans and paths to profitability. "This is a gut check moment in the tech trade," said Dan Ives, tech analyst at Yorkville Ives. "Investors are trying to better discern between the winners and losers and if there are any weak links in the tech AI food chain." "Patience is wearing thin and scrutiny will be elevated especially for those taking on a major debt load like some of the neoclouds," he added. The weak debut underscores a broader shift in sentiment toward the AI trade, where rising borrowing costs and concerns over debt-fueled expansion may force investors to distinguish between companies generating cash from the boom and those spending heavily in anticipation of future demand. "The AI trade has moved from a phase where the size of the capex announcement was itself viewed positively to one where investors are asking who can actually earn an adequate return on that capital," said Billy Leung of Global X ETFs. "The market is distinguishing between companies that need capital to survive the build-out and companies that are being paid as the build-out continues." The most vulnerable companies are neocloud providers expanding faster than their ability to generate cash, particularly those heavily dependent on external financing, according to Leung. CoreWeave, one of the largest neocloud providers, is "the poster child of this whole thing," according to John Blank, chief equity strategist at Zacks Investment Research. "This is broad market stress, not just speculation," he said, pointing to widening credit spreads. Companies borrowing heavily to build computing capacity could face a squeeze if financing costs rise faster than revenue, particularly where construction expenses and depreciation mount before facilities reach full utilization. The shift is particularly significant for Asia, where technology markets are heavily exposed to the semiconductor and memory-chip industries that have powered the global AI investment frenzy. "U.S. semiconductor and AI plays are overbuilt. And in South Korea, even more overbuilt," Blank said. South Korea's SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics have been among the biggest beneficiaries of soaring demand for advanced memory chips, but their shares have come under pressure as investors reassess the sustainability of AI spending. "Asia is simply much more directly geared to the hardware and memory side of the AI trade, so when investors question AI capex and financing, Korea and other North Asian technology markets feel it disproportionately," Leung said. He added that rising earnings estimates across South Korea and Taiwan suggest the recent selloff reflects deteriorating sentiment and shrinking valuations rather than a sudden collapse in demand. The change reflects a growing divide between companies with the financial firepower to sustain aggressive AI investments and those relying heavily on borrowing to fund expansion. HSBC Chief Executive Officer Georges Elhedery warned that investors and lenders must become more discerning about which data-center projects deserve financing. "You have to look at the quality of the tenancy agreements," he said. "You have to look at the pricing of these contracts. Not all of them are of that level of virtuosity that you can support strongly. Some of them may be more challenging."

A Guatemalan man has been sentenced to 30 years in a United States prison for his role in a human-smuggling operation that killed 53 migrants trapped in a truck – a disaster that had been described as one of the deadliest such incidents along the US-Mexico border in recent history. US District Judge Orlando Garcia handed 39-year-old Rigoberto Ramon Miranda-Orozco a 30-year prison term on Tuesday, more than a year after his extradition from Guatemala in March 2025. list 1 of 4 Two more men plead guilty in US for deadly 2021 human-smuggling truck crash list 2 of 4 The deadly business of migrant smuggling list 3 of 4 Texas migrant deaths: Families anxious amid efforts to ID victims list 4 of 4 ‘Horrific tragedy’: At least 50 people found dead in Texas truck He was first arrested in Guatemala in August 2024, as part of a cross-border effort to dismantle the human-smuggling network. The charges stem from a fatal incident on June 27, 2022. According to the US Department of Justice, emergency crews discovered dozens of people trapped inside an abandoned truck in a remote area on the southern outskirts of San Antonio, Texas. A total of 64 migrants had endured a lengthy journey that began in Guatemala and continued through Mexico across the border into the US. By the time the truck was driving from Laredo, Texas, to San Antonio – a distance of 250km (155 miles) – prosecutors say the air conditioning had stopped functioning. When the truck was discovered, temperatures were approaching 32C (90F). Forty-eight people were pronounced dead on the scene, and five more died while receiving emergency medical treatment for heat-related illness and dehydration. Among the dead were six children and a pregnant woman. Of those killed, 21 were Guatemalan nationals. Miranda-Orozco has admitted to arranging travel and accommodation for two of the migrants who died in the truck and another who survived but suffered grave injuries. He pleaded guilty in July to conspiring to bring a migrant into the US resulting in death, as well as aiding and abetting the unlawful entry of migrants resulting in death and serious bodily injury. According to The Associated Press news agency, Miranda-Orozco is among a group of nearly 20 people sentenced in the US and Guatemala in connection with the tragedy. Felipe Orduna-Torres, identified as the leader of the operation in the US, was sentenced to life in prison in a federal court in San Antonio in June 2025. Armando Gonzales-Ortega, described by prosecutors as Orduna-Torres’s top assistant, received an 83-year sentence. Further proceedings remain pending, including in the case against the truck driver. According to prosecutors, investigators found signs of passengers’ desperate attempts to escape the abandoned truck. Some had reportedly removed clothing. Scratch marks on the trailer’s interior, meanwhile, suggested that some people had clawed at the walls in a futile bid to escape. The prosecutors said the passengers had paid as much as $15,000 for passage across the border. “It was clear that they suffered tremendously in their last few hours on this earth,” US Attorney Justin Simmons told reporters at a Tuesday news conference following the sentencing. The I-35 highway near where the truck was found runs through San Antonio from the Mexican border. It is considered a popular smuggling corridor because of the large volume of truck traffic, Jack Staton, a former senior official with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), told the Reuters news agency at the time. The administration of President Donald Trump has cited the need to end human trafficking as a rationale for his crackdown on irregular immigration across the southern border. Reserve Bank deputy governor Andrew Hauser says the inflation outlook is "materially worse" than the RBA had forecast, raising the prospect of another interest rate hike as soon as November. Just under a fortnight out from the next interest rate decision, Mr Hauser warned high inflation was becoming entrenched in the Australian economy. "We are beginning to see some signs that some people in the community are not sure if we're going to bring inflation back into target at all, or certainly not for an extended period," Mr Hauser told the Citi Investment Conference in Sydney. The RBA targets headline inflation between 2 and 3 per cent on average over time. Inflation currently sits at 4 per cent, according to the August consumer price index . Mr Hauser said the central bank's liaison program and surveys showed there was "an increasing share of businesses who are thinking that, maybe, sort of 3 per cent, 3.5 per cent [inflation] is the new normal". "Look, that is the central banker's nightmare. "We can't allow expectations to shift away from target." events.title: When AI models refuse to fight hackers
events.summary: In the race to fend off AI-enabled cyber threats , security teams are confronting a new problem: The AI models they rely on to investigate attacks can suddenly refuse to help. Why it matters: While AI giants race to build AI tools that can respond quickly to hacking or other malicious online threats, strict guardrails on their most powerful models lock out defenders mid-investigation, leaving them scrambling for alternatives at critical moments. What's happening: OpenCode, an open-source AI coding agent, said it was compromised over the weekend, allowing attackers to obtain API keys belonging to some customers, including keys for OpenAI, Anthropic and Google services. OpenCode said the breach was "related to a large scale distillation attack that impacted 1.4% of OpenCode Console users." OpenCode co-creator Dax Raad said attackers had been targeting its systems continuously for 48 hours, forcing the company to keep its own AI agents running around the clock to respond. OpenAI , Google and Anthropic have said they worked with affected customers to revoke exposed API keys and address unauthorized usage charges. Zoom in: Raad said on X that frontier AI models initially helped investigate the breach but then "started refusing." The models' safety restrictions reportedly began blocking requests as the investigation turned to potentially malicious code, even though OpenCode was trying to defend its own systems. OpenCode then gained access to OpenAI's Daybreak Blue program, which gives vetted cybersecurity defenders access to models with fewer restrictions. "We definitely need to be more proactive and we've made so many improvements over the last few days," Raad wrote on X Monday. The big picture: The incident underscored a dilemma facing cybersecurity teams trying to figure out when to use powerful proprietary AI models, which come with built-in restrictions, or open-weight alternatives that offer greater control over how they're deployed. When Hugging Face discovered suspicious activity on its systems that it later linked to OpenAI's own agents, its security team turned to a Chinese open-weight model to help investigate after encountering restrictions on frontier models. Yes, but: AI companies maintain that they need to gate access to their most powerful models to ensure that malicious actors can't abuse their cyber capabilities. Between the lines: Cybersecurity teams will have to figure out how to balance the need for faster AI-powered defenses with restrictions designed to keep those same capabilities out of attackers' hands, Chris Jones, chief technology officer at Nightwing, told Axios. "We're all going to have to figure out how that race gets modulated over time," Jones said. "That's a big piece here." Go deeper : Anthropic and OpenAI are now cybersecurity's kingmakers

events.title: Chinese automaker reports set to shine before challenges mount
events.summary: Chinese EV stocks have underperformed in 2026 as mounting concerns over weak domestic demand and regulatory uncertainty weighed on investor sentiment. Chinese automakers are set for a strong third-quarter earnings boost from hybrid exports, with BYD, Geely and Leapmotor likely posting higher profits. The outlook is clouded by new barriers, including the EU’s 350,000 hybrid import cap from 1 December and China’s lower export VAT rebate from 13% to 9% on 1 April. Investors are watching 2027, as firms face weaker domestic demand, trade risks and lower margins, while pushing local production in Europe to cut tariff exposure. A surge in hybrid-vehicle exports is set to give Chinese automakers a much-needed third-quarter earnings boost. Import curbs in Europe and exports tax changes at home are now clouding their outlook. BYD’s net income likely jumped the most in six quarters, estimates show, while Geely Automobile Holdings’ profit probably grew 36% based on the average of two estimates, and Zhejiang Leapmotor Technology is set to post record earnings. All will have benefited from strong exports, making up for sluggish domestic demand, though their views of the months ahead will be monitored closely, given growing export hurdles. The European Union has set an import cap of 350,000 hybrid vehicles per year from China as soon as Dec 1. Meanwhile, China plans to reduce its value-added tax export rebate to 9% from 13% effective April 1, denting profitability from overseas sales. “Investors are focusing on 2027: Whether domestic demand can stabilise, and how automakers will absorb higher costs from a lower tax rebate on NEV (new energy vehicle) exports and rising trade barriers,” said Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Joanna Chen. The EU’s annual quota could potentially exclude 60% of Chinese automakers’ hybrid volume in Europe, with BYD, SAIC Motor and Chery Automobile the most vulnerable, Chen said in a note. The global auto industry is struggling to come to terms with an influx of cars from China as the country’s automakers look overseas for growth and profit. While Chinese automakers are cut off from the US market by tariffs and other restrictions, they have grown increasingly dependent on other overseas markets like Europe to bolster their bottom lines. China’s trade surplus with the EU reached a record in September, with exports to the region exceeding US$60 billion (S$76.7 billion), making Brussels increasingly receptive to import restrictions. While progress in trade talks between Beijing and the EU and China’s reduction of export VAT tax rebates have cleared some policy ambiguity, carmakers will still need to demonstrate margin resilience to reignite share momentum. BYD’s Hong Kong-listed shares have dropped 23% in 2026 , underperforming a Bloomberg gauge of global electric vehicle-related stocks that slid 14%. Smaller rivals Xpeng and Xiaomi have suffered even steeper losses, slumping 53% and 31% in the same period, respectively. While trade frictions and tax changes pose headwinds, “we believe greater policy visibility should reduce some of the uncertainty that has weighed on the sector”, HSBC analysts led by Yuqian Ding wrote in a note. Key earnings catalysts include potential shipment front-loading through early 2027 to beat trade curbs and a rapid ramping up of local overseas manufacturing, Jefferies analysts led by Xiaoyi Lei said. Xpeng already makes cars in Austria, BYD plans to start production in Hungary this quarter and Leapmotor already has a sales and manufacturing partnership with Stellantis NV. While localisation involves additional investment and execution risks, it should support long-term growth, reduce exposure to tariffs and export quotas and strengthen the competitive position of leading Chinese automakers in Europe, HSBC’s Ding said. events.title: Japan exports post huge miss in September as growth slows to 16.7%
events.summary: Reuters-polled analysts had pegged exports growth at 20.1%. This is the second straight month that shipments from Japan have recorded a slowdown. Shipments to mainland China — Japan's largest trading partner — rose 8.6%, while exports to the U.S. climbed 22.9%. Japan's exports in September rose 16.7% from a year earlier, missing market expectations by a huge margin. Reuters-polled analysts had pegged exports growth at 20.1%. This is the second straight month that shipments from Japan have recorded a slowdown, after hitting a near four-year high in July. Growth was supported by continued strong semiconductor exports, with shipments rising 49.4% year on year by value. Exports of machinery also bolstered growth, with semiconductor-related machinery shipments up 43.9% and power generation machinery exports climbing 22.6%. In terms of destinations, shipments to mainland China — Japan's largest trading partner — rose 8.6%, while exports to the U.S. climbed 22.9%. Exports have been the main driver of Japan's growth for the first two quarters of 2026, helping the world's fourth largest economy beat expectations in the first quarter, and supporting growth in the second. Japan's imports in September grew 18.9%, also missing expectations of 19.6% from Reuters. Tokyo's imports of petroleum climbed 51.1% by value in September, with inbound shipments from the U.S. surging nearly 820%, while those from the Middle East inching up just 1.5% as the conflict in the region continues to impede supplies. Following the data release, the benchmark Nikkei 225 was up 1.8%, while the Topix gained 1.14%. The data comes as the Bank of Japan is set to meet next week, and Reuters poll estimates indicate that the central bank is set to hold its policy rate steady at 1%.

events.title: Why former FDLR fighters are returning to Rwanda
events.summary: From the forest to Mutobo, former fighters face the challenge of rebuilding their lives after leaving the armed group. Musanze, Rwanda – Jean Claude Hategekimana feared that returning to Rwanda could cost him his life. After years with the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), he decided to leave the armed group and return home. At Rwanda’s Mutobo Demobilisation and Reintegration Centre, he began preparing for civilian life. Born in 1996 in Rutsiro District, in western Rwanda, Hategekimana moved to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) with his parents and grew up in an area controlled by the FDLR. He joined the group in 2018, underwent military training and eventually reached the rank of captain. “I arrived at the Mutobo Centre after fighting to defend Goma. Following our defeat, I fled to Masisi. After realising that I was fighting for nothing, I decided to return to Rwanda. I came back on February 24,” he told Al Jazeera. Hategekimana said FDLR members had been taught that anyone who returned to Rwanda would be killed. “Upon arriving in Rwanda, I realised that the FDLR had been lying to us. For me, returning home felt like embarking on a suicide mission,” he said. His experience illustrates the challenge of reintegrating former fighters whose beliefs and fears have been shaped by years in an armed group. Francis Musoni, secretary-general of the Rwanda Demobilisation and Reintegration Commission, said the Mutobo centre, located in Musanze in Rwanda’s Northern Province, was established in 2001 to receive members of the FDLR and other Rwandan armed groups returning from the DRC. The FDLR emerged in the aftermath of the 1994 genocide against the Tutsis. After the genocide, members of the former Rwandan armed forces and militia groups fled to what was then Zaire, now the DRC. The Rwandan government accuses the FDLR of carrying out attacks against Rwanda and contributing to cross-border insecurity. At Mutobo, the rehabilitation programme includes medical care, psychosocial support, civic education and assistance with reconnecting with families. Returnees can also contact relatives and friends through a telephone service, Musoni said. “We help them to build confidence among themselves, build trust, and empower them to go back into the community and contribute to the development of the country together with their families,” he said. The centre also allows visitors and media representatives to meet returnees. Musoni said those undergoing rehabilitation can visit their communities for short periods to help rebuild their confidence in returning home. “They can travel to their communities [during rehabilitation]. They are given written permission for a week or two, and we even facilitate transport,” he said. For the former commanders interviewed by Al Jazeera at Mutobo, the decision to leave the FDLR was shaped by family ties, disillusionment and concerns about personal safety. Major-General Anastase Munyaneza served in the former Rwandan armed forces in Kigali’s Kicukiro District during the 1994 genocide. He said he left Rwanda after the genocide and later joined the FDLR, eventually commanding its South Kivu sector. Although he had come to accept the group’s beliefs, Munyaneza remained in contact with his family in Rwanda. News of their lives made him question his own circumstances. “I was the only one who had fled to the DRC. I regularly received news about them. I knew they were still alive, attending school, working for the government and improving their lives. I began asking myself what I was doing in the forest,” he said. He added that seeing other members return safely encouraged him to consider going home. Munyaneza said he contacted personnel from the United Nations Organisation Stabilisation Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO), who transported him from South Kivu to Bukavu and then to the Congolese-Rwandan border. He subsequently proceeded to Mutobo. Lieutenant-Colonel Idrissa Bizimana, who was responsible for ideology, propaganda and recruitment within the FDLR, said his decision to return followed a change in his convictions. “I no longer believed in the ideology I had been promoting. After receiving verified information about what was happening in Rwanda, I decided to return home,” he said. Bizimana said he had been in contact with a MONUSCO general who had offered to help him return. Using a satellite phone equipped with GPS, he sent his location and the date. A helicopter was then dispatched to retrieve him, he said. Lieutenant-Colonel Emilien Mpakaniye, who joined the FDLR in 1998 and was responsible for economic affairs at its headquarters, said he began questioning the organisation after becoming disillusioned with what he described as its lies. Colonel Augustin Nshimiyimana, a former FDLR intelligence commander, returned to Rwanda in 2022 and underwent rehabilitation at Mutobo.

events.title: One year on: Has Kenya’s opposition lost its way without Raila Odinga?
events.summary: Odinga’s legacy faces a test as ODM splits over its alliance with President Ruto. Nairobi, Kenya – One year after Raila Odinga’s death, the political movement he led for decades is struggling to define its future. Within the Orange Democratic Movement (ODM), a bitter dispute over cooperation with President William Ruto has exposed divisions over the party’s identity and independence. The struggle raises a question that extends beyond ODM’s leadership: Can Kenya’s opposition remain a credible force without the man who helped shape it? Raila’s death prompted tributes and commemorations celebrating a political career defined by the struggle for multiparty democracy, constitutional reform, freedom of expression and social justice. Yet the divisions now confronting his party reveal the difficulty of sustaining a political movement built around one dominant figure. His legacy remains a source of inspiration, but also a point of contention over what ODM should stand for and how it should exercise power. At the centre of the dispute is ODM’s relationship with Ruto’s administration. The removal of Secretary-General Edwin Sifuna, who opposed closer cooperation with the president, has become a flashpoint in a wider struggle over the party’s direction. The disagreement is about more than personalities: It raises questions about whether ODM can work with the government while retaining the independence to challenge it. A vacuum at the heart of the opposition For decades, Raila occupied a central place in Kenya’s reform movements, challenging successive governments and campaigning for political change. To his supporters, he represented resistance and the promise of a more accountable political system. His influence, however, also meant that the opposition’s ability to unite often depended on his personal authority, political networks and capacity to negotiate competing interests. Political analyst Professor Herman Manyora argues that Raila’s absence has left a vacuum that the opposition has struggled to fill. “One year after Raila’s death, he is larger than life. I think there’s a way in which people thought Raila was not going to die. We had immortalised Raila,” Manyora says. He argues that the opposition has yet to find a figure capable of bringing its competing interests together. “The opposition is in disarray. There isn’t a figure that people can rally around,” he says. The assessment points to a challenge that predates Raila’s death but has become more visible since it: A movement can inherit a leader’s political legacy without necessarily inheriting the authority that held it together. Whether that vacuum becomes a lasting weakness will depend on the ability of other leaders to build trust, establish a common agenda and organise beyond individual loyalties. The alliance that divided his legacy Raila’s decision to work with Ruto in 2024, amid nationwide protests against the Finance Bill, remains one of the most contested chapters of his political career. The protests, driven in large part by young Kenyans, developed into a wider expression of anger about taxation, governance and political accountability. As pressure mounted on the government, Raila’s move towards cooperation with Ruto raised questions about whether dialogue could deliver meaningful change or whether it risked drawing the opposition closer to the establishment it had long challenged. Manyora views the intervention as a decisive moment for Ruto’s administration. “What happened then was that Raila came to the rescue of President William Ruto because, had he not come to rescue Ruto, I think the government would have collapsed,” he says. Although Manyora’s assessment of the political consequences of the alliance is debatable, his interpretation captures the significance of Raila’s decision: A politician long associated with opposition politics had become a partner in an arrangement with the president against whom many Kenyans were protesting. For some young Kenyans, the alliance was a betrayal of the political struggle that had made Raila a symbol of resistance. The Gen Z-led protests emerged largely outside traditional political structures, driven by demands for accountability and frustration with established political elites. Many protesters rejected the idea that their movement should be absorbed into negotiations among familiar political figures. Joshua Okayo, a lawyer and human rights activist who identifies with the Gen Z generation, says Raila’s decision left him feeling betrayed. “As a Gen Z, I recognise the kind of politics he fought for. I recognise the years he put into fighting for social justice, democracy, rule of law, constitutionalism, and many good things. But I also have a spot in my heart where I feel he betrayed the generation,” Okayo says.

events.summary: Britain’s King Charles III has welcomed Oman’s Sultan Haitham bin Tariq for a state visit, praising the Gulf Arab monarch’s efforts to broker peace in the region. Haitham bin Tariq said his country has chosen the path of diplomacy in a region rife with conflict, following a day of ceremonies including a reception by a red-uniformed military honour guard at Windsor Castle. list 1 of 3 Tourists face legal action over turtle-riding video in Oman list 2 of 3 US bombs cargo vessel in Gulf of Oman ‘trying to run Iran blockade’ list 3 of 3 Oman evacuates injured crew from attacked tanker in Strait of Hormuz “In a region that has known too much conflict, Oman has chosen a different path, an independent path,” the Omani ruler said during a state banquet on Tuesday. “Britain has been a friend on this path and has stood beside us in this duty,” he added. King Charles III praised Oman’s peacemaking attempts in the Middle East, paying tribute to Muscat’s “noble efforts” to help reopen the choked Strait of Hormuz. “I would especially like to recognise, at a time when conflict has returned so painfully to the region, Oman’s enduring commitment as a trusted interlocutor to all parties,” Charles told about 160 guests at the lavish dinner. “Oman’s role across the Gulf and her ‘constructive neutrality’, as you put it, matters far beyond Hormuz, and is worthy of our utmost respect,” Britain’s king added in a toast to the Omani sultan. The sultan’s visit, the first state visit to Britain by a sultan of Oman in 44 years, comes amid severe turbulence in the Middle East prompted by the Iran war. Oman, a key United Kingdom military ally which borders the vital Hormuz waterway, has acted as a mediator in talks between the United States and Iran since the US-Israel war against Iran started in late February. The Omani sultan is due to hold talks on Wednesday in Downing Street with Prime Minister Andy Burnham, where security, trade and investment are expected to be high on the agenda. Burnham was among those at Tuesday’s banquet, alongside the chief executives of Shell, BP and Airbus, as well as various royals and other dignitaries.

events.title: Exclusive: Ramaswamy doubles down on explosive ad featuring rival's mother, despite backlash
events.summary: Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign for Ohio governor is pouring $4 million into a bombshell ad in which his opponent's estranged mother attacks her daughter — doubling down on the message despite fierce bipartisan backlash, Axios has learned. Why it matters: Ramaswamy is gambling that the deeply personal attack by Amy Acton's mother — who Acton has said sided with her stepfather after he sexually assaulted Acton when she was 12 — will resonate with voters. After the ad began appearing Tuesday on social media, many fellow Republicans urged Ramaswamy to distance his campaign from it. They warned it could backfire at a time when the controversy over the Epstein files has elevated the sexual abuse of children as a national campaign issue. Driving the news: Ramaswamy's campaign confirmed to Axios that it produced the ad, which began circulating on social media late Monday without language identifying its sponsor. Sources close to Ramaswamy's campaign said the ad tested well with "persuadable" voters, prompting the decision to launch a $4 million statewide campaign that began streaming Tuesday night. Catch up quick: The minute-long commercial features Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur, accusing her daughter of lying about her childhood and urging Ohioans not to vote for her. "She lies about her past," Arthur says. "She's lied her entire life." Arthur also disputes Acton's account of experiencing homelessness as a child. The other side: Acton, a physician, has said she was sexually abused at age 12 by her stepfather, who faced criminal charges, and that her mother sided with him. Acton and her brother were removed from their mother's custody. According to her brother, their mother remained married to Acton's alleged abuser until his death. Acton, 60, has said she hasn't seen her mother since childhood. In a statement posted to Facebook on Tuesday, Acton said that "between the ages of 10 and 12, I was sexually abused by her husband, while my birth mother did nothing to protect me." "I've always known that she was deeply sick and unwell, and it's sad to see Vivek Ramaswamy exploit her all for his own political gain." Acton's brother, Philip Stearns, called Ramaswamy's ad "disgusting." What they're saying: Despite bipartisan criticism, Ramaswamy's campaign continued to treat the mother's statements as campaign gold. "This is a campaign-ending moment for Amy Acton. The people who know her best keep warning Ohioans about her," Ramaswamy campaign manager Jonathan Ewing told Axios. Several prominent Republicans and conservative commentators blasted the ad, arguing that it could generate sympathy for Acton. Republican strategist David Urban on CNN drew a parallel to the Epstein controversy, warning that voters are especially sympathetic to victims of sexual assault and that the ad could backfire. "It seems crazy to me one would assume this would work and not backfire," conservative commentator Mary Katharine Ham posted on X. Yes, but: Some conservatives defended the commercial, including Donald Trump Jr., who urged Ohio voters to "watch [it] and think about what it means." By the numbers: A mid-October Marist survey showed Acton leading Ramaswamy 50% to 43% among likely voters. What's next: Ramaswamy and Republican Sen. Jon Husted are set to campaign with Vice President Vance in Cincinnati on Wednesday.

events.title: House Democrats forced to make tough choices with limited midterm cash
events.summary: House Democrats' main super PAC is winding down its spending in several races where the party has struggled to make headway despite national trends working in their favor . Why it matters: Democrats' ambitions of winning heavily Republican districts are running into the reality of finite resources at the end of a long and expensive midterm campaign. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and its corresponding super PAC, House Majority PAC, have struggled to keep pace with their GOP counterparts' monster fundraising this cycle. Republicans also have the bonus advantage of a network of cash-rich outside groups, namely President Trump's MAGA Inc. and Elon Musk's America PAC . Driving the news: HMP pulled back its spending this week in three Republican-leaning districts, according to AdImpact and a source familiar with the matter. TN-05: Democrats were bullish about their star recruit, Columbia Mayor Chaz Molder, until redistricting made the district redder and embattled Rep. Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.) lost his primary to former state Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher . HMP has drawn down its ad reservations in the district from nearly $1.6 million this month to a little over $500,000 as of Monday. Trump carried the newly reconstituted 5th district by 21 percentage points in 2024. Cook Political Report rates the race as "solidly Republican." FL-07: Facing a situation similar to Tennessee, Democrats liked their odds of unseating scandal-tarred Rep. Cory Mills (R-Fla.), who lost his primary to former local news anchor Ryan Elijah. Like Molder, Democratic candidate Bale Dalton, a former NASA chief of staff, was a top DCCC recruit and is part of the committee's coveted "Red to Blue" program. HMP essentially halved its investment in the district on Monday, cutting ad reservations from $3.9 million to just $1.95 million. Cook rates the race as "likely Republican," though a poll released by the DCCC on Tuesday had the two candidates tied at 45% each. CO-03: A top target for Democrats when Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.) represented it, the seat has become a heavier lift for the party since she abandoned it and Rep. Jeff Hurd (R-Colo.) took office last year. Democrat Dwayne Romero, a real estate company CEO and Army veteran, is seen by party operatives as having failed to build the kind of momentum shown by Jessica Killin in the neighboring 5th District. HMP halved its investment in this district too, from more than $2.1 million last week to less than $1.1 million as of Monday. Between the lines: The group has also made partial cuts — what it calls "shaves" — in districts where Democrats have struggled to gain traction but still see a glimmer of hope. That includes Arizona's 2nd District, where Rep. Eli Crane (R-Ariz.) is locked in a rematch with former Navajo Nation President Jonathan Nez in a race Cook rates as "likely Republican." HMP has also taken some money out of Texas' 23rd District, where Republican Brandon Herrera, a right-wing YouTuber, is facing Democratic lawyer Katy Padilla Stout in another race rated "likely Republican." Yes, but: Some HMP triages are in districts where they feel confident the Democratic candidate will prevail. That includes Reps. Greg Landsman (D-Ohio) and Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-Mich.), both of whose races are rated "likely Democratic" by Cook. The PAC has also pulled back in the districts of retiring Reps. Darrell Issa (R-Calif.) and Don Bacon (R-Neb.), which Democrats are increasingly bullish about flipping. The money from these cuts is funneled to districts the party views as more core battlegrounds — including some seats Trump carried by double digits in 2024 that Democrats nevertheless view as winnable. HMP has added at least $4.7 million to its existing investments in nearly two dozen districts over the last two days. What they're saying: Phil Gardner, a senior adviser for Blue Dog Action — a centrist group backing Dalton — told Axios of the cuts in Florida, "I'm not sure what HMP was thinking here." "The rest of the party is not triaging this seat," he said, citing the DCCC's poll and House Minority Whip Katherine Clark's (D-Mass.) plans to campaign there on Wednesday. Gardner said he agrees with "95% of the decisions HMP's made this cycle," but that it is "bonkers they're dumping so much money" into Maine's 2nd District "while leaving one of the party's best recruits high and dry in Florida." Blue Dog Action spent nearly $500,000 to help Dalton win the primary, but it hasn't yet invested any money in the general election. The bottom line: "We're focused on taking back the House," CJ Warnke, a spokesperson for HMP, told Axios in response to Gardner's criticism. Said Gardner: "I'm confident they'll rethink and make the right decision for the final week. Bale can win and hold that seat with everyone's help."

events.title: Elon Musk says Tesla-SpaceX merger being considered
events.summary: Elon Musk is the top executive of both Tesla and SpaceX Elon Musk has said he likes the idea of a merger of Tesla and SpaceX, two of his most notable companies, and it is under active consideration. "Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said during a call with financial analysts over the quarterly business results of SpaceX on Tuesday. While Musk noted the certainty of such a merger should not be assumed, and it would need shareholders' support, he said special committees within both companies have been formed to examine the move. "The special committees have not reached agreement on terms of any transaction and there's no guarantee that they will," Musk added. "But I do think there is a lot of merit to merging and a lot to be gained." With Tesla valued roughly $1.5 trillion and SpaceX valued at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history. The company, which builds space rockets and Starlink internet satellites, is now expanding into offering cloud compute capacity for other tech companies, like Anthropic and Google. That line of business has become the most profitable part of SpaceX, bringing in $7.5bn according to the latest quarterly results. Starlink also tallied revenue of $5.2bn. SpaceX as a whole, however, is not profitable and has lost $1.1bn so far this year. Over the last year, Musk has taken to bringing more of his various companies under fewer banners. Before it went public earlier this year, SpaceX acquired xAI and X , the platform formerly known as Twitter, both of which Musk owned. The recent launch of Terafab, a combined effort to manufacture computer chips between Tesla and SpaceX, was another signal that Musk sees his companies as potentially more effective when working together. Musk said on Tuesday a full merger between the two companies would make sense for the work each is doing around chips, artificial intelligence, software and more. Musk, who became the world's first paper trillionaire after the SpaceX stock market debut earlier this year, said he is not included in either of the special committees considering the mega-merger. He described himself as a "conflicted party" as the chief executive of Tesla and of SpaceX. Even commenting on the possibility of a merger between the two companies, Musk compared to "tap dancing through a minefield". He added a merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders. At least 50% of Tesla's shareholders would need to approve the merger, which Musk described as "quite a high hurdle to achieve". While Tesla is known as an electric car company, Musk has lately been shifting resources there to work around robotics. SpaceX, with its growing focus on AI infrastructure, quickly outstripped Tesla on the stock market in terms of value when it made its stock market debut. NATO is deploying additional patrol aircraft and intelligence personnel to the Black Sea, a spokesman for the alliance said, after a series of deadly drone attacks in the region widely blamed on Russia but denied by the Kremlin. “Allies have or will send additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, explosive exploitation teams, intelligence personnel, drones and more to the Black Sea,” said Colonel Martin O’Donnell on Tuesday. list 1 of 3 NATO says will do ‘anything and everything’ if alliance is attacked list 2 of 3 ‘Block, blunt, break’: What’s in NATO’s new Russia war plan? list 3 of 3 Will NATO’s ‘theory of victory’ work? “The most important thing we can do, however, is to increase our situational awareness in the region through increased sensors and data sharing,” he added. NATO, along with Bulgaria and Romania, has not directly attributed the recent spate of attacks to any country. Military analysts have said Russia almost certainly carried out the attacks but Moscow has not acknowledged any responsibility. In an attack on October 5, Romania reported two people dead after their ship caught fire and sank in Black Sea waters. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Moscow of being responsible. Kallas warned that the latest strikes were adding to a “perfect storm” facing global food supplies already being battered by droughts in multiple regions and the war in the Middle East. Last week, seven sailors were reported missing after drones struck two chemical tankers near Romania’s Black Sea coast, setting them ablaze and raising fresh security concerns along a vital shipping route used by Ukraine. events.title: Musk calls Tesla-SpaceX merger a ‘good idea’ as SpaceX posts first profit as a public company
events.summary: Speculation about SpaceX buying the EV maker has gained traction recently. Musk said a Tesla-SpaceX merger would be “a good idea”, and special committees are now discussing it. Shareholders would need to approve any deal. SpaceX posted its first profit as a public company, with net income of US$4.4 billion. Revenue rose 161% to US$14.58 billion, helped by fast-growing AI income. Starlink reached 13.6 million subscribers, but average monthly revenue fell to US$69. SpaceX still faces heavy spending, and Starship remains central to its future plans. WASHINGTON – Elon Musk said on Oct 20 that a merger of his two companies SpaceX and Tesla would be “a good idea” and that they had formed special committees to discuss a union, sending shares of the space and technology company up 4.9% in extended trading. The company earlier posted its first profit as a public company and Musk said it was tracking an annual revenue run rate of up to US$1 trillion (S$1.28 trillion). Musk has in the past tantalised shareholders with the idea, citing growing overlap between the companies. Speculation about SpaceX buying the EV maker has gained traction recently, with Barclays suggesting earlier in October that a deal could be announced before Tesla’s annual meeting in December. “I think it would be a good idea, but it’s really up to the special committees of both companies,” Musk said in the first official confirmation that the companies were formally talking. “Because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussion of the special committees,” he told investors on a conference call. Shareholders ultimately would need to approve a deal, he added. SpaceX’s revenue climbed 161% to US$14.58 billion for the three months ended Sept 30 from a year earlier. AI revenue surged by almost 10 times to US$7.56 billion, mostly from renting out datacentre capacity to developers such as Anthropic, Alphabet’s Google and Reflection AI rather than from its own models. “We are in an inflection moment for SpaceX across launch, connectivity and superintelligence,” Musk said on the call. He ended his portion of prepared remarks with a seemingly off-script remark: “In a nutshell, what this implies for SpaceX annual recurring revenue by the end of 2027 is somewhere between US$500 billion and a trillion.” The third quarter offered the clearest evidence yet that SpaceX’s heavy investment in AI is translating into revenue, even as spending on compute infrastructure remains enormous – capital expenses nearly tripled. The shift is reshaping a company whose financial engine has long been its Starlink internet services business and whose longer-term ambitions still hinge on getting Starship rockets into regular service. For now, though, its main business looks closer to a cloud provider’s than an AI lab’s. AI revenue drives SpaceX transformation SpaceX’s chief financial officer, Bret Johnsen, reiterated that SpaceX expects annual recurring revenue of about US$100 billion by the end of 2026. He said the company expects US$35 billion to US$40 billion in capital expenditures in the fourth quarter. AI took US$16.4 billion of the company’s US$19.6 billion in capital spending in the third quarter. “SpaceX delivered the quarter the bulls wanted, at least on the top line,” said Will Rhind, CEO of asset manager GraniteShares. “The story now is all about AI. The compute contracts signed earlier in 2026 are turning into revenue faster than a lot of people thought.” The company’s AI business spans Grok, social media platform X and a fast-growing datacentre operation. Operating losses at the AI unit have been large and SpaceX has cautioned it will need sustained investment before it can consistently generate profits. But it turned a profit in the third quarter, compared with a year-ago loss. “With AI revenue now the company’s biggest business line, the company’s hyperscale business is quickly providing operating strength and leverage which will carry into the advancements of its satellite and launch business,” said Daniel Newman, CEO of tech research group the Futurum Group. “Increasingly, the strength and diversification of SpaceX makes a merger with Tesla feel imminent.” SpaceX reported net income of US$4.4 billion versus a net loss of US$1.1 billion a year earlier and analysts’ expectation for a profit of US$1.57 billion. On a per-share, adjusted basis, it earned 45 US cents according to IBES calculations, outstripping a 13-cent average estimate. The satellite-internet unit has continued to expand its subscriber base, aided by additional satellite launches and a growing range of consumer, enterprise, aviation, maritime and government services. Starlink reached 13.6 million subscribers in the third quarter, above the 12.19 million analysts expected, but growth is coming at a price: Average monthly revenue per subscriber has fallen from US$99 in 2023 to US$69 in the third quarter as it expands abroad with cheaper plans.
