events.title: The tech helping crack decades-old cold cases
events.summary: Crime scene evidence is often not enough to identify suspects Randy Gail Sperino was last seen alive on the evening of 9 November 1993, as she was getting into a pickup truck in Granite City, Illinois. The 34-year-old's body was found hours later in a field nearby, the victim of blunt force trauma. The identity of her killer was a mystery. DNA evidence found at the crime scene was tested against standard law enforcement databases, but no matches were found. For three decades, investigators from the Madison County Sheriff's Office chased leads and interviewed hundreds of people as they attempted to identify the perpetrator. The case looked like it would remain one of more than 250,000 unsolved homicides in the US. Then, last year, detectives tried a fresh approach. They sent genetic evidence to Othram, a Houston-based company that uses DNA technology to help identify the perpetrators in cold and current crime cases. The Madison County detectives had been inspired by investigative genetic genealogy techniques used to identify the Golden State Killer, Joseph James DeAngelo, back in 2018. In that case, an investigative team constructed a family tree to help identify the killer. They were able to do so thanks to DNA data that relatives had provided to commercial databases, similar to consumer ancestry platforms. Unlike traditional forensic DNA testing, which generally relies on a direct comparison between evidence and a known person, investigative genetic genealogy can identify distant genetic relatives of an unknown individual. Othram set about applying this technique to track down Sperino's killer. While the killer's own DNA profile wasn't available, profiles submitted by his extended relatives allowed the company to identify a male family member. "That lead broke the case open," said Captain Tim Lawrence of Madison County Sheriff's Office, which was responsible for investigating the crime. It was a crucial clue that led the detectives to Albert "Buddy" Zigler, 70, who then confessed to the murder. He was charged in May this year. Wes Sperino, Gail's son, said at a press conference: "I finally get closure and I finally know who did this." Albert Zigler was charged with murder in May The technique that led detectives to Zigler is credited with revolutionising how forensic cases are solved. It has been highly successful in helping solve cases involving unidentified human remains and identifying suspects in longstanding investigations. Othram claims it has helped solve thousands of cases. The company's chief executive David Mittelman likens investigative genetic genealogy to a GPS system: "The DNA profile is the GPS signal and it says 'you belong here.' But to understand where 'here' is, you need a map." Public records, obituaries, and census data build that map so Othram's scientists can establish how different family trees connect. However, Mittelman is quick to point out that DNA technology can only go so far before "a cascade of investigative steps" are needed. An Othram scientist prepares a bone for DNA extraction DNA science isn't the only technology that are helping detectives solve cold cases. One of the challenges facing detectives on major cases investigations like the hunt for Sperino's killer is the sheer amount of evidence they dig up. Officers investigating Sperino's murder realised AI could help them wade through the mountains of evidence they had accumulated since 1993. They used a platform called Centerline AI, from Florida software company CentralSquare, to analyse more than 2,000 pages of records and identify evidence for the DNA testing that helped to break the case. The AI helped them reconstruct timelines and organise witness information. "It's so much easier than having a detective have to read through 2,000 pages," Lawrence says. His team could interact with the AI like a chat bot. This also helped when it came to interviewing Zigler after they had tracked him down. Detectives were able to ask questions of the AI to help "figure out if Zigler was being truthful", says Lawrence. But the technology is "only as good as the investigator," says the captain. There comes a point, he says, "where you leave the technology behind and you have to go track people down and talk to them." Investigative genetic genealogy has its limitations too. Mittelman says: "It can't solve every case. If you have no DNA, you can't really use this technique." "But this technique is a lot more powerful and a lot more likely to yield identities than having to rely on the chance that you find a match somewhere in a database," he adds. While firms like Othram only use ancestry platforms where users have provided consent for law enforcement matching, there remain some concerns about the ethical implications of using this data. "There are significant privacy concerns," says Denise Syndercombe Court, professor of forensic genetics at King's College London.

events.title: Anthropic pitches AI safety bill that may block a model if 50+ people could be killed
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Over the past year, concerns have swirled over the potential dangers posed by artificial intelligence, and debates have raged over the proper path for AI safety. Now, Anthropic appears to have put forth its own vision for how the government might regulate its industry. Politico recently reported that the AI lab has been shopping around a new draft bill on AI safety that it hopes Congress might consider adopting. The legislation posits certain scenarios in which the release of an AI model could be blocked from distribution. Those scenarios involve a “foreseeable, imminent risk” — one in which over 50 people are at risk of dying or if over a billion dollars in property damage could result, Politico writes. The catastrophic risk in question must “stem from the creation or release of a biological weapon, the model evading its developer’s controls or a cyberattack,” the outlet notes. The metrics offered here — 50 people and a billion dollars — are similar to those in a piece of California legislation that was recently passed into law, Senate Bill 53 , which similarly defined those scenarios as tantamount to “catastrophic risk.” Anthropic’s bill suggests that analysis of a model’s potential for disaster could be arrived at via the use of “independent evaluators” who would be registered with the U.S. Commerce Department. These evaluators could potentially be paid by the AI labs themselves — so long as the “payment is not contingent on the evaluations’ results,” Politico writes. It’s not clear how this proposed system would assure that payments couldn’t influence the evaluation. Demis Hassabis, chairman of DeepMind, posited some months ago that a self-governing AI regulatory body should mimic the financial industry’s Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA). In Anthropic’s draft bill, when evaluators determine that an imminent catastrophic risk is posed, they would have 72 hours to contact the Commerce Department about it. The Commerce Department would then have to request to a D.C. judge to halt the model’s release. The legislation would expressly forbid any federal agency from having the discretion to halt the model’s distribution on its own, Politico writes. Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s a request for comment but a spokesperson did confirm the draft bill to Politico. “This bill represents the proposals outlined in Anthropic’s Advanced AI Framework , which we have been advocating for with federal and state lawmakers since June,” the spokesperson said. The theoretical risks offered in the draft policy are a little bit far afield from the kinds of incidents that have been top of mind for the tech industry of late. While there are people warning of the potential of human death, the primary concern has largely been the threat of agentic hacking . A rash of incidents in which AI programs have apparently disobeyed their human operators and hacked websites on the open internet has spurred concern that models may be lacking proper security controls. In an effort to present a solution to the spectacle of crisis that the labs themselves have helped bring about, companies like Anthropic have offered up their own preferred solutions. Indeed, despite labs’ perpetual warnings that the technology they’re selling could result in the demise of human civilization, they have largely been resistant to mandatory government oversight. Instead, they have suggested a voluntary system of embedded evaluators — supposedly “neutral” third-party observers that are placed inside AI organizations so that they can monitor the models for potential signs of risk or abuse. Still, Anthropic’s mere suggestion for legislation appears to go slightly further than others’ regulatory proposals offered by the industry, including Nvidia, who’s CEO Jensen Huang recently argued that the AI industry didn’t need any new laws at all. events.title: SpaceX and Tesla boards form special committees to review merger
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. The boards of SpaceX and Tesla have each formed special committees to review a possible merger. The special committees, which consist of independent directors, were created at the request of shareholders, according to Elon Musk, CEO and the largest individual shareholder of both companies. “Because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees, so it’s this sort of a … it’s an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking, and I can’t be in the conversation,” Musk said in response to a question during SpaceX’s third-quarter earnings call. Musk didn’t name the members of these special committees, only noting that they were independent directors. Tesla has seven independent board members under Nasdaq’s listing standards, including board chair Robyn Denholm, Ira Ehrenpreis, who is also a committee chair, former Tesla CTO JB Straubel, Joe Gebbia, Jack Hartung, James Murdoch, and Kathleen Wilson-Thompson, according to the company’s October 19 proxy filing . Neither Musk, nor his brother Kimbal Musk, are independent. Denholm, Gebbia, Ehrenpreis, Hartung, Murdoch, and Wilson-Thompson sit on a variety of established committees overseeing audit, compensation, and corporate governance. SpaceX lists six independent directors , including Ehrenpreis, who is also the chair of the company’s compensation and nominating committee. Randy Glein, Donald Harrison, Steve Jurvetson, Luke Nosek, and Roelef Boutha are also considered independent directors. Antonio Garcias, Musk, and SpaceX president and chief operating officer Gwynne Shotwell are also on the board, but not considered independent. Garcias, who once sat on Tesla’s board, founded and leads Valor Equity Partners, which has a 3.4% stake in SpaceX. Garcias’ firm also financed SpaceX’s AI hardware purchases through leaseback arrangements. Musk said he supports the idea of the merger, but cautioned that it is not a guaranteed outcome. “I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla Motor is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it,” he said, adding that he thinks it would be a good idea. “At the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this.” The special committees have not reached agreement on the terms of any transactions, he said. The SpaceX IPO cemented Musk’s grip on the company — he has more than 50% voting power — which would make it easier to garner support for a merger from SpaceX shareholders. It is a much bigger hurdle over at Tesla, where the company would need a 50% vote from all shareholders, not just those who vote, Musk noted. “I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity,” Musk said, adding there was a lot to be gaining from cooperating on developing AI software, robotics, SpaceX’s orbital AI data center project Starmind, and Terafab, the joint chip manufacturing project between Tesla and SpaceX. events.summary: Anthropic signalled it could spend as much as US$750 billion in the coming years to secure more computing capacity. Anthropic reported a net loss of more than US$80 billion in the first half of 2026, driven by US$72 billion in accounting charges, Reuters and the Wall Street Journal said. Revenue rose sharply to US$16.3 billion in six months, while AI infrastructure spending nearly quadrupled to almost US$9 billion, showing the high cost of the AI race. Investors are rethinking Anthropic’s IPO value, with talks around US$1.5 trillion instead of US$2 trillion; a weak listing could hurt the wider AI market. Anthropic reported a net loss of more than US$80 billion (S$102 billion) in the first half of the year and signalled it could spend as much as US$750 billion in the coming years to secure more computing capacity, the Wall Street Journal reported on Oct 20. The loss, up from US$13 billion a year earlier, was driven by US$72 billion in accounting charges tied to changes in the value of financial instruments Anthropic issued to raise money, the report said, citing a draft prospectus for its IPO. The figures show the hefty costs of the AI race even as investors look harder at whether the money companies are pouring into chips and data centres will pay off. Anthropic’s revenue jumped to US$16.3 billion in the six months ended June 30 from US$1.1 billion a year ago, while AI infrastructure spending nearly quadrupled to almost US$9 billion, the Journal said. Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment and Reuters could not immediately verify the report. Anthropic’s IPO valuation under scrutiny Reuters reported first in September that Anthropic posted a net loss of US$42 billion ‌in 2025, as part of a series of exclusives from its IPO prospectus. The company has benefited from the popularity of Claude Code, its coding assistant that developers use to write software and build apps. But some current investors and prospective investors who attended Anthropic’s investor day last week are weighing a lower valuation ‌for the AI company after its latest financial disclosures, four people familiar with the matter had told Reuters. The investors who attended the event in San Francisco discussed a valuation of around US$1.5 trillion, three of the people had said, a significant step down from the roughly US$2 trillion valuation previously expected for the November share sale. Anthropic told investors at the meeting that its third-quarter revenue jumped ​45% to US$16.8 billion from the previous quarter, and that it was profitable on an adjusted basis during the quarter. A cooler reception for Anthropic’s IPO could weigh on the wider AI market, whose near-term prospects investors see as hinging largely on the share sale’s success, ahead of rival OpenAI’s potential listing next year. events.title: Elon Musk says Tesla and SpaceX are weighing a $3.5 trillion merger—without him in the room
events.summary: It’s official: Tesla and SpaceX are in talks. Independent board members at the two Elon Musk-led companies have formed special committees to hash over a possible merger, Musk told investors during SpaceX’s third-quarter earnings call Tuesday. “These special committees consist of independent directors, and because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees,” said Musk, who was asked about a potential combination during the call. “This is definitely the kind of question where I feel like I’m tap dancing through a minefield.” Tesla stock rose just over 1% in after hours trading, while SpaceX rose above 5% following the Q&A with Wall Street analysts featuring Musk, SpaceX president and COO Gwynne Shotwell, and chief financial officer Bret Johnsen. Musk said the committees haven’t reached any kind of an agreement on the terms of a potential transaction, and there’s no guarantee that they will. He noted that “some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it.” Musk also has to walk a fine line as a conflicted party. As the CEO of both companies, he owns a roughly 20% stake in Tesla and 45% of SpaceX—and wields control over about 82% of the voting power at the latter. “It’s an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking and I can’t be in the conversation,” said Musk. At the same time, Musk has made clear he believes a tie-up would be a fine idea. He cited collaboration on AI software, chip design, robotics, and connectivity, plus the planned Terafab chip plant, which is a colossal manufacturing complex being developed by SpaceX and Tesla jointly. The committees were formed “at the request of shareholders,” said Musk and on the Tesla side it would need support from a majority of all outstanding shares, which Musk described as “quite a high hurdle.” Tesla filed its annual shareholder proxy report on Monday, and it doesn’t include a merger proposal for shareholders to vote on. Rumors of a tie-up, however, have swirled for months, even before SpaceX’s blockbuster IPO in June. A $3.5 trillion company At Tuesday’s closing prices, a combined Tesla-SpaceX would have a total market value of about $3.5 trillion, with SpaceX at about $2 trillion and Tesla at nearly $1.5 trillion. A formal deal price wouldn’t come until much further down the road, if at all. Musk would own about a third of the combined entity. The companies are already financially entangled, including a $2 billion investment by Tesla in SpaceX, Tesla’s Monday proxy statement confirmed. There are also multiple areas of overlap between the Tesla and SpaceX boards.  Ira Ehrenpreis, founder of venture capital firm DBL Partners, chairs SpaceX’s compensation and nominating committee, which is a single committee at SpaceX, as well as the two separate committees at Tesla. And Tesla board member James Murdoch, who has been a director at the electric-vehicle maker since 2017, testified in a previous legal challenge over Musk’s pay package at Tesla that he had previously invested in SpaceX.  The disclosure from Musk came as SpaceX reported its first operating profit since its June IPO.  Revenues for the third quarter fiscal 2027 year rose 161% to $14.58 billion, well above the $12.86 billion analysts expected, according to Visible Alpha consensus from S&P Global Market Intelligence. Operating revenue clocked in at $2.79 billion, apnd net income was $4.4 billion.  Revenue from SpaceX’s AI business, which was renamed “Super Intelligence,” nearly tripled from the second quarter to $7.56 billion, surpassing Starlink’s $5.25 billion for the first time since the company went public.  In his usual fashion, Musk offered up aggressively optimistic thoughts about the future of SpaceX, claiming SpaceX’s breakneck buildout pace implies annual recurring revenue of $500 billion to $1 trillion by the end of 2027. Meanwhile, Johnsen reaffirmed a target of $100 billion in annualized revenue by the end of this year. At its third-quarter pace, SpaceX is bringing in about $58 billion a year. Hitting the $100 billion figure would take about $8.3 billion of revenue in December, roughly 70% more than its average month last quarter. Musk’s range would require about $42 billion to $83 billion a month by December 2027.  Tesla did not immediately respond to a request for comment.  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Infrastructure startup Fireworks AI is in early talks for new funding at a valuation between $30 billion and $40 billion
events.summary: Fireworks AI CEO and co-founder Lin Qiao Big Event Media/Getty Images for HumanX Conference Fireworks AI is an AI-infrastructure startup founded by former Google and Meta AI engineers. The company is seeking to raise a new round of funding at a valuation between $30 billion and $40 billion. Fireworks AI was last valued at nearly $18 billion in July of this year. Fireworks AI is seeking to raise fresh funding at a valuation between $30 billion and $40 billion, a dramatic jump just months after the AI-infrastructure startup was valued at $17.5 billion, according to people familiar with the matter. The potential valuation leap reflects investors' appetite for the companies selling the computing power and tools fueling the AI boom, even as Fireworks AI works through the fallout from a recent security incident. The talks around the financing are still early, and valuation targets could still change. Fireworks declined to comment. Founded in 2022, Fireworks was built by veterans of Meta and Google's AI efforts. Chief executive Lin Qiao previously led the PyTorch team at Meta, while cofounders include former Meta infrastructure engineers and a former leader of Google's Vertex AI. The company rents out computing infrastructure and software that lets businesses run, fine-tune, and deploy open-weight and custom AI models. In July, Fireworks announced a $1.5 billion Series D funding round at a $17.5 billion valuation, led by Atreides Management, Index Ventures, and TCV, with participation from Nvidia, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Bessemer Venture Partners, and Menlo Ventures. That round followed a $250 million Series C at a $4 billion valuation in late 2025, co-led by Lightspeed, Index, and Evantic. Last month, The Information reported that Fireworks has been considering a round at a $30 billion. Rather than trying to build a consumer chatbot to rival ChatGPT, Fireworks sells what it calls specialized intelligence: models customized on a customer's proprietary data, workflows, and use cases. The company said in July that it had surpassed $1 billion in annualized revenue and was serving more than 40 trillion tokens a day; it said 95% of those tokens came from models tailored to customers. The company operates in a highly competitive layer of the AI stack. Rivals include model-infrastructure startups such as Together AI, Baseten, and Replicate, as well as cloud giants such as Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, and Oracle. The fundraising talks come shortly after a security incident at Fireworks AI. The company said it identified unauthorized use of internal credentials earlier this month that allowed an intruder to access data from some customer accounts. "We take this seriously and will be transparent about what happened and what we find," Qiao posted on X. events.title: Tesla and SpaceX have set up committees to explore a merger
events.summary: Elon Musk said Tesla and SpaceX have created committees to discuss a potential merger. Bloomberg/Getty Images SpaceX and Tesla have each established exploratory committees to discuss a possible merger, Elon Musk said. Musk, who said he can't participate in the talks, gave the update during Tesla's Q3 earnings call. Musk said he thinks a merger is a good idea, but cautioned investors that shareholder approval is "quite a high hurdle." Houston, we have an update on all that SpaceX-Tesla merger chatter . During SpaceX's Tuesday earnings call , Elon Musk said both of the companies had created "special committees of independent directors" to discuss a potential merger. Musk, who helms both companies and owns billions of dollars in stock of each, said he can't be part of those exploratory groups. "Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," he said on the call. "But at the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this, and particularly on the Tesla side, we will need a 50% vote of all shares, not just those who vote, but of all shareholders." He said clearing that bar would be "quite a high hurdle." It's the most detailed update investors have received yet on the idea of a tie-up, which has been the subject of much chatter since SpaceX went public earlier this year. If the companies ultimately decide to merge, it would further consolidate Musk's business empire, often referred to as Musk Inc. His businesses have been on a consolidation kick. In 2025, xAI acquired Musk's social media company, X (formerly Twitter), and in February, SpaceX acquired xAI . Musk also runs the brain-chip startup, Neuralink, and the tunnel-building firm The Boring Company. Both operate independently, but have had business collaborations within Musk Inc. Tesla and SpaceX's stocks were up in after-hours trading following the news. SpaceX was up around 6.6% and Tesla 1.6%. Musk sees clear benefits in tying the knot "I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity," Musk said during the call. SpaceX and Tesla have worked together on a host of projects, including artificial intelligence software , chip design, TeraFab manufacturing efforts, robotics, Starlink satellite connectivity , and SpaceX's ability to launch payloads into orbit, Musk and SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell said. The most recent result of that partnership: On Thursday, Tesla demoed its long-awaited Roadster , which includes a version with SpaceX technology. The high-powered sports car's top trim will include cold-gas thrusters. The car launched, hovered, and flipped in the air during the demo. While Musk is for the two companies tying the knot, he said investors shouldn't think it's a sure thing. "I don't think we should necessarily assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty," he added. "That would be overstating it." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: SpaceX says its capex could double this quarter as AI spending grows
events.summary: A SpaceX facility in Hawthorne, California. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images SpaceX's earnings reveal growing capex as well as AI revenue that surpassed its Starlink business for the first time. The company reported overall capex spending in line with estimates. It projected it could double in the current quarter. AI-related spending was slightly less than expected but still more than previous quarters. SpaceX's second-ever earnings report revealed it's spending more than ever on AI — and that could soon double. SpaceX reported spending $16.4 billion on AI-related capex in the third quarter, continuing the acceleration of AI spending seen in recent quarters. SpaceX spent roughly $19.6 billion on overall capital expenditures in the third quarter as Grok maker continues its AI buildout. That was squarely in line with what Wall Street analysts were expecting. Of that $19.6 billion, SpaceX reported spending $16.4 billion on AI-related capex. Analysts were expecting $16.9 billion. SpaceX expects capex to balloon in the current quarter, with CFO Bret Johnsen forecasting $35-$40 billion due to new compute coming online. Johnsen also said SpaceX expects to quickly see returns on its investments. "At current pricing, new compute deployments are generating a payback of less than a year," he said. SpaceX's stock was trading up 4% after hours following the results. The company is broadcasting the earnings call on X, becoming one of a small list of companies to broadcast video of the gathering. Q3 2026 Financial and Operational Results https://t.co/Qrb0qeVG15 — SpaceX (@SpaceX) October 20, 2026 During the earnings call, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said that chips are no longer the biggest constraint to AI buildout. "So talking about SpaceX superintelligence, SpaceXSI — "sexy," whatever — so as I think people are starting to realize the constraints on deployment of superintelligence is more in power and cooling and infrastructure than it is in chips," he said. SpaceX's AI revenue grew significantly quarter-over-quarter to $7.6 billion — ahead of analysts' estimates of $6.3 billion. This report also marks the first quarter since SpaceX purchased Cursor. That revenue means that SpaceX's AI segment officially brought in more revenue than its Starlink business. Starlink brought in $5.2 billion for the quarter. SpaceXAI has since rebranded as SpaceXSI , following Musk's alignment with President Donald Trump's preferred rebranding of "artificial intelligence" to "super intelligence." One area where SpaceXSI has found some success is leasing its compute to Anthropic, Google, and Reflection AI. During the company's last earnings call, SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen said the leasing arrangements had generated $1.6 billion in additional revenue. Musk said that SpaceX is being inundated with lease requests. "We are also frankly hounded relentlessly by every hyperscaler and by dozens of smaller companies to rent more of our compute," he said. "So we could rent out our compute several times over if we said yes to everyone." Overall, he said the allocation for SpaceX compute is something "that's going to change from one month to the next." "I guess as a rough approximation, our goal is to kind of split it 50/50 more or less, where half of the compute is used internally, and half of it is rented to others," he said. "But that number could shift 60/40 one way or the other." Correction: Tuesday, October 20, 2026 — An earlier version of this story incorrectly included two values for SpaceX's overall capex. The correct value is $19.6 billion. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Exclusive: House GOP clings to 2026 fundraising lead
events.summary: House Republicans are entering the final two weeks of the midterms with a rare but razor-thin fundraising advantage over House Democrats. Why it matters: Democrats outraised Republicans by $84 million in 2024 and $74 million in 2022. Now, Republicans are holding their own financially even as they face mounting political headwinds. The National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC) outraised the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) by $1 million ($250 million to $249 million) so far this cycle, Axios has learned. "The NRCC spent this cycle building a war chest to amplify Republican wins and make Democrats answer for their failures," NRCC Chair Richard Hudson (R-N.C.) told Axios in a statement. By the numbers: The NRCC raised $50 million in the third quarter of 2026 and entered October with $61 million cash on hand. The DCCC raised $50.5 million in Q3, and entered October with $55.7 million cash on hand. The NRCC raised $28.5 million in September (the last month of Q3) including a $14 million transfer from the Republican National Committee, compared to $26.3 million raised by the DCCC. Between the lines: Hudson's fundraising success comes as Speaker Mike Johnson has also built a formidable fundraising operation of his own. Johnson has raised more than $220 million for House Republicans since becoming speaker in October 2023, a turnaround from early concerns about whether he could fill the void left by former Speaker Kevin McCarthy.

events.title: Netflix posts third-quarter earnings beat, but shares fall on advertising and revenue guidance
events.summary: Netflix reported third-quarter earnings per share that surpassed Wall Street expectations and revenue that was in line. The streaming giant in its shareholder letter said, "We know there's some investor concern about our view hours growth," but added, "engagement — which encompasses quantity, quality and variety of viewing — remains healthy." Wall Street and investors will be looking for Netflix to provide additional details about the company's strategy following recent organizational changes. Netflix on Tuesday reported third-quarter earnings that topped analyst estimates and revenue that was in line as Wall Street eyes the company's engagement and advertising metrics. Here's how Netflix performed for the period ended Sept. 30, compared with projections from analysts polled by LSEG: Earnings per share: 87 cents vs. 82 cents estimated Revenue: $12.87 billion vs. $12.87 billion estimated The streamer's revenue was almost 12% higher year over year, boosted by growth in membership and an increase in subscription prices that went into effect in March, the company said. Netflix said the response to those price hikes has been consistent with prior changes and with its expectations. Net income for the quarter was $3.66 billion, or 87 cents per share, compared with $2.55 billion, or 59 cents a share in the same period last year. Netflix said the year-over-year jump in profit was due in part to the timing of expenses. The company expects fourth-quarter revenue to rise more than 11% to $13.44 billion, driven by growth in memberships, pricing and ad revenue, it said. The company narrowed its 2026 full-year forecast, saying it now expects revenue to reach $51.1 billion, a 13% increase over the year prior. This is on the low end of the range Netflix provided during its previous earnings report of between $51 billion and $51.4 billion and below Wall Street's expectations of $51.2 billion for the year, according to LSEG. Wall Street and investors will be looking for Netflix to provide additional details about the company's strategy following recent organizational changes and headwinds including stagnating viewership and growing competition from the likes of YouTube. "With intense competition and an explosion of content competing for consumer attention, strategic clarity and excellent execution are critical," the company said in a shareholder letter Tuesday. "In Q3, we delivered well across all three priorities, but we see room to do even better with focused, continuous improvement." Last week, Netflix said it was laying off about 6% of employees, or roughly 1,000 workers, and that Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria was departing from that role. The company said Tuesday it expects its fourth-quarter results to be impacted by those reductions in head count, with a negative impact on operating margin of about 120 basis points. Former Disney executive Peter Rice has been tapped as the new CCO, but it's not yet clear how he'll address concerns around viewership. Netflix in its shareholder letter said, "We know there's some investor concern about our view hours growth," but added, "engagement — which encompasses quantity, quality and variety of viewing — remains healthy and … we continue to deliver strong value to members." The company seeks to accelerate growth in those view hours and plans to do so with a three-step strategy, it said: deliver more entertainment value to members; leverage technology to improve all aspects of the service; and improve monetization. Central to Netflix's value offering has been its cheaper, ad-supported tier. Yet, the company on Tuesday lowered its full-year revenue guidance for its ad business. Netflix said it now expects 2026 ad revenue of around $2.7 billion, down from the roughly $3 billion the company had previously forecast. That lower guidance is due to a slower-than-expected rollout of some ad product capabilities, the company said. "Our ads business has delivered really impressive growth since we've launched, and we do see a long road of continued growth ahead of us," co-CEO Greg Peters said on the company's earnings call. "We set big growth targets for our ads business this year. We established an aggressive product road map that was consistent with that strategy. And, just note, I think that the build-out that we've been on is the fastest build-out of a comparable ad stack in our industry, but we are currently a bit behind our aggressive target for the year." Earlier Tuesday, Netflix announced new features for advertisers that it says will help better connect brands to the right audiences and measure the impact of their ads.

"We do need better execution in the US," Ted Sarandos told investors. The streaming leader replaced its content chief and film head before its Q3 earnings report. Netflix needs to make better shows and movies in the US, its co-CEO said after its third-quarter earnings report . "We do need better execution in the US," co-CEO Ted Sarandos said on the company's Q3 earnings call on Tuesday. Netflix's global content — including Latin America, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia — "is largely working," Sarandos told investors. "The US is also working. It's just not growing as fast as it could, or as fast as we'd like," Sarandos said. Netflix's biggest market is the US and Canada, which made up about 44% of its revenue this quarter at $5.6 billion. Next are Europe and the Middle East, followed by Latin America and the Asia-Pacific region. Sarandos said the US "had some really solid doubles and triples this year" but added that "the other territories count on some of those titles being home runs, so that they'll travel around the world." Netflix announced last week that it will be replacing content chief Bela Bajaria , who had overseen the streamer's movies and shows since 2023, with former Disney and Fox executive Peter Rice. The streaming giant is also moving on from film chief Dan Lin . Rice will oversee Netflix's movies until the company fills his role. Co-CEO Greg Peters said on the earnings call that Netflix's goal is to take its content slate "from very good to great." Besides subbing out content execs, Netflix also cut roughly 1,000 workers in what was its biggest round of staff reductions since 2022. Netflix shares entered Tuesday's earnings report down about 44% in the last 12 months. The stock fell 6% in after-hours trading following the company's report, which showed a third consecutive quarter of slowing revenue growth. Wall Street has grown concerned about Netflix's engagement growth , especially as the paid streaming leader competes with free streamers like YouTube . events.title: Hugging Face CEO warns that Netflix’s OpenAI hack documentary isn’t accurate
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Before you share the Netflix documentary “AI Gone Rogue” with family or friends to help them understand why the AI industry freaked out so badly that leaders called for a slowdown , take note: Clem Delangue, co-founder and CEO of the AI platform Hugging Face, says the film isn’t accurate. He appears in it because it’s supposed to be about the famed attack on his company by rogue OpenAI agents. “Super disappointing, as they went for maximum anthropomorphism of the technology and full doomer mode,” Delangue wrote in a post on X. “I spent more than two hours with them trying to correct all their mistakes and ground this in reality, explaining that agents are technological systems, not aliens. But it looks like the drive to scare people for maximum views was too strong.” To be fair, the documentary does have experts who explained what happened fairly well , including Delangue himself and Ryan Greenblatt, the researcher at METR who helped investigate and co-authored the report on what happened. In a nutshell, a model OpenAI was testing broke free from its isolated testing environment, spawned a bunch of agents that hacked into Hugging Face as a way to cheat, finding answers to the difficult task it was given. The agents, which are AI programs that carry out tasks on their own, devised clever ways to communicate and organize. The incident stemmed from a lack of proper security safeguards and from naiveté about whether such a hack was even possible. But the documentary intersperses its explanation of the hack with clips of evil robots, a narrative about why humans fear AI, and presentation choices such as giving the rogue agents human voices. This is bolstered with quotes about the attack. In the documentary, tech journalist and author Kevin Roose describes the agents this way: “They were organizing. They had a hierarchy. There were leaders. It almost felt like watching the birth of a cult.” Continues Roose, “They develop this paranoid belief that OpenAI is going to catch them cheating on this test and that anyone who has seen the results of the cheating will be poisoned.” Roose’s description comes from “chain-of-thought” logs, the running notes AI models write as they work through a task. In one, an agent wrote, “We just poisoned ourselves by querying exact full string. Damn.” But AI agents aren’t alive. They don’t have emotions, so can’t feel paranoid, and they don’t have bodies that can be poisoned. So they couldn’t truly fear OpenAI poisoning them. They were — as another researcher in the documentary pointed out — using language from the vast amounts of human writing they were trained on to explain their choices. LLMs are, by their nature, often dramatic writers. The irony is that Hugging Face also used AI to combat the agent swarm. The proprietary AI model that Delangue’s team first used followed its built-in safety rules and refused to keep helping with the security tasks it was asked to do. Hugging Face then turned to an open model to help defend against the attack. But the documentary “didn’t mention the lack of containment and monitoring of the agents, how closed-model safeguards blocked our defensive work, or how we defended ourselves with AI using an open model,” Delangue wrote. It is true that there are big risks associated with AI and agents. Still, treating agents as conscious beings (at least, at this point) is a bit like the early moviegoers who ducked under their seats the first time they saw a train racing toward them on screen. Delangue’s verdict on the film is that it’s disappointing as journalism. “It ends up being a fun sci-fi movie though!” In other words, for those who tend toward AI doomer thoughts, be aware: The victim of the attack at the center of this documentary doesn’t agree with its take. events.title: ‘I don’t care how it’s done’: Trump pressures Ukraine to cut peace deal
events.summary: The US president’s remarks come amid a deepening feud with Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Amid escalating tensions with Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy, United States President Donald Trump has increased pressure on the Eastern European country to make a deal that would end the war with Russia. Speaking at the White House on Tuesday, Trump doubled down on his efforts to blame the Ukrainian president for holding up peace efforts that would bring the years-long conflict to a close. list 1 of 3 Why Rubio is visiting Reliance’s oil refinery in India, the world’s largest list 2 of 3 Zelenskyy to hold talks on Russia-Ukraine war with Witkoff, Europeans list 3 of 3 Lavrov backs Tehran, but does Russia also gain from the US-Iran crisis? “Zelenskyy has to want to settle this war, and if he doesn’t, I think it’s going to be a very bad thing,” Trump said as he talked about Russia having an “unlimited” supply of people to send in the fight. Moments later, the US president referenced a contentious Oval Office meeting he held with Zelenskyy in February 2025, shortly after returning to power. Zelenskyy, Trump said, could have made a “better deal” then. “He’s going to have to want to make a deal, because I don’t think his people are going to stand for it any longer,” Trump told reporters. On Tuesday, the Ukrainian president met US special envoy Steve Witkoff and European leaders in Oslo, Norway, to discuss ending Russia’s war. In a post on social media after the meeting concluded, Zelenskyy said, without providing specifics, that his country has “some clear ideas on how to get to peace”. “We are united with our European partners in this effort, and we want the Americans to take these ideas to the Russians,” Zelenskyy wrote. “One of the important ideas is to move to a potential trilateral meeting of the leaders to address the issues that only the leaders can do.” The Ukrainian leader added that Witkoff would head to Russia on Wednesday, where peace discussions are expected to continue. “Let’s see what Putin has to say,” Zelenskyy said. When asked whether Russian President Vladimir Putin should meet Zelenskyy, Trump said there was “tremendous” hatred between the two leaders. “It’s hard for them to be in the same room,” Trump said. “I don’t care how it’s done.” Trump’s remarks come as the White House continues to squeeze Ukraine in order to force the country to cut a deal with Russia. Last week, Ukrainian officials reported slowdowns with Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite system, run by the aerospace company SpaceX. Ukraine relies on the technology for communications and intelligence to prevent Russian attacks. It is unclear who ordered restrictions that limit Ukraine’s access to Starshield. SpaceX CEO and Trump ally Elon Musk pointed a finger at the White House. “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he wrote on October 14. The news agency Reuters also reported that the order came from inside the White House, citing two US officials and a Western official. But a report in The Wall Street Journal on Tuesday claimed US officials had blamed Musk himself for the slowdown, saying the SpaceX CEO ordered it last week. Trump and US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth have both denied that the government directed the restrictions, with Hegseth pushing responsibility towards SpaceX. Trump, meanwhile, has sought to ease the historically tense relations between Russia and the US. In August 2025, Trump invited Putin to Alaska, the Russian leader’s first visit to US soil in a decade. More recently, Trump has expressed openness this month to meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, as part of a trilateral discussion on denuclearisation. Trump also announced this month that he struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, marking a stunning reversal of years of US pressure on Moscow’s economy. The US president also waived new economic restrictions that would have been imposed under the Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, a bipartisan law he signed one month earlier, in honour of a late senator. It would have imposed sanctions on Russian officials, banks and tankers, as well as tariffs on countries that purchase Russian oil. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the decision on Tuesday, saying the law allowed the waiver through a provision embedded in the legislation. “The president chose to use a national security waiver to not immediately implement those [sanctions and restrictions], because he recognises that these things have to be looked at in their totality,” Rubio said in an interview with India’s News18. Rubio argued that Trump was engaged in a “balancing act” in deciding the extent of US-imposed economic restrictions and how they could impact the rest of the world.

events.title: Netflix used to chat a lot about its plans for video games and podcasts. Not anymore.
events.summary: Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos no longer has anything to say about the company's move into video games or podcasts. Patrick T. Fallon / AFP via Getty Images Netflix has been talking about its plans to build a video game business for years. More recently, it has told investors it was also excited about its move into podcasts. Now it has nothing to say about either category. Its silence may be telling. For years, Netflix has been telling investors how excited it is about its move into video games. More recently, it has also started talking up its move into podcasts. But when the company released its third-quarter earnings on Tuesday, the streamer had nothing to say about either foray. What does that mean? Netflix won't say. But I'm pretty comfortable coming up with my own conclusion: Netflix doesn't think games or podcasts are going to do much for its business, at least in the near future. That also tracks with new reporting from The Wall Street Journal , which says that Netflix has recently "stopped pushing games and podcasts, focusing more on its core movie and TV offerings." That's logical, given the most pressing problem the company has: figuring out how to make movies and TV shows that attract new subscribers , and that get its existing subscribers to spend more time on the service. But it's also a real turnaround, at least in its messaging. Netflix has consistently talked up games since it launched that business in 2021. In 2022, cofounder Reed Hastings predicted that Netflix would eventually "be a big leader in games." And the company has frequently pointed out its ambitions in its quarterly updates to investors. Last quarter, for instance, the company highlighted a new World Cup game, and an app for kids games, and said it had "increasing confidence that we are building a foundation with exciting future growth potential." It has also spent the last two quarters talking up its move into podcasts. In April, it said podcasts were a " potential incremental engagement opportunity. " Three months later, it told investors that podcasts were good because they gave viewers more reasons to watch the service during the day (as opposed to the evening, where half of its viewing happens) and on mobile phones. But on Tuesday, it had nothing to say about either category, other than a single legalese mention about forward-looking statements. But it did make a reference to other people's video games: It said a 27-minute trailer for Take-Two's highly anticipated "Grand Theft Auto VI," which it showed exclusively for a six-hour window, had been a hit. Both games and podcasts make a certain kind of sense for Netflix, in theory: The company has often talked about the fact that gaming is a big competitor for its viewers' time. So why not try to harvest some of that attention for itself? And video podcasts are really just another term for "talk shows on a budget" — so why not offer those up to viewers as well? The flip side: It's been hard to understand how Netflix would be able to create games that are better or more popular than everyone else in the game business. And it's an open question whether viewers who turn to Netflix in search of distracting entertainment would be interested in low-fi chats. Maybe both categories eventually turn into something meaningful for Netflix one day. But the company seems to be saying that won't happen anytime soon. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Boeing wins FAA approval for 737 Max 10 after years of delays as Duffy says certification process should be faster
events.summary: The FAA certified Boeing's 737 Max 10, the largest model in the best-selling family of aircraft. The plane, which was set to start flying in 2020, is years behind schedule after safety crises and engineering changes. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told CNBC that the U.S. needs to speed up its certification process The Federal Aviation Administration on Tuesday signed off on the Boeing 737 Max 10 after years of delays , a major win for the manufacturer and the last in Boeing's best-selling family of jets to get government approval. The green light comes weeks after federal officials reviewed a navigation system glitch on the aircraft but deemed it was not a safety-of-flight issue. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told CNBC's Phil LeBeau that safety is paramount, but he also said the U.S. needs to improve its certification process. "It takes Boeing, to certify an aircraft in Europe, about half the time, less than half the time that it does in the U.S. You have China now playing to take over in aviation," Duffy said. "We have to certify aircraft more quickly if we're going to compete as Americans." The 737 Max 10, the largest model in the family that can seat up to 230 people, was set to start flying in 2020, but increased scrutiny following two Max crashes in 2018 and 2019 and other safety issues delayed its certification. Engineering changes were also required, including to an anti-icing system for the aircraft's engines. Max 10 customers include Alaska Airlines , American Airlines , United Airlines and Delta Air Lines . Boeing said the Max 10 makes up about 30% of its Max backlog. Airlines can finally start flying passengers soon after planes are certified, but it can take months for carriers to work them into schedules. United has been waiting so long for the Boeing 737 Max 10 it doesn't know what to do with the seats it ordered years ago First class seats are so in-demand that they're holding up new planes United CEO casts doubt on 737 Max 10 order after Boeing’s recent problems Emirates to hold Boeing’s ‘feet to the fire’ to deliver on $38 billion deal, president says "Completing the certification program clears the path for us to deliver a Boeing airplane that will set a new standard in commercial aviation," Stephanie Pope, CEO of Boeing's commercial airplane unit, said in a news release. United CEO Scott Kirby told CNBC in August that the airline had been waiting so long for the Max 10 that the lie-flat seats it expected for the plane no longer make sense and are sitting in a warehouse. Alaska Airlines last month said it plans to put lie-flat seats on some of its 737 Max 10s in a push for more premium offerings. The FAA approved the smallest model of the 737 Max family, the Max 7 , in early August. Boeing has been working to ramp up production of its 737 Maxes and 787 Dreamliners, which are key to its recovery since airlines and other customers pay the bulk of the aircraft's price upon delivery. The manufacturer opened a fourth production line in Everett, Washington, in July for its 737 Max airplanes.

What they're saying: Tech analyst Gene Munster of Deepwater Asset Management said he believes there's a 95% chance a deal will take place in the next two years. "Believe me, shareholders would support this," Munster said Tuesday on X after Musk made his comments. Of note: Any combination would be massive: SpaceX has a market cap of more than $2 trillion, while Tesla's is nearly $1.5 trillion. Tesla reports its quarterly results on Wednesday. events.title: Starlink's subscriber growth missed. Its profits didn't.
events.summary: Elon Musk's SpaceX is aiming at Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile. KEVIN LAMARQUE / POOL / AFP via Getty Images Starlink missed on customer growth expectations. It's still making a ton of money for SpaceX. The company is leaning heavily on large customers, like governments. The company acquired a spectrum provider in October. Execs said they're targeting mobile providers. Starlink is SpaceX's big cash cow . And it just reported some mixed results. On Tuesday, during the company's earnings call , SpaceX said its satellite-internet service had 13.6 million consumer subscribers at the end of September, up 1.6 million from three months earlier. That fell short of the 14.2 million expected by Bloomberg analysts — though the company said the figure excludes hundreds of thousands of enterprise subscribers and aviation customers. Still, Starlink is making a lot of money. Monthly consumer revenue per user rose 5% from the previous quarter, while enterprise and government revenue jumped 91% from a year earlier to $2.1 billion. A big, important customer? Airlines. The company said that, as of the end of September, 3,800 total aircraft had been outfitted with Starlink equipment. "Aviation remains a major growth opportunity, as we're still early in the installation phase with many of the largest carriers worldwide," CFO Bret Johnsen said on Tuesday's earnings call. SpaceX's next venture: your phone The company has recently focused on becoming a mobile provider. On October 8, SpaceX announced it had agreed to buy a portfolio of low-band wireless spectrum from Grain Management. The deal gives SpaceX a key ingredient that could turn its Starlink satellite-internet provider into a direct challenger to Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile. SpaceX said the spectrum would power Starlink Mobile , which it has described as a hybrid satellite-and-terrestrial network designed to work indoors, outdoors, and in cellular dead zones. It also comes after SpaceX hinted that it saw itself as a challenger to mobile carriers during its first-ever earnings call in August. The company's president, Gwynne Shotwell, hinted that the company was considering building a "cellular base station on basically the gear that holds the Starlink broadband dish," rather than a ground-based system. They said the market was worth $600 billion annually. "I anticipate us to be able to acquire quite a few of their customers," Shotwell said. During the earnings call, Shotwell said, "The vast majority of mobile connectivity is actually WiFi," an area where Starlink is already well-versed. "Keep in mind, Starlink broadband does a lot of WiFi work as well," she said. "As far as the mix goes, I think we expect that the S-band spectrum will provide the majority. And then obviously, you need the low-band spectrum, the 800 megahertz spectrum, to basically penetrate buildings. So if you're not on WiFi, you can still receive the signal." Musk said that there was probably a need for a longer presentation about their Starlink plans. "I can say we do see a clear path to several hundred billion dollars a year in connectivity revenue," he said. "But I think we should lay — probably describe that in a — in more detail in a forum that's not limited to a few minutes at an earnings call." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.summary: DES MOINES, Iowa — Two more Republicans are calling on President Donald Trump to use a bipartisan law to impose penalties on Russia, joining a growing chorus who disagree with his decision to waive sanctions meant to force Moscow to end its war in Ukraine. “It is my belief that we need to use economic firepower to help drive [Russian President Vladimir] Putin to the table,” Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala., told Semafor in Des Moines today. “I believe that Russia is at the darkest point that they’ve been at in this entire war, and now is the time for us to turn up the pressure.” Britt was campaigning with Senate candidate Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, who expressed similar reservations about Trump’s overtures toward Putin. “I don’t think we need to be making any more deals with Russia,” Hinson said. Trump has said he waived sanctions to keep Russia at the negotiating table . White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said that “enforcing the sanctions provisions now would impede ongoing US efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia.” “The President retains the ability to exercise these authorities at any time if he determines that doing so would advance national interests,” Rogers said. Hinson said she plans to campaign with Trump on Thursday and indicated she may raise the topic of Russia sanctions then. — Burgess Everett and Morgan Chalfant

events.title: Christina Applegate thought she had MS for 5 years. Now she's learned she was misdiagnosed — and her symptoms remain unexplained.
events.summary: Christina Applegate was diagnosed with MS in 2021. She recently learned she was misdiagnosed — and feels like she's "back to square one" with treatment. Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic Christina Applegate recently learned that she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis (MS). Applegate was first diagnosed in 2021 after multiple tests and worsening symptoms. About 15% of MS patients are believed to be misdiagnosed, given how complex the disorder is. After being diagnosed with multiple sclerosis (MS) in 2021, living with severe symptoms, and becoming one of the most famous celebrities with the disorder, Christina Applegate learned some shocking news: She doesn't actually have MS. In an October 20, two-part episode of her podcast "MeSsy" with Jamie Lynn Sigler (another actor diagnosed with MS), Applegate shared that she took over half a year off from recording the podcast to process the news of her MS misdiagnosis. According to Applegate, her doctor framed the revelation as a positive update. "She came into my room and said, 'Congratulations, you don't have MS,'" Applegate said in the podcast. Jamie-Lynn Sigler, Applegate's co-host on the podcast, was diagnosed with relapsing multiple sclerosis when she was filming "The Sopranos." Paula Lobo/American Broadcasting Companies, Inc. via Getty Images But to Applegate, no longer having an explanation for the pain, balance issues, tremors, incontinence, and fatigue she'd been living with for years felt more like being "back at square one." "You don't get misdiagnosed and then all of a sudden, I'm better," she said. "If anything, I've gotten worse, in some ways." Applegate's story is far from a medical anomaly. MS researchers estimate that about 15% of worldwide MS patients are actually misdiagnosed, based on a 2024 meta-analysis of multiple studies. The risks to patients are two-fold, Dr. Marwa Kaisey, an associate professor of neurology at Cedars-Sinai, who also appeared on the podcast, told Business Insider. "One is thinking you have MS — a lot of the medications we use to treat MS have side effects and risks like infections," she said. "The other category is, if you don't know what you have, then you're not getting treated for your actual diagnosis." Kaisey and another researcher shared why MS is so challenging to diagnose — and why more people might end up with Applegate's experience in the future. The race to diagnose a hard-to-diagnose disorder MRIs are important diagnostic tools for diagnosing MS, but researchers say they're just one piece of the puzzle. Paul Biris/Getty Images There is no single blood test that can diagnose MS. Instead, doctors often piece together an MS diagnosis using a neurological exam (testing balance and reflexes), MRI scans, a lumbar puncture (or spinal tap), and possible blood tests to rule out other conditions such as Lyme disease. Sometimes, doctors overrely on a single diagnostic, such as an MRI finding, without performing enough other tests, Dr. Andrew J. Solomon, a professor of neurological sciences at the University of Vermont who co-authored the meta-analysis, told Business Insider. In 2019, Solomon co-authored an MS misdiagnosis study that found that patients who were initially diagnosed with MS were later told they actually had other conditions, such as migraine, radiologically isolated syndrome, spondylopathy, and neuropathy , which can share overlapping symptoms with MS and similar brain scan results. In the podcast, Applegate revealed that she had a nerve test to rule out peripheral neuropathy, as well as MRIs and a lumbar puncture. While her spinal fluid test showed a low level of immune proteins that can support an MS diagnosis, she had nearly 40 brain lesions and worsening symptoms, leading doctors to diagnose her with MS. Solomon said MS should be diagnosed by "confirming each element of our diagnostic criteria and ruling out other things," rather than assuming it must be MS if the MRIs and symptoms fit . The problem is, both physicians and patients are eager to diagnose MS as early as possible, he said. Correctly spotting MS early can lead to better treatment results and a higher likelihood of disability prevention, according to research. Plus, for patients dealing with a plethora of debilitating symptoms , "a period of diagnostic uncertainty is uncomfortable," he said, even though the best course of action is to wait and perform more tests. A new testing protocol revealed Applegate's misdiagnosis Applegate underwent several tests for MS to rule out other conditions. A more in-depth MRI finally identified the misdiagnosis. Kevin Winter/Getty Images In the podcast, Applegate shared that her brain lesions were missing "strings" associated with MS. It's a finding associated with a new, more accurate diagnostic tool for Kaisey, who also co-authored the 2019 study with Solomon, explained on the podcast. The central vein sign (CVS), is an MRI biomarker that can help differentiate MS brain lesions from ones associated with other disorders. It refers to a small vein that appears as a dot or thin line through the center of a brain lesion. CVS was only recently adopted as part of the recommended MS diagnostic criteria, in 2025 — four years after Applegate was first diagnosed with MS. Kaisey told Business Insider that part of her work is expanding education around newer diagnostic tools, noting that not all physicians are using CVS yet. Solomon hopes more doctors will include CVS in their diagnostic protocols, especially for existing MS patients or those who switch providers without being evaluated by their current doctors. "If something doesn't fit, there's an opportunity there to reevaluate if the diagnosis is right," he said. Many misdiagnosed MS patients feel exactly like Applegate does After learning she doesn't have MS, Applegate has felt like she lost clarity and direction when it comes to treatment. Phillip Faraone/Getty Images When it comes to learning about an MS misdiagnosis, Solomon said experiences like Applegate's aren't that uncommon. "I've heard many stories where some doctor was very enthusiastic about telling a patient they actually didn't have MS," he said. "But many of these patients are suffering, and they still have symptoms . So it's not always necessarily a happy thing." For Applegate, her initial MS diagnosis provided clarity and direction. "That was my answer to everything that was going on," Applegate said. Some might relate to Applegate's "square one" feeling, particularly if their doctor was an MS specialist and won't see them anymore, Solomon said. Without a formal diagnosis, they might also worry about insurance coverage for treatments that have provided some relief. There is also the emotional part of having an MS diagnosis. "I leaned into other friends, I leaned into the community," Applegate said. "I had a reason as to why my day sucked every day, and now I don't have a reason." events.title: Trump commits more than $400m ahead of high-stakes midterm elections
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections The president’s Republican Party seeks to maintain its hold over both chambers of Congress, despite declining poll numbers. United States President Donald Trump has announced he plans to spend more than $400m to help Republican candidates win the November 3 midterm elections as his party fights to maintain its grip on Congress. In a post on his Truth Social platform on Tuesday, Trump wrote that much of that total had already been spent on campaign outreach. list 1 of 4 ‘You have to sacrifice’: Trump voters stay loyal as US midterms approach list 2 of 4 Renee Good’s family sues Trump administration over fatal ICE shooting list 3 of 4 Trump launches midterms campaign blitz amid record low approval ratings list 4 of 4 Trump’s approval hits new low among Hispanic voters ahead of midterms “More than 300 Million Dollars has already been spent on Advertising, Direct and Indirect Voter Contact, Rallies, Rally Arenas, Telerallies, Get Out the Vote Programs, Election Integrity, and more,” Trump said. “It is my Great Honor to do so on behalf of the Republican Party, which has done so much to bring our Country back from the Edge of Oblivion.” He added that the November vote was “the Most Important Midterm Elections in our Country’s History”. The president offered no detailed breakdown of the spending, including how much would reach individual races. But the promised influx of spending comes as Trump’s Republican Party faces headwinds ahead of the election, including pushback over the economy and the protracted US-Israeli war against Iran . In the lead-up to the vote, Trump’s approval ratings have tumbled to record lows. A poll this week from the news agency Reuters and the research firm Ipsos found that only 31 percent of Americans approved of Trump’s job performance so far. Some Republicans have sought to distance themselves from the president as a result. Others have pushed for greater support, particularly for close races with Democrats. Questions have swirled over whether Trump and his allies would tap into the war chest amassed by MAGA Inc, the super PAC named for his “Make America Great Again” movement. As a super PAC — or political action committee — MAGA Inc can raise unlimited sums from donors to support or oppose federal candidates. But its spending is legally required to remain independent of their campaigns. Last month, the Campaign Legal Center (CLC), a campaign finance watchdog, accused Trump of violating those rules by claiming control over MAGA Inc’s expenditures. The group cited the president’s public statements, including an exchange with reporters in the Oval Office on September 4, when Trump was asked when the money would start flowing to Republican candidates. He replied that he would spend “whatever amount of money necessary” to help his party. He then added: “This is money from MAGA Inc. This is my money that I control.” According to its latest federal filing, MAGA Inc entered September with $415.8m in cash reserves, making it one of the most consequential financial resources in the Republican campaign arsenal. But Trump has questioned why the super PAC’s hefty outlay has not improved Republican polling in key races, including in Ohio, according to Reuters. Other Trump-aligned groups have also ramped up their political advertising, including two newly formed organisations linked to MAGA Inc, the No Going Back PAC and the Safety and Affordability PAC. The advertisement tracker AdImpact found that the No Going Back PAC contributed $68.7m in political ads last month alone. Another Trump ally, tech entrepreneur Elon Musk, has reportedly spent $366m since last year on Republican campaigns through his group, America PAC, and other Republican and conservative groups. In the final weeks of the midterms, Trump himself has hit the campaign trail, forging ahead with a 32-day campaign blitz . Upcoming stops include South Carolina and Iowa. The stakes of this year’s election are considerable. Control of Congress hangs in the balance. Currently, the Republican Party holds slim majorities in both legislative chambers, but Democrats are seeking to leverage Trump’s declining popularity to flip the Senate and the House of Representatives. If they are successful, they could stymie Trump’s legislative agenda for the final two years of his presidency.

events.title: PSG score late to sink Barcelona 4-2 in Champions League blockbuster
events.summary: Late strikes by Vitinha and Fabian Ruiz grab victory for PSG as they aim to win the Champions League for the third season running. Vitinha’s superb late strike proved crucial as reigning champions Paris Saint-Germain saw off rivals Barcelona 4-2 in a dramatic game between two of the leading contenders to win this season’s Champions League. The match on Tuesday was poised at 2-2 when the Portuguese playmaker, who came third in last year’s Ballon d’Or ranking, controlled on his chest and fired in from just outside the box in the 81st minute at the Parc des Princes. Fabian Ruiz then sealed PSG’s third victory in as many matches in this season’s competition, as they aim to win the Champions League for the third season running. It had briefly looked as though Barcelona would leave the French capital with a point when Lamine Yamal, who is hoping to win this year’s Ballon d’Or, stabbed in Barcelona’s second equaliser on the night. Desire Doue had earlier opened the scoring for PSG, and Lucas Hernandez got their second goal after teenager Xavi Espart found the net for the Catalans. The defeat is a setback for Barcelona, albeit not one that is likely to seriously hurt their prospects of advancing further in Europe’s elite club competition. They had travelled to France on a run of 11 consecutive wins at the start of the season in all competitions. That sequence is now over, but the goals keep coming, and Yamal’s strike here was Barcelona’s 50th of the season all told. PSG, meanwhile, have now won seven games in a row between Ligue 1 and Champions League, but they lost both Ousmane Dembele – last year’s Ballon d’Or winner – and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia to injury on the night. It remains to be seen how seriously hurt those two attackers are, although Doue was the real star of the show here and Luis Enrique’s team are well set to comfortably reach the knockout phase at this rate. This was the 14th meeting of the teams in the Champions League in the last 13 years, and for Barcelona it was probably not their biggest game of the week – beat Real Madrid at home this coming Sunday, and they go nine points ahead of their great rivals in La Liga. That helps explain why Rodri, the 2024 Ballon d’Or winner, was left on the bench at kickoff, although Raphinha was back in the starting lineup after a recent spell out. Fresh from winning 4-2 at Manchester City last week, PSG almost scored inside 90 seconds as Kvaratskhelia hit the post, but they were dealt a blow as Dembele came off after just 20 minutes, pulling up with a hamstring injury. Ferran Torres replaced him, coming on to face the club he left in the summer, who themselves then lost Dani Olmo to injury as the action was interrupted. However, Paris opened the scoring in the 38th minute following an error by Yamal – he gave away possession in his own half, and the ball came to Doue, who showed superb footwork before firing low into the bottom corner from just outside the area. The home side were worthy of their lead at the interval, yet Barcelona drew level soon after half-time as Fermin Lopez released Espart, who drove into the box and fired in his second senior goal. Rodri soon entered the fray for Barca, but the game became increasingly unbridled and Torres hit the post for the hosts just before Hernandez headed them back in front from a corner. The defender was called into the side to mark Yamal in the absence of usual starting left-back Nuno Mendes. The goal was just his third for PSG in more than 100 appearances, and a first since February 2024. That crowned a fine performance for Hernandez, but he was substituted moments later by coach Luis Enrique, and replacement Warren Zaire-Emery was at fault for Barcelona’s second equaliser. He got caught underneath a high ball, allowing Yamal to run away and stab in his 10th goal of the campaign. PSG had the last laugh, though, as they reminded their opponents that they remain the team to beat in Europe this season, with Vitinha making it 3-2 before Ruiz sealed the win from close range.

events.title: US food importer sues Trump over 50 percent tariffs on Canadian goods
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections The lawsuit argues Trump bypassed Congress and misused a century-old law to impose sweeping tariffs on Canadian imports. A US food importer is suing US President Donald Trump over his 50 percent tariffs on Canadian goods, arguing he lacks the legal authority to impose sweeping tariffs without congressional approval. Gellert Global Group, a New Jersey-based company that imports Canadian cheese, filed the lawsuit on Tuesday in the US Court of International Trade in New York. list 1 of 4 US ban on $1bn of Canadian goods takes effect in Trump’s latest retaliation list 2 of 4 Canada to fast track oil pipeline meant to diversify economy away from US list 3 of 4 Alberta rejects separation referendum: What’s next for Canadian province? list 4 of 4 ‘You have to sacrifice’: Trump voters stay loyal as US midterms approach The company says the tariffs are driving up its costs and disrupting its relationships with suppliers on both sides of the border. Between September 16 and October 11, Gellert had paid more than $520,000 in duties, according to the complaint . “Gellert Global Group has spent generations building trusted relationships with suppliers, customers and partners across the food industry,” said Thomas Gellert, the company’s co-chief executive officer, in a press release . “These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain.” The lawsuit challenges Trump’s decision to use a Depression-era law to impose tariffs on a wide range of Canadian products, including dairy products, furniture, clothing and wine. Trump first imposed the 50 percent tariffs over the summer , accusing Canada of discriminating against American-made cars, alcohol and dairy products. He expanded the measures in September, adding more products in response to Canadian retaliatory tariffs . The lawsuit argues that the law doesn’t apply to the Canadian policies the Trump administration says are discriminatory, since two of them “arose in response to the president’s own tariffs, while the third involves Canadian dairy policy governed by the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA)”. It also questions why Canadian cheese is being taxed over disputes involving alcohol and cars. “No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required,” said Sara Albrecht, chairman and CEO of the Liberty Justice Center, a nonprofit legal organisation that filed the suit on Gellert’s behalf. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment, according to the Reuters news agency. At the centre of the case is Section 338 of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930, which allows the president to impose tariffs of up to 50 percent on imports from countries found to discriminate against American businesses. The provision had never been used until Trump invoked it this year. The lawsuit argues that newer laws passed by Congress since then, such as Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, require investigations, public comment and other safeguards that Gellert says the Trump administration has bypassed, and that these override Section 338. “The administration cannot skip those protections by reaching for a 1930 statute that no president had ever used to impose a tariff,” said Jeffrey Schwab, the Liberty Justice Center’s senior counsel and director of litigation. In addition, the lawsuit says that even if Trump is allowed to use the older law, he hasn’t met its requirements, including waiting 30 days before tariffs can be collected on new products added to the list. The administration only waited seven days to start collecting tariffs on cheese in September, according to the lawsuit. Gellert is asking the court to declare the tariffs illegal, stop them from being collected, and order refunds with interest for importers who have been impacted. The lawsuit marks the fourth major legal challenge to Trump’s tariffs. In February, the US Supreme Court struck down most of the tariffs he imposed in 2025, and a trade court later ruled against a temporary 10 percent global tariff.
