events.title: Dow leads Wall Street higher, investors focus on health care stocks
events.summary: Traders working on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, on Oct 19 in New York City. The Dow led Wall Street higher as investors moved into healthcare and other value stocks. The S&P 500 rose 0.31% and the Nasdaq slipped 0.03%. Healthcare hit a record high, helped by Eli Lilly, UnitedHealth, Merck, Johnson & Johnson and Amgen. Moderna also reached its highest level since 2022. Tech paused after a rebound, as investors stayed wary about AI spending and profits. Earnings from SpaceX, Netflix, Meta and Tesla were next in focus. NEW YORK - The Dow led Wall Street higher on Oct 20 as investors focused on value stocks such as healthcare, while technology lagged after rebounding a day earlier. Healthcare led gains among the S&P 500’s 11 major sector indexes, hitting a record high on Oct 20. Eli Lilly boosted the benchmark index along with Dow components UnitedHealth, Merck & Co, Johnson & Johnson and Amgen. Vaccine company Moderna hit its highest level since 2022. Defensive sectors such as real estate and utilities were also outperforming, along with the small-cap Russell 2000 index. Declines in megacap stocks pulled the communication services sector down while energy shares underperformed as oil prices dipped after touching a five-month high. Oil traders were weighing a meeting between the Iranian president and Pakistan’s army chief, a key US-Iran mediator, against Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and reports of vessel attacks in the Gulf. Trading was muted in the heavyweight technology sector, which had rebounded on Oct 19 from a selloff last week. Technology investors have been worried about steep spending and financing costs for AI developments. “Equity investors are still a little sceptical around the AI trade and the ability for some of these companies to monetise their investments, so you’re seeing a bit of a rotation into other areas of the market,” said Jim Baird, chief investment officer at Plante Moran Financial Advisors, pointing to advances on Oct 20 in small caps and sectors including healthcare. “Investors are looking for other opportunities outside of tech, and healthcare is one of the beneficiaries of that,” he said. According to preliminary data, the S&P 500 gained 23.79 points, or 0.31%, to end at 7,714.52 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 9.05 points, or 0.03%, to 26,421.84. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 547.95 points, or 1.05%, to 52,513.98. The S&P 500 value index was outperforming its growth counterpart on the day. Investors were looking ahead to earnings reports from SpaceX and Netflix, due after the market close. Meta and Tesla are scheduled to report on Oct 21. Meta and Netflix shares were among the weakest stocks in communication services on Oct 20, along with Alphabet. General Motors shares dropped after the automaker signalled pressure in coming months from higher commodity costs and lower truck sales. 3M rose after the company said it was expanding its data-centre partnership with Amazon and issued a warrant to an Amazon subsidiary to purchase 3M common stock worth over US$521 million (S$665 million). The industrial conglomerate also raised its full-year profit forecast. Credit reporting firm Equifax rallied after it reported third-quarter profit above analysts’ estimates.

events.title: Why do the US midterms matter for Trump and Congress?
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections Republicans and Democrats jockey for control of Congress, which will set course for Trump’s final two years in office. The United States midterms on November 3 are dominating national and international headlines. The stakes of the election are high. The midterm race will determine which party controls the US Congress, and in turn, shape the direction of Trump’s final two years in office. It will also decide key state and local positions. list 1 of 3 Trump faces bipartisan backlash over Russia sanctions waiver list 2 of 3 There is no split in MAGA list 3 of 3 ‘No Kings’ protests spread across the US ahead of midterm elections But notching big wins in the midterm election may not be enough to shake up the balance of power in Washington, DC. To understand the implications of this year’s midterm election and what may come next, Al Jazeera has put together this simple primer. Here’s why the US midterms matter at the federal level. Battle for the US House of Representatives and US Senate Midterm elections fall at the halfway point of a president’s term, meaning the executive office will not be on the ballot. Front and centre will be the battle for control of Congress. Two chambers make up the US legislature: the House of Representatives and the Senate. Because members of the House serve two-year terms, all 435 seats in the chamber are up for election on November 3. However, most races are already considered formalities, with a clear frontrunner. That leaves only a handful of races — about 50 — to decide who will win the House majority. While subject to change, nearly every reputable election prognosticator has predicted that Democrats will win control of the House, some by as many as 15 seats. The Democrats have a slimmer chance of winning a majority in the Senate, however. That chamber has only 100 seats. But because senators have staggered six-year terms, only 35 seats are up for election. Only about a dozen of those races are considered competitive. Still, Democrats have seen their odds of seizing the Senate increase, as the number of competitive races has grown. Left-wing candidates have made inroads in deep-red states like Texas and Kansas, creating more opportunities for the Democratic Party to claim a Senate majority this election cycle. Because the US vice president breaks ties in the Senate, Democrats would need 51 seats to control the chamber. Congress passes laws and approves federal budgets. But even if a party secures a majority in both chambers of Congress, it may not be enough to control the country’s legislative agenda. Laws can pass by a simple majority in the House, but they typically need a supermajority of 60 votes in the Senate to overcome a process known as the filibuster . That process can allow a minority group to stall legislation indefinitely, barring a supermajority. Therefore, unless a party wins more than 60 seats in the Senate, most legislation will still require at least some level of bipartisan support to pass. Even if legislation passes both chambers, the president can veto any bill that comes across his desk. Overriding a presidential veto requires a two-thirds supermajority in both the House and the Senate. Achieving the broad bipartisan support needed to overcome a presidential veto is exceedingly rare. The last time it happened was in January 2021, during Trump’s first term. At the time, the US president had lost the 2020 election, and he saw his support from Republican lawmakers dissipate when he attempted to veto a defence spending bill. Still, there are instances when bipartisan support overcomes presidential objections. A bill to increase the housing supply passed both the House and Senate with veto-proof majorities earlier this year, despite Trump’s stated opposition . So what happens if Republicans maintain control of Congress? Republicans currently hold two majorities in Congress, with 53 seats in the Senate and 218 in the House. With Trump in the White House, that means the party has held a so-called government “ trifecta ” over the last two years, with three levers of power under its command. The Republican majorities in Congress have helped Trump pass some of his signature legislation, including surging funding to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and cleaving back some forms of publicly funded healthcare as part of a sweeping 2025 tax bill. But Republicans’ numbers have not been enough to pass Trump’s entire legislative wishlist. Notably, he has been unable to pass his signature federal voter identification law, dubbed the “ SAVE America Act “, amid Democratic opposition. There have also been a handful of issues where Republicans have defied Trump, particularly on tariffs . A few Republicans have also voted to assert congressional authority over the US-Israel war with Iran.

events.title: It’s a bird, it’s a plane … it’s a robo-puffin?
events.summary: MIT engineers’ design for a robot that both swims and flies could lead to a new class of vehicles for ocean exploration. Given that water is 1,000 times denser than air, moving through those two mediums requires very different mechanics—or so one might assume. Yet birds like gulls and puffins can plunge into the sea, swim underwater, and leap back into the air to fly away. And now engineers at MIT and EPFL in Lausanne, Switzerland, have designed a robot that can do likewise. The “flapping-wing aerial-aquatic vehicle,” or FAAV, weighs less than 300 grams (about half a pound) and is equipped with a central fuselage, two flexible wings, and a steerable tail. The body contains a battery and a waterproof electric motor that drives a crankshaft, which pumps the wings up and down at preset frequencies. The wings are made of thin membranes that are coated with hydrophobic nanoparticles to help wick away water. And the tail is motorized, enabling it to change its angle to help the robot fly up or dive down. In experiments carried out in a water tank and at Lake Geneva, a team led by Raphael Zufferey, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at MIT, identified combinations of wing size, flapping frequency, and tail angle that enable the robot to smoothly transition from swimming to flying. The best results came with medium-size wings that were flexible enough to minimize flapping amplitude in water and also firm enough to keep the robot aloft in the air. The speeds and flapping frequencies were similar to those used by actual birds, and a pitch of 70 degrees—a relatively steep angle—allowed the robot to make the leap from water to air. Interestingly, although many diving birds paddle their feet to help them take off from the water’s surface, the team found that the bot didn’t need feet at all. The engineers’ results could help pave the way for a new class of drones and vehicles that could fly to and sample from aquatic regions too dangerous for traditional vessels to access. “Our dream vision is for oceanographers, marine biologists, and members of coastal communities to launch this robot from a boat, or from shore, and it would fly close to the area of interest, such as an iceberg or a port facility, or over a pod of whales,” says Zufferey. “It would dive into the water to take a measurement or collect a sample, and fly back to deliver the data at a fraction of the cost of traditional methods. Then it could go back out to dive for more.” The researchers are now trying to design wings that can turn as well as flap. They will also test the robot’s performance under turbulent conditions, such as swimming in choppy waters and flying through wind. Then they hope to deploy the vehicle to help answer questions in ocean science. “One of the major challenges in ocean science is collecting data both frequently and across many locations, which is something this robot could do in the future,” Zufferey says. “You could send this out not just every week, but every hour. It could fly out at high speeds, dive in, fly back, deliver its data, and go back out, multiple times.” This story was part of our November/December 2026 issue. events.title: Here’s the tea
events.summary: An MIT historian uncovers the true origins of an artifact once thought to be a relic of the Boston Tea Party. When Tristan Brown, an associate professor of history at MIT, first examined a Chinese tea chest label displayed at Old South Meeting House, he had no reason to doubt its story. Descendants of the Boston blacksmith Thomas Wells had donated the label in 1987, saying it had been recovered after colonial protesters threw tea into Boston Harbor in 1773. But after a year of research, Brown reached a different conclusion: The label was made nearly a century later. The decisive clue came when he read the Chinese text in Cantonese rather than Mandarin, as previous scholars had done. He found that the characters had been used phonetically, in slightly variant forms across contemporary sources, to represent the name of Smith, Archer & Co., a US firm that acquired Asian tea for shipment to American markets during the 1860s and 1870s. Working with the Wells family, he traced the label to a relative who traveled from Michigan to California during the Gold Rush era before returning and operating a business known as the California Tea Store. Brown argues that claims for its revolutionary pedigree probably developed later, amid the centennial commemorations of the 1870s. The discovery does not make the label historically insignificant, he says. Instead, what began as an inquiry into a supposed artifact of the Boston Tea Party became a study of how ordinary objects acquire historical authority, and how historical memory itself is made. “History is never finished,” he says. “Even objects that have sat in museums for decades can reveal entirely new stories when we ask new questions.” This story was part of our November/December 2026 issue. events.title: Melt it, spin it, use it again
events.summary: A plastic-based recyclable yarn is as strong and stretchy as spandex. The average American throws out around 81 pounds of clothing each year, and there are few options for recycling it. MIT engineers hope to cut down on that textile waste with a new type of yarn. The thermoplastic yarn mimics the properties of conventional elastic yarns, which typically combine spandex with polyester or nylon. Those fibers would have to be separated for recycling—a process that isn’t practical. But the MIT team found a way to create a similarly stretchy yarn from two variations of polyethylene, a material commonly used in milk jugs and grocery bags. Because they come from the same chemical family, the yarn can be melted as is. Svetlana Boriskina, who led the work as a research scientist in the Department of Mechanical Engineering, says a garment made from this material could then be spun into new yarn for a next generation of clothing. Even after 10 cycles of melting and respinning, the yarn stays as strong and flexible as conventional thread. “Now we have something that can be knitted and woven,” Boriskina says. “That is the next stage.” Someday, the researchers hope, a polyethylene garment could be dropped in a collection bin and sent to a recycling facility, promoting a more sustainable, circular textile economy. events.title: A reason to eat carbs
events.summary: MIT researchers have found that a ketogenic diet may fuel the growth of some intestinal tumors. A high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet can help some people lose weight, and some research has shown that it may protect against colon cancer. But a new study suggests that such a ketogenic diet may also increase the risk of cancer in the small intestine. This type of diet forces the body to burn fatty acids instead of carbohydrates for fuel, producing by-products called ketone bodies. One of these, BHB, was thought to be responsible for the protective effect observed against colon cancer. Omer Yilmaz, director of the MIT Stem Cell Initiative, worked with colleagues including MIT postdocs Jessica Shay and Fangtao Chi to investigate whether the effects were similar in the small intestine. But instead, they found that mice on a ketogenic diet were more likely to develop tumors in that part of the gastrointestinal system than those on a control diet were. Additional studies revealed that this tumor growth was driven by the way intestinal cells burn dietary fat for energy—a metabolic pathway called fatty acid oxidation. This pathway activates proteins that signal stem cells to multiply more rapidly. “Having more stem cells means that when you injure the small intestine, it can repair itself better, but the downside is that having more active stem cells can lead to tumor formation,” Yilmaz says. Though the researchers confirmed that a ketogenic diet suppressed the development of colon tumors, their findings suggest that ketone bodies are not involved. “These molecules are essentially metabolic bystanders,” Yilmaz says. One implication is that commercial ketone supplements probably do little to either help or harm people who take them. But the deeper issue is “why the same diet has opposite consequences in two adjacent parts of the gut,” Chi says. “That is what we are working to understand next.” Whatever they discover, as Yilmaz says, “the message here is that we need to be very careful in generalizing the effects that these diets can have.” This story was part of our November/December 2026 issue. events.title: Robotic therapy for stroke patients
events.summary: An adaptive physical rehab system uses generative AI to learn from physical therapists and offer personalized support. Strokes leave 5 million people with long-term impairments each year, and a growing shortage of physical therapists makes it hard for them to get the care they need. A new approach tries to solve that problem by combining artificial intelligence and human therapy. Johannes Lachner, a former MIT postdoc who is now an assistant professor at Purdue University, and Noah Geiger, a former visiting student at MIT, developed a robotic system that uses generative AI and real-time force feedback to learn from real therapists. Drawing on what it’s learned, it gives patients just the right amount of assistance during physical rehabilitation exercises like reaching, lifting their arms, and performing tasks of daily living. The goal is “not to replace therapists, but to extend their reach,” Lachner says. “Initial robotic experiments have already demonstrated the feasibility of this approach,” he reports. “The next phase of the project aims to develop therapist-specific models and evaluate them in a long-term clinical study with the same patients who previously received manual therapy.” Beyond that, he envisions possible applications in contact-rich industrial settings or collaborative workspaces. events.title: Taking a swing at a pickleball startup
events.summary: In corporate America, Stanley Anderson ’79 says, executives often assume that their peers grew up in privileged circumstances. “I spent my early years trying not to get recruited into gangs, getting shot at, watching my friends get murdered, and thinking that if I don’t leave, I will die,” says Anderson, who was raised in Chicago. “I was fortunate to survive.” But he thrived, building an impressive career at the likes of HP, Intel, and the Palo Alto Research Center. Now he is applying his management expertise as CEO of Costa Pickleball, a Las Vegas–based startup that sells high-performance paddles in decorative designs. Beyond giving customers a way to, as he says, “bring their identity to the court,” he is also betting on technology: He’s developing a quieter type of paddle he expects will provide a competitive advantage. Succeeding in today’s pickleball market will be tough, but Anderson thinks he has what it takes, partly thanks to an important lesson he learned at MIT: “There’s nothing you can’t accomplish if you are willing to put effort into it.” This story was part of our November/December 2026 issue. events.title: A good TA: priceless
events.summary: These are images of quizzes I took in 3.091, Introduction to Solid-State Chemistry, in the fall of 1980. One is my very first exam at MIT, and getting 49 out of 100 was a soul-crushing experience. I can still picture the TA, Leszek Pawlowicz, PhD ’87, returning my paper. He had a big smile on his face, and he said something to the effect of “I expect to see you double your score on the next quiz!” Well, I got the message. Studying at MIT was not like studying in high school, but I got 100 on the next quiz and graduated with good enough grades to get me into grad school. All it took, it seems, was that initial kick in the seat of my pants, then a kind hand helping me up off the ground. Recently, I connected with Leszek, and he replied with a charming note. It felt good to let him know how much his encouragement meant to me. A good TA can really have lasting impact! This story was part of our November/December 2026 issue. events.title: Nebraska native explores galaxies far, far away
events.summary: Growing up on a small farm in Nebraska, Megan Donahue ’85 discovered the wider world by reading her way through her local library. Today, she is learning how the wider universe works by studying galaxy clusters. Donahue discovered her passion for physics in that library at age 12 and started her path into astronomy thanks to “a providential interaction.” Through MIT’s Undergraduate Research Opportunities Program, she got introduced to cutting-edge x-ray imaging—work she found “really cool.” Now a professor of physics and astronomy at Michigan State University, she researches galaxy clusters and baryonic matter (matter made of protons and neutrons, as opposed to dark matter) in an effort to learn more about the composition of the universe and its evolution. “Clusters of galaxies are very large scoops of the universe,” says Donahue, who served as president of the American Astronomical Society from 2018 to 2020. “It’s like taking a sample from the ocean. If you’re trying to find out the average composition of the ocean’s water, you’d want to study as big a scoop as possible.” This story was part of our November/December 2026 issue. events.title: A champion for brain injury patients
events.summary: Alissa Totman ’13 was a sophomore when she joined MIT BrainTrust, a student-run organization that connects Institute undergraduates and people with brain injuries for support and socializing. “That group was a great way to learn about the human experience of what people go through when they experience a brain injury,” she says. And it laid the foundation for her life’s work. Today, Totman is a physician specializing in brain injury medicine at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, where she treats adults with head trauma, stroke, brain tumors, and more. She is also the founder of Synapse, a nonprofit focused on providing support for such individuals. The organization grew out of a group she started with Jaclyn Konopka ’14 during medical school at Stanford, and Totman launched it as a national service organization in 2016, while pursuing her master’s degree in public health at Harvard. There are now chapters at 28 universities across the country—and Totman still runs the organization. “There’s a big need for more resources like this,” she says. events.title: A cleaner path to rare earth metals
events.summary: Tomás Villalón Jr. ’14 was raised in San Antonio, Texas, but vividly remembers smog hanging over the city his family came from—Monterrey, Mexico, a steel manufacturing and metal fabrication hub. Even as a child, he realized it was problematic to breathe that air. “I’m motivated because I’ve seen what metal-making does,” says Villalón, who majored in materials science and engineering. He started thinking about sustainable metallurgy senior year while working at Boston Metal, an MIT spinoff focused on decarbonizing steelmaking. In 2019 he cofounded Phoenix Tailings, which has developed an efficient process for extracting rare earth metals from mining waste. “The mining ecosystem by itself makes over several billion tons of waste,” says Villalón, who serves as chief technology officer. (Others on the founding team are Michelle Chao ’17, Nick Myers, and Anthony Balladon.) “We have to get rid of this pollution.” The company asserts that its proprietary electrochemical technique for processing rare earths generates no toxins and is carbon-free when fueled by renewables. events.title: Netflix posts higher Q3 profit but revenue growth worries pull shares lower
events.summary: Netflix, which announced layoff plans last week, posted a third-quarter profit above Wall Street’s expectations Netflix, which announced layoff plans last week, posted a third-quarter profit above Wall Street's expectations, but investors sent shares down after the streaming company lowered its ad sales guidance, prompting worries about slowing revenue growth. Netflix said Tuesday it earned $3.66 billion, or 87 cents per share, for the July-September period. That's up 44% from $2.55 billion, or 59 cents per share, a year earlier. Revenue rose 12% to $12.87 billion from $11.51 billion. Analysts surveyed by FactSet predicted earnings of 82 cents per share on revenue of $12.87 billion. “With Netflix under pressure to find alternative lines of revenue beyond subscriptions, it’s concerning that the company lowered its estimate for its ad business,” said Emarketer senior analyst Ross Benes. "Revamping content strategy is not enough to fix this challenge but it is a worthwhile start. Guidance is not as aggressive as investors have grown accustomed to.” Last week, the Los Gatos, California-based company announced that it plans to lay off about 6% of its workforce, amounting to nearly 1,000 positions, as the company makes wider “organizational changes.” At the end of 2025, per regulatory filings, Netflix had about 16,000 full-time employees worldwide. The most recent layoff announcement marks the biggest round of cuts that the company has rolled out in years. Bajaria was with Netflix for nearly a decade. Rice will lead Netflix’s global content organization, overseeing scripted and unscripted series, film, live events and more across all regions. He takes over the post on Oct. 26. While Netflix has benefited from membership signups and price increases, the company is dealing with intense competition in the streaming sector from companies such as Amazon’s Prime Video and Disney+. There's also Skydance , after Paramount’s $81 billion buyout of Warner Bros. Discovery put HBO Max and Paramount+ under the same roof. Netflix walked away from its offer to buy Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming business in February. As of Tuesday's close, Netflix's stock is down about 25% for the year to date. Analysts see several factors contributing to its difficulties. “Investors are concerned about soft engagement trends, decelerating revenue growth, a slower margin expansion outlook, and most recently content executive leadership changes,” said John Belton, portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds. events.title: Audit regulator looking into Manchester City accounting
events.summary: The UK audit regulator has confirmed it is leading inquiries into accounting irregularities at Manchester City. The Financial Reporting Council confirmed in a letter to the House of Commons business select committee it had taken over "regulatory consideration" of the case from the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales on 30 September. No formal investigation has started, but the FRC is making inquiries into the case. It comes after Manchester City were found guilty by an independent commission of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, including by artificially inflating the club's financial position by more than £900m. City are appealing the verdict. The FRC has greater resources, and greater powers, to apply sanctions if it does find evidence of violations. It routinely oversees accounting standards at bigger institutions such as listed public companies, but not football clubs. The FRC can look into the conduct of BDO, Manchester City's auditors, to ask whether the audit was in line with the rules. It can also apply sanctions to individuals such as directors or employees of the Etihad club, if they are members of professional accountancy bodies. BDO is the UK's fifth-biggest accounting firm, but claims to be a market leader in football, advising more Premier League and Championship clubs than any other firm. The independent commission which looked into Manchester City found that the club gave a "misleading impression" of the scheme used to disguise the origin of shareholder funds injected into the club to its auditors, who were "unaware" of the scheme. Manchester City have said they will appeal against the commission's decision, arguing that it contains "material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe". Liam Byrne, chair of the business select committee, called for greater powers for the FRC to look into similar cases. He wrote on X: "The regulator's letter exposes gaps in its ability to compel evidence from the club and pursue directors who fall outside its disciplinary rules. "This raises serious questions about the powers available to hold companies and directors to account. "The government has a responsibility to explain why reforms to close these gaps were abandoned - and what will now be done to strengthen accountability." events.title: Netflix shares sink on earnings after a dramatic content executive shake-up
events.summary: Netflix hired Peter Rice as its new content chief as co-CEO Ted Sarandos tries to boost growth. Frank Micelotta/Tubi via Getty Images; Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images; Chris Pizzello/AP Netflix shares sank up to 6% after a Q3 earnings beat and weak guidance for the rest of the year. Shares had fallen about 44% in the last year as investors worry about slowing growth. The streaming leader laid off about 1,000 employees last week and changed its content leadership. Netflix's third-quarter earnings failed to excite investors, a week after a major content executive shuffle and its biggest round of layoffs since 2022. The streamer turned in results above expectations for the third quarter, but provided weak guidance for the rest of the year. Netflix said its earnings beat was primarily due to the timing of expenses. Netflix's revenue growth slowed for a third straight quarter, and the company projected it would continue to decelerate in the fourth quarter. Shares fell up to 6% in after-hours trading on Tuesday. "While Netflix is growing, the pace of that growth is slowing," Forrester's Mike Proulx said. "That's a wake-up call for the company that once defined the streaming market and is now in need of growth reacceleration." Here's how the streaming giant's Q3 financial results compared to the company's forecast: Revenue: $12.87 billion vs $12.86 billion estimated ($11.5 billion in Q3 2025) Earnings: $0.87 per share vs $0.82 per share estimated ($0.59 per share in Q3 2025) Netflix told investors to expect earnings of $0.67 per share in the fourth quarter, below Wall Street's $0.73 per share estimate. The company's $13.44 billion revenue projection for Q4 was also lower than analysts' estimate of $13.51 billion. The streaming leader cut its annual advertising forecast from $3 billion to $2.7 billion, citing a slower-than-expected rollout of its ad products. "With Netflix under pressure to find alternative lines of revenue beyond subscriptions, it's concerning that the company lowered its estimate for its ad business," said analyst Ross Benes of Emarketer, Business Insider's sister company. Heading into Q3 earnings, Netflix's stock was down over 44% in the last year as investors worried about engagement growth and stiff competition from YouTube and other free streamers. Netflix said in its third-quarter shareholder letter that it knows "there's some investor concern about our view hours growth" but added that engagement "remains healthy." "We do seek to accelerate growth in view hours as well, and we're confident we'll do that by relentlessly focusing and executing" its strategy, the shareholder letter said. The company has invested in video games and podcasts but didn't mention either in its letter, outside a disclosure section on "forward-looking statements." Netflix's results came less than a week after it shook up its content leadership team and cut about 1,000 workers . Content chief Bela Bajaria is leaving her role after more than three years, Netflix announced last week. The company said Monday that film chief Dan Lin is also out. Bajaria will be replaced by Peter Rice, a former Fox and Disney exec who ran Disney's TV division, including ABC and FX. Netflix hasn't yet said who will replace Lin; Rice will oversee film in the meantime. "It's our goal to go from very good to great," co-CEO Greg Peters said of Netflix's content slate on the company's earnings call. The leadership changes come as Netflix battles slowing viewership growth. The streaming powerhouse generated 97 billion viewing hours in the first half of the year, which was up 2% year-over-year. Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos said at an industry event hosted by Bloomberg last month that Netflix was "not growing as fast as I want us to, and we're working on making that move faster." "Revamping content strategy is not enough to fix this challenge, but it is a worthwhile start," Benes said. Netflix layoffs were across its product, tech, HR, and legal teams. Co-CEOs Sarandos and Peters said in a memo to staffers that the company was downsizing so it can be "disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources." Other media companies have laid off employees in the last month. NBCUniversal cut a few hundred global streaming tech employees in early October, and Disney trimmed its tech and HR teams in late September. In the second quarter, Netflix's results were roughly in line with analysts' expectations. The stock sank 8% after the report as Netflix said it would cut back on how frequently it shared viewership data. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Instacart settles federal claims of discrimination against US-born job seekers
events.summary: The federal government has reached a $5 million settlement with Instacart for allegedly discriminating against U.S.-born workers in its hiring practices The federal government has reached a $5 million settlement with Instacart for allegedly discriminating against U.S.-born workers in its hiring practices. According to the U.S. Department of Justice Civil Rights Division and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, Instacart was advertising jobs through the Permanent Labor Certification, or PERM, program. The program lets employers hire temporary visa holders and sponsor them for permanent resident status as long as they have also made a good-faith effort to hire U.S. workers. The agencies said Instacart created a burden for U.S. workers by requiring that applications be physically mailed to the company for jobs that were listed as part of its PERM recruitment program. Instacart allows electronic applications for its standard job recruitment process. San Francisco-based Instacart said Tuesday that its hiring practices complied with U.S. laws and regulations, but it agreed to the settlement in order to remain focused on its business. “We’re proud to be a U.S.-based grocery technology platform, employing thousands of American workers and serving millions of customers, retailers, shoppers and brands,” the company said. “Hiring and investing in American workers across our U.S. business is our priority, and we actively promote every role across many channels to ensure qualified U.S. candidates are always first in line for opportunities.” Instacart is the latest tech company to reach a settlement with the government over allegations that it favors foreign workers for certain jobs. Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say 'United in grief': 4 dead, 39 injured in explosion at Canadian military training base DOJ official clashes with judge in DC golf course case after Trump attacks her In 2023, Apple agreed to a $25 million settlement after federal regulators said its hiring practices discriminated against U.S. candidates for jobs that went to immigrant workers seeking permanent resident status in the country. Facebook agreed to pay $14 million in 2021 to settle claims about its hiring practices. “Our record demonstrates that the Justice Department is holding companies who prefer workers with temporary employment visas accountable," Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon said in a statement. "We will not stop fighting for U.S. workers until there is a fair playing field.” The settlement requires Instacart to establish a fund of up to $4 million to compensate job applicants and people who were allegedly deterred from applying to Instacart between December 2023 and February 2026. Instacart will pay $1 million in civil penalties to the federal government. The company is also required to post jobs that are part of its PERM recruitment program on its public career website and accept electronic applications. events.title: SpaceX’s AI business is beating expectations
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. SpaceX’s data centers and Grok agents were more profitable than investors expected in third quarter of the year, as the company leaves its roots as a space company behind to focus on artificial intelligence, which now makes up 52% of its income. CEO Elon Musk’s deep tech conglomerate reported $14.6 billion in third-quarter revenue on Tuesday, according to its regulatory filing . That number was driven by growth in all segments, but especially its renamed “Super Intelligence” business line, which generated $7.5 billion in revenue from the recently acquired Cursor coding tool, Grok bot, and most importantly, the company’s burgeoning neocloud business, which now boasts 1.7 GW of compute. The AI business generated $431 million in profit, which would have been higher without $1.2 billion in one-time stock-based compensation expenses related to the Cursor acquisition. The top-line revenue number was also boosted by about $1 billion in income related to the recovery of Bitcoin prices and unspecified related-party income that might be attributed to a SpaceX investment in another company. The growing revenue is balanced against total capital expenditures of $19.6 billion, as SpaceX continues to build out a second data center project, Colossus II, and increase investment in Starship, the heavy-lift rocket it sees as vital to deploying a new generation of Starlink satellites and developing orbital data centers. CFO Bret Johnsen said the company would spend $35 billion to $40 billion on new capital investments in the fourth quarter. During a live-streamed discussion of the results with investors, Musk said he was spending four days a week in Memphis, Tennessee, the site of Colossus II, working to bring the data center online. “People are starting to realize [that] the constraint on deployment of of super intelligence is more in power and cooling and infrastructure than it is in chips,” Musk argued, saying that he had tasked a team of SpaceX engineers to solve that problem. “This is a bit like the New York Yankees playing in Little League. It’s not fair, but the net result is being able to deploy power cooling infrastructure at a rate that is vastly faster than any anyone else.” In one example, Musk noted that manufacturers of turbines to power data centers are facing 12 to 18 month delays in obtaining the metals blades and vanes required for those machines. Now, SpaceX is using the metal casting capabilities developed for SpaceX to make those components and obtain turbines more quickly. Musk also said that the next test flight of the Starship rocket, expected in November, would see SpaceX attempt to recover both the first-stage booster and the second stage. Recovering both segments of the vehicle would be a “massive technology milestone,” Musk said, but the true milestone will be reflying both stages. SpaceX also saw growth in subscribers to its Starlink space internet network, reaching 13.6 million consumers, with Musk predicting that the growth of AI agents would lead to more demand for connectivity. Despite of those capital expenditures, the company’s revenue boost was substantial enough to push it back into profitability. SpaceX reported net income of $4.4 billion, a turnaround from the $1 billion loss in the same quarter last year. It will still have some catching up to do if it wants to remain profitable for the year, however. In the first nine months of the year, SpaceX still had a net income loss of $413 million. Musk took a particularly bullish stance on the company’s Super Intelligence business segment, predicting that SpaceX’s annual recurring revenue by the end of 2027 will be “somewhere between $500 billion and $1 trillion.” More concretely, Johnsen forecast total revenue for the first quarter of 2027 in the range of $33 billion to $37 billion. events.title: Foursquare cofounder says acquisition gave $0 to equity holders, leaving him 'heartbroken'
events.summary: Foursquare cofounder Dennis Crowley wrote that "watching the company slowly decay has been a grind on my soul." Bloomberg/Getty Images Foursquare cofounder Dennis Crowley said the company's acquisition paid $0 to equity holders. "I am sorry the Foursquare story ended in such a way," he wrote to employees. Crowley said the company decayed after a private equity investment. Foursquare's acquisition left its cofounder sad and angry. Dennis Crowley helped launch the location technology company in 2009. Seventeen years later, Foursquare was acquired by Infillion. Crowley wrote on Substack that one point of the acquisition left him "heartbroken." Foursquare's acquisition earned equity holders exactly $0, Crowley wrote, with no money offered for preferred or common stock. "To our ~1600 former employees over 17 years, I am sorry the Foursquare story ended in such a way that makes it seem like our collective efforts were worth… nothing?" Crowley wrote. Crowley left the CEO role in 2016, though he continued to lead Foursquare's research and development lab through 2021. After that, Crowley kept a seat on the board. Foursquare raised capital from The Raine Group , a private equity firm, in 2019. Less than two years later, Gary Little became CEO. Little was one of The Raine Group's managing directors. "Leadership was unable to preserve the value it inherited or create new value during those six years," Crowley wrote. Foursquare employees reached out to Crowley to express their frustrations with leadership, he wrote. He cited the company's Glassdoor reviews , which rate it 2.1 stars out of 5. The Raine Group did not respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Crowley also wrote that the $0 equity outcome was buried in a 125-page PDF for Foursquare's legal team. "No single individual stood up to own (or even acknowledge) the outcome," he wrote. Calynn Krieger, an executive vice president of marketing for Infillion , told Business Insider in an email that Foursquare had "remarkable technology and a talented team." "We have nothing to say about Foursquare's former leadership, but we're glad the business and its value continue, and we're committed to creating even more of it," Krieger said. The lesson Crowley learned Crowley took responsibility for his role in the lead-up to Foursquare's $0 outcome for equity holders. His decisions as CEO led to the need for a private equity investment, Crowley wrote, and he said he wished he were louder on the board. His takeaway: "Maybe the biggest mistake I've made in my career is falling in love with this company." Crowley was too loyal to "making it work," he wrote, and stayed longer than he should have. "Watching the company slowly decay has been a grind on my soul," he wrote. In a footnote, Crowley gave founders a piece of advice . "It's okay to fall in love with the company you're building, but don't deny yourself the ability to get closure and move on just because the company itself hasn't yet experienced an exit or ending," he wrote. events.title: Prediction-market odds rise for Marine Le Pen in France 2027 presidential race as protests roil nation
events.summary: Protests over poor schooling conditions and the cost of living have been roiling France since September. Kalshi traders see a greater likelihood that far-right candidate Marine Le Pen will win France’s 2027 presidential election. Odds have surged to 53% from 39% in the past month. As protests intensify in France, Kalshi traders see a growing likelihood that far-right candidate Marine Le Pen will win that country's presidential race in 2027. Student-led protests first erupted in Paris over frustration with school conditions and teacher shortages in September but rippled into national outrage over the country's living costs and public services, including in education and healthcare. Authorities said over 500,000 people demonstrated nationwide over the weekend. Since the protests have started, Kalshi trading activity over who will be the next French president has jumped on Kalshi. Odds for far-right candidate Marine Le Pen have jumped to 53% from 39% in the last month. Just days after the protests began, speculators placed a 44.7% chance on Sept. 26 that David Lisnard, the current mayor of Cannes, would become the country's next president. Those odds came in just a day after he held a major campaign rally for the presidential race. Lisnard's Kalshi odds of winning the 2027 presidential contest dropped to 11% by Tuesday afternoon. The contract asks "Next French presidential election winner?" and will be verified by French government next year. Le Pen has repeatedly criticized the escalating civil unrest, cementing it as a key message in her campaign and arguing that leadership under Emmanuel Macron's centrist government has contributed to the conditions behind the protests. "You saw yesterday our cities, our streets, our country, battered, mistreated, ransacked," Le Pen wrote in an Oct. 18 post on social media platform X , following some of the country's worst unrest in years , with over 2,000 arrests and nearly 1,000 police officers and gendarmes injured, according to the country's ministry. "We are living through a profound crisis of trust, of authority that poses a threat to democracy. This observation must alert us: our country is caught in a vise, or even taken hostage, between violence and powerlessness," Le Pen added. French stocks are also facing volatility, with the CAC 40 index down 2.8% in the last month and off almost 6% in the last six months. The country's bond yields, which measure the government's borrowing costs, have also been on the rise, with the 10-year government bond yield trading above 4.9%. "It will be difficult to see the budget deficit come down without painful measures," Sharon Bell, senior European equity strategist at Goldman Sachs, told CNBC's " Squawk Box Europe " on Monday. events.title: SpaceX posts first operating profit as public company as AI revenue nearly triples to $7.6 billion—cruising past Starlink
events.summary: Elon Musk’s SpaceX said Tuesday that third-quarter revenue rose 161% to $14.6 billion year over year, cruising past the $12.86 billion analysts expected, according to Visible Alpha consensus from S&P Global Market Intelligence. The company reported net income of $4.4 billion, or 35 cents a share compared with a net loss of $541 million in the second quarter and $5.5 billion a year ago. Operating income rebounded to $2.79 billion, from a loss of $143 million in the second quarter, well above the $2.33 billion analysts expected. SpaceX’s buzzy AI segment—renamed “Super Intelligence”—which includes computing capacity leased to Claude-maker Anthropic, Google, Grok, and X, clocked in with revenue of $7.56 billion, compared with the $6.47 billion analysts had expected, and up from $2.56 billion in the second quarter. SI revenue nearly tripled this quarter. Connectivity revenue, mostly from Starlink, rose 69% to $5.25 billion, against the $4.92 billion analysts expected, and connectivity operating income nearly doubled to $2.37 billion. Starlink added 1.6 million consumer subscribers, falling short of the 2.29 million analysts were predicting. Overall, Space revenues rose 6% to $1.77 billion, above the $1.46 billion expected. Capital spending came in at $19.6 billion in the quarter, although the release did not include a full-year forecast, which analysts are eagerly awaiting to make projections about the outlook. SpaceX’s capital investments are expected to nearly triple from about $70 billion this year to $197.4 billion in the 2028 fiscal year, according to figures cited by Melissa Otto, global head of Visible Alpha research at S&P Global. In a note before third-quarter numbers were released, Otto wrote that consensus estimate projections pegged connectivity capital expenditures surging from $4.2 billion in fiscal 2025 to $22.8 billion in fiscal 2028. Alongside it, SpaceX’s debt is expected to rise nearly sevenfold from $50.7 billion in 2025 to $350 billion in 2029, according to Otto. Earlier this month, SpaceX agreed to buy investment firm Grain Management’s 800-megahertz-band licenses to boost its Starlink Mobile phone service indoors. The deal with the global investment firm, which specializes in digital infrastructure, is subject to FCC approval. Financial terms were not disclosed, but Wall Street Journal reporting put the amount SpaceX will pay at $8 billion. The Q3 results also come a day after Musk posted on X that he planned to offer a share of SpaceX stock to “every kid in America” next year, calling the donation the first of many. Census figures show there are roughly 72 million children under 18 in the U.S., making the gift worth about $10.5 billion. Currently, all of Musk’s shares in SpaceX are locked up until 2027, based on an extensive agreement he signed before SpaceX’s IPO in June. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: United Airlines slashes 2026 profit outlook on fuel prices, but travelers keep booking despite higher fares
events.summary: United Airlines' fourth-quarter earnings outlook came in below Wall Street estimates. The outlook means United expects lower earnings overall for 2026 as fuel costs bite. Even still, United said passengers continued to book, with passenger counts up more than 2% from last year. United Airlines is slashing its profit forecast for the year as fuel costs continue to bite, but the carrier said passengers keep booking. United said Tuesday that it expects to earn between 50 cents and $1.50 a share on an adjusted basis in the fourth quarter, well below the $1.76 a share Wall Street analysts expected. At the high end of that range, it would bring United's 2026 adjusted earnings to no more than $7.22 per share. In mid-July, United said it was expecting full-year earnings of $9 to $11 a share. The carrier expects to pay an average of $4.80 a gallon for fuel in the fourth quarter, up from an average price of $3.90 a gallon in the third. A surge in fuel prices this year has added billions of dollars to airlines' costs, eating into profits, despite strong demand, and driving up airfares. Here is what United Airlines reported for the quarter that ended Sept. 30 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on estimates compiled by LSEG: Earnings per share: $2.54 adjusted vs. $2.57 expected Revenue: $17.88 billion vs. $17.9 billion expected United's third-quarter net income rose 8.5% from a year earlier to $1.03 billion, or $3.14 a share. During the same period last year its net income totaled $949 million, or $2.90 a share. "Our employees met the challenge of our ever-changing environment and our results prove the resilience of focusing on building a brand-loyal airline for customers," United CEO Scott Kirby said in an earnings release. United's fuel bill rose close to 62% in the quarter from a year earlier to $4.84 billion. Revenue for the three months ended Sept. 30 rose 17.4% from a year earlier to $17.88 billion, compared with $15.23 billion the year before. Domestic passenger unit revenue rose 14.5% from a year earlier, while international unit revenue was up 17.4%, a sign of higher fares. Passengers continue to book, United said, with passenger counts up more than 2% from last year. Adjusting for one-time items, United reported net income of $833 million or $2.54 a share. events.title: Deloitte U.S. human capital chief warns: Broken trust cuts employee motivation by more than half
events.summary: At a time when every company is warning employees not to blindly trust in anything—even corporate emails, lest they be from fraudsters trying to manipulate and socially engineer—trust has become more challenging to engender and maintain.  Advisory firm Deloitte breaks it down into four factors, said U.S. Human Capital Practice leader Simona Spelman, who spoke at Fortune ’s Most Powerful Women Summit in Santa Barbara, Calif., last week. Those pillars are reliability, transparency, capability, and humanity, said Spelman, who added trust seems like a “soft” word, but has the power to galvanize or drag on momentum as companies try to advance. Moreover, maintaining balance among the four pillars on a go-forward basis will continue to be an evolving issue to measure as companies press further into AI, particularly after some layoffs have been blamed on replacing employees with AI instead. “Getting the right balance of those four things is really what measures trust,” Spelman said. That means a single factor that veers into distrusted territory drags down the whole trust infrastructure, even when a leader is strong everywhere else. Spelman, who shared additional data after the panel, said 82% of employees are motivated to give their best when they distrust none of the four factors. One distrusted factor cuts that to 37%, a drop of more than half. A second brings it down to 28%, and by the time all four factors are distrusted, only 7% of employees are motivated. Meanwhile, a robust 96% of employees who trust their leader on all four factors are motivated to work. “So think about that,” Spelman advised the room. Jennifer McCollum, president and CEO of gender equity and workplace inclusion nonprofit Catalyst, said periods of massive transformation offer “a huge opportunity to either engender trust or really screw it up.” Catalyst’s research has shown how large the gap can be. McCollum, who spoke on a panel with Spelman, said Catalyst found 68% of leaders claim they have plans in place to reskill employees, but among employees, only 34% said they believe their organizations make AI training open to everyone. “Our intentions are good, but we can really get it wrong,” McCollum said.  The same study found only one-third of employees believe their leadership teams act with integrity during business disruption, and just 16% said leaders remained confident and supportive during AI-driven change. Employees are watching how leaders carry themselves during the transition, she said. There’s also a hidden double bind for women, McCollum warned. Forthcoming research will show that when women use AI at work, their credibility is questioned—but when they don’t use AI, their capabilities are questioned. The evolution of the double bind means shifting challenges as new generations enter the workforce, she said. Therefore, as AI spreads, technology alone will eventually cease to be much of a competitive advantage, noted Francesca Cornelli, dean of Northwestern University’s Kellogg School of Management. What will set companies apart, Cornelli said, is “investment in the people, in the human capital.” Moreover, how a company introduces AI matters. When a leader announces that a new tool will simplify processes, there’s an inadvertent message sent to employees.  “All they hear is, ‘you won’t need me anymore,’” Cornelli said. People become more invested when AI is framed as a way for everyone to help the company get better—but only if the investment is real. “If you just use words, people will see through it,” she said.  Spelman cited a statistic showing the imbalance: About 93% of AI investment goes to the technology while 7% goes to the human side. “You can sit here and say, ‘yes, we’re invested,’” she said. “But if you’re only spending 7% on what the impact is to the work, the workforce, or the workplace, you’re really missing the mark.” As technology and knowledge become democratized, she said, businesses will be set apart by “enduring human capabilities like empathy, curiosity, and judgment.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: UK police rearrest two men on suspicion of assisting Iran’s intelligence
events.summary: The duo was first arrested for a suspected link to an incident at a US-run airbase used for striking Iran during this year’s war. Police in the United Kingdom have rearrested two men on suspicion of assisting Iran’s intelligence service after an incident at a United States-run airbase in England last month. Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK said the men, a 24-year-old British national and a 25-year-old dual British-Iranian national, were arrested under the National Security Act. list 1 of 3 UK police arrest British national linked to RAF Fairford airbase incident list 2 of 3 UK police charge Royal Navy member accused of working with foreign power list 3 of 3 Two Latvian men arrested inside UK military base after breach One of the suspects was first arrested on September 27, when the suspected plot against RAF Fairford took place. The airbase in Gloucestershire in western England has been used to launch strikes on Iran during this year’s war. The second suspect was first arrested on October 1. Until Tuesday, the men had been released on bail pending more investigation. Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK, said the investigation was “hugely complex” and that detectives were looking at “many lines of enquiry”. “This is very much a live investigation,” Taylor said in a statement, adding: “We consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement.” “Our investigators are continuing to examine what that level of involvement was and the ambition behind it,” he added. British police declared a major incident in the area around RAF Fairford after a member of the public reported seeing three “suspicious” vans driving near the base. Residents were forced to leave their homes as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swarmed the rural area. Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant – petrol – in three vans at the site, but no explosives. The incident prompted the US to pull its bombers out of RAF Fairford, while British authorities blamed Iran. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the apparent plot was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Ken McCallum, the UK’s domestic intelligence spy chief, warned that Iran and Russia were expanding attacks against military bases in the UK, adding that the RAF Fairford incident was not unique. In all, more than 50 people have been arrested over Iran-linked plots in the past year, McCallum said. Iran has denied involvement, although it has previously said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target. Five other men in their 20s were arrested earlier then released on bail pending further investigation. No one has yet been charged.

events.title: United Airlines CEO—who made $32 million last year—calls for a national wealth tax and a nearly 100% inheritance tax: ‘I would pay them’
events.summary: United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby earned $32.3 million last year, roughly 334 times the compensation of his company’s median employee. Now he says America’s wealthiest people should pay more in taxes, including an inheritance tax that could approach 100%. That puts Kirby alongside other wealthy business leaders, including Bill Gates and Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff , who have publicly supported raising taxes on the rich. “Wealth inequality has become a danger to our society, and we need to address that,” Kirby said in an interview with the New York Times published Sunday. He continued: “We should have a national wealth tax—it won’t work by state because people will just move. And I think we should have inheritance taxes that get close to 100% at some level. I would pay them.” The comments came in response to a question about declining public trust in CEOs. Kirby’s own pay offers a striking illustration of the economic divide he described. What Kirby made last year Kirby’s total 2025 compensation, according to United’s proxy statement, was $32.28 million and included $1.2 million in base salary, $22.6 million in stock awards, $8 million in non-equity incentive compensation, and roughly $500,000 in other compensation. United’s median employee, meanwhile, received $96,670 in total compensation, according to the same filing. The gap mirrors a broader trend: CEO pay rose 11% in 2025 while worker pay rose just 0.5% , according to a study by the International Trade Union Confederation and Oxfam. In the Dallas area, where Kirby lives , even though United is headquartered in Chicago, United advertised a part-time airport customer service representative position with a starting wage of $19.64 an hour. The job includes assisting passengers at boarding gates. Even working 40 hours a week at that rate, it would take roughly 790 years to match Kirby’s 2025 compensation, assuming no raises, bonuses, or overtime. A widening wealth gap Kirby’s warning comes as the wealth gap continues to widen. The richest 1% of American households held 32.5% of the nation’s total net worth in the second quarter of 2026, up from 31.1% a year earlier, according to Federal Reserve data . The bottom half of households held just 2.3%, down from 2.4% a year earlier. Other top executives have acknowledged the backlash. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said in July that he understands the anti-rich sentiment in some communities, and a survey earlier this year found that one in five Americans thinks it’s morally wrong to be a billionaire . Not everyone welcomed Kirby’s remarks. Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry wrote on X that if Kirby feels that strongly, “he could simply cut a check,” linking to the Treasury’s fund for public donations to pay down the national debt. What the U.S. taxes now Kirby did not specify the threshold for his proposed national wealth tax or how much someone would need to inherit before facing a rate approaching 100%. The U.S. has no federal inheritance tax, though a handful of states levy one. The federal estate tax, which is paid by the estate rather than heirs, carries a top marginal rate of 40%, with a $15 million basic exclusion amount for people who die in 2026, according to the IRS . Kirby, a longtime airline executive who joined United as president in 2016 and became CEO in 2020, has lately made headlines for other reasons, including his reported interest in acquiring American Airlines . Fortune asked United whether Kirby believes the gap between CEO and employee pay contributes to the inequality he described, and what tax thresholds and rates he would support. The airline did not respond. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Salesforce announces $5.66 billion deal for Braze, sending BRZE stock soaring 51%
events.summary: Salesforce announced an agreement to buy Braze in a $5.66 billion deal Tuesday. Braze shareholders will receive $47.50 in cash per share under the terms of the deal. Salesforce announced an agreement Tuesday to buy customer engagement platform Braze in a deal worth about $5.66 billion. Under the deal, holders of Braze Class A common stock will get $47.50 in cash per share. Braze shares closed at $30.04 on Monday. The transaction is expected to close in fiscal 2028, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals, according to a Salesforce blog . The stock skyrocketed more than 51% on Tuesday to close at $45.57 after a brief halt premarket following the news. The company makes artificial intelligence marketing tools to manage customer data and messaging. "Salesforce shares our commitment to marketers, and we'll continue building as Braze and investing in the Braze community of customers and partners who built this company with us," Bill Magnuson, CEO of Braze, said in a statement. "Salesforce's platform will help us innovate faster and together we'll help marketers around the world build deeper, more lasting relationships with their customers." The latest deal comes just months after Salesforce announced it would buy AI customer service platform Fin for about $3.6 billion, in a move meant to bolster the company's agentic AI offerings for enterprises. In August, Salesforce and Anthropic announced an expanded partnership , including a new plugin called "Claudeforce" with pre-built sales skills for salespeople to better compose emails, update records and more with the frontier lab's model. events.title: Google is bringing a more personal version of its Gemini AI assistant to your car
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Google is making the Gemini AI assistant that’s already in millions of cars, trucks, and SUVs a lot more personal — a move that could push consumers even deeper into the company’s ecosystem of products. The company said Tuesday it’s upgrading Gemini in vehicles with a personal intelligence feature that can draw on information from Gmail, Google Calendar, YouTube, Maps, Google Search history, and other connected Google services to understand your preferences, activities, and past experiences. Google said it will roll out “Personal Intelligence with Gemini” to vehicles in two ways — through Android Auto, an app that runs on the user’s phone and wirelessly communicates with and projects navigation, media, and messaging to the vehicle’s infotainment system, and Google Built-in , software and services that have been directly integrated into the vehicle. The feature will launch in Android Auto, starting today, and expand to cars with Google Built-in in the coming months. Google initially launched Gemini last November in Android Auto. Meanwhile, Gemini’s “Personal Intelligence” feature rolled out across the U.S. in March and is now in beta in global markets. This latest upgrade would connect the dots — as Google put it in its blog post — across users’ Google apps. Drivers will have to opt in for Personalized Intelligence to work. Once a user does so, they should expect all sorts of cross-pollination. For instance, a driver who is navigating to the airport may be alerted that the flight on their calendar is delayed. Google said the feature will allow users to make complex requests using natural language. Returning to that airport example, a user might ask the AI assistant for their flight gate before quickly following up with a question about whether it’s still on time. Gemini will give the user answers to both questions at the same time, the company said. That level of emmeshing might make consumers uncomfortable, although Google says users do retain full control over their data with Personal Intelligence. The feature can be turned on or off at any time, and users can selectively choose which apps they’d like to connect, Google said. events.title: TCM physician, musician, rail engineer: Three S’poreans who made a mid-career switch into tech
events.summary: These individuals say the right programmes and people helped them make the move, and their non-tech backgrounds are proving an asset on the job (From left) Ang Jun Jia, Soh Wen Ming and Woo Jia Jian made mid-career moves into technology from Traditional Chinese Medicine, music and rail engineering respectively. PHOTOS: PETER CHUA (CENTRE), AND COURTESY OF ANG JUN JIA AND WOO JIA JIAN When Soh Wen Ming’s daughter said she was bored and wanted to play a video game, he asked her to build one herself. The former musician, now a senior software developer, turned to the AI assistant he developed, which coached the eight-year-old into building her own game from scratch. “Now she doesn’t even want to play iPad games anymore. She just wants to make them,” says 43-year-old Soh. Grocery shopping has become easier too. Every two weeks, an automated assistant reviews the household’s needs, fills a RedMart cart and pings his wife for final approval. Soh says such moments are proof that his mid-career pivot into technology has yielded far more than just a new profession. It has transformed how he approaches learning and problem-solving at work – and at home. He is among a growing number of professionals joining Singapore’s tech sector, a workforce that includes both fresh entrants and mid-career switchers. At home, Soh turns AI into a teaching tool – nudging his daughters to build and experiment. According to the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA), the number of tech professionals grew by 3.8 per cent to 222,200 in 2025 , up from 214,000 the year before. Tech jobs also continue to offer strong wage outcomes. In 2025, the median monthly wage for Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents in tech roles was $8,000 – 60 per cent higher than the $5,000 median across all occupations. As Singapore steps up efforts to drive AI adoption across enterprises and equip its workforce with the skills needed for an AI-driven economy, the Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB) is working with leading global companies and enterprises to deepen their AI capabilities here. Beyond attracting investments, EDB works closely with companies to create good jobs and grow Singapore’s pool of AI talent. This includes supporting companies as they build teams with specialised AI expertise, and encouraging industry partnerships and training opportunities that help Singaporeans develop in-demand skills. Two other Singaporeans took similar routes as Soh: Ang Jun Jia, a former Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) physician now helping Microsoft’s clients adopt the latest tech and AI tools; and Woo Jia Jian, a former rail engineer who manages generative AI projects at PwC today. None has a computer science background. Each took a calculated leap into a new technology role. Balancing family, stability and a move into tech Soh had spent most of his working life in music, first as a professional session musician performing with some of the biggest artistes in South-east Asia, then managing about 20 performers at So Drama! Entertainment. The music manager role was, he says, “as close to an iron rice bowl as possible”. But something else had been quietly pulling at him. “It wasn’t really that I hated the job; it was just that I knew I really, really wanted to do programming,” he says. He first became curious about programming while running a food and beverage business, where he saw vendors pitching software to manage operations. Years later at So Drama!, he taught himself Python to automate spreadsheets. But with a mortgage and two young daughters then aged five and two, turning that early interest into a career was a decision he had to weigh carefully. The turning point came when he spotted Temus’ four-month Step IT Up programme on LinkedIn in 2023. Soh (centre) receiving his certificate after completing Temus’ four-month Step IT Up programme, the leap that took him from music management into software development. Supported by IMDA’s Company-Led Training programme, Step IT Up offers participants an accelerated pathway into the tech sector. It follows a Place-and-Train model, where participants are hired from the outset before undergoing structured instructor-led and on-the-job training. Soh and his fellow trainees also received a monthly stipend during the four-month programme. Close to 80 Singaporean career-switchers have since been placed in technology roles through the programme, with a 100 per cent placement rate. Today, Soh is a senior software developer at Temus, leading a team that builds and maintains a student app used daily by thousands at one of Singapore’s largest universities. He also develops AI-powered internal tools to help colleagues work more efficiently. Much of his work involves helping non-technical users communicate their exacting specifications in a syntax the engineers are familiar with. “In the end, all businesses, even technology ones, are people businesses. And they are built on empathy,” he says.

events.title: Data, applications, computing power: Get the network wrong, and AI adoption stalls
events.summary: As companies move AI from testing to daily use, they will need networks flexible enough to keep pace or risk falling behind, says Tata Communications’ chief strategy and innovation officer Tri Pham As companies move AI into everyday operations, a flexible network helps keep data, applications and teams connected, so work stays fast and efficient. For eight years, a family car has been a reliable companion for school runs and grocery trips. Lately, however, visits to the authorised service centre have become more frequent as the vehicle begins to show its age. At around the same time, the family starts exploring replacement options through the same dealer – checking the trade-in value of their current car, comparing newer models on its website and enquiring about a test drive. Individually, these interactions may not mean much. Put together with information the dealer already holds, such as the car’s age and service history, they can signal something more useful: The family may be ready for a new car. A good salesperson might spot these clues and follow up. Artificial intelligence could do the same across thousands of customers simultaneously, helping the car dealer identify potential leads and respond to them in real time. This is one way AI could help companies generate business, says Tri Pham, chief strategy and innovation officer at Tata Communications. But for that seemingly simple AI-enabled sales process to work, different sources of data, computing power and communications tools have to connect with one another, and do so quickly, seamlessly and securely. As companies move from AI experiments into incorporating AI into everyday operations, they need to look beyond the AI tools themselves and ask whether the digital infrastructure underneath them is ready, says Pham. The current AI boom has “re-energised” the importance of networks and connectivity, says Pham. In a 2025 survey by market intelligence firm International Data Corporation, 94 per cent of companies said their networks limit their ability to run large data and AI projects in some way. The survey covered 650 global enterprise technology leaders across Asia-Pacific, Europe and North America. Part of the problem is that AI is developing rapidly but traditional network infrastructure – comprising hardware, software and connectivity services — has been comparatively static. “Historically, network infrastructure is not as flexible or malleable as what we see in the cloud,” says Pham. Tata Communications is making network infrastructure “cloud-like” – the same way cloud storage lets people pay for – and use – only the space they need, rather than buying a fixed hard drive upfront. This means companies can easily use what they need from their network and adapt as requirements change. For example, the car dealer’s AI use might grow from simply answering customer questions to running AI agents that handle more complex tasks. Rather than buying new hardware and software at each stage, it can draw on what it needs from Tata Communications’ suite of digital solutions, which brings together network, cloud, interaction and Internet of Things solutions. “Our customers are seeing that this will actually help improve their sales efficiency and be able to deliver potentially more revenues,” says Pham. As companies start using AI, their networks must link the right data to the applications and computing resources that need it, securely and in line with regulations, says Tata Communications’ chief strategy and innovation officer Tri Pham. However, upgrading the network is not necessarily the first step for a company preparing to use more AI. “The challenge for most companies, even before thinking about the network or infrastructure, is thinking about where their data is,” says Pham. Companies first need to understand whether their data is accurate and relevant, where it came from, where it can be stored and whether it can be moved. The car dealer, for example, may have information spread across customer management systems, offices, connected devices, private data centres and cloud platforms. If it was a multinational company, it may also have data in different countries, with different requirements governing where information can be stored and processed. When the company starts using AI, its underlying network has to connect the appropriate data to the applications and computing resources that need it, while meeting security and regulatory requirements. This is what Pham describes as “network agility”. Rather than requiring a company to buy an entire suite of components and services that may include parts they do not need, Tata Communications identifies the company’s business problem and provides the combination of solutions it needs. Companies can also control how much they pay for each separate service. The car dealer may set a target of 1,000 text messages and 500 AI voice calls to customers, but pay for only what they use.
