events.title: The release of Sarah J. Maas' 6th 'ACOTAR' book is one week away. Here's everything we know.
events.summary: Sarah J. Maas is publishing the sixth "A Court of Thorns and Roses" book. Alexandra Genova / SAINT LUCY Represents Sarah J. Maas is returning to the "ACOTAR" world with two new books. The sixth book will be released on October 27, 2026, and the seventh on January 12, 2027. Teasers shared ahead of its release confirmed four characters who will return in book six. Sarah J. Maas fans, gather round. We're just one a week away from returning to Prythian. On August 17, 2026, Maas announced the titles of the sixth and seventh "A Court of Thorns and Roses" books, along with initial descriptions of the novels. Book six is called "A Court of Splintered Harmony" and will be released on October 27, 2026, and book seven is "A Court of Forgotten Melody," hitting shelves on January 12, 2027. Maas first announced she would publish the sixth and seventh installments of her "ACOTAR" series in March 2026, remaining tight-lipped about them until the title announcement in August. The books are eagerly awaited not only by fans but also by Maas' publisher, Bloomsbury. The company's sales fell 10% for the 2025-2026 fiscal year because Maas didn't release a new book, Publishers Weekly reported . Ahead of the release, Bloomsbury shared quotes from "A Court of Splintered Harmony" on social media, building hype for the novel and teasing what's to come. Maas joined in the fun a week before the release (after asking fans to stop sharing any leaks of book six). Here's everything we know about "ACOTAR" six so far. Warning: Some spoilers for Maas' work — including "ACOTAR" and "Crescent City" — ahead. Maas is releasing the sixth 'A Court of Thorns and Roses' story in multiple volumes In March 2023, Bloomsbury announced that Maas had signed a deal for three more books with the publisher. At the time, she was already under contract for four titles, including "House of Flame and Shadow," the third installment in her "Crescent City" series , published in January 2024. Readers didn't find out what the next book she would write would be until her March 2026 appearance on the "Call Her Daddy" podcast with Alex Cooper. She told Cooper she finished the sixth "ACOTAR" book while writing in Montana over the summer of 2025, but she didn't share details about it because of its nontraditional release structure. "This book's coming out October 27, and then on January 12, like two months later, I can't do math, whatever that is, the next ACOTAR book will be coming out," Maas said. "So there will be two books within, like, a very short span." Sarah J. Maas for "Call Her Daddy." Call Her Daddy As her fans will know, Maas' books are typically split into parts, separating different sections of the story she is telling. However, when it comes to the sixth "ACOTAR" story, Maas said the individual parts became longer than she anticipated as she started writing, with part one coming in at 400 pages at one point. As she continued writing, Maas decided the parts didn't have to be in a single physical book. "What if this book was really long?" she said. "What if it took me more than a thousand pages to tell the story that needed to be told, the arc that I wanted to create from start to finish?" Maas said the story for "ACOTAR" six was ultimately divided into four parts, though it is still one cohesive story. Part one is the novel Bloomsbury will publish  on October 27, 2026, and parts two and three will be published together on January 12, 2027. Maas has yet to write or give a publication date for part four, but she told Cooper all three volumes would be published "in a very short time." "It's meant to be read, ideally, as one massive, massive story as opposed to in a trilogy," she said. "It's not a trilogy. Like, arcs aren't wrapped up." Maas finally shared some details about the books in August 2026 On August 16, Maas cleared her Instagram of all its posts, changing her profile photo to a black-and-white illustration of a monster and a spider. Then, on August 17, she shared the covers and titles of books six and seven on social media. The "Splintered Harmony" cover features a pink-and-orange backdrop with a sketched drawing of a monster with teeth and bones, and the subtitle is "The Valkyrie Cycle: Movement I." The Valkyrie were introduced to "ACOTAR" in "A Court of Silver Flames," when Nesta Archeron brought the legendary all-female fighting squad back to life alongside her friends Gwyn and Emerie. "A Court of Splintered Harmony." Bloomsbury Maas posted the book alongside the tagline, "What was broken will be remade." The blurb shared on booksellers' websites reveals that the Night Court is facing new threats when book six opens: Koschei the Deathless, one of three legendary monster siblings introduced throughout "ACOTAR," and those willing to ally with him to claim the newly freed human lands. The description also notes that there is tension among the members of the Night Court because of "recent betrayals and revealed truths," which they must work through if they want to defeat Koschei. "A Court of Splintered Harmony" will be 352 pages and will include three bonus chapters from the "ACOTAR" series. Those bonus chapters were previously published in specific editions of Maas' novels, but they will be in all copies of "ACOSH," as the publisher shared on its social media on September 24. One chapter focuses on Feyre and Rhysand, one on Cassian and Nesta, and one on Azriel's experience on the Winter Solstice that takes place in "A Court of Silver Flames." Teasers from the new book In mid-September, Bloomsbury began sharing quotes from "A Court of Splintered Harmony," offering more insight into the novel than the vague blurbs. It released six quotes in total, and the first, shared on September 17, revealed that at least some of the novel will be told from Lucien Vanserra's perspective. "Lucien's heart thundered, throat drying out," the quote read . "Maybe this had been a terrible idea." Lucien has only played a supporting role in the "ACOTAR" books so far, but Maas has been teeing up his expanded role in her books through his unaccepted mating bond with Elain Archeron, Feyre's middle sister, and his connection to Koschei. He serves as an emissary to the human lands for the Night Court in "ACOSF," alongside Jurian and Vassa, a human queen who was sold to Koschei and cursed to turn into a firebird each day. It would be surprising if Vassa — and by extension Lucien — weren't involved in fighting against Koschei in book six. Likewise, the final quote Bloomsbury shared on October 9 appeared to confirm that Azriel will narrate some of "ACOSH." The quote didn't include his name, but the unnamed narrator was communicating with shadows: "'We are here,' the shadows whispered in his ear. 'We are always here.'" events.title: Trump administration punts on releasing Fannie, Freddie
events.summary: The Trump administration isn’t loosening the federal government’s grip on mortgage giants Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac any time soon. “I would imagine that the next year, the year after, we will be tackling the ownership structure,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday , calling it “unclear” for now how “a change in the arrangement of the shareholder structure” would benefit homeowners. President Donald Trump said this summer that he was still considering selling some of the government’s shares in Fannie and Freddie, purchased after the 2008 financial crisis. But any move to release them from conservatorship is likely to spike mortgage rates , which Bessent called “our North Star.” Housing starts dropped 5.2% in September, the Commerce Department said this morning , as residential construction slumped. Mortgage rates, meanwhile, recently reached their highest levels since November 2023 . — Eleanor Mueller

events.title: Amazon is buying billions in Nvidia AI systems it can't yet turn on
events.summary: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images AWS expected to get $5 billion of Nvidia GB300 racks, followed by $3 billion more each month. Some of these GPU systems are being stored elsewhere due to lack of data center power. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy sees AI as a major opportunity, but getting capacity online is a challenge. Amazon is racing to secure AI hardware earlier than before, even as data center power shortages leave some GPU systems waiting in warehouses. Under a new Early Rack Receipt process, AWS expected to receive roughly $5 billion in Nvidia's GB300 server racks at US facilities before final deployment, according to August internal emails reviewed by Business Insider. The company projected roughly $3 billion more in GB300 racks each month "for the foreseeable future," one of the emails said. Some AWS sites had room for more racks but not enough available power to turn them on, people familiar with the effort said, leaving finished equipment to be staged at intermediary warehouses until the facilities were ready. At least one AWS team did not have "a clear forecasted path" for getting the incoming racks into data centers at the time, according to one of the emails. Dark GPUs A lack of new electricity capacity is one of several bottlenecks slowing the buildout of some AI data centers. This has led to a phenomenon known as dark GPUs , where AI chips and servers are purchased but can sit idle due to power supply issues or other challenges. (Dark GPUs can also refer to system design flaws that mean this gear isn't fully used after being plugged in). This is partly why financial pressure is mounting on big data center projects. Money must be spent upfront to secure supplies of Nvidia GPUs and other valuable AI components. But if some data centers aren't ready to run, those early investments can tie up huge amounts of cash. Debt financing can fill in the gaps, but the market has become less willing to lend against some of these projects lately. Trade-off Amazon's early-rack program is one piece of the cloud leader's broader AI buildout, which is putting new pressure on its cash flow, as Business Insider exclusively reported this week. Amazon expects roughly $220 billion in capital expenditures this year — more than any Big Tech peer. Its free-cash-flow turned negative last quarter for the first time since 2023, and could stay negative for a while. For AWS, the trade-off is securing scarce GPU racks before competitors do, even if some data centers are not yet ready to turn them on. But taking ownership earlier can tie up billions in equipment before it starts generating cloud revenue. Previously, AWS took ownership of a finished rack only upon delivery to a data center, according to internal documents. Under the new approach, it can pay for and record certain racks earlier in the supply chain. An Amazon spokesperson said the company routinely stages finished hardware near deployment sites so it can install it once capacity becomes available, calling the practice "best business practice." The spokesperson added that Amazon has long-established systems for tracking infrastructure assets and disputed that the broader company lacked a path for getting racks into data centers. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy previously said the company has a "clear line of sight" to strong returns from its AI investments, calling the technology a "once in a lifetime opportunity." "We've been through this cycle with the first big AWS growth wave, and liked the results," Jassy wrote in Amazon's annual shareholder letter. "We expect to feel similarly about this next wave." events.title: 17 actors who transformed into real-life tech company CEOs and founders
events.summary: Elizabeth Holmes (and Amanda Seyfried's portrayal of her) is back in the news. A24; Hulu Amanda Seyfried is making headlines for again playing Elizabeth Holmes in "You Can See Everything." Seyfried first played the Theranos founder in the Hulu series "The Dropout." She's part of a growing class of actors who've taken part in the latest trend: playing tech moguls. We've all heard of musician and actor biopics — now, it's all about the stories of tech CEOs. These days, startup founders can be just as famous (or infamous) as any other celebrity, and the dramatic lives they've lived in business or at home make great fodder for TV and film. To play these figures, some of the best-known actors had to ditch their signature looks to take on Steve Jobs ' turtleneck and wire-frame glasses, Elizabeth Holmes ' red lipstick and frizzy blowout, or SBF's signature curls. Here are 17 celebrities who transformed to play some of Silicon Valley's most prominent figures. Amanda Seyfried as Elizabeth Holmes in 'The Dropout' and 'You Can See Everything' Hulu; David Orrell/CNBC/NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal/ Getty Images In the 2022 Hulu limited series " The Dropout , Seyfried played Holmes from her time at Stanford in 2003 (when she did the titular dropping out) through the fall of her company, Theranos, after The Wall Street Journal's 2015 exposé. Theranos purported to manufacture a device that could do a litany of blood tests from a single finger prick, but, infamously, it did not work as promised. In 2022, Holmes was sentenced to 11 years in prison after being convicted of defrauding investors. Four years after the Hulu series, comedian and documentarian Nathan Fielder asked Seyfried to once again play Holmes in some reenactments he wanted to do in his doc about her final days before prison, " You Can See Everything ." We won't say much else besides that you need to see it to believe everything that goes down. Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman in 'Artificial' Neon; Mike Coppola/Getty Images for TIME "After the Hunt" wasn't enough for Garfield and director Luca Guadagnino — the two have since teamed up to tell the story of OpenAI CEO and cofounder Altman. " Artificial ," which is set for release in select theaters on Christmas Day, will focus on Altman's 2023 firing by cofounder Ilya Sutskever (Yura Borisov) and subsequent rehiring one week later. Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in 'The Social Reckoning' Sony Pictures Releasing; David Paul Morris/Bloomberg/Getty Images "Succession" star Jeremy Strong played the Facebook founder in " The Social Reckoning ," a film about the release of Facebook Files , a staggering number of internal documents leaked by whistleblower and employee Frances Haugen and published by The Wall Street Journal in 2021, and the subsequent congressional scrutiny that followed. The film, released in October 2026, was written and directed by Aaron Sorkin, the screenwriter of "The Social Network," making this something of a sequel to the 2010 classic. Jesse Eisenberg as Mark Zuckerberg in 'The Social Network' Sony Pictures Releasing; Adam Berry/Bloomberg/Getty Images "The Social Reckoning" wasn't the first time Zuckerberg has been portrayed on screen — most famously, Eisenberg played the founder in " The Social Network ," which chronicled the earliest days of Facebook, back when it still had a "the" in front of it. It juxtaposes the wild, early days of the website with two lawsuits Zuckerberg settled a few years later: one from cofounder Eduardo Saverin and another from his Harvard classmates, the Winklevoss twins. Justin Timberlake as Sean Parker in 'The Social Network' Sony Pictures Releasing; Ramin Talaie/Corbis/Getty Images The other famous "disruptor" portrayed in "The Social Network" is Parker, one of the cofounders of Napster , the original music streaming platform. He's played by Timberlake in a career-best performance. Parker comes in as an early believer and executive at Facebook, which ruffles the feathers of cofounder Eduardo Saverin. Anthony Boyle as Sam Bankman-Fried in 'The Altruists' Netflix; Craig Barritt/Getty Images for CARE For Special Children Sam Bankman-Fried , also known as SBF, will get the biopic-miniseries treatment this November on Netflix in a series titled "The Altruists." Bankman-Fried co-founded the crypto trading firm Alameda Research in 2017 and later co-founded the cryptocurrency exchange FTX in 2019. After making millions, FTX collapsed in 2022 , and Bankman-Fried was eventually convicted of several crimes , including fraud and money laundering, in 2024. He was sentenced to 25 years in prison. SBF's onetime girlfriend and former CEO of the FTX-affiliated trading firm Alameda Research, Caroline Ellison , will also be in the show, portrayed by Julia Garner. Joseph Gordon-Levitt as Travis Kalanick in 'Super Pumped' Showtime; D Dipasupil/FilmMagic/Getty Images Gordon-Levitt played Uber cofounder and former CEO Kalanick in "Super Pumped," a 2022 Showtime limited series. It focuses on the rise of Kalanick and his eventual fall from power, culminating in his 2017 resignation from the company. Ashton Kutcher as Steve Jobs in 'Jobs' Open Road Films; Tom Munnecke/Getty Images The first mention of Jobs on this list goes to Kutcher, who played the Apple founder in the 2013 biopic "Jobs." It traces his career from Apple's founding in 1976 to the introduction of the first iPod in 2001. Michael Fassbender as Steve Jobs in 'Steve Jobs' Universal Pictures; William STEVENS/Gamma-Rapho/Getty Images Two years after "Jobs," the late founder was portrayed again on screen, this time by Michael Fassbender in "Steve Jobs." Instead of a standard cradle-to-grave biopic, " Steve Jobs " checks in with the enigmatic figure at three different points in his career: first in 1984, before the introduction of the first Apple Macintosh computer; second, in 1988, when Jobs is the head of a new company, NeXT, and is preparing to launch its first computer; and finally, in 1998, as Jobs gears up to release the iMac. Noah Wyle as Steve Jobs in 'Pirates of Silicon Valley' TNT; Matthew NAYTHONS/Gamma-Rapho/Getty Images In 1999, the TV movie "Pirates of Silicon Valley" aired, starring Wyle as the Apple founder. It chronicles Jobs' career from the '70s to the '90s, from the founding of Apple to his return as CEO. Anthony Michael Hall as Bill Gates in 'Pirates of Silicon Valley' TNT; Doug Wilson/CORBIS/Corbis/Getty Images The other half of the "Pirates of Silicon Valley" narrative focuses on Gates, the cofounder of Microsoft . He's played by "Breakfast Club" star Anthony Michael Hall. The film's climax is based on the real-life falling out Gates and Jobs had in 1985, when Jobs felt that Gates had ripped off Apple. events.title: Mamdani takes on AI chatbot ‘doom loops’ in New York
events.summary: New York City could be the first place in the country where consumers are protected from a “doom loop” of AI-powered customer service chatbots, per a rule proposed today by Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration. The rule would require businesses to connect people to a human customer service agent quickly if a chatbot cannot fulfill their requests. “When corporations force you to fight your way through an endless doom loop of AI-generated responses to speak to another human being, they’re stealing your time, money, and patience,” Mamdani said in a release. “This rule makes clear: Customer service cost-cutting can’t come at New Yorkers’ expense.” Businesses would have to disclose when customers are talking to AI and offer an “easy off-ramp” to a human representative, with violators subject to fines that would start at $525. At the helm of Mamdani’s consumer protection efforts are several Biden administration alumni: Samuel Levine, commissioner of the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, previously led the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection under the agency’s then-chair Lina Khan, and Deputy Mayor Julie Su was acting labor secretary during the Biden era. Khan is also part of Mamdani’s administration, serving as board chair of the city’s Economic Development Board. — Ashley Gold

events.title: The Internet goes on high alert after discovery of 8 compromised TLS certs
events.summary: Security personnel around the world are on high alert Tuesday following the discovery of eight TLS certificates with private keys so weak they could allow anyone to mint trusted browser and app credentials for any site on the Internet. As of late morning Tuesday, browser makers and some major apps and programming languages had blocked all eight of the intermediate certificates. There are no reports of certificate transparency logs, which track the issuance of all browser-trusted certificates, showing the compromised keys being used maliciously. The threat remains far from over, however, because it will be hard and time-consuming to update other key parts of the Internet, such as Linux distributions and embedded and Internet of Things devices. One word: bonkers The eight intermediate certificates belong to India-based certificate authority eMudhra Limited. An informal advisory published to emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com over on Tuesday posted the message “We have a problem here - Wayne.” The words were digitally signed using the private key of one of the eMudhra certificates. With proof that the reporting party had control of the key, defenders scrambled because the same key could be used to sign unauthorized certificates that would be trusted by millions of servers worldwide. events.title: Travellers weigh up the cost to get to Sydney's new airport opening this week
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts What travellers flying from Western Sydney International Airport can expect to pay to get there Commercial flights take off from Western Sydney's new airport on October 25. ( ABC News: Dylan Goolagong ) The freshly built terminals of Western Sydney International Airport (WSI) will open to eager holiday-makers in a matter of days. Located 45 kilometres from Sydney's CBD and 18 kilometres from Penrith's city centre, the Badgerys Creek aviation hub will run around the clock when commercial flights take off on October 25. It is set to bring the world to Western Sydney's doorstep, but is a trip from there worth it for all travellers in Greater Sydney? Rico Merkert, chair in transport and supply chain management from the University of New South Wales, said it was ultimately important to consider the door-to-door journey for those chasing a cheaper holiday. "You have to account for two things, transit time and then also the cost to get to and from the airport as well," he said. The new airport will complement Sydney's Kingsford Smith in Mascot, which is limited to a curfew between 11pm and 6am and is heavily congested by slot allocation constraints. With less restrictive scheduling, the 24/7 operations of WSI are attractive for international low-cost carriers that want to capitalise on profitable peak flying times. WSI has announced a number routes from low-cost carriers. ( ABC News: Digby Werthmuller ) Gulf carrier Qatar Airways is the latest airline to call WSI home, announcing on Wednesday it would offer flights to Hamad International Airport at Doha from December 2027. It is expecting to offer daily flights from late 2028. Qantas, Jetstar, Air New Zealand and Singapore Airlines have also announced routes from WSI. The most recent airlines to sign on were VietJet and Fiji Airways, with cheap flights on offer to service Western Sydney's Vietnamese and Fijian communities. According to WSI, over 500,000 people travelled between NSW and Vietnam in 2025 alone, while 400,000 passengers travel to Fiji annually. The 24/7 operations of WSI are attractive to airlines that are after attractive slot times. ( ABC News: Therese Banna ) Premier Chris Minns was also hopeful Western Sydney could provide a steady stream of passengers into New Delhi and met with Air India representatives last month , although no deal was reached. How much does it cost to get there? There will be three main ways to get there when flights begin taking off. The Sydney Metro line is due for completion in 2027. ( ABC News: Supplied: NSW government ) The Sydney Metro Western Sydney Airport Line will be the fastest mode of public transport to WSI when it is completed in 2027. But until then, travellers will have to make the commute via shuttle bus from St Marys station, located about 20km away. From there, free WSI Linkshuttle bus services will run every 30 minutes though the commute via bus will take twice as long as a ride on the metro. Transport for NSW said when the line does become operational, "passengers will be able to travel from the broader rail network via St Marys Station to Western Sydney International Airport in around 15 minutes". To cope with the lack of rail options, there are additional bus routes operating through Mount Druitt, Penrith, Liverpool, Campbelltown and Leppington. A trip from anyone of those locations could take anywhere between 30 minutes to over an hour, with an adult fare starting from $5.77 during peak time, according to Transport NSW's trip planner website. There will be no direct public transport route for people travelling from inner-Sydney. ( ABC News: Patrick Thomas ) At the moment there is no direct public transport route for those living in inner Sydney, so people who are travelling from Central Station will need to change over at either Mount Druitt, Leppington or Penrith. The quickest way to get there will be via a train from Central then a bus from Penrith with a commute time of about 1 hour and 40 minutes and a $10.31 fare. For people willing to spend a little extra to save a bit of time, the Super Shuttle WSI offers express bus services from Parramatta CBD and Sydney CBD. For an adult travelling from Sydney CBD to WSI, a one-way ticket costs $55 and a return trip is $80. The journey is expected to take 45 minutes to 60 minutes, depending on traffic. Those heading from Parramatta CBD will get the best deal, with one-way adult tickets going for $25 and $45 return, and a commute time of up to 45 minutes. The Super Shuttle also provides the only direct airport transfer from WSI to Kingsford Smith, which will cost $65 one-way and take around 60 to 75 minutes.

events.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wins dismissal of sister's lawsuit
events.summary: OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman has won a dismissal of a lawsuit brought against him by his sister that claimed he had sexually abused her more than two decades ago. A US district judge dismissed the case after Ann Altman had refused to attend an independent medical examination, adding she was warned a failure to do so would result in the case being thrown out. Ann Altman had claimed the OpenAI founder had regularly sexually abused her between 1997 and 2006. Sam Altman has denied those accusations. The Altman family has said Ann Altman has mental health challenges and they have supported her financially, adding the claims were made as she continued to demand more funds. District Judge Zachary Bluestone said that despite multiple accommodations and multiple opportunities to do so, Ann Altman did not appear for an independent medical exam on three separate occasions, and "failed to meaningfully prosecute her case". "Because Annie has continued to violate her discovery obligations and forced this case to a halt through her intransigence, the Court has run out of options and, thus, dismisses her claims with prejudice," he said in his written order. The case was filed on 6 January 2025 in the Eastern District of Missouri. In it, Ann Altman claimed that her older brother Sam Altman began abusing her when she was three, and he was 12. However, in a joint statement released by Sam Altman along with his mother and two brothers at the time, the family said they were concerned for Ann Altman's wellbeing and have spent years trying to support her financially and to look after her wellbeing. The family said she receives monthly financial support, and her bills and rent were also covered, while also trying to assist with medical help. The statement said her claims against Sam Altman had changed drastically over time, but all of those claims were "utterly untrue". Sam Altman is the co-founder of OpenAI, which launched its popular ChatGPT artificial intelligence chatbot in 2022. events.title: Oil prices fall as traders hope for diplomatic progress in Middle East
events.summary: Crude oil prices fell Tuesday as traders hoped for diplomatic progress between the U.S. and Iran, though attacks on tankers and strikes against Saudi Arabia have escalated recently. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for November fell 1.8% to close at $101.79 per barrel, pulling back dramatically from a session high of $110.48. The November contract expired on Tuesday. The WTI December contract was down 26 cents at $98.28 per barrel. Global benchmark Brent crude futures for December delivery fell 0.7% to settle at $108.79 per barrel, well off a session high of $111.99. Developments in the Middle East remain in focus, with attacks on commercial ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz escalating in recent weeks. At least 18 vessels have come under fire over the past two weeks, according to ship tracker Kpler. Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said Tuesday that two "non-compliant" oil tankers had been set ablaze in the strait after hitting mines laid by its naval unit, Iranian state-affiliated news agency Tasnim reported. Meanwhile, Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said at a weekly news conference on Tuesday that Tehran would respond to any American strike "in equal measure, if not more forcefully," according to Tasnim. U.S. President Donald Trump said earlier this month that American forces will not attack Iran before the midterm elections on Nov. 3. Tamas Varga, analyst at PVM Oil Associates, told CNBC in an email on Tuesday that front-end WTI strength ahead of the contract expiry is a sign of tightness in the global crude oil market. "It is a reflection of falling export volumes from the Middle East as tanker attacks and Houthi strikes on Saudi oil infrastructure intensify," he said. "Secondly, the U.S. decision to exempt Russian shadow fleet from sanctions will push freight rates possibly lower, which was a prohibitive factor to increase demand for U.S.-sourced crude." "With this hurdle removed, at least temporary, U.S. crude oil grades are back in play as replacements of Mideast crude oil," he added. "Thirdly, U.S. commercial oil stocks are expected to have declined last week."

events.title: Trump goes full apocalypse in anti-Dems midterms message
events.summary: President Trump is escalating his doomsday warnings about a Democratic takeover of Congress, painting a nightmarish vision of an America consumed by burning cities, economic collapse, mutilated children and the destruction of Western civilization. Why it matters: Trump has long portrayed Democrats as an existential threat to the country. But in an effort to preserve Republicans' grip on Washington, he's taking that rhetoric to new extremes as he casts the election as a choice between Republican rule and national catastrophe. At the same time, Trump is offering voters a financial incentive to keep Republicans in power: $5,000 checks for every adult American citizen if the GOP retains control of Congress. The pledge would cost more than $1 trillion and has no clear path to becoming reality. What they're saying: "President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress," White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Axios in a statement. "The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump's winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats' extreme liberal policies and obstruction." Reality check: Even if Democrats take control of Congress, Trump will remain president and retain veto power over legislation they pass. Here's what he's been telling voters. America will burn like France On Monday night, Trump told Kansas voters that under Democrats, America will burn like France, which is facing widespread student and union protests over public spending cuts and deficit concerns, per Reuters . "When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical Dumocrats want to do to America." Trump has blamed the riots in France on immigration , suggesting that border policies under Democratic Party leadership would unleash the same chaos in America. Yes, but: The unrest in France has been driven by disputes over living costs and public funding. There's no evidence that Democrats in the U.S. want to take up similar forms of violence. America will fall into another Great Depression Trump predicts Democrats will cause economic catastrophe and trigger a depression similar to the one that began in 1929. "If the Democrats win you will have a 1929-style economic depression," Trump told Tennessee voters on Saturday. "I hope I'm wrong on that." By the numbers: Unemployment peaked at roughly 25% during the Great Depression, compared with about 4% today. What's next: House Democrats, should they gain power, plan to repeal Trump's tariff policy, bring back Affordable Care Act tax breaks and undo Medicaid cuts as part of a general affordability push. Democrats will "mutilate your children" In Arizona, Trump warned last week that Democrats want to "mutilate, cut your children." "I mean, they can do whatever they want, and they do. Your son leaves as Jimmy and comes back home in three days as Janet, and they don't even ask you," Trump said . "They can take your child out of school and do whatever the hell they want." Reality check: Trump's claims about schools secretly performing gender-transition procedures misrepresent how such medical care works. Schools cannot perform gender-transition surgeries. Those operations take place in medical settings under relevant state laws. Democrats will "get rid of the border" Trump warned Democrats would dismantle the border and allow criminals from around the world to enter the U.S. He told voters in Kansas that "the Dumocrat agenda is a plan to extinguish Western civilization. They want to open the borders." Trump claimed prisons around the world will empty prisoners into the United States. The other side: A coalition of Democrats have proposed using advanced technology to protect the border, while rejecting mass deportation strategies. Trump: Democrats will take your guns — and wild animals will feast Trump also warned that Democrats will "take away your guns" if they control Congress. "You know who would love that to happen? Some of the wild animals you have up here that like eating you," he told voters in Montana. "... They would gain a lot of weight." Context: Mainstream Democrats have not called for repealing the Second Amendment. While some Democrats support banning certain types of guns, that's different from eliminating the constitutional right to own firearms. Democrats will destroy farms Trump also warned that Democrats would "decimate Kansas farms." On Monday, the Trump administration announced $8 billion in relief for farmers facing soaring fuel costs, driven in part by Trump's own policies and the Iran war. What's going on: Democrats have been making a push in farm country by appealing to rural voters in Kansas and Iowa . House Democrats have also proposed expanding support for rural development and family farms .

events.title: Trump sued over Canadian tariffs in latest legal challenge
events.summary: US President Donald Trump is facing another legal challenge on tariffs after the group that successfully sued over his so-called "liberation day" import taxes filed a new lawsuit over the latest Canadian levies. The White House imposed a 50% levy on some $20bn of Canadian goods after trade talks between the US and Canada broke down in August. The Liberty Justice Center filed a suit on behalf of US food business Gellert Global Group, urging the US Court of International Trade to find the levies unlawful and to order refunds with interest for affected importers. The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the tariffs and caused "immediate harm to American businesses". The White House has been contacted for comment. Gellert Global Group is a third-generation family business that is paying 50% tariffs on cheese exported from Canada. The New Jersey-based firm is also facing retaliatory tariffs from Canada on American-made cheese it sells north of the border. Co-chief executive Thomas Gellert said the firm had spent generations building relationships with suppliers and customers in the food industry. "These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain," he said on Tuesday. The Liberty Justice Center is challenging the administration's use of Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act to hit Canadian goods from wine to dairy products and hockey sticks. That section of the nearly 100-year-old Act is aimed at protecting US business against foreign discrimination, but the legal group is arguing that it does not allow the executive branch "to impose sweeping tariffs or import restrictions whenever a trade dispute arises". The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts Published 31 August The lawsuit seeks to challenge the White House's reliance on retaliatory tariffs imposed by Canada to justify its own duties under Section 338. Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures against numerous US tariffs. Last month, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney matched the Section 338 US tariffs "dollar for dollar" after Trump imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US cars, dairy and alcohol. It also points out Section 338 requires a 30-day waiting period before levies can be imposed, but the tariff on products including cheese was added to the list just a week before tariff collection began. Sara Albrecht, chief executive of the Liberty Justice Center, said the case was not about Trump himself but about the presidency. "No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required," she said. The lawsuit argues that Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 has been superseded by Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. It also argues that if Section 338 still applies, the White House has not established the legal basis for the sweeping tariffs against Canada. "The case is not an objection to tariffs as such. It asks who has the power to impose them and whether the executive branch followed the law Congress wrote," the Liberty Justice Center said. The law group has also filed a motion for a preliminary injunction to block their collection. It is the fourth case brought by the group against Trump's tariffs, including its successful case against the sweeping tariffs brought in under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) that were struck down in February this year. Albrecht said the group had brought all the cases for the same reason: "the Constitution gives tariff power to Congress. The executive branch cannot keep moving the same policy from one statute to another and pretend the limits disappear". As Trump shares an AI goose meme amid the trade war, the BBC's Jessica Murphy examines how much Canada can fight back. events.title: Housing is flashing warning signs just as the Fed weighs more interest rate hikes
events.summary: Fresh data points from September showed the housing market continues to deteriorate just as the Federal Reserve is considering raising interest rates again. Building permits, new starts and pending sales all were considerably worse than Wall Street forecasts. Under some circumstances, Fed officials would use easier policy to spur demand. However, the central bank is currently battling inflation, which it could prioritize over a flagging housing picture. The Federal Reserve's inflation fight is running into a growing complication: The housing market is slumping even as broader price pressures persist. Housing data deteriorated further in September , according to separate reports Tuesday, adding to an already complicated policy landscape for the central bank as it contemplates its next move on interest rates. Things appear poised to get worse before they get better. If the Fed raises short-term rates as expected over the next several months, mortgage rates that are already at 7.43% could push even higher, putting a further damper on affordability. Higher home borrowing costs have coincided with a general rise in inflation and a housing shortage. "The housing market is about to go into a deep sleep unless Washington can do a 180 on its policies and make the cost of a new home more affordable," wrote Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds. "It is not winter yet but housing is going into a deep freeze." The National Association of Realtors reported that pending sales, a forward-looking index that measures home sales under agreement but not completed, hit an all-time low in records that stretch back to 2001. The index slid 7.3% for the month and was off 11.3% from a year ago. The Wall Street estimate was for a decline of just 0.4%. Housing starts, another important metric when evaluating the state of the market, also posted a decline well outside already-muted expectations Tuesday. Privately owned housing starts fell at a seasonally adjusted annualized rate of 5.2% on the month, against expectations for a decline of just 0.4%, while building permits were off 0.2%, against the Dow Jones consensus outlook for a 2% gain, according to Commerce Department data. Moreover, single-family permits totaled just 845,000, down 4% from August and the lowest number since 2023. "Market conditions weakened in September due to fast-rising mortgage rates," said Lawrence Yun, the NAR's chief economist. "Although job growth and income gains can support home purchases, housing affordability is more affected by changes in mortgage rates." The rate for a 30-year mortgage was above 7% for most of September, ending the month around 7.6%, according to Mortgage News Daily . Five years ago, rates were closer to 3%, feeding into the Covid-era housing boom that saw an explosion in demand and, consequently, prices. Outside of the pending sales number, home builder sentiment is at lows not seen in 14 years. Under some conditions, Fed officials might respond to the housing weakness with easier monetary policy. Lower rates generally help spur demand by lowering borrowing costs. But the Fed has a bigger fight on its hands in its effort to bring inflation under control. Readings last week on consumer and producer prices provided few signs of optimism, with wholesale final demand goods prices rising 2.6%, the fastest pace in a Bureau of Labor Statistics data series going back to December 2009. Fed officials have said they are tracking the inflationary effects of the robust investment in artificial intelligence, which is driving up the cost of chips and electronics. At the same time, they believe that benefits from AI investment could offset weaker sectors of the economy such as housing. However, conditions generally point to a housing market likely to weaken further before stabilizing, Goldman Sachs economist Ronnie Walker said in a client note Monday. "In 2027, we expect the headwind from affordability—reignited by the recent rebound in mortgage rates—to increasingly dominate, weighing further on activity," Walker wrote. "Sustained higher mortgage rates will continue to have their most pronounced impact on housing turnover, and the recent run-up in rates is likely to push existing home sales lower in the coming months." Several data points tell the story: More than 95% of mortgage borrowers have rates below the prevailing level, and 65% are 2 percentage points below. Goldman forecasts residential investment to decline 2.5%, 4% and 1%, respectively, over the coming three quarters, with a possibility for a steeper decline if mortgage rates don't fall. The firm sees single-family starts of just 875,000 in 2027, little changed from this year, while existing sales are forecast at 3.9 million, also about the same as 2026 but notably 26% below pre-Covid 2019 levels.

events.title: 'Dark fleet' under spotlight in latest US move to ease rising energy costs
events.summary: The US is turning to an unlikely saviour in its latest efforts to ease rising energy prices: the “ dark fleet ” that it has spent years sanctioning. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright revealed the administration's latest endeavour on Monday, telling those at a New York event that Washington wants to “move some of the ships from what I call the 'bad-guy fleet' to the 'good-guy fleet'". The dark fleet, sometimes referred to as the shadow fleet, refers to a group of ships that sail outside conventional shipping regulations. These vessels use deceptive shipping practices to transport cargo that is under sanctions or high risk, deliberately concealing it to avoid detection. Estimates on the size of the fleet vary. Mr Wright said he believes there are about 1,600 vessels. Data from TankerTrackers set the number at 1,480 active ships, while maritime company Windward said it has identified 1,100 dark fleet vessels. The dark fleet has grown in recent years after sanctions were imposed on Russian oil in response to Moscow's invasion of Ukraine. Many of these vessels are past the 15-year threshold that marks the point at which technical failures begin to mount, adding to environmental safety risks. Mr Wright said the administration's plan would involve investors buying and refurbishing these idle sanctioned vessels before using them to transport legitimate oil. “They will not carry sanctioned oil any more,” he said. The US has delisted sanctioned vessels before. In March, the Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control removed sanctions on the Panama-flagged crude oil supertanker Kiara M, which had been placed as part of the Trump administration's pressure campaign on Venezuela . This morning, U.S. military forces, in support of the Department of Homeland Security, apprehended… pic.twitter.com/UPADtiw681 — U.S. Southern Command (@Southcom) January 20, 2026 Richard Nephew, a senior research scholar at Columbia University's Centre on Global Energy Policy, said the move does little to address the security issue facing seafarers today in the Strait of Hormuz. At least 15 container ships have been struck in the waterway in the past 10 days. “You can repurpose all the ships you want. If you can’t solve the security problem, then you’re not solving the security premium shippers are charging and thereby the consequence to energy markets,” Mr Nephew said. War risk insurance premiums have surged since the start of the conflict. Rates have climbed to as high as 10 per cent of hull value, compared to 0.25 per cent before the conflict, adding millions to the premiums ship and cargo owners pay. Mr Wright's comments also come less than two weeks after US President Donald Trump waived sanctions on Russian diesel in an agreement with President Vladimir Putin. Mr Trump said the agreement would include Moscow supplying millions of barrels of diesel to US and global markets. You can repurpose all the ships you want. If you can’t solve the security problem, then you’re not solving the security premium shippers are charging and thereby the consequence to energy markets Richard Nephew, senior research scholar at Columbia University With only two weeks until the US midterm elections on November 3, diesel prices at the pump have risen to more than $6 a gallon [$1.59 a litre] on average, compared to about $3 the same time last year. Wholesale diesel prices passed $200 a barrel in Singapore in mid-September and hit all-time highs of about $220 a barrel in Europe and the US, the International Energy Agency said in an October 14 report. The seven-day moving average for tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz was seven vessels for the week ending September 18, a small fraction of its pre-war levels, according to the International Monetary Fund's PortWatch monitor. Analysts at Kpler estimate only 24 of the about 160 vessels under sanctions from the US Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control could return to mainstream trade after taking into account their age and ownership restrictions. “If this is about getting ships out of sanctions, fine, no problem, proceed as you wish. If this is about solving the problem with whether we can get enough diesel and other products to market, this is not it," Mr Nephew said.

events.title: Golden North's ice cream factory starts production at new site
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Golden North's ice cream factory starts churning at Murray Bridge Topic: Food and Beverage Processing Industry Dimi Kyriazis (left) and Paul Connelly plan to expand production at Murray Bridge. ( ABC Rural: Cassie Hough ) Golden North has begun producing ice cream at the Murray Bridge processing plant it purchased last year. The company expects to employ 20 more people at the new site. The company will also start making cheese and use the increased processing capacity at Murray Bridge to expand production. Where cheese was once piled high, ice cream now swirls as production begins at Golden North's new processing plant in Murray Bridge, South Australia. The South Australian ice cream company bought the former Beston Global Food Company plant after administrators failed to find a buyer when it was liquidated in 2025. Golden North managing director and co-owner Dimi Kyriazis said the move to Murray Bridge would bring the company closer to SA's central milk-producing region. Golden North's ice cream is sold across Australia and overseas. ( ABC North and West: Viki Ntafilis ) It would also allow the company to increase its ice cream production and expand into other products such as cheese. "We're kicking things off with ice cream," Mr Kyriazis said. "Ice cream is the most important thing; that's what's going to pay the bills in the beginning of this story of Golden North here in Murray Bridge. "Cheese will be equally as important in time." Mr Kyriazis said the ice cream would be produced using the same recipe and equipment brought over from the plant in Laura, but it could be frozen much quicker in Murray Bridge. The new Golden North factory at Murray Bridge. ( ABC Rural: Cassie Hough ) Golden North will source milk from another company for the first year, with Mr Kyriazis saying he wanted to gauge its needs before signing direct contracts with farmers. Only about one-third of what Golden North made stayed in SA and the rest was sold interstate and overseas. With the larger facility, Mr Kyriazis said he hoped to expand the products and amount they produced. The move to Murray Bridge meant leaving Golden North's home of 103 years in the Mid North town of Laura. Golden North gave priority to Laura workers to move to Murray Bridge, but only three staff took the opportunity. The new factory will need about 20 more people than the Laura plant, taking overall employment to about 100. Golden North has left its home of 103 years. ( ABC North and West: Viki Ntafilis ) Former Beston staff are among those employed by Golden North, including head of operations Paul Connelly. He has seen the factory change hands several times and was excited to see ice cream being produced. Mr Connelly was also involved in cheese production at the site over the years. "The recipes stay with the factory. They don't usually get sold off to someone else," Mr Connelly said. "Sometimes they do get sold with the brand, but all the recipes here are from probably 20 or 30 years ago, even more. Golden North was Laura's largest employer and will leave a big hole in the town even with $1 million in government assistance to support it during the company's transition. However, Laura's loss is Murray Bridge's gain, and after riding the highs and lows of dairy processing in Murray Bridge, Mr Connelly said the move would boost the town. "As I walk around the community, people are always asking me, 'How's Golden North going? How's the project going?'" he said. "So, there is a level of engagement and excitement that I can feel as I'm walking around the town.

( Supplied ) Family-owned and operated restaurant Parwana Afghan Kitchen was inducted into the Michelin Guide last week with a Bib Gourmand award. The award recognises restaurants which serve high-quality food for great value. The restaurant, which has been open since 2009, is one of 77 eateries recognised in the inaugural Michelin Guide South Australia. Parwana Afghan Kitchen in Adelaide has been plating up vibrant, traditional food since 2009. Now, it is celebrating being recognised on the global stage. The family-owned and operated restaurant was recently inducted into the Michelin Guide with a Bib Gourmand award, an accolade recognising restaurants which serve high-quality food at great value. It was an emotional moment years in the making for the family behind the business. The Ayubi family left Afghanistan during the Cold War, immigrating to Australia as refugees in 1987. "There was a lot of violence in the country, and the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan was happening and then there were tensions between the US and Soviet Russia," Durkhanai Ayubi said. "It was a time of great devastation for Afghanistan and Afghan people." Durkhanai Ayubi says her family's mission is to share warm hospitality and rich culture. ( ABC News: Steve Opie ) Durkhanai was one of four young daughters who fled Kabul with their mother and father. "We left Afghanistan on foot into Pakistan where we stayed in a UN refugee camp for about a year and then eventually, by luck and chance, made our way to Australia as refugees on humanitarian grounds," she said. "For my parents to have made that journey into the unknown, leaving everything that they loved behind and literally stepping into uncertainty, was a huge move." Her mother Farida Ayubi recalls the journey being fraught with risk. "From Kabul to Pakistan, that was really hard to get over the border and there were a lot of police," she said. "If they know we are running away from Afghanistan, they will not let us, so that was really hard, really scary." Farida Ayubi says the food is a connection to her homeland. ( ABC News: Steve Opie ) The pair described food as being a central part in their lives and connection to their homeland. "There's something about the beauty of that food; that it has such a strong pull and allure and is so life-giving and community building, that it just became a really natural part of our life and something really incredible to be able to share with people here," Durkhanai said. Becoming restaurateurs was a far cry from her parents' former lives in Kabul where her mother had been a high school teacher and her father had worked as a lawyer. The family started catering before purchasing the store, which they now operate from, in 2009. "We thought … if nothing else we'll have a kitchen to do our catering from," Durkhanai said. "Sure enough, people loved the food and word of mouth spread and we just got busier and busier." Food is a central part of the Ayubi family and is a connection to their homeland. ( ABC News: Steve Opie ) Parwana then expanded into the property next door and released a best-selling book of family stories and recipes. "That was a continuation of that ethos of being able to share something about Afghanistan and Afghan food and history and culture," Durkhanai said. "To have that book be in people's homes and kitchens and be dear to so many people … that's been a really incredible part of spreading and sharing a different narrative about Afghanistan too." The family said the latest Bib Gourmand accolade was a huge moment, with Farida and her son-in-law Sayed Ayaz Ashna who works alongside her in the kitchen collecting the award at a ceremony in Adelaide last week. Sayed Ayaz Ashna says the food he cooks has "lots of love" in it. ( ABC News: Steve Opie ) "That was a big surprise for us … it was a great honour, I was a bit emotional," Sayed said. "We haven't changed much from day one; we cook with love, simple food, lots of love in it." And while the award has created a bit more demand in their already busy kitchen, Durkhanai said their mission to share warm hospitality and rich culture at the very place where Parwana first began was as pertinent as ever. "Hopefully more and more people are intrigued about these stories of Afghanistan that are in the morsels of the food rather than the headlines that can be so alienating and so fragmenting for so many people.

events.title: Mystery mailings put Congress and election offices on edge
events.summary: Over three dozen congressional lawmakers and election offices in at least 32 states have been targeted with suspicious letters, many containing a white powder. Why it matters: The letters have forced evacuations and disrupted election offices just weeks before the 2026 midterms , raising concerns about political intimidation . Driving the news: Rep. Adam Smith's (D-Wash.) district office received a letter Monday, prompting staff to evacuate. In an emailed statement, Smith's office confirmed it "received a suspicious letter containing a powdery substance, like others sent to Congressional offices across the country." Staff returned to the office Tuesday. What they're saying: "The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices, and Congressional offices," an FBI spokesperson said in an emailed statement. "Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident." Catch up quick: The U.S. Capitol Police, the House and Senate sergeants at arms and other officials sent notices to congressional offices last week warning about letters containing suspicious substances and urging staffers to be vigilant. Over 100 letters were estimated to be circulating around the country, law enforcement sources told ABC News. The USCP referred Axios to the FBI for comment. Here's what we know about the suspicious letters: Who was targeted At least three dozen lawmakers have been targeted with the letters, including both Democrats and Republicans. That includes prominent leaders such as Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Sens. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.). Election offices in at least 32 states were targeted with similarly suspicious letters, according to WIRED . Authorities intercepted many of the letters, including those addressed to election offices in Ohio , Minnesota and Connecticut . But in places like Oklahoma , Arizona and Delaware , the letters arrived and prompted evacuations. What's inside Many letters contained a white powder-like substance. So far, preliminary testing of the powder has found no hazardous materials. Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) and Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) also reported receiving suspicious letters but did not disclose their contents. Nebraska officials received a letter that they didn't open and instead turned over to the FBI for further analysis. Flashback: The Capitol Police's notice went out on the 25th anniversary of the anthrax attacks that terrified Capitol Hill in the wake of 9/11. On Oct. 15, 2001, a staffer opened an anthrax-laced letter in then-Senate Majority Leader Tom Daschle's office, forcing the Hart Senate Office Building to close for months. Anthrax attacks killed five people that year. Where are they coming from Law enforcement has not yet determined where the letters are coming from or if they're part of a coordinated attack. The FBI declined to say if the letters are linked, nor are they confirming "specific instances or letters." However, the bureau told Axios in an emailed statement it is working to identify whoever sent the letters. Worth noting: Some of the letters claimed to come from the Democratic Socialists of America, the left-wing insurgent organization that denies any involvement. Some letters bore a New York City return address that DSA previously used but has not occupied since 2013, a spokesperson said . DSA did not respond to Axios' request for comment. events.title: Google has joined Amazon in attacking Nvidia’s stronghold with AI app developers
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. On Tuesday, Google announced that TorchTPU, its long-awaited version of PyTorch, is now available as an open-source project. With this, Google joins Amazon in trying to break Nvidia’s stranglehold on the AI industry, where most AI apps are written by default to run on Nvidia’s chips, or GPUs. PyTorch is the popular open-source toolkit that AI app developers and startups use to build, train, and run AI models. It is, by some accounts, used by 85% of the AI apps. PyTorch was originally developed by Meta (then Facebook) in 2016, long before the world had an inkling that LLMs would change the world. At the time, Nvidia’s GPUs were already the standard hardware for AI research, so many of PyTorch’s features were built to work specifically with them. In 2022, Meta turned PyTorch over to the Linux Foundation, a nonprofit that manages many important open source projects. Google’s version, TorchTPU, lets AI apps run on Google’s AI chips, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). It also makes it easy to move existing PyTorch apps to TPUs and, therefore, to Google Cloud. Developers can do this with a simple configuration change and no re-writing of their apps. Amazon made a similar announcement Monday, when it released its own version of PyTorch, called TorchNeuron. TorchNeuron allows AI apps to be ported to Amazon’s homegrown AI chip, Trainium, and to AWS with no rewriting. Amazon also said it going even further in its effort to loosen Nvidia’s hold on PyTorch. It is submitting code to the main PyTorch project that decouples various features from Nvidia’s chips, making it more open to any hardware by default. Google may be one-upping Amazon in a few ways, however. It says it worked directly with Meta, Hugging Face, Inferact (maker of vLLM) RadixArk (maker of SGLang), and others to ensure that TorchTPU’s features and code libraries work well with these popular AI development tools, just as the original PyTorch does. Plus the search giant has launched a dedicated tool, the TPU agent suite , to help developers move their apps to Google’s chips and cloud and fix errors along the way. It even updated its popular LiteRT tool, which runs AI on phones, laptops and embedded devices, to work better with PyTorch AI apps. None of this means AI app developers will automatically ditch Nvidia’s hardware en masse just because they can now easily move to alternative chips and clouds. But Amazon and Google are clearly working to end Nvidia’s advantage. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. events.title: Steven Bartlett started ‘The Diary of a CEO’ with a $100 microphone. Now he says it’s on track for $60 million in annual revenue
events.summary: Steven Bartlett started his podcast with just a laptop and a sock pulled over a $100 microphone. Before there were guests, it was just Bartlett, reading from his diary at 2 a.m. and trying to make sense of what he had written that week. He eventually began interviewing other people about theirs. Now, The Diary of a CEO is one of the world’s biggest podcasts and is on track to overtake Joe Rogan as the most-subscribed podcast on YouTube. The show has grown into a business Bartlett forecasts will generate about $60 million in revenue this year. But growing it has also meant turning down money—including a deal that would have required more advertising and taking the show off YouTube. He described the proposed arrangement as a trade: Accept a large payment, put 12 advertisements in the podcast, and have little say over those ads. “One of the central reasons why I turned down such an offer is because that is four times more ads than I have to put in now,” Bartlett told Fortune’ s Ellie Austin on Fortune Daily . Working with what he calls “fragmentation vultures”—companies seeking exclusive podcast distribution deals—can mean sacrificing revenue or control over the relationship with an audience, Bartlett argued. Instead, he sees the relationship with his audience as worth protecting, even when a lucrative offer like that comes along. The business he aims to preserve already makes money beyond advertising through products, subscriptions, and events. Beyond the podcast ad Bartlett, who dropped out of college to pursue entrepreneurship, launched The Diary of a CEO in 2017 by turning his own diary entries into podcast episodes. He later began interviewing other people about their own diaries, finding it more intellectually stimulating to learn about their own lives than to read about his own. Those conversations explored his guests’ motivations, insecurities, and ambitions, eventually broadening the show’s scope to subjects ranging from neuroscience and psychology to performance and sports.  And with it, the business has expanded too. When asked where the show’s projected $60 million comes from, Bartlett pointed to brand partnerships, products his business owns and manufactures, subscriptions, memberships, and events. On top of that, he runs an investment fund.  “It’s a wide range of things and again, this goes to the point of diversification,” he said. Steven.com, Bartlett’s holding company, houses the podcast and his other creator businesses. It also includes other creators, helping them build media brands and develop products and ventures. Bartlett forecasts about $90 million in revenue for his broader media company this year, including the projected $60 million from The Diary of a CEO . He also put next year’s holding-company forecast at about $160 million. But he’s not the only person to see nine-figure valuations as a result of the podcasting business: Call Her Daddy podcast host Alex Cooper’s holding company Unwell raised investment at a $500 million valuation in August . Bartlett sees that evolution as part of a wider shift of how creators work with brands. Early in his career, he said companies treated influencers like billboards: Pay them, and they would post something. Then came the creative-director titles, equity arrangements, and opportunities to cofound businesses. That is most evident with Sydney Sweeney, who became an equity partner and creative director at sports prediction market Novig, shaping its advertising rather than just simply appearing in it. He believes the next stage involves creator businesses making acquisitions and operating more like large holding companies.  “You’re no longer an influencer, you’re no longer an equity partner, a creative director,” he said. “You are an owner or cofounder.” The business of audience trust Distribution has become a point of negotiation across podcasting, perhaps most famously in 2024, when Spotify ended Rogan’s exclusivity and allowed his show to stream on rival platforms. Bartlett prefers fewer partnerships, and only with businesses that matter to him personally. About 70% of his podcast partners, he said, are companies whose founders he approached himself.  Choosing sponsors is only one part of maintaining audience trust—what guests say on the podcast matters too. On Fortune Daily, he was questioned about a 2024 BBC investigation into health claims made on his show. He said his team had contracted a full-time medical PhD to review health episodes, adding context on screen and removing material that could not adequately be contextualized. Now, an independent review team fact-checks every episode —not just those focused on health—before it is published.  When asked whether an unsupported scientific statement would be removed from the audio, he said the decision depends on its framing: A definitive claim would be treated differently from a guest discussing a hypothesis based on early research. But despite his growing influence, Bartlett doesn’t consider himself a journalist. He described his interviews as an exercise in pursuing his own curiosity, whether he’s sitting across from Kamala Harris or JD Vance. Viewers will always have questions they wish he had asked, he said, but he believes his approach needs to remain anchored in that curiosity. “If you’re not anchored to, like, your own curiosity, you’re going to be a plastic bag in the wind,” he said. As the business continues to grow, Bartlett’s advice to other creators is to think beyond the next deal—while acknowledging that his own success gives him more freedom to choose.  “If you want to build a durable business in this creator economy, you have to prioritize sovereignty,” he said. “You’re renting your audience at the moment.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: ChatGPT now lets you lock your chats
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. OpenAI announced on Tuesday that users can now lock ChatGPT conversations to keep sensitive chats private when others may have access to their screen or device. Users can secure their locked chats with a four-digit PIN, or use Face ID or Touch ID on supported devices. Unlike the app’s Temporary Chats, which provide a separate session that doesn’t appear in chat history, users can return to Locked Chats at any time. The company says the feature is designed for situations where users might be discussing something personal or planning a surprise and want to keep those conversations private when handing their device to friends or family to show them something in another chat. The addition of locked chats adds a new layer of privacy to ChatGPT, as the app is increasingly used for personal conversations . Of course, while locking a chat can limit access, it doesn’t address concerns about how sensitive information is stored or handled. OpenAI notes that locking a chat doesn’t create end-to-end encryption or a separate encrypted vault, change how long it retains the chat, remove information that ChatGPT remembered before a chat was locked, or change the “Improve the model for everyone” setting. Once users lock a chat, it moves to a dedicated “Locked Chats” section, where it’s kept separate from regular chat history, pinned conversations, and chat search results. With Memory enabled, Locked Chats has its own separate memory shared across conversations within the section. New messages sent after locking a chat can update that memory, but don’t update regular Memory. That means new information from locked chats won’t leak into regular chats. OpenAI says resetting a PIN permanently deletes all locked chats, files, and other content protected by the previous PIN. Additionally, the Locked Chats option isn’t available for temporary chats, archived chats, group chats, chats created from a shared link, chats with scheduled tasks, and chats with meeting recordings. Locked Chats will be available to users on ChatGPT Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu plans. The company notes that the feature is not available on ChatGPT for Healthcare. The feature is starting to roll out on Tuesday, so it may not be live yet for all users. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Loan of $20m to troubled smelter deemed high risk, govt went ahead anyway
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Tasmanian government advised of high risk of loaning $20m to troubled Liberty Bell Bay smelter Topic: State and Territory Government Liberty Bell Bay partly used a $20 million loan from the Tasmanian government to purchase ore. ( ABC News: Maren Preuss ) The Tasmanian government loaned Liberty Bell Bay $20 million to buy ore when the manganese smelter was rapidly running out of money. An internal document shows the government was advised that the loan risks were high. The government is trying to get its money back by selling the ore. The Tasmanian government was advised to approve a $20 million loan to the country's only manganese smelter last year despite knowing the risk of not getting all the money back was high, as inaction was deemed too risky, an internal document shows. The Liberty Bell Bay manganese smelter, in Tasmania's north, closed in July this year and was subsequently liquidated, resulting in the loss of more than 200 jobs. More than two years earlier, a tropical cyclone damaged South32's GEMCO manganese ore operation in the Northern Territory, hobbling Liberty Bell Bay's access to its main source of ore and sparking a chain of events that would lead to its liquidation. In May 2025, the smelter had entered limited operations due to what its then-owner — UK billionaire Sanjeev Gupta's GFG Alliance — said were ore supply issues, international price volatility and US tariffs. More than 200 workers lost their jobs when Liberty Bell Bay closed. ( ABC News: Kelsey Reid ) A document obtained by the ABC under right-to-information shows in July 2025, the Tasmanian government was told Liberty Bell Bay "may run out of available capital by the end of July" and was given four options. The paper, from Tasmania's coordinator-general John Perry, recommended the government provide an urgent loan of up to $20 million to Liberty Bell Bay — stating there was a "very high risk" the smelter would not be able to restart without an immediate capital injection. Every risk category for loan was rated high The Tasmanian government ultimately decided to proceed with the $20 million loan to allow Liberty Bell Bay to purchase ore and restart operations at the smelter. But the document from the coordinator-general shows his office rated every risk category for the loan as "high". The document stated manganese producers carried "industry and sector risks" including fluctuations in steel demand and pricing — as manganese is used to make steel — exchange rate volatility, supply chain disruptions, geopolitical instability, and environmental regulations. Liberty Bell Bay's administrators ordered its closure in July. ( ABC News: Maren Preuss ) It also stated there was a "high risk that the value of security provided would not be sufficient to cover the outstanding loan amount" — meaning the government may not see the full value of the loan returned. But ultimately, the document stated the risks of Liberty Bell Bay's closure were greater. Doing nothing considered riskier than loan The paper from the coordinator general canvassed three other options, in addition to the $20 million loan. Option 2: provide a staged financial support package with an immediate $20 million loan. Option 3: support a "solvent" sale of Liberty Bell Bay through US-based private equity firm White Oak. Option 4: provide a smaller loan, conditional on security strong enough to force administration of the smelter. Liberty Bell Bay was Australia's only manganese smelter. ( Supplied ) "Do nothing" was deemed a "significant risk" to the smelter, with the paper estimating its closure could impact the state economy by $500 million a year if it failed to reopen. Option 3, the sale of the smelter through White Oak, was considered "more than what is required" and "does not represent good value for money for the Tasmanian government". The paper said option 4 would have enabled the Tasmanian government "to take control of the business" but was "fully expected this is likely to be unpalatable to GFG". Liberty Bell Bay said it was solvent at time of loan Minister for Business, Industry and Resources Felix Ellis said the government stood by its decision to loan Liberty Bell Bay $20 million to give "its workers the best possible chance of a future". "We understood the risks were present, but the released documents show the advice was that the consequences of doing nothing were greater," he said in a statement. Felix Ellis says the Tasmanian government will recover funds through the sale of the ore.
