events.title: Mike Bloomberg spent $80M to boost Democrats in midterms: NYT
events.summary: Former New York Mayor Mike Bloomberg spent $80 million in September and October to help Democratic candidates in November's midterm elections, The New York Times reported. The billionaire's contributions are part of a Democratic effort to regain majority control of the House of Representatives in the upcoming midterm elections. President Donald Trump has vowed to spend $400 million to help Republican candidates this election cycle. Mike Bloomberg spent $80 million in September and October to help Democrats regain majority control of the House of Representatives in the upcoming midterm elections, The New York Times reported Tuesday, citing his team. Shortly after The Times published its article about Bloomberg's campaign spending, his fellow billionaire, President Donald Trump , in a social media post reiterated his vow to spend $400 million to boost Republican candidates. The dueling announcements came as Republicans are increasingly worried about retaining their majorities in both chambers of Congress. Many political analysts expect Democrats to win control of the House, and multiple polls show Democrats within reach of winning a majority of seats in the Senate. Bloomberg "is of the view that resources matter in campaigns," his political advisor Howard Wolfson told The Times. Bloomberg, a former New York City mayor, "expects a result," Wolfson said. With the $80 million in spending, Bloomberg is among the top five largest individual Democratic donors according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings for the 2025-2026 election cycle. Wolfson did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC. Before Tuesday's announcement, Bloomberg was known to have donated $23 million to Democrats and affiliated causes this election cycle, according to Federal Election Commission records through Tuesday. As of the beginning of October, Bloomberg had put $11 million behind a super PAC supporting Micah Lasher in New York's 12th Congressional District and $2.5 million toward Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro's reelection, according to campaign-finance records . Trump waives broad new Russia sanctions and tariffs under Graham Act 2026 midterms money race: Democrats surge as Musk backs Republicans Why Trump and GOP's billion-dollar midterm election blitz isn't working Trump, in a Truth Social post, said that he and his affiliated political action committee have spent more than $300 million to help Republican candidates with advertising, voter contacts, rallies and turnout efforts. Trump promised that his spending will top $400 million by Election Day, Nov. 3. FEC filings as of Tuesday afternoon so far show roughly $200 million in identifiable spending and ad reservations tied to Trump's political operation, leaving a gap between what's publicly visible and Trump's broader claim. In September, Trump said he had " close to a billion dollars " in his super PAC, MAGA Inc., and planned to spend $400 million to $500 million on the midterms. At the time, MAGA Inc. reported about $403 million in cash on hand — less than half the amount Trump cited.

events.title: Andy Burnham faces climate revolt after approval of North Sea gas drilling
events.summary: Jackdaw gasfield announcement signals UK’s commitment to North Sea industry but undermines green credentials What does the approval of the Jackdaw gasfield mean? The Jackdaw gasfield will be given the go-ahead on Wednesday, signalling Andy Burnham’s commitment to the North Sea fossil fuel industry and threatening to trigger a row with climate campaigners and Labour MPs. Miatta Fahnbulleh and John Healey, the energy secretary and chancellor respectively, will make the announcement from Aberdeen on Wednesday morning after more than a year of deliberations over whether doing so would violate the UK’s climate commitments. The approval for drilling at one of the biggest undeveloped fields in the declining North Sea basin is a big boost for Britain’s oil and gas industry – and especially for Shell and the Norwegian company Equinor, which operate it. It will be met with outrage from climate campaigners, who say it undermines Labour’s green credentials and will exacerbate the climate crisis. Tessa Khan, the executive director of the anti-oil campaign group Uplift, said: “Jackdaw will provide around just 2% of our gas demand for roughly 10 years. It has been oversold and won’t stop the overall decline in North Sea jobs, as it will be largely unmanned and operated remotely.” She added: “Labour’s climate credibility is on the line. No new oil and gasfields are compatible with safe climate limits.” When fully operational, Jackdaw will account for 6% of North Sea gas production, making it one of the biggest gasfields not yet under production. Along with the Rosebank oilfield, its status has become symbolic of the government’s commitment to the oil and gas industry, which is facing heavy job losses as reserves decline and platforms become increasingly automated. The field was approved by the Conservative government in 2022, with ministers arguing it would help shield the UK from the volatility in the energy market caused by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Labour came to power in 2024 on a promise not to grant any new licences in the North Sea, not expecting to have to make a decision on Jackdaw or Rosebank. However both fields were cast into doubt last year by a landmark ruling that said their environmental approval had been incorrectly granted. A judge ruled that when deciding whether the two fields would violate the UK’s climate commitments, regulators should have taken into account the carbon emissions generated by burning the oil and gas they would produce. Shell and Equinor resubmitted their application for environmental consent last September. Since then, Fahnbulleh and her predecessor, Ed Miliband, have spent months deciding whether to use their ministerial power to block it. Both the prime minister and his predecessor, Keir Starmer, have come under heavy pressure to allow the fields to go ahead in recent months, not least from Donald Trump, who urged both men to “open up the North Sea”. Burnham signalled he was sympathetic to the US president’s arguments earlier this summer, promising to take a “pragmatic approach” to the decision. “There is a resource there,” he said in July. “When people are struggling – you can’t ignore that.” He told the Commons last week: “I will take a pragmatic approach on oil and gas. We will set out our decisions shortly.” Several sources have told the Guardian that Fahnbulleh has decided not to block the field, allowing the North Sea Transition Authority (NSTA), which regulates the industry, to give the go-ahead based on financial and logistical concerns. Making the announcement alongside Healey and the NSTA’s chief executive, Stuart Payne, they will say that granting the environmental approval does not violate Labour’s manifesto commitment because it is not a new licence. Fahnbulleh is understood not to have made a final decision on the larger Rosebank field, but energy department officials are looking at ways the tax proceeds from the project could go to green projects if it was given. A decision is expected later this year. The Jackdaw announcement could boost Labour’s position in north-east Scotland, where much of the industry is based and where unions have been campaigning heavily for the permits to be granted. But it is likely to cause angst among some Labour MPs, especially those in seats where they face a challenge from the Green party. A poll by Savanta for the climate group E3G and seen by the Guardian shows that nearly a third of voters say they would be less likely to vote Labour if it gives the go-ahead for more North Sea oil drilling. That includes almost exactly a third of those who voted Labour at the last election, and around half of 18- to 24-year-olds. Ellie Mae O’Hagan, the UK energy programme lead at E3G, said: “After a summer of deadly heatwaves, the public has made up its mind: more drilling is the wrong answer.

events.title: Secret review into Seven West Media reveals 'diabolical' culture problems
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Seven West Media sexism and bullying allegations detailed in secret 2024 review into company culture One staff member told the review they saw a manager throw a chair at another employee. ( Getty Images: Brendon Thorne/Bloomberg ) A 2024 review found allegations of sexism, bullying and a toxic culture at Seven West Media. The review was commissioned after court claims the company reimbursed Bruce Lehrmann for drugs and sex workers to secure an interview. The company's new owner says it has since had a "cultural reset". A bombshell review of Seven West Media in 2024 has been told of a "diabolical" corporate culture, with allegations that sexism, bullying and harassment were rife and "sacred cow" executives favoured by then-chairman Kerry Stokes were protected amid a ratings obsession. The ABC has seen a copy of the 65-page review, conducted by independent consultancy Interchange. It was concluded in July 2024 and has never been made public. The review was commissioned by the former Seven West board in May that year in the wake of Federal Court claims by former Spotlight producer Taylor Auerbach that the network had reimbursed ex-Liberal staffer Bruce Lehrmann for drugs and sex workers in order to secure an interview with him. Former producer Taylor Auerbach's claims to Federal Court were partly why the culture review was commissioned. ( AAP ) Mr Auerbach acknowledged he had never seen an invoice for this and Seven vehemently denied the claims, saying it was "appalled" by them. Former Seven chief executive James Warburton resigned in April 2024 following those claims as well as the network's on-air misidentification of the Bondi stabber , and was replaced by Jeff Howard . Mr Warburton had previously announced his intention to step down in June. Kerry Stokes was chairman of Seven West Media at the time of the review. ( ABC News: Andrew O'Connor ) Mr Lehrmann was ultimately found by the Federal Court, on the balance of probabilities, to have raped colleague Brittany Higgins in a federal Parliament House office in 2019. That finding was made as part of a defamation trial and remains untested in a criminal court. Mr Lehrmann has denied the rape allegation. The Interchange review into the network's corporate culture interviewed Kerry Stokes and the rest of the board, as well as half a dozen advertising clients and agencies, and did 127 interviews or small focus groups with Seven employees across Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Perth. Interchange also drew on more than 800 responses to a company survey. The report does not suggest that Mr Stokes, Mr Warburton or other senior management were aware of or involved in the alleged incidents discussed by staff. Mr Stokes declined to comment for this story. "Immoral, unethical and illegal behaviour has been prevalent for a very long time," one anonymised NSW Seven West leader told the review. The Seven West Media board commissioned the review in 2024. ( ABC News: Glyn Jones ) Another interviewee said: "There are people in this office every day crying and there is nothing I can do about it." "The culture here is abhorrent … I know the stuff they have been exposed to. Some of them have been touched up; the less pretty ones get verbally abused. Pick your poison. It's not just the girls either, but they cop it the worst." "We've had some diabolical situations culturally, but they've been allowed to keep going," another said. "Certain people in power who have continually abused their position time and time again; nothing happens because they are a protected species." Interviewees told Interchange that they immediately believed the Lehrmann allegations "because of other misconduct they witnessed". Other testimonies in the final report include: "The news guys are ruthless and get away with really bad behaviour because of their legacy and results. People are scared to cross them because they're sacred cows." A senior leader in NSW said: "I think decisions made in the past indicate that people are protected by the Stokes'." One executive said: "The way to leave Seven with very heavy pockets is to behave appallingly". A Queensland leader said: "The ambulance was called due to someone who 'mentally snapped' after an incident of bullying at the office — it included seven senior males piling onto a female". A Victorian leader said: "We are a man's world in media. It is a big swinging dick culture, unfortunately. It's got better than it used to be, but everyone's having affairs, and people are getting ahead because of those things." A Victorian team member said a manager once threw a chair at a colleague.

events.title: At least $963K in trading cards were stolen from a FedEx truck in California
events.summary: Police in California are investigating the theft of trading cards worth at least $963,000 from a FedEx truck SANTA ANA, Calif. -- Police in California are investigating the theft of trading cards worth at least $963,000 that were taken from a FedEx truck parked outside of a company that verifies memorabilia. The truck was broken into on Oct. 13 near Professional Sports Authenticator, also known as PSA, which authenticates trading cards, autographs, comic books, and other memorabilia and grades their condition, Santa Ana Police Department spokesperson Natalie Garcia said in a news release. Pokémon and sports cards were among the items that were stolen, the release said. The driver had left the truck unattended, Garcia said in a follow-up email Tuesday. How long the driver was gone is part of the investigation, she said. The truck's lock was gone and two pallets were taken, she said. A third pallet was disturbed. “The estimated value of the stolen cards at the time of the incident was $963,000. However, the exact value of the stolen items has not yet been determined,” Garcia said in the news release. Nick Andrews, a card collector near Boston, told The Associated Press the value of what was taken could be much higher. PSA's parent company, Collectors, said it has “deactivated the certificates for the stolen cards and notified marketplace partners so they can be on the lookout for rare and serialized items.” The company also said it contacted affected customers directly and arranged for compensation based on fair market value. Both FedEx and Collectors said they are working with law enforcement. “The security of our customers’ shipments is a top priority,” FedEx spokesperson David Westrick said in a statement. FedEx referred additional questions to police. They were worried they would never see them again or receive proper compensation. Andrews, who collects vintage sports and Pokémon cards, told the AP in a phone interview that he was not affected by the theft but has heard from at least two dozen people who were. “Thousands of cards, most likely, and millions of dollars, most likely,” he said of the losses collectors suffered. He said one person who submitted cards for grading on behalf of several people told him that they lost half a million dollars in declared value. PSA's parent company did not get into specifics on losses in its statement. “We understand the impact this has on collectors involved, many of whom see these cards as far more than a financial asset,” the statement from Collectors said. “Our team is focused on supporting them. We take this incident seriously, and we will continue working with law enforcement to hold those responsible accountable." events.title: Right after my ex and I broke up, I started packing my things. Then, we decided to continue living together.
events.summary: I've been living with my ex while saving money and building a life abroad. Aaliyah Alexander I was living with my boyfriend when we broke up, and he suggested that we stay roommates. After looking into my options, I realized that living together might be the best financial move. It was awkward at first, but acknowledging the situation and setting boundaries helped. I met my ex in Spain, on a warm October night in 2024. He approached me as we were both walking home from a boxing class and confidently started a conversation. About two weeks later, we went on our first date . A few months after that, we took our first weekend trip together. In April, he surprised me with a key to his home. By June, I'd moved in. Our relationship was built on genuine care for one another. Throughout our relationship, we always sought to support each other's well-being and growth. Of course, we had bumps here and there, but they were never significant enough to change our respect for each other. That's why, when we agreed to break up in August because we saw our lives going in different directions, I wasn't at all surprised that we found a way to continue living together. We broke up, but I stayed at my ex's house I normally wouldn't have continued living with an ex, but it felt like the best option. Aaliyah Alexander Under normal circumstances, I would've moved out as soon as possible. I've always believed that you can't start to heal from a breakup until you cut all ties and communication with your ex. So, I bought the boxes, tape, and bubble wrap, started looking for apartments , and began packing. But then two weeks later, I lost a freelance contract that contributed a significant portion to my income. This, coupled with the fact that I was already in the middle of a lengthy visa process to make Spain my long-term home, only added to the stress of going through a breakup. Seeing the distress I was enduring, my ex sat me down and suggested that I continue to live with him until I was able to get back on my feet again. My first thought was that people would think I was out of my mind for choosing to live with an ex . Then, I started weighing the pros and the cons. If I stayed, housing would be one less thing I'd have to worry about … but every day, I would have to see someone I'd just broken up with. Worst of all, I'd have to treat my ex like a roommate, as if we didn't just spend the past two years in an affectionate relationship. If I decided to move out, I wouldn't have to see my ex every day, and I could focus on healing my broken heart alone — but I'd be in a tough financial situation. Unlike my ex — who's lenient and open to pulling some extra weight when I can't make rent or contribute 50/50 on utilities — I knew that a landlord wouldn't necessarily care about my personal situation once the first of the month rolled around. I chose to keep living with him. At first, there was an adjustment period Having honest conversations and setting boundaries helped. Aaliyah Alexander Those first few weeks were awkward. We'd already had separate bedrooms because of my ex's insomnia, but the changes to our routines and interactions felt foreign. Instead of getting a text inviting me to come cuddle with him on Sunday mornings, my phone remained silent. Instead of getting ready and walking to the gym together in the afternoon, I started going in the morning. Instead of sitting down to have dinner together, we ate at different times in different rooms. Whenever we saw each other, we would force a smile, say hi, and go our separate ways. We didn't acknowledge the strangeness of our situation until one moment broke down the barrier. I was used to having crying sessions in my room, but this time, one snuck up on me while I sat in the living room. The stress of my breakup, finances, and living situation had just built up too much. My ex was passing through the living room when he saw me crying and gently asked if he could give me a hug. I nodded. This interaction prompted us to finally discuss the elephant in the room (well, house): Living with your ex is weird. Simply addressing the situation and talking about how we were both coping instantly made it feel a little bit lighter. We found a new way to live together What followed was a conversation about how we wanted living together to look like. We knew we were doing something unusual, which was daunting, but also meant we were free to make our own rules. Our first decision was to stop acting like strangers. Barely acknowledging each other's existence just didn't work for us, so we welcomed a level of friendliness into our new relationship. Then, we decided we'd continue offering each other a certain level of emotional support. My ex recently took a leave of absence from work to heal from burnout and contemplate his next career move. Meanwhile, I was struggling to find full-time work and sustain the life I was building abroad. Being there for each other when one of us needed a listening ear felt important. Lastly, we agreed not to cross any lines that would confuse the other person. We weren't in a romantic relationship anymore, so we decided that any affection beyond a friendly hug would be prohibited. With this, our living situation went from something that felt unbearable to something that works for us. In the next few months, I plan to save enough from my freelance work to move out. Until then, I'm happy knowing I have a home, even if it's with my ex. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Traders are betting Netflix's stock drama may be coming to an end
events.summary: Current options prices are implying a 9% post-earnings move for Netflix. This time around, a hint of optimism is replacing what has become an almost automatic quarterly disappointment. The stock has had a median move of 7.25% over the last eight quarters. A slumping stock price. C-suit shakeups. Corporate layoffs. A failed takeover bid. It's not a new drama on Netflix, but rather the drama that has surrounded the streaming giant as it limps into earnings with its stock nearly off 50% from its all time highs. Option traders are betting the drama might be coming to an end. Current options prices are implying a 9% post-earnings move, which is the highest since its Q3 2022 report, when it was priced for an 11% move. Netflix shares beat that implied move that quarter surging 13%. This time around, a hint of optimism is replacing what has become an almost automatic quarterly disappointment. The stock has had a median move of 7.25% over the last eight quarters. As of 12 p.m. ET on Tuesday, one-and-a-half times more calls had been bought than puts in Netflix, while more puts had been sold than bought on more than 150% of average daily volume. Six of the ten most-bought contracts were calls, with five of those expiring this Friday. When traders sell puts, its a bullish strategy. The single largest trade on Netflix's tape was a seller of a string of Nov. 20 expiration 70-strike puts for a total of just about $2 million. Notably, those contracts are right at the money, making this trade a major vote of confidence for a stock desperately in need of some reassurance heading into this afternoon's print. There was also notable call buying of the 80-strike calls expiring this Friday. Traders bought more than 3,500 of those contracts for more than $210K worth of premium. For context, that would require Netflix stock to surge at least 20% by Friday to break even, a jump of more than double its implied move to the upside. Trader appear to be betting that Netflix earnings losing streak could be ending shortly.

events.title: Trump sued over 50% tariffs on Canada in latest trade challenge
events.summary: A new lawsuit challenges President Donald Trump's 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods. The suit by the Gellert Global Group, a New Jersey food importer, asks the U.S. Court of International Trade to declare Trump's "Section 338" tariffs unlawful and order refunds for duties already paid. Gellert Global is represented by the Liberty Justice Center, the same legal group that dealt a major blow to Trump's trade agenda by successfully contesting his "reciprocal" tariffs at the Supreme Court. A new lawsuit filed Tuesday challenges President Donald Trump 's invocation of a Depression-era law to impose 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods . Trump in July used Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to slap those steep tariffs on Canadian hockey sticks, wine, honey, wigs, and other products in response to alleged trade discrimination by Ottawa. It was the first time the 96-year-old law had ever been used to impose a tariff. "Section 338 is a relic of the retaliation-based tariff policy" that has been "impliedly repealed" by subsequent legislation, the civil complaint filed in the U.S. Court of International Trade says. The suit was filed by Gellert Global Group, a New Jersey-based food importer that says its cheeses are covered by the tariffs. The complaint asks the court to declare the tariffs unlawful, block their enforcement, and order the Trump administration to issue refunds for duties already paid, with interest. Trump waives broad new Russia sanctions and tariffs under Graham Act 2026 midterms money race: Democrats surge as Musk backs Republicans Why Trump and GOP's billion-dollar midterm election blitz isn't working Gellert Global is represented by the Liberty Justice Center, the same legal group that dealt a major blow to Trump's trade agenda by successfully contesting his "reciprocal" tariffs. The Supreme Court struck those tariffs down in February. The administration is in the process of refunding the estimated $166 billion that the federal government collected from importers through the reciprocal duties. The Liberty Justice Center is currently engaged in two other lawsuits against what it says is Trump's misuse of laws to impose sweeping tariffs. "This case is not about the president. It is about the presidency," the group's CEO Sara Albrecht said in a statement Tuesday morning announcing Gellert Global's suit. "No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required." The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on the suit. Trump on July 20 signed three presidential proclamations targeting different sets of Canadian imports with the Section 338 tariffs in response to alleged unfair treatment in the U.S. motor vehicle , alcohol and dairy sectors. The tariffs took effect Aug. 22, after last-ditch trade talks with Canadian officials in Washington fell apart. Canada later retaliated with "dollar for dollar" tariffs on U.S. goods. Tuesday's lawsuit argues that even if the 1930 tariff law is upheld, the Trump administration did not meet the legislation's requirements when it imposed the duties on Canada. It says that the law permits tariff action "only upon finding 'as a fact'" that a foreign country is unequally imposing unreasonable charges or trade limitations on U.S. products, or that its customs rules otherwise unfairly disadvantage the U.S. "Even then, the President may impose only such duties 'as he shall determine will offset such burden or disadvantage,'" the lawsuit states. But the Canadian actions cited in Trump's proclamations "do not discriminate against the United States," it says. Two of those actions are "Canada's responses to the President's own tariffs, including tariffs the Supreme Court has held unlawful, and retaliation is not discrimination," the lawsuit contends. Another centers on dairy quota terms that were negotiated in USMCA, the U.S.'s trilateral trade deal with Canada and Mexico. Those terms "give American cheese better access to Canada than the cheese of most of the world receives," the suit states. The suit says Gellert Global boasts more than $1.7 billion in annual revenue. In 2025, the company imported $71 million worth of Canadian cheese — including sheep's and goat's milk cheese, mascarpone, brie, camembert and the hybrid cheese borgonzola, the complaint says. Gellert says it paid no tariffs on its imports of Canadian cheese under USMCA. The Trump administration said in July that it would not renew that trade pact for another 16-year term. Under the Section 338 tariffs, "Gellert now pays a 50 percent duty on the entered value of its Canadian cheese, an estimated $40 million per year," according to the suit. While it plans to absorb the costs through the end of the year, the situation is "not sustainable long term," the company says.

events.title: Google resolves cloud outage affecting UK banks and websites
events.summary: Google Cloud says it has resolved disruption at its UK cloud site which caused an outage affecting UK banks, businesses and the courts. The company, one of a few large cloud computing firms whose infrastructure and services underpin many online platforms, reported an "issue with multiple services" at its London data centre complex "europe-west2" early on Tuesday. Revolut, Lloyds Bank and HSBC were among popular UK services that confirmed disruption on Tuesday morning, after thousands of reports of problems were raised by users online. The tech giant apologised to those affected and thanked customers for their patience. "We have resolved a disruption to Google Cloud services at a third-party facility in our europe-west2 cloud region due to a power event," a Google Cloud spokesperson said in a statement on Tuesday evening. They added that the company would publish an analysis of the incident on its service health dashboard , external , where it provides customers with updates about the status of its cloud services globally. Cloud computing giants like Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud make their services available to clients in local or regional sites around the world, which they call "regions", containing their data centres. In updates to its service dashboard on Tuesday morning, Google Cloud had said a number of its cloud services were "experiencing elevated errors and intermittent network failures in europe-west2 region" - its UK cloud facility in London. It later said that the issues had stemmed from a "power event" within one of its smaller data centre zones, europe-west2-b. These seemingly affected a host of popular UK platforms and services, with customers flagging issues with sites including Royal Mail, DPD and e-bike service Forest. The HM Courts and Tribunals Service also said it was aware of an issue affecting the video platform used for remote hearings. Banks appeared to be among the most badly affected, with customers reporting problems ranging from being unable to access funds abroad to struggling to complete a property purchase. Rachael Ellen, 25, a Revolut customer from Glasgow, told BBC News she was left unable to access her money. "Today I was unable to pay for my parking at a shopping centre because my Revolut account wasn't working properly," she told the BBC. "This left me in a difficult situation as I had no way to access the money I needed at the time." She said the outage also meant she could not view a transaction from a relative and was told by the app's help bot that there were no pending incoming transactions. "It's frustrating not knowing where the payment is or when I'll receive it," Rachael added. Rachael Ellen said the outage caused her "real inconvenience" when she couldn't access her funds on Revolut More than 1,500 reports of issues affecting Revolut services were flagged to platform outage monitor shortly after 08:00 BST on Tuesday. A spokesperson for the company said some Revolut services were disrupted earlier as a result of the Google Cloud outage. "We can confirm that services are now fully restored. Our customers' money and data are safe and remained safe throughout. "We apologise for any inconvenience caused." Customers of Lloyds Bank, Halifax and Bank of Scotland - all owned by the Lloyds Banking Group - also reported issues affecting some online banking services. A Lloyds spokesperson did not confirm the cause of issues affecting some of its services, but told the BBC later on Tuesday "we understand the root issues have been resolved, so we expect all our services to be back to normal soon". Guy Baybutt, who works for a family-run business The Veg Box Company also said he was "severely affected" by Tuesday's outage. Baybutt, who is from Preston, told the BBC the firm - which supplies fresh fruit, vegetables and other produce to customers across the UK - could not access its website to download and process customer orders amid the technical issues. "We were also unable to book parcels onto DPD's system for collection, meaning orders that should have been dispatched today were at risk of being delayed," he said. "To make matters worse, customers were unable to access our website to place new orders, meaning we lost valuable sales during the outage." He said that such disruptions can have "serious financial consequences" for small businesses like his own. "We don't have the resources of larger companies to simply absorb lost revenue, particularly when we're dealing with fresh, perishable produce that needs to reach customers promptly," Baybutt added. Guy Baybutt told the BBC its services had recovered, but it was frustrating "that a technical failure completely outside our control brought so much of our business to a standstill" Tuesday's incident came exactly one year after more than 1,000 sites, including UK banks, were knocked offline for hours during an outage at AWS' largest cloud site .

events.title: The Wall Street Journal has been planning a big push into streaming TV, and courted Feed Me's Emily Sundberg for a show
events.summary: Emma Tucker has been involved in a video push at The Wall Street Journal. John Nacion/Variety via Getty Images The Wall Street Journal has been planning a big streaming TV push with an ambitious slate of shows. It's explored shows around editor in chief Emma Tucker and creators like Feed Me's Emily Sundberg. Sundberg dropped out of talks a few weeks ago, Business Insider has learned. The Wall Street Journal has been ramping up its push into video and had plans for an ambitious slate of streaming TV shows. Internal documents viewed by Business Insider described an initial six-series offering that would include a flagship live morning program and an interview show hosted by the Journal's editor in chief, Emma Tucker . The docs are from the summer, and a person familiar with the Journal's strategy said that its plans, including dates and partners, are in flux. The docs said the Journal had been "in negotiations" with creators such as Feed Me Substacker Emily Sundberg, as well as with the restaurant discovery platform The Infatuation . Sundberg dropped out of the talks a few weeks ago, Business Insider has learned. The plans called for the shows to launch on the Journal's own channels, YouTube, and social media. Journal parent company Dow Jones is also hiring a head of programming and content, who would be tasked with building "something ambitious in video." The live job description says the role will pay up to $330,000 in base salary, and involve developing talent that includes employees and external creators, translating the company's journalism into streaming formats, and creating live and on-demand shows. The Journal and Dow Jones's effort shows how news outlets traditionally known for the written word — including The New York Times — are racing to beef up their video offerings in a media landscape that's seeing both the rise of social video and the decline of cable TV news. It also demonstrates that Tucker is taking a flexible approach to the market by looking to both build shows around in-house talent, including herself, and partner with creators and other media companies. "Expanding our video presence across Dow Jones and The Wall Street Journal is a major strategic priority, as we have widely communicated," a Dow Jones spokesperson said. "We are actively hiring leadership to shape and execute our go-to-market strategy for video across Dow Jones, and we look forward to sharing our updated plans when ready." events.title: Sydney firm linked to suspected scammers investigated, $138m feared lost
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Australian firm investigated over fears investors may have lost up to $138 million Candice Driver is demanding answers over how Main Group FX was licensed to legally offer financial products in Australia. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) Australian investors lost millions to a licensed investment scheme they allege was an international scam with possible terrorism links. They are now asking how it went undetected by authorities and its financial licensor. ASIC is investigating the Sydney company that authorised the alleged scammers to have a financial services licence, but the firm denies due diligence failures. An Australian company that extended its financial licence to a group of suspected scammers is under investigation over fears that its failures cost investors $138 million. More than a dozen Australians claim they were duped by a sophisticated investment scheme called Main Group FX, which appeared legitimate because it had a financial licence. An ABC investigation into the alleged scam found ghost addresses leading to Caribbean headquarters, a famous Australian cricketer acting as ambassador, and an enigmatic chief executive listed as having alleged connections to terrorism. The corporate regulator is now investigating the Australian Financial Services Licence (AFSL) provider company that gave the alleged scam legitimacy by making it an authorised representative. The ABC has traced an alleged ghost investment scheme across the globe and found its enigmatic CEO may have links to terrorism. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) regulates financial services providers through a licensing scheme, but these companies can also act as licensors — supplying an effective sub-licence to others who become their authorised representatives. Sydney-based company MGF Capital holds an AFSL, and its sole director is Matthew Starkey, a former Goldman Sachs trader. Corporate records show Main Group FX was an authorised representative of the parent licensor MGF Capital between February and December 2023. Matthew Starkey declined an interview with the ABC. ( Supplied: LinkedIn ) It is understood Australians may have lost as much as $138 million from financial products they believed were being offered by multiple authorised representatives under the umbrella of MGF Capital, including at least $2 million from Main Group FX. It has sparked fears the alleged criminals behind Main Group FX were effectively given a licence to scam. Main Group FX is alleged to be a sophisticated investment scam. ( ABC News: Guido Salazar ) Do you know more about this or have a similar story? Email turner-cohen.alex@abc.net.au ASIC told the ABC it was "actively investigating" whether there were "oversight, due diligence and compliance failures" related to MGF Capital's corporate authorised representatives. MGF Capital's Matthew Starkey declined an interview and referred the ABC to a lawyer and crisis PR manager, who denied any due diligence failures had occurred, but would not say what checks had been carried out to allow Main Group to be its licensee. Monthly dividends arrive late, then not at all Candice Driver is among 13 investors the ABC knows of who have collectively lost more than $2 million to Main Group FX. The Sydney marketing executive said she was glad ASIC was investigating, but she had "no trust whatsoever" in the system that allowed the alleged fraudsters to have a financial licence. The reason she invested with Main Group was because their financial services licence meant they were regulated by ASIC. Candice Driver is the only Main Group FX customer to get an AFCA complaint in in time against its AFSL provider. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) Ms Driver poured tens of thousands into Main Group FX in 2023 believing she was investing in commodities on a trading platform. By year's end, the company was unravelling, with her monthly dividends arriving late and then not at all. She could not withdraw her cash and felt staff were "making excuses", with two separate workers claiming they had been slow to respond because their fathers were in hospital. An example of Main Group's sophisticated online portal. ( Supplied ) Another financial authority called in Ms Driver reported Main Group's licence provider, MGF Capital, to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA). The complaints body acts as an ombudsman for external dispute resolution between financial institutions and customers. Within days of the complaint, MGF Capital's director, Mr Starkey, contacted her urging her to withdraw her complaint.

events.title: Retired judge lashes NSW decision to rewrite laws to support coalmine
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts The Mount Pleasant coalmine has acknowledged it kept expanding during High Court proceedings over its planning approval. ( Supplied: Nearmaps ) A former Supreme Court judge says the NSW government's decision to draft laws to circumvent a court ruling on the Mount Pleasant coalmine is "reprehensible". The government has denied it is undermining the High Court ruling, but Anthony Whealy says there should be an independent review into the decision. The NSW government will introduce laws to underwrite the mine's expanded capacity, as the court process over its planning approval continues. A former Supreme Court Judge says a NSW government plan to draft special laws for a Hunter Valley coalmine "obliterates" the legal process and should be independently reviewed. The premier has announced the government will legislate to allow the Mount Pleasant mine to continue operating at expanded production rates, despite a High Court ruling against it this month. "The idea that a substantial mining venture can approach the government and say look, let's go behind the court processes and sort this out between ourselves is a very dangerous precedent, and that's exactly what appears to have happened here," said Anthony Whealy, who is now on the board of the Centre for Public Integrity. "They've effectively ignored what I would call respect for the rule of law by overriding it. "It is, on the face of it, reprehensible". Anthony Whealy says there is no evidence 400 jobs are under threat. ( ABC News ) The ABC can reveal the Hunter Valley mine is already being investigated over allegations it breached its coal production limits, as it scaled up construction during the court process. In 2022, the mine was given approval to double its capacity, from 10.5 to 21 million tonnes of coal per year, until 2048. But that approval was deemed invalid after a NSW Court of Appeal ruling in July 2025 that planning authorities had failed to consider the effect of overseas or Scope 3 emissions caused by the 406 million additional tonnes of coal exports over the life of the mine. The Court of Appeal ordered a lower court, known as the Land and Environment Court, to revisit the expansion's approval, which was now "invalid", subject to that lower court's review. But MACH Energy did not want to wait for a decision from the lower court. In August 2025, weeks after the ruling, the company started earthworks to pave the way for millions more tonnes of coal to be produced, in what it described in company documents as "the next phase of the Mount Pleasant expansion". The company lodged a swift appeal with the High Court, and by December 2025 the mine had produced 12.78 million tonnes of coal. The Mount Pleasant coalmine is in the Hunter Valley region of New South Wales. ( Supplied: Nearmaps ) Department increases mine output while under investigation The residents' group that had won the NSW Court of Appeal case, known as the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (DAMSHEG), lodged a complaint with the planning department through its lawyer, Elaine Johnson. By her reading, the NSW Court of Appeal decision meant the company should not be furiously expanding while the matter was still before the courts. And the mine should instead be required to rely on its first planning approval from 1999, which only allowed 10.5 million tonnes of coal to be extracted. A department spokesman told her that it would "consider" her concerns. As the expansion gained pace, Elaine Johnson wrote another letter, and the planning department finally confirmed it was investigating. A close-up of the open pit at the MACH Energy coalmine near Muswellbrook in NSW. ( Supplied: Nearmaps ) "The Department is committed to timely and appropriate compliance action," its letter from August 14, 2026 stated. "Thank you for your correspondence." On the same day, the department announced it would "modify" MACH Energy's first planning approval from 1999, which was not being challenged in court, to increase its 10.5 million tonne coal output to 12.5 million tonnes per year. It also extended the mine's life for another six years, so there was no threat of it closing in December, when the existing 1999 permit was due to expire. The "modification" could be done at the stroke of a pen because it met the "substantially the same development" test, according to a department spokesman. High Court loss puts mine on back foot When the High Court ruled against MACH Energy this month, it threw its expansion plans into disarray.

events.title: United CEO Scott Kirby says he wants a nationwide wealth tax
events.summary: United CEO Scott Kirby said there should be a nationwide wealth tax. Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images United CEO Scott Kirby says he's all for a nationwide wealth tax. Kirby said wealth inequality "has become a danger to our society." While Kirby doesn't want a state-by-state approach, California voters will soon vote on a proposed billionaire tax. United CEO Scott Kirby says "wealth inequality has become a danger to our society." That's why Kirby said he supports a nationwide wealth tax. "We should have a national wealth tax — it won't work by state because people will just move," Kirby recently told The New York Times. Kirby, who lives in the Chicago area near United's headquarters, was one of the highest-paid CEOs of a public company in 2025, according to Crain's Chicago Business. Kirby's 2025 total compensation was valued at over $32 million, according to United's filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Wealth taxes are facing one of their biggest tests yet this November. Californians will vote on what, if approved, would become the world's first billionaire tax. The fight is pitting some of the state's wealthiest individuals against the proposal. Google cofounder Sergey Brin alone has donated $102 million to a group seeking to undercut the proposed wealth tax by proposing competing initiatives that could effectively cancel it out. In addition to a wealth tax, Kirby also said that inheritance taxes should be increased. "We should have inheritance taxes that get close to 100 percent at some level," he said. "I would pay them." Kirby's views may seem unusual among corporate leaders, but others are at least open to the idea of wealth taxes. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang recently reiterated his willingness to pay potentially billions of dollars if California's wealth tax goes into effect. "I don't mind paying taxes," Huang said. "The more you make, the more taxes you pay, so I'm OK with it." Huang, who famously got his start working at Denny's, said he worries about other things. Bloomberg estimates that the Nvidia CEO is now worth $180 billion, making him the ninth richest person in the world. "The fact that I can afford to pay $8 billion in taxes over five years is a privilege," he said. "I'm not afraid of paying taxes. I'm just afraid of being poor." events.title: Exclusive: OpenAI has acquired Orchestra Bio
events.summary: OpenAI has acquired Orchestra Bio, a startup building AI agents to help pharmaceutical companies manage drug development, the ChatGPT maker shared exclusively with Axios. Why it matters: Rival AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic are both pushing into science as they look to expand beyond their core competencies in coding and cybersecurity. State of play: OpenAI will integrate Orchestra's team and technology into Rosalind, its suite of AI models and tools designed for life sciences researchers, the company said. Orchestra's platform allows scientists to delegate tasks like monitoring studies, tracking drug development timelines and identifying potential delays to AI agents. Both companies aim to deploy agents that can connect scientific findings with the decisions and next steps required to advance potential treatments. Financial terms of the acquisition were not disclosed. Between the lines: AI companies don't just want to increase productivity, they want to say they are responsible for, say, curing cancer, solving math, and fundamentally changing every critical industry in the world. Those ambitions have fueled acquisitions from rival AI labs. Anthropic acquired AI biotech startup Coefficient Bio for roughly $400 million in April, according to The Information . Zoom in: OpenAI introduced its specialized GPT-Rosalind model in April to help researchers tackle complex problems in biology, chemistry and drug discovery. OpenAI has also partnered with pharmaceutical giants including Novo Nordisk and Moderna to bring AI into research and development workflows. OpenAI says developing a new medicine typically takes 10 to 15 years, a timeline it hopes AI can shorten. Zoom out Anthropic has been making its own aggressive push into life sciences. In June, Anthropic launched Claude Science , an AI-powered research platform that connects scientific databases, analysis tools and specialized agents. In September, the company announced a new biological research lab and said Claude had helped discover a previously unknown enzyme system with similarities to CRISPR, though some scientists said these finders were overblown, per Bloomberg . The bottom line: The AI race is shifting from building the best models to applying that intelligence across industries. Several AI investors told Axios a key question as AI companies go public is how far they can expand into new markets.

events.title: Elon Musk says 'AI and robots' are the only way to solve America's debt burden
events.summary: Elon Musk said his stint at DOGE led him to this conclusion. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images Elon Musk said that "AI and robots" are the key to fixing America's national debt. On a podcast, Musk said it would be "impossible" to tackle any other way. He predicted "digital superintelligence" could boost the output of goods and services by 20% to 30%. Elon Musk said artificial intelligence and robots — not government spending cuts — are the only way to fix the US national debt problem. Speaking on a newly released episode of author Walter Isaacson's "The Builders" podcast, Musk said his 130-day stint as a special government employee in the second Trump administration led him to that view. Musk, the world's richest person, served as the de facto leader of the White House DOGE office from January to May 2025, where he sought to slash federal spending. "I came to the conclusion that the only way we're going to solve the national debt is with AI and robots. We're not going to solve it by trying to save our way there," Musk told Isaacson, calling the latter "impossible." The US national debt load hit a record $40 trillion in August and has continued to climb, according to Treasury data. "Maybe if the president made that his, you know, primary goal, we could do that, but the problem is if you try to solve the deficit and stop wasteful spending, you make a lot of enemies in that situation," Musk said. The Tesla and SpaceX CEO said political leaders in Washington are mostly unwilling to rein in federal spending enough to significantly shrink the deficit. "The appetite is not there, and it's not just at the presidency. The appetite is not there at the presidency, the House, the Senate, or the judiciary," Musk said. He added, "Basically, no one in authority in the government whatsoever, really, with maybe a few rare exceptions of like the Rand Pauls of the world type of thing, actually wants to reduce spending — no, they don't." Musk estimated that "digital superintelligence" could boost the global output of goods and services by 20% to 30% — an increase he estimated could add roughly $30 trillion a year to the world economy. "If you have robots and you get to space and can do a mass driver on the moon, then you can get to, I think, potentially a million times the size of the Earth economy," he said. This could ultimately make money "irrelevant," Musk said. "There will still be currency, but I think currency will be measured in fundamental physics metrics like wattage and tonnage, mass and energy," he said, predicting, "Conventional currency will not matter." During the interview, Musk also reflected on his chainsaw-wielding time with the Department of Government Efficiency, admitting he got "carried away." "I think I should have been more in the background and probably only had it last for a month or two, because at that point you've sort of seen most of what there is to see," Musk told Isaacson. Musk said he should have left and "focused on AI a little sooner than I did." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: French Government Calls Emergency Meetings With Platforms Over Protests
events.summary: TikTok and eBay were among six online platforms summoned by the French government this week, as authorities sought to contain widespread rioting and looting and prevent the resale of stolen goods. Anne Le Hananff, France’s minister of digital affairs, convened representatives from social media firms on Tuesday for an emergency meeting, after their platforms were blamed for fanning the flames of the worst civil unrest the country has seen in years. The goal of the meeting was to remind platforms that they need to moderate content on their sites, including livestream video, to avoid violent content or anything that could encourage people to break the imposed curfew, according to French TV station BFM . A review by WIRED of TikTok found that the search term “blocus”—meaning blockade in French— showed videos that were potentially altered or AI-generated, including viral images of a protester in a Pink Panther costume. The search term is also being used to promote “Act II” of the protests for October 24. The platform issued an “evolving situation” tag on the search term that said: “This situation is developing rapidly. Information available now may be unverified, incomplete, inaccurate, or subject to change. Take care when viewing this content, and report anything that may violate our Community Guidelines.” A separate meeting, confirmed by Serge Papin, minister for small and medium-size enterprises on X, was held on Monday with major online reselling platforms where “an agreement was signed” to crack down on the resale of looted goods. French newspaper Le Monde reported that Vinted, eBay, Amazon, LeBonCoin, Meta, and TikTok were at the meeting. Platforms agreed to forward reports to investigators, monitor ads for goods stolen specifically during the protests, and send the government reports of their actions, with the first one coming within 48 hours, according to Papin. Peaceful demonstrations against high living costs and strained public services, including schools, erupted into rioting and the looting of more than 1,500 shops and businesses over the weekend. Police “lost control” in some cities, Interior minister Laurent Nuñez admitted, as they responded with tear gas, water cannon, and batons. They have since arrested more than 2,400 people, according to authorities. French penal law can hand down a five-year sentence and a €375,000 fine to anyone who is concealing, possessing, or transferring an item that they know was obtained through a crime or offense. Police issued a warning in the Netherlands that online ecommerce sites could have a higher number of stolen goods online due to the riots. The French Alliance of Marketplaces, a nonprofit representing French online retailers such as Back Market, eBay, Etsy, LeBonCoin, ManoMano, and Vinted, said in a press release that its members are relying on user reports, human oversight, and tech tools to monitor ads that resell stolen goods from the riots. When identified, a fake ad is removed and “measures are taken against the accounts involved,” which could include permanent suspension of the seller’s account, according to a statement from eBay. The time it takes for eBay to take action “depends on the nature of the report and the necessary verification process,” the company said. Vinted, Amazon, LeBonCoin, Meta, and TikTok did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. events.title: Hugging Face CEO says the Netflix doc about its famous hack went 'full doomer mode'
events.summary: Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue criticized the Netflix documentary about his company's hack. Bloomberg/Getty Images Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue isn't a fan of the Netflix documentary about his company's hack by OpenAI's AI agents. Netflix released a short documentary called "AI Gone Wild" in October. Delangue, who was interviewed for the project, called the result "super disappointing." Clément Delangue isn't wild about Netflix's new documentary. Delangue cofounded Hugging Face, an AI startup acquired by Nvidia for almost $13 billion in September. Two months prior, Hugging Face became the face of AI risk when rogue OpenAI agents hacked the business. The hacking saga sparked a Netflix documentary titled "AI Gone Wild." On Tuesday, Delangue criticized the so-called "instadoc" in a lengthy X post. "Super disappointing, as they went for maximum anthropomorphism of the technology and full doomer mode," Delangue wrote. Delangue sat for an interview in the documentary, along with a METR researcher , the director of the AI Futures Project, and two tech journalists. In the X post, Delangue wrote that he spent over two hours trying to correct what he described as the documentary's mistakes. He wanted to explain that AI agents were "technological systems, not aliens." "It looks like the drive to scare people for maximum views was too strong," Delangue wrote. Delangue listed some things the Netflix documentary omitted: the lack of agent containment, how safeguards for OpenAI's closed model blocked Hugging Face's defense, how Hugging Face defended itself with an open model , and "that we still lack a lot of information and transparency including full agent traces and that companies need to remain accountable for what their agents do." Netflix did not respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Some techies responded to Delangue's post with their own criticism of the documentary. Alex Imas , Google DeepMind's director of AGI economics, called Delangue's post "important reading." Brigitte Tousignant, Hugging Face's head of communications, posted on X that the documentary widened the gap between the public's understanding of AI and how it actually works. Tousignant wrote to Netflix: "If you can't tell this story responsibly in 26 minutes, maybe 26 minutes isn't enough." Despite his criticism, Delangue suggested a way to frame the project to make it an enjoyable watch: "It ends up being a fun sci-fi movie though!" Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: UK government to make Jackdaw gas field announcement
events.summary: The Jackdaw gas platform and drilling rig stand east of Aberdeen in the North Sea The UK government is expected to announce a long-awaited decision on whether to approve the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea. It is widely believed in Westminster that Jackdaw will be approved but that a decision on the Rosebank oil field off Shetland will not yet be made. The question of whether to approve the two sites has become hugely politically significant and has been delayed for several months. Multiple Whitehall sources have told BBC News the government would make an announcement on Jackdaw on Wednesday morning with the Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh expected to address MPs in the afternoon. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has spoken repeatedly of the need for a "flexible" approach to energy and is believed to be in favour of drilling more where licensing already exist in the North Sea. Labour's 2024 manifesto pledged not to issue any new oil and gas licences in the North Sea but to honour existing ones such as Jackdaw. Jackdaw, about 150 miles (241.4km) east of Aberdeen, is a gas field which its operators say could be connected to the UK network within months. Rosebank, about 80 miles (128.7km) north-west of Shetland, is Britain's largest untapped oil field, which would also produce some gas. The controversial fields have been the subject of years of debates, legal wrangling and public consultations, with arguments from both industry bodies and environmentalists being weighed up by the UK government. Licences for the fields were granted by the Conservative UK government in 2022 and 2023, which sparked legal challenges from environmental groups. The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that Rosebank and Jackdaw had been unlawfully approved because the government had failed to take into account the climate impact of burning extracted oil and gas from the sites. Environmentalists insist more drilling would be unconscionable, and hamper efforts to cut planet-warming carbon emissions as deadly heatwaves and extreme weather affect people across the globe. They also claim starting production would not protect energy security and transitioning sooner to greener technologies would be better for supporting jobs. Industry bodies argue starting production at Rosebank and Jackdaw will provide jobs and improve the UK's energy security as overseas conflicts threaten supply. events.title: Meta’s Muse hits 10M U.S. downloads in 40 days, a milestone reached by only 11 other apps
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Meta’s AI companion, Muse, is now one of only a dozen mobile apps to have reached 10 million U.S. downloads in its first 40 days on the market. According to new data from market intelligence provider Sensor Tower, Muse has seen 10.9 million downloads since its September debut, 10.2 million of which were in the United States. Only 11 other apps to date have reached this type of post-launch milestone, said Sensor Tower’s Senior Insights Analyst Kara Lee. The most recent of these was Meta’s Threads, back in July 2023. Other apps that saw this kind of scale were largely mobile games, Lee noted, like Fortnite, PUBG Mobile, Pokémon GO, and others. Besides Threads, Disney+ was the only other non-game app to make it into the exclusive club. Meta’s success is tied to the company’s ability to scale its new apps by marketing them across its other services, which it has done with both Threads and Muse. Threads was built on top of Instagram’s social graph, and its content has been integrated into both Facebook and Instagram. However, Muse isn’t only benefiting from Meta’s ability to market the AI agent across its family of apps, which today includes 3.6 billion daily active users; the company is also heavily investing in advertising to drive new users to Muse. Per Sensor Tower’s data, Meta has allocated 39% of its total advertising spend to market Muse in October, up from 23% last month. In addition, Muse now ranks as the 21st largest brand in the U.S. by advertising impressions this month, up from 73rd in September. Still, marketing an app and retaining users after the initial shine wears off are two different things. In this case, Muse is seeing better retention rates than its AI competitors like ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok. In the U.S., the app had a 30% retention rate after 7 days and a 23% retention rate after 14 days. By comparison, its rivals saw an average of a 19% 7-day retention rate and a 16% 14-day retention rate, according to the firm’s data. Muse also hit another milestone that demonstrates active engagement with the AI app. Its daily active users reached 2.5 million for the first time on October 16, a 15% week-over-week increase. Meta’s latest AI app, which can handle various tasks on users’ behalf, has seen breakout success since its debut. It shot up to No. 1 on the App Store, and, at one point, even outpaced some of the metrics ChatGPT saw following its launch. Its latest milestone sees it topping its rivals again, as ChatGPT saw 3.7 million U.S. downloads in its first 40 days on the market. Grok and Claude saw only 500,000 and 200,000 U.S. downloads, respectively, in their first 40 days. Globally, ChatGPT beat out Muse, having scaled to around 15 million global downloads in its first 40 days. But this isn’t a fair comparison, as ChatGPT benefited from a wider reach. Muse is only available in the U.S. and Canada for now, while ChatGPT’s app attracted attention from markets like Japan, Brazil, and Germany, too. (Japan, for instance, accounted for 25% of its global installs during its first 40 days.) Since launching, Muse has retained its No. 1 rank on the U.S. App Store for all days except October 19, when streaming app Kick briefly beat it out. It has since reclaimed the top spot as of Tuesday. events.title: NatWest cracks down on 13,000 staff attending office two days a month
events.summary: Union furious as bank scraps remote-first policy from February 2027, forcing all UK employees to come in at least twice a week NatWest has ordered 13,000 staff to increase their in-office days from two days a month to two days a week, angering its staff union. The banking group, which serves customers under the Royal Bank of Scotland, NatWest, Ulster Bank and Coutts brands, will require all of its nearly 40,000 UK staff to follow a strict two days a week office schedule from February 2027, abolishing a remote-first policy for thousands of employees. Unite said it was a “kick in the teeth” for the 13,000 employees who attend the office only two days a month, and accounted for some of NatWest’s lowest-paid workers, including staff involved in technology, security, data analytics and human resources. The union said the change would pile additional financial pressure on staff already struggling with rising living costs, while undermining flexible arrangements for those with caring responsibilities or disabilities. Many had also structured their lives around flexible working agreements that were expanded during the Covid pandemic, it said. “This is yet another kick in the teeth for workers who have suffered years of real-terms pay cuts and who are struggling to make ends meet,” said the Unite general secretary, Sharon Graham. “NatWest’s decision is completely out of touch with the realities facing its workforce,” she added, noting that thousands of staff would face higher travel and childcare costs as a result. “For NatWest to impose these changes while reneging on existing agreements shows complete contempt for its workforce. NatWest must ditch these proposals and engage properly with its workers.” The bank said its policy was meant to “help teams collaborate,” echoing arguments made by other banks ranging from JP Morgan to Revolut , which clamped down on remote working, saying it harms the training of younger staff . Last month Barclays was forced to push back its return-to-office plans after a staff backlash , backed by Unite. It had ordered staff to come in at least three days a week from early October, up from two days a week. The bank eventually softened its stance and allowed some staff to delay the requirement until next year. Some staff at NatWest – including traders, branch workers and relationship managers – are already required to be in the office four days a week. Others, including its communications, administrative and analytics staff, work a hybrid schedule where they are in six times a month. A NatWest spokesperson said: “Flexible working remains an important part of how we work but we’ve also learned more about the value that spending time together brings for our colleagues and customers – helping teams collaborate, share ideas, build relationships and learn from one another.” The bank added: “We recognise this will be a change for some colleagues and we’re giving them time to plan ahead and will support them through the transition.”

events.title: Ahead of massive IPOs, AI companies are sketching plans to share their wealth
events.summary: As they steam toward massive public offerings on Wall Street, the companies at the forefront of artificial intelligence have begun sketching plans to share their wealth with the public NEW YORK -- As they steam toward massive public offerings on Wall Street, the companies at the forefront of artificial intelligence have begun sketching plans to share their wealth with the public — a commitment they say is imperative to address disruptions the technology could bring to the workforce and people’s livelihoods. Executives at Anthropic and OpenAI have long argued the technology's arrival will bring many benefits for everyday people , and they've promised that will include a share of the profits. The companies are outlining a range of proposals for distributing AI fortunes, but so far they have not resolved key questions over how they would work, how transparent they will be, and who will determine beneficiaries. On Sunday, Anthropic said it would commit 5% of its shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity within the company, pending approval from stockholders. The stake could increase “as the company grows” in the future. The maker of AI assistant Claude said the fund “might explore” larger donations to traditional nonprofits or potentially distribute money to “specific populations.” The San Francisco-based company shared little information about the types of organizations supported by the fund and the issues they will address. One area it will not support, Anthropic said, is lobbying and political giving. Phil Buchanan, the president of The Center for Effective Philanthropy, said he welcomed Anthropic’s commitment — especially at a time when he said some billionaires are “diminishing the importance of philanthropy.” But he cautioned that Anthropic should avoid the “arrogance” of previous technology barons who assumed their professional expertise would translate to philanthropic wisdom. Buchanan recommended the fund support highly effective, existing nonprofits but said it is “hard to talk about any of this because it’s all so abstract.” “I guess I’m hopeful,” Buchanan said, “but I’m not going to get too excited until I see some evidence of what’s actually happening.” Anthropic, which was valued at close to $1 trillion earlier this year , is preparing for an initial public offering as soon as next month that is shaping up as one of the biggest ever. Once a company is public, donations might be made through the selling of future shares, or potentially turning to cash dividends in the future, explained Jay R. Ritter, director of The IPO Initiative at the University of Florida’s Warrington College of Business. The specifics on how charitable donations will be made through Anthropic’s fund are not clear yet. Regardless, Ritter said the announcement now is helpful for potential investors to “know what they’re buying.” Anthropic has already committed $200 million to study the economic effects of AI more broadly. Combined with Sunday’s announcement, Anthropic said roughly 20% of its shares will be dedicated to the “public good,” plus any additional percentage that could be added if the company’s valuation reaches certain milestones. In announcing the benefit fund, Anthropic offered labor market impacts as one example of its philanthropic focus. “AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers,” Anthropic said in a blog post Sunday. It added the fund will have the “versatility” to pursue “bolder approaches” that might be necessary to offset that. The company said it would share more details about the fund's structure and governance in the coming months. In a May interview with The Associated Press, Anthropic president Daniela Amodei said she expected the company’s success would generally lead to more philanthropic support for disease research and “ensuring that everyone around the world gets to share in the prosperity that we hope AI creates.” The companies' pledges have met with skepticism from some critics. “Anthropic is playing games here,” Gary Marcus, a longtime AI expert and professor emeritus at New York University, wrote on social media Sunday. “Trying to curry public favor while still holding control and resisting disclosure is annoying.” Airman killed rappelling from Alamodome's ceiling in Salute to Armed Forces ceremony 'United in grief': 4 dead, 39 injured in explosion at Canadian military training base Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Anthropic and OpenAI are each structured as a public benefit corporation , a designation that requires the companies to pursue not just profit but a social good. OpenAI Foundation, the nonprofit that controls OpenAI, promised to build out its grantmaking capacity earlier this year with a $1 billion commitment. Separately, OpenAI in April proposed the creation of a “Public Wealth Fund” with a stake in “AI-driven economic growth” across companies more broadly.

events.summary: Supermarkets and gas stations in Naples are facing shortages due to week-long protests by truck drivers against high gasoline costs MILAN -- Some supermarket shelves and gas station pumps were empty in the southern city of Naples on Tuesday due to a week-long protest by truck drivers against the high cost of diesel driven up by the Iran war. Protesters blocked the loading and unloading of fresh food and other goods at supermarket distribution warehouses near Naples on Monday, Sky TG24 reported. The truckers are adding their voices to demonstrations that have spread across Europe as the war disrupts economies. One supermarket in the city posted a note on empty shelves apologizing that “some products may be temporarily unavailable or available in a reduced range" due to the truckers' strike. Shortages of fresh pasta, packaged cheeses and meats as well as produce have been reported in Sicily, partly due to stockpiling by shoppers. Partially empty supermarket shelves were also reported in the southern regions of Calabria and Puglia.
