events.title: Microsoft opens a hands-on STEM and AI hub for students at its Grange Castle data center campus
events.summary: Microsoft opens €1m Dream Space hub at its data centre campus in Grange Castle to bring STEM and AI skills to young people in surrounding communities Microsoft Vice Chair and President, Brad Smith, today joined students, teachers and community representatives from Dublin and Kildare at the company’s data centre campus in Grange Castle to officially open its new €1m Dream Space hub. Dream Space @ the Data Centre marks the next step in Microsoft’s mission to create lasting benefits for people living near its current and proposed data centre operations. More than 5,000 students from schools in Dublin and Kildare are expected to participate in learning sessions at the hub over the next 12 months. Providing a wide range of tailored STEM and AI experiences for primary and post-primary students, Dream Space @ the Data Centre will also help to build awareness of the wide-ranging career opportunities that exist in the digital infrastructure sector. Through the new hub, Microsoft is delivering on its Data Centre Community Pledge to be a responsible and supportive neighbour to communities that host its data centres. Since 2018, Microsoft has invested over €6.5 million in Irish communities close to its current and future data centre operations, supporting programmes that advance community prosperity, sustainability and wellbeing and directly benefiting more than 135,000 people. Dream Space was first introduced at Microsoft’s Leopardstown campus, One Microsoft Place, in 2018. Since then, more than 550,000 students have taken part in its STEM and AI education sessions, developing the skills and confidence to become the next generation of digital leaders. Building on Dream Space’s strong foundations in coding, robotics and AI, the new hub at the data centre features a new curriculum that introduces learners to the specific technology and skills needed to support the digital infrastructure sector. These will range from electrical engineering and physical computing to cloud operations. Supported by a mini data centre lab and many other hands-on learning experiences, the facility will bring to life the technology, skills and careers powering the digital world for learners. Microsoft has invested €1m in the development of the new hub. This comes from a €4m investment fund that was set aside by the company in March last year to help ‘Skill Up Ireland’ for the era of AI. An integrated approach to STEM skills development across Dream Space @ the Data Centre and Microsoft Ireland’s other skilling and education initiatives, such as the Collinstown Data Centre Academy, will help to build awareness of pathways into further education, apprenticeships and careers in the data centre and broader technology sector. Brad Smith, Vice Chair and President, Microsoft, said: “We have been part of Ireland for more than 40 years and see it as Microsoft’s home in Europe. As our presence continues to grow, so too has our commitment to creating lasting benefits for the Irish people. Since 2018, we’ve invested over €6.5 million in local data centre communities, benefitting more than 135,000 people. Microsoft ‘s Dream Space is the next step in that journey, giving thousands of young people the chance to experience and understand the technology behind the digital services they use every day, and envision a future career for themselves in Ireland’s digital economy.” Lavinia Morris, General Manager, Microsoft’s EMEA Data Centre Operations said: “Today is an exciting milestone for Microsoft as we officially open Dream Space @ the Data Centre. This new hub builds on Dream Space’s strong foundations in STEM, AI and digital skilling, while bringing students closer to the real-world skills, careers and opportunities shaping Ireland’s growing digital infrastructure sector. “Over the next year, more than 5,000 students and teachers from communities near our data centre will enjoy the hub. Through hands-on experiences in areas such as physical computing, electrical engineering and cloud operations, learners will gain practical skills and direct exposure to the technologies that power the digital world. The new hub will deepen our connection to the local community, helping young people develop vital STEM skills for the future and gain a better understanding of the exciting possibilities that exist in the sector.” To learn more, visit the Microsoft Dream Space website: https://DreamSpace.ie

It’s the moment everyone is waiting for — the ChatGPT moment for robotics, Amulya Vishwanath explained to TechCrunch’s Equity. She is the founder and managing partner of Techable Ventures, a VC firm focused on physical AI, which she started after spending nearly seven years as a product marketer at Nvidia. Before that, she held the same role at a company that was later bought by Intel and was a digital signal processing engineer at Interconnect Systems, which was later bought by the electronics manufacturer Molex. She stopped by Equity to talk about the future of physical AI — one of the industry’s latest buzzwords. “ A lot of companies and experts have been talking about the ChatGPT moment for robotics,” she said, adding that right now the industry was more in a “LEGO era.” “There are a lot of foundational software and building blocks for robotics that are being rethought right now as we speak, and it’s super important in order for innovation to scale,” she continued. Right now, people are building the basics — the robotic hands or the actuators — that can one day come together and build that big-ticket-item, like a bunch of LEGOs coming together. There’s general- and special-purpose robots being built right now too, and eventually, as people continue building them, they will get better and more advanced. “We’ve done this during the internet era,” she said. “We’ve done this long, long time ago with the Industrial Revolution. I think it’s just a matter of time before things fall into place.” “Talent is also going to be very critical,” she continued, adding elsewhere in the convo that talent is still a key definer of the U.S. market. This is one of the “moats” of her firm, she said, helping connect founders to top talent so they can stay competitive right now, as so much talent is going to big companies like Anthropic and Nvidia. She pointed out that she’s built up a strong network to help founders from her years of working in this space. “This just make sit a lot more easier for me to be the strength or the first call for founders,” she said. events.title: Novo's next-generation obesity drug shows 25% weight loss in women in late-stage analysis
events.summary: Novo released new evidence that its experimental CagriSema injection can improve upon the weight loss with its blockbuster GLP-1 obesity injection, Wegovy. The Danish company said its next-generation obesity drug showed 25% weight loss on average at 68 weeks among adult women in a new analysis conducted after a late-stage trial. A second analysis found that the drug was associated with significant weight loss across menopause statuses. Novo on Tuesday said its next-generation obesity drug, CagriSema, showed 25% weight loss on average among adult women in a new analysis conducted after a late-stage trial. The Danish company said further work is needed to confirm the hypotheses of two post-study analyses. Still, the results are the latest evidence that the experimental injection can improve upon the weight loss and other benefits offered by Novo's GLP-1 drug semaglutide, the active ingredient in its blockbuster obesity shot Wegovy and diabetes counterpart Ozempic. CagriSema, a combination of semaglutide and another drug called cagrilintide that targets the amylin pathway, is expected to launch early next year. Obesity drug leaders Novo and Eli Lilly have built new treatments around amylin , which involves a hormone released in the pancreas alongside insulin that helps regulate hunger and fullness, hoping it will give them a new revenue stream beyond existing GLP-1s. In an analysis of roughly 2,300 women with obesity or who are overweight, CagriSema was associated with 25% weight loss on average at 68 weeks compared with 3% with placebo. The results are based on an ideal scenario in which all patients stayed on treatment without interruptions. A second analysis of around 1,900 women grouped by their menopausal status found that weight loss reached 26.7%, 24.8% and 23.1% in premenopausal, perimenopausal and postmenopausal women, respectively, at 68 weeks, if all patients remained on the drug. That compares with approximately 2% across menopause groups with a placebo. Across both analyses, CagriSema was linked to reductions in abdominal fat, based on waist circumference, among women overall and across menopause stages, Novo added. The results suggest that women may experience slightly more weight loss on CagriSema than a broader population of both men and women with obesity saw in the Phase 3 trial. Initial results from the study showed that CagriSema helped adults lose 22.7% of their weight on average at 68 weeks versus 2.3% in the placebo group. However, the majority of patients in the trial — around 67% of roughly 3,400 — were women. Weight gain is very common for women during menopause. Declining estrogen levels can contribute to a slowdown in metabolism, making it easier for women to gain weight and harder to maintain muscle mass. After menopause, estrogen generally remains low and does not return to previous levels. More than 86 million women in the U.S. are 40 and older, according to the U.S. Census Bureau , which are the years in which perimenopause, menopause and postmenopause occur. "Many women with obesity or overweight experience weight gain as they move through menopause, and it is important to explore investigational products such as CagriSema across the reproductive lifespan," said Michelle Skinner Moore, Novo's interim head of clinical development, medical and regulatory affairs. Wall Street has not appeared particularly excited about CagriSema, whose previous late-stage clinical trial results disappointed investors because the drug showed weight loss efficacy below their expectations. Novo, however, maintains CagriSema is effective and differentiated enough from its other drugs to draw significant demand. Analysts expect CagriSema to generate $11.84 billion in sales for obesity specifically in 2028, according to a consensus estimate compiled by FactSet.

events.title: The non-gamer CEO racing to save Microsoft’s Xbox
events.summary: Asha Sharma returns from one of her walking meetings around Microsoft’s sprawling campus in Redmond, Wash., to her relatively new office in the Xbox building, reached via a 1,100-foot-long bridge from the main offices. It’s a brisk early September afternoon, and Sharma is wading through the next series of changes she’ll make at the legacy gaming business. There are more layoffs to complete and more studios to consolidate. Much is still new for Sharma, the 38-year-old executive whom Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella in February put in charge of turning around one of entertainment’s biggest brands. Her office, adorned with Xbox controllers, framed Halo game discs, and a Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater skateboard, at first seems like an odd fit for an executive who famously had zero past video game experience. Yet the Xbox CEO who’s replaced gaming legend Phil Spencer is moving fast. Xbox’s finances have been in shambles while its market share has tanked from its peak years ago. Sharma must fix its economics while improving its brand. She has been blunt about Xbox’s poor performance; has cut thousands of staff members; is reimagining how Xbox markets and sells its products; is upending its tech stack; has divested or reorganized smaller studios; and is focusing Xbox around its biggest franchises and publishing groups, including Blizzard Entertainment. If Spencer was a gamer’s gamer, Sharma is the decisive boardroom boss. Only Xbox’s is a very big, and opinionated, board. Every gaming conference Sharma attends, every decision she makes, and every post she publishes on social media is being closely watched by rabid gaming fans and Microsoft’s top brass. “It’s hard to be a first-time CEO … where everybody sees everything you do,” Sharma told Fortune, sitting in one of her office’s blue velvet chairs, with several packs of NeeDoh stress balls by her side and wedding invitations from fans on her desk. “We are trying to get done an inordinate amount of things in an inordinate amount of time.” The attention, Sharma said, is a reflection of how much Xbox matters to people. “The benefit of everybody caring is that you’re going to be able to pick out things that people really care about to actually make our product better,” she said.  Unafraid to create tensions, the jacket- and sneaker-loving executive has come in clear-eyed and with swagger, indirectly questioning her predecessor’s strategy, and has shown a remarkable knack for marketing that plan with deftly written employee memos , new slogans, and strategic posts on social media, where meme after meme of Sharma also appear. (One deepfake video shows her yelling, “You’re all fired!” to a group of studio employees.) Sharma inside Microsoft’s campus store in Redmond, Wash. MERON MENGHISTAB for Fortune Flashy moves aside, Sharma has a challenging road ahead. Turning around a sprawling $21 billion business that includes hardware, creative studios, and thousands of video game titles is a task that would test even the most experienced of CEOs. And at a time when Microsoft is intensely focused on competing in the AI race, many industry observers wonder how committed the company is to the gaming business, and if Nadella has put Sharma in charge to prepare for an eventual sale or spinoff. For an enterprise software company like Microsoft, a consumer gaming business stands out as a bit of an “odd condiment,” said Joost van Dreunen, a gaming expert and professor at NYU’s Stern School of Business. “How you value, operate, manage, and finance a creative division is very different than most of the other parts of the Microsoft empire.” As Sharma works to revitalize the storied gaming unit, Microsoft employees, investors, analysts, and gamers are all focused on a key question: Can a gaming industry outsider bring Xbox back to its glory days—and if she can, under what structure will that happen? A storied franchise  For all its current challenges, Xbox is a Microsoft success story. In the quarter-century since the software giant launched its first console , Xbox has grown into one of the company’s most visible and influential global consumer brands. Even if you’ve never picked up a game controller, there’s a good chance you recognize some of its hits. There are cultural touchstones like Halo , a first-person shooter game that became a global multimedia franchise spanning a television series, comic books, and toys. There’s Xbox Live , which helped make multiplayer online gaming a mainstream form of entertainment. And there’s the beloved Xbox 360 console of the mid-2000s, which at its peak rivaled Sony’s PlayStation in sales, and on which a generation of young gamers—including this writer—cut their teeth. With Microsoft’s 2023 acquisition of game publisher Activision Blizzard for $69 billion, Xbox gained custody of blockbuster titles like Call of Duty, World of Warcraft , and Overwatch , making it one of the most significant players in a video game market that has ballooned to several times the size of the global theatrical box office.  The fact that Xbox now finds itself in fix-it mode instead of on a victory tour for its 25-year milestone is the result of what current and former employees say has been a series of strategic miscalculations, conflicting internal priorities, and a loss of focus on the basics. Game Pass, a Netflix-style monthly gaming service , helped Xbox build a subscription business. But it also led to a cannibalization of sales for the company’s higher-priced first-party game titles, especially during the critical launch period. And competing internal metrics within different teams—such as subscription revenue versus store revenue—exacerbated the problem, said former employees. As Microsoft acquired more game publishers—including Minecraft -maker Mojang Studios —it didn’t pay enough attention to its core console, which still represents 80% of its business, former Xbox employees said. PlayStation and Nintendo have offered more exclusive titles that lock in gamers. The Activision Blizzard acquisition, in particular, made the overall business more complex and intensified pressure to show returns. The purchase vaulted Xbox to become Microsoft’s third-largest business by revenue. “If there’s any place that we got out of sync maybe in the last five years, it’s not that any one of those [individual bets] wasn’t working. It’s just that we hadn’t connected the dots maybe as well as we should have,” Matt Booty, Xbox’s chief content officer, told Fortune . Bill Gates, then Microsoft chairman, unveils the company’s first Xbox at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas, on Jan. 6, 2001. JOHN GURZINSKI/AFP via Getty Images While Xbox remains one of the three major console platforms, it’s seen a big drop-off. Current-generation Xbox consoles have sold just a little over a third as many units as the PlayStation 5, according to third-party estimates. events.title: As billionaires fight a tax hike, Jensen Huang says paying $8 billion is a ‘privilege’: ‘I’m just afraid of being poor’
events.summary: California is home to dozens of entrepreneurs who have made billions off their companies. Now some are packing up and leaving as the coastal state weighs tax hikes against the rich, but Nvidia CEO and longtime California resident Jensen Huang is happy to pay his fair share.  “I don’t mind paying taxes. The more you make, the more taxes you pay. I’m okay with that,” Huang said in a recent interview with CBS Sunday Morning. “I am the ultimate American Dream.” Billionaires like Google’s cofounder Sergey Brin and former CEO Eric Schmidt have been waging war against Proposition 40 in California: a one-time 5% tax on residents with assets over $1 billion. The state hopes this will increase temporary revenue by tens of billions spread over several years to fund health care and education. And some of California’s ultrarich are fighting back. Tech billionaires have raised more than $340 million and spend more than $1 million daily in a campaign to defeat Prop 40, according to the Guardian. Others like Palantir’s Peter Thiel and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg have already left the state for more tax-friendly areas.  But Huang, the world’s ninth-richest person with an eye-watering $180 billion net worth, isn’t afraid to pay up. The leader of the world’s largest chip company reasoned that his success wouldn’t have been possible without the opportunities America afforded him. He was able to pursue a high-level education, create a new company, pursue his dreams, and meet the people that “made Nvidia possible.” Huang has lived a success story that millions dream of—and he’s happy to contribute to the same system that nurtured his ambitions.  “The fact that I can afford to pay $8 billion in taxes over five years is a privilege,” Huang continued. “I’m not afraid of paying taxes. I’m just afraid of being poor.” Fortune reached out to Nvidia for comment.  Huang urges people, ‘Move to California, don’t leave’ as billionaires flee The “Make Billionaires Pay Their Fair Share Act” was introduced in March by Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) and Sen. Bernie Sanders (D-Vt.). Ahead of Prop 40’s Jan. 1, 2026, residency cutoff, a slew of billionaires left the state. Google cofounders Larry Page and Brin moved their business entities to Florida and Nevada, and Travis Kalanick, the former CEO of Uber , also changed addresses to Austin.  As some billionaires balk at the tax hike, Huang has said that “I haven’t thought about it even once.” Instead, he’s continued to be outspoken about the upsides of living in the Golden State—and called on others to make California their permanent home.  “I say to everybody, ‘Move to California, don’t leave.’ It’s the highest taxes in the world, but it’s okay,” Huang said at the Stanford Graduate School of Business earlier this year.  Aside from having great weather, California is also a hotbed for innovation, Huang has reasoned. Nvidia’s office is located in Santa Clara, right in the heart of Silicon Valley where “the talent pool is,” Huang has said. He argues that it’s a choice to set up shop in the tech hub—and whatever taxes come with operating there, “so be it.” However, Huang isn’t sold on being taxed for everything. While he has no issue with Prop 40, he is skeptical that company robots and AI tokens should be taxed. Microsoft cofounder Bill Gates championed the idea; the tech mogul argued that by not taxing those tools, but still forking over payroll taxes on employee earnings, employers are incentivized to replace humans with machines. In response, Huang said his “remedies will be a little different.” “I’m in favor of taxes,” Huang said in an interview with Fox Business’s The Claman Countdown earlier this year. “And I think that…for anybody who is productive, it’s a great way for us to contribute back to society and the economy. But the fact of the matter is, there are probably lots of different ways to approach this.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Jamie Dimon says CEOs should be more like Ted Lasso instead of like ‘autocrats’—and tell their employees how they truly feel
events.summary: When Ted Lasso took over AFC Richmond, the fictional England soccer team at the center of Apple TV’s hit series, his relentlessly positive attitude and folksy charm made him an unlikely leader. But beneath his optimism was a coach who understood how to bring out the best in people—even when that meant confronting their insecurities, calling out bad behavior, and demanding better. It’s a leadership style that even JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon admitted he’s learned from. “I love Ted Lasso,” Dimon recently told the Wall Street Journal . “He comes in and he doesn’t know anything about football, and he’s just gracious. He’s working with people—their insecurities, their bad behavior, their work ethic—and he’s getting them to function as a team.” The 70-year-old added that Lasso gets at something many corporate leaders struggle with: balancing humility and empathy with an unwavering drive to win. “Most of these companies have huge capabilities, IP, and great people. But a lot of big companies are political and bureaucratic,” Dimon said. “The people would like to get out of that, most of them—but some of the bad people want to keep it that way, like autocrats, they want to keep things suppressed because they benefit from it.” That often shows up when unnamed “terrible companies” have to bring in a new CEO to clean up a culture problem, Dimon said. However, it would suit many to be more like Lasso to begin with—and speak up when there are problems, even if it may not be easy to hear. “A good leader over time figures it out, removes some of the bad ones, and the place starts to shine,” Dimon added. “It can take some time because these bullshitters have been doing it for 25 years, and they’re usually pretty good at it. It’s hard to notice in real time.” Chevron’s CEO agrees with Dimon: The ‘best leaders’ ask questions and listen to others Dimon isn’t the only business leader who saw leadership lessons in the show, now in its fourth season and starring Jason Sudeikis and Hannah Waddingham . Chevron CEO Mike Wirth has also praised Lasso’s approach, particularly his willingness to listen before jumping to conclusions. “In our work, it’s easy to assume we already know the answer,” Wirth told the WSJ . “Easy to think we know what caused a problem, what a customer wants, or what the best option is. But the best leaders I’ve worked with do something different. They ask questions. They listen. They seek to understand before they decide.” That philosophy is central to Lasso’s unlikely coaching career. Hired to lead an English soccer club despite having coached American football, he had to learn a new sport while earning the trust of players who initially doubted him. Rather than pretend to know everything, he leaned on others, stayed curious, and adapted as he went. Wirth said that the same willingness to learn from people with different backgrounds has helped him throughout his career at Chevron, the energy giant ranked No. 21 on the Fortune 500 . “Some of the most important lessons I’ve learned came from conversations with people with different experience than me—in a refinery control room, at a drilling site, or on a trading floor,” Wirth added. “Curiosity creates learning. And learning leads to better decisions.” Lasso’s lessons are embodied in one word: ‘Believe’ There’s also a more academic explanation for why Lasso’s approach resonates with business leaders. Bruce Avolio, professor of management at the University of Washington, sees the fictional coach as an example of a leader who prioritizes learning, humility, and the people around him. “Ted [Lasso] views each situation with childlike wonder and curiosity,” Avolio said in a university Q&A. “He seeks out opportunities for development and performance, while delaying judgment. He transmits genuine humility, which allows others who know more to step in and contribute to the collective potential.” That approach puts people before metrics, Avolio argued, with Lasso focusing on the human dynamics that can be among the hardest parts of leadership to get right. Ultimately, he added, great leadership is about stewardship: creating an environment where people can grow, make their own decisions, and succeed even after their leader is gone. Lasso’s “Believe” sign captures that philosophy in a single word. The message has even made its way into the corporate world: Dimon reportedly brought a version of the sign into JPMorgan’s offices, a fitting reminder that building a winning team starts with believing in the people on it. events.title: Streaming guide JustWatch becomes a streamer itself
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. JustWatch, a company offering a search engine and guide for streaming movies and TV shows, is now moving directly into the streaming business itself. On Tuesday, the company behind the popular guide that’s used by 50 million people is launching JustWatch TV. The new streaming service will feature content from 30 partners and will offer both free and paid tiers, as well as a movie rental store. The media and entertainment company behind the streaming guide, the JustWatch Group, initially announced its plans to venture into streaming last month. At the time, it said partners like Paramount, New Regency, Fremantle, Bleecker Street, and Vortex Media were on board. The company has since announced other content partners, including Cineverse in the U.S., LEONINE Studios in Germany, SND in France, and Altitude in the U.K. The 12-year-old company has long been known for its online guide to movies and TV. Essentially, it’s a “TV Guide” for the streaming era, helping users navigate a landscape where movies and shows move from one service to another, making it harder to keep up with what’s streaming where. Available in 140 markets globally, the guide provides streaming options for more than 500,000 movies and shows across more than 1,500 service providers worldwide. This “where to watch” information and streaming chart data are also used to power some 1,400 partner websites and apps and are valuable to studios, distributors, streamers, and agencies that use the data to target their campaigns across social media platforms like Meta, YouTube, TikTok, and others. Now the company believes there’s an even bigger opportunity to grow its audience data and insights by running its own service. “At a time where there is so much choice, yet with so many people constantly searching for a place to find their favourite film, the series they just heard about, or something exciting that fits them, it is a great moment to be a hub for all things entertainment,” said Quentin Carbonell, JustWatch SVP of Global Content Acquisitions and Strategy, in an email shared with TechCrunch. “By having our own service with titles to watch directly on JustWatch TV, we can grow our already massive audience, while continuing to direct them to all our streaming partners. This is a natural continuation of our mission to contribute to the entire ecosystem, from the big screen to the small one.” The new streaming service will be available within JustWatch’s existing apps and website across 12 markets, including the U.S., Canada, the U.K., Ireland, Germany, Austria, France, Italy, Spain, Switzerland, Australia, and New Zealand. Its free tier will offer a selection of ad-supported titles, while the ad-free version, JustWatch TV Plus, will offer more than 300 ad-free titles in the U.S., as well as other exclusive features, like advanced filters and the option to hide previously seen or disliked titles in the guide. A movie rental store will also initially be available in the U.S., U.K., Ireland, Australia, and New Zealand, with more markets to follow in time. While the ad-supported tier competes with free streamers like Tubi and Plex, the Plus tier will compete with low-cost streamers like Roku’s $2.99 per month ad-free service , Howdy. It will be similarly priced at $3.99 per month or $49.99 for a lifetime subscription. (The latter is an interesting way to price streaming, given the evolving content costs, but JustWatch believes there will be additional value in the data collected.) Paid subscribers will also be able to take 10% off on hundreds of rentals in the JustWatch TV Store, the company noted. Like most low-cost services, JustWatch’s content lineup focuses on older movies and shows, as well as more indie content. Another unique feature is that users will be able to influence the service’s content to some extent. events.title: Plants can speak using electricity, so this startup built an AI model to decipher their language
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Justin Mast’s life was changed by a cyborg plant. A few years ago, Mast was reading through some scientific literature when he stumbled upon research about a houseplant wired to a motorized stand . When the plant wanted more light, electrical signals flowed through the living tissues. A control board sensed the current and wheeled the plant closer to the light source. “I’m like, what the heck?” Mast told TechCrunch. “That was the entry to the rabbit hole for me.” Mast wound up partnering with Lee von Kraus, a neuroscientist who has worked with DARPA, to found Electric Plant , which has been spending the past three years collecting data to build a large language model, Bombadil, capable of interpreting the subtle electrical signals coursing through a plant’s stem and relaying details about the plant’s needs to growers. The founders believe their model could one day lead to a tool that would let people “speak” to plants. “We’re listening more than we’re speaking, but listening’s the first step,” said Mast, co-founder and CEO of Electric Plant. To bring its sensors and Bombadil to market, Electric Plant recently raised an $11.2 million seed round led by Onto Ventures and Climactic, with participation from Ponderosa, Endeavor Catalyst, Ludlow, Michigan Rise, The Fund, Schox VC, and Dug Song. Even in the most controlled greenhouses, farmers and growers don’t have full visibility of what their plants require, Mast said. Traditionally, farmers, growers, and foresters have relied on coarse tools that react to plants’ demands for water, nutrients, or light. And tools like soil probes, handheld spectroscopes, and satellite imagery work well enough, but they leave much to be desired, Mast said. “That technology is sophisticated, but its ability to get at the inside of the plant isn’t very sophisticated. Most of that stuff still lags quite a bit behind the real-time needs of the plant,” he said. Electric Plant had to start somewhere, though, so it used those devices to train its Bombadil model, which is capable of interpreting electrical signals in about 125 different species. “We know the model will surpass a lot of that equipment,” Mast said. The startup’s sensors are also significantly cheaper than existing tools, which generally cost thousands of dollars. “This is tens of dollars,” he said. The sensors, about the size of a regular iPhone folded lengthwise, are attached to a plant using stainless steel screws. The screws must penetrate the cambium — the layer of living tissue just under the bark — to connect to the microvolt changes occurring within the plant. Data collected from these sensors is sent to a base station via a low-power wireless network. Electric Plant only needs a couple sensors per acre for accurate results, Mast said. The data gets interpreted by Bombadil in the cloud, and the results are sent back to the customer, who can use it to, for example, adjust their watering or fertilizer schedules. Mast claims such a system can boost yields while reducing water use by 20% or more. Mast wouldn’t disclose who Electric Plant’s initial customers are, but it’s easy to imagine applications in agriculture and forestry. Bombadil’s first hundred-plus species runs the gamut of plant forms, from ferns, redwoods, and tomatoes to dahlias, Mast said. “This is the most diverse model ever created on biological electrical signals,” he said. “No one’s ever done anything equivalent to this in the animal world.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Homebuilder sentiment is at a 14-year low
events.summary: The AI boom is sucking up all the capital. The Federal Reserve is raising rates to try to cool inflation. And one sector is bearing the brunt of the pain from both: housing . The big picture: The situation is lose-lose for both homebuilders and homebuyers. Builders are facing more expensive capital and bidding for scarce construction-related resources. Would-be buyers are being quoted some of the highest mortgage rates of this century. New September housing starts data out Tuesday morning puts an exclamation point on what has been a slow-moving disaster for a sector that plays an outsized role in the economic cycle and in Americans' basic living standards. By the numbers: The number of housing units started by builders fell 5.2% last month, the Census Bureau said , to 1.22 million. It's down 7.4% year over year and near post-pandemic lows. Starts of single-family homes fell 4.6% to their lowest level since March 2023. Pending home sales fell 7.3% last month, the National Association of Realtors said Tuesday morning, to the lowest since the data was tracked going back to 2001. Homebuilder sentiment fell this month to its lowest level since 2012, the National Association of Home Builders said Monday. State of play: The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate was 7.4% earlier this month, Freddie Mac said in its most recent weekly reading. The rate was briefly higher than that in 2023, but has not been consistently above that level since the fall of 2000. That has kept homebuyers on the sidelines — while a parallel rise in borrowing costs for developers has made it harder for new projects to pencil out. In effect, the bottomless demand for capital from AI hyperscalers and the U.S. government has to squeeze something, and that something has been the housing sector. Residential investment has subtracted from overall GDP for five of the last six quarters. Zoom out: Housing affordability is the crux of Americans' broader dissatisfaction with economic conditions, and all signs point to it getting worse, not better. For all the bipartisan emphasis on increasing housing supply — most prominently in the passage of a law to encourage more building earlier this year — conditions are weighted against a building boom. Housing developers are competing with data center builders for labor and materials like copper, concrete and HVAC equipment. Of note: Restrictionist immigration policy has also crimped the supply of construction workers . "Nationwide, more than one-third of builders reported immigration enforcement activity in their market areas during the past month, causing construction delays and discouraging legal workers from reporting to work," said NAHB chairman Bill Owens, an Ohio homebuilder, in the sentiment release . Between the lines: An unfortunate side effect of relying on Fed interest rate policy for macroeconomic stabilization is that interest-sensitive sectors, particularly housing, take it on the chin when the economy shows signs of overheating. It's particularly problematic now, when persistent undersupply of housing is a defining economic challenge of our age. The bottom line: The current alignment of interest rates, housing supply and construction costs isn't making anybody happy. Builders can't afford to build, buyers can't afford to buy, and even the people sitting pretty with pre-2022 mortgages can't afford to move.

events.title: Paddy Power cuts 1,400 jobs and blames betting tax rises
events.summary: Paddy Power-owner Flutter has announced plans to cut up to 1,400 jobs as its boss claimed the company "cannot fully absorb" tax rises imposed on the gambling industry. Staff based in Leeds and Dublin, as well as workers for its UK and Ireland business at Flutter's Portugal and Romania sites, will be most affected, but what roles are at risk has not been disclosed. The government announced taxes rises on online casino and sports betting, with an exemption for horse racing, in the Budget last year. Flutter boss Kevin Harrington said the tax hikes had "fundamentally changed" the economic model of the UK betting and gaming industry, arguing it had helped "fuel the unlicensed, unregulated market". "We continue to expect these tax increases to have a very significant impact on the overall market," Flutter Entertainment said on Tuesday. Flutter, which also owns Sky Bet and Betfair, employs 28,500 people across the world, including 9,000 in the UK and Ireland. As well as its Leeds and Dublin offices, the BBC understands the cuts could also affect staff based in London and Sunderland, as well as Malta and Gibraltar. Harrington, who is chief executive of the betting giant's UK and Ireland business, said: "As we warned a year ago, we cannot fully absorb a rise of this magnitude without reducing our fixed cost base and therefore must restructure our business so that we can best position ourselves for the future." A government spokesperson said the job cuts were a "commercial decision for Flutter, not the UK government". "However, we understand this will be a difficult time for the workers," they added. Flutter delisted from the London Stock Exchange in August in a blow to the UK, with its shares now solely traded in New York. In its most recent results, the company reported a $299m (£224m) pre-tax loss for the three months to June for its entire business worldwide, compared to a $205m profit in the same period last year. Sales rose 3% to $4.3bn. However, revenues in the UK and Ireland rose by 4% over the period, due to strong growth in online gambling games. Some online gambling tax rises announced in last year's Budget took effect in April. This included remote gaming duty, which is paid on online casino betting, rising from 21% to 40%. General betting duty, paid on the profits made from various forms of sports betting, was kept at 15% in betting shops, but is set to rise from 15% to 25% online in April next year. Betting firms had warned that cost increases would lead to job losses and betting shop closures, but MPs dismissed the warnings as "scaremongering". During the summer, Ladbrokes owner Entain announced job cuts, with news agency Reuters reporting 500 roles were being removed. Punters' winnings from gambling are not taxed in the UK, nor is VAT charged on bets. Flutter said its restructuring plan would cost between $80m and $90m. The company has claimed in previous financial results that the impact of UK tax rises would hit its underlying profit by $320m this year and $540m in 2027, before any savings or restructure to mitigate the impact. events.title: Data center stocks remain under pressure after Korea IPO plunges 30%
events.summary: Elice Group has been compared to CoreWeave, the U.S. neocloud at the center of last week's sell-off. Concerns about overcapacity in computing power amid lackluster AI revenues are persisting. Data center stocks are being squeezed on Tuesday following a lackluster initial public offering overnight from a South Korean cloud company that has been compared to U.S. neocloud CoreWeave. The bearish sentiment spilled into U.S. tech equities before some names clambered back into the green. CoreWeave shares are up 1.6% after dropping 4% just after market open Tuesday; Nebius shed about 1% while Iren was down about 4% in late morning trading. HSBC said in a Monday note that the troubles for the heavily levered CoreWeave are not going away. "Debt market woes and moderating LLM revenues are exacerbating structural concerns for neoclouds ," HSBC analyst Abhishek Shukla wrote. Shukla has a reduce rating on CoreWeave with a price target of $39, implying 36.5% downside. Elice's IPO was small, having raised just $150 million, according to Reuters . Its market cap also equates to roughly $1.3 billion. The company provides a range of AI-related services, including cloud computing equipment, training libraries and application interfaces for businesses. Despite its size, investors are likely looking at it as a a signal of investor sentiment toward the AI build-out. Trouble for neoclouds, which some investors see as the weakest link in the emerging AI value chain, started earlier this month with less-than-stellar revenues reported by the private AI algorithm companies and pressure from higher interest rates. Frontier model Anthropic showed a deceleration in quarterly revenues, with sales dropping from 140% growth in the second quarter to 45% in the third. OpenAI also disappointed, reporting revenue that was $20 billion shy of what analysts expected, analyst Stephanie Roth at Wolfe said in a Sunday note. Profitability concerns for AI algorithm companies were the focus of a report last week from advisory firm Gartner predicting that 80% of neoclouds could cease independent operations by 2030. "Our research indicates that enterprise and consumer AI revenue will be insufficient to support profitable returns on all planned AI capital expenditures" between 2027 and 2030, Will Sommer, senior director analyst at Gartner, said. Gartner stood by its analysis in a Monday interview with CNBC. "At the moment, we have more compute capacity than we have demand, and we have a lot of the tokens and processing power being given away in freemium solutions," Gartner chief forecaster John Lovelock told CNBC. "Everyone in the AI race is running for a last-man standing position. Pretty much every market that Gartner is tracking in our AI race is likely to collapse down to a duopoly."

events.title: Dh1m gets you in the queue for Tesla's new Roadster in the UAE
events.summary: Tesla has opened the ordering process for its next-generation Roadster in the UAE – but the “flying” version is not yet available. The Roadster, unveiled by Tesla chief executive Elon Musk at a demonstration in Texas last week, comes in three models: Performance, Thrust and Rocket. UAE customers can reserve the Performance with an initial refundable payment of Dh20,000 ($4,847), followed by another Dh190,000 within 10 days. The more powerful Thrust requires the same initial payment, followed by Dh1 million within 10 days. The car's built-in thrusters are purely for acceleration, not flight. The Rocket model – which is fitted with SpaceX -made thrusters – demonstrated its ability to “fly” last week. It can be bought through invitation only and remains unavailable in the UAE. It has yet to be revealed how Tesla will determine who can get hold of this top-end version. Tesla has made clear payments are deposits, as the final prices have yet to be decided. The Texas-based company plans to start production of the next-generation vehicles in 2028. Tesla has said availability of the Rocket is subject to domestic laws and regulations, and that configuration will not be offered in all regions. What does UAE law say? The “flying” capabilities of the Rocket Roadster have raised questions about the legality of such vehicles on roads, whether it would be classified as an aircraft and what approvals would be required. Flying raises a separate set of legal questions. UAE law states that aircraft operating in the Emirates must meet registration, licensing and airworthiness requirements. Hefty fines await those who breach these laws. However, the UAE is already developing regulations and infrastructure for flying taxis. In July, the General Civil Aviation Authority certified Dubai 's first purpose-built commercial vertiport for electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft. The UAE has separate laws governing road vehicles and aircraft but there is no publicly established approval framework specifically addressing a vehicle such as the Rocket Roadster. Federal regulations in the Emirates stipulate all vehicles must be registered and licensed, meet approved technical and safety standards and undergo inspection as part of the registration process. They require approval for substantial changes to the body, chassis or engine power, although this concerns modifications and does not necessarily apply to factory-built vehicles. The authority has also published operating procedures for such aircraft at Abu Dhabi's Al Bateen Executive Airport. But these frameworks do not automatically establish whether a vehicle designed for both roads and flight, such as the Rocket, would be permitted to operate. The Roadster would still need to meet UAE road regulations – and the Rocket version is expected to require particular aviation approval.

events.title: France riots become Republican midterm boogeyman
events.summary: As the French right-wing National Rally is seizing on fiery protests in the country for its pre-election pitch, so are President Trump and his Republican allies in the U.S. The big picture: The Trump administration has used the unrest, which began over education grievances , to bolster its messaging on immigration and the threat of "communists," a group Trump has repeatedly claimed is threatening American civilization. Driving the news: "When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical 'Dumocrats' want to do to America," Trump said before a Kansas rally crowd Monday. He claimed France was being "conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists and communists who hate Christianity" and "the Western civilization itself." Speaking earlier to reporters, the president claimed, without evidence, that the situation in France was about "immigration, not schools." He's repeatedly blamed immigration for the protests. The White House referred Axios to the president's Truth Social post echoing that rhetoric. Catch up quick: Localized demonstrations by high school students that began in Paris last month have broadened into a massive nationwide movement over poor school conditions and costs of living, sparking thousands of arrests and clashes between police and protesters, Axios' Bec Falconer reports. The civil unrest gave way to rioting and looting, leading French President Emmanuel Macron to condemn "unrestrained violence" by "insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals," per the AP . Some 550,000 people demonstrated in France Saturday, per the interior ministry, though Reuters reported that a key union estimated 800,000. On the sidelines, "thugs" chose "violence," per a translation of the interior ministry's statement , which added that some 500 police officers and firefighters were injured. The forceful police response to student demonstrators has also been scrutinized , sparking dozens of probes into officer conduct. Zoom out: Other U.S. Republicans have followed Trump in evoking the protests, which have spread to other countries , to rally voters and condemn immigration . Vice President Vance wrote on X, " Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion," sharing a video of a historic town hall reportedly set ablaze by masked protesters, per AFP. "This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country," Vance contended. Yes, but: Macron, per a translation of his nationwide address over the weekend protests, said the hundreds of thousands of demonstrators had " legitimate demands" and should not be conflated with violent rioters. He said those concerns included the cost of living and fuel price spikes triggered by the war in Iran. The bottom line: The spiraling violence has created global shock that Trump is harnessing as a boogeyman ahead of an uphill midterm battle. events.title: Amazon to hire over 300,000 workers for holiday season, up 20% from 2025
events.summary: Workers unloading Amazon packages from a Prime delivery truck in New York on Oct 6. Amazon is offering full-time, part-time and seasonal roles to cover the holiday shopping season. SEATTLE – Amazon.com plans to hire more than 300,000 workers during the holiday shopping season, up 20% from 2025, making it a stand-out in an otherwise lacklustre holiday jobs market. The positions include full-time, part-time and seasonal roles, with temporary workers earning an average of US$20 (S$25) per hour, Amazon said in a blog on Oct 20. The Seattle-based company is incentivising seasonal workers to stay through the year by offering medical benefits to those who remain in January and work at least 30 hours each week. Seasonal retail hiring will likely fall below 450,000 jobs created in 2025, which would mark the lowest holiday recruitment since 2008, according to outplacement firm Challenger, Gray and Christmas. Large retailers like Walmart and Target have again refrained from announcing their seasonal recruiting plans, marking a departure from pandemic-era hiring sprees. Seasonal hiring for logistics and warehouse companies will be about flat from 2025, Challenger, Gray and Christmas estimated. “Almost every hiring announcement we’ve seen in the last three years is smaller and more surgical than the pre-pandemic playbook,” said Andy Challenger, the firm’s chief revenue officer. US shoppers will spend US$275.1 billion online in November and December, up 6.7% from 2025, according to Adobe. Amazon captures almost 40 US cents of every dollar spent online, according to EMarketer. United Parcel Service, which has been reducing package volume from Amazon to focus on more profitable business segments, earlier in October announced plans to hire more than 100,000 seasonal workers, which is roughly in line with previous years. events.title: To get a reply when reaching out to people, make 1 simple change, says LinkedIn career expert
events.summary: Work Use this 4-word phrase to stand out after a job interview: 'It can be really powerful,' says career coach Work Ex-Google recruiter: Why this common mistake makes your resume 'invisible' Work Your AI interviewer will see you now—what experts think job seekers should know Work 'Doomjobbing’ can hurt your job search and worsen anxiety, experts say: Why it happens and how to avoid it Work Some job seekers 'time travel' to cram more AI skills onto LinkedIn profiles Having a strong professional network may be more important than ever in a tough job market . U.S. job applicants with an inside connection at a company, defined as a first-degree connection working there, are nearly seven times more likely to be hired than those without one, according to a LinkedIn analysis of 5 million members across multiple countries. But having a network and effectively tapping into it aren't the same thing. In fact, many professionals could stand to be a little more strategic when reaching out to people with an ask , says Catherine Fisher, vice president of communications and career expert at LinkedIn. "That first step of reaching out to someone is being really specific about what you're asking for," Fisher tells CNBC Make It. "The more specificity you can give, the better." When you ask for an informational interview, for example, you should explain what you're looking to get out of a conversation and what you can offer in exchange. You might offer to take them out to coffee and say you have three questions you want to ask them. Given people's busy schedules, you might also make your requests time-bound by, say, asking for 15 minutes of someone's time. Specificity helps people know just what they'd be agreeing to, and demonstrating that you have a game plan shows you've done your homework and are respectful of their time. "You don't want to put a lot of the work on the person," Fisher says. And if the person doesn't feel they're the right fit to help you, extra information might help them introduce you to someone else who can, Fisher adds. Fisher says someone reached out to her recently to ask if she could spare 15 minutes to talk about a few ways Fisher might get involved with the person's charity. The specificity of the request made the decision easy: "I can spare 15 minutes, I know what she wants to talk about, and that's it," Fisher says. While you can build relationships through these types of meetings, networking can also be much simpler. It's "a spectrum," Fisher says: Some actions you can take to build and sustain your network are as easy as commenting on someone's post or sending someone a quick text to say you're thinking of them and want to check in on how they're doing. Many people have a larger network than they may realize. Recent college graduates , for example, may worry they don't have many connections because their work experience is limited. But everyone from college advisors and professors to peers and even families they've babysat for can constitute a network, Fisher says. Your social networks, not just your professional ones, can also aid in your job search, Bonnie Dilber, a recruiting leader at the software company Zapier, previously told CNBC Make It . A neighborhood Facebook group, your workout buddies, or acquaintances and friends can help keep an eye out for opportunities you might be a fit for. "People should get out of the traditionally professional spaces and go get in spaces where they have some connection with people," Dilber says. From these kinds of "inner circles," Fisher says, you can build "concentric circles" of your network, say, in asking a mutual connection for an introduction to someone at a company you're applying to. "If you've been at it, applying, applying, applying," she says, "that network is going to help bridge some of those gaps." events.title: TikTok staff raised child safety concerns, but executives reportedly failed to act
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. TikTok was repeatedly warned by employees about the risks the social media platform posed to children, according to court records obtained by NPR . The documents say employees were frustrated with how executives responded to their concerns about risks to children, including sexual exploitation and exposure to suicide-related content. Depositions of employees filed in March 2026 are shedding new light on TikTok’s child safety practices. According to NPR, TikTok employees warned that minors were appearing in sexual content that was available for purchase on TikTok, raising concerns that the company could profit from potentially illegal activity. They also flagged that minors were exploiting loopholes to access age-restricted content and hide their activity from parents. Additionally, the court documents show that TikTok didn’t conduct surveys to determine the age of its users out of concern that it would have to share the results with the Federal Trade Commission. “These citations and claims are clearly cherry-picked at the behest of trial lawyers and used to inaccurately rewrite our history and mislead the public about our commitment to youth safety and how our platform works,” a TikTok spokesperson said in an emailed statement to TechCrunch. “It’s unfortunate that NPR has chosen to ignore the numerous documents and resources we have provided that demonstrate how these claims mischaracterize our record and platform features.” The statement continues, “We have invested billions of dollars in Trust & Safety and rolled out more than 50 preset safety, privacy, and security settings for teens, including Family Pairing, which helps parents and guardians customize the experience for their teens. We remain steadfast in our commitment to the well-being of our community.” TikTok, in addition to Meta, Google, and Snap, faces hundreds of lawsuits consolidated in federal court. The lawsuits allege that these companies’ platforms harm minors and that they failed to disclose known risks to young users. TikTok has reached settlements in several of these cases before they went to trial, including one in Los Angeles where a jury found that Meta and YouTube had designed their platforms to be addictive to young users. events.title: France to deploy military as it braces for fresh unrest this weekend
events.summary: France plans to tap its military to help maintain order at planned protests coming weekend. French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said Tuesday that some areas would remain under curfew after a weekend of violent rioting. Criticism is growing of President Emmanuel Macron's decision to embark on a tour of the Middle East amid the turmoil at home. France will deploy some military forces to help maintain order during a fresh wave of protests expected this weekend, officials said Tuesday. French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told lawmakers in the National Assembly that the government would ⁠deploy forces from France's Sentinelle force — a domestic military operation that was launched in 2015 following terrorist attacks in Paris — "mainly on static security missions." This would free up police and gendarmes — a military police force — to carry out law enforcement objectives, Nuñez added. Also addressing parliament on Tuesday, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said authorities planned to mobilize a "massive" security presence this coming Saturday, adding that the government's objective was to achieve "an immediate return to order." Lecornu also said there would be fresh curfews "where the situation requires it," according to French newspaper Le Monde . Curfews contributed to a "calm" night across France, he said earlier on Tuesday, even as public discontent remained high following the weekend's mass protests, looting and violent scenes . Certain areas of several French cities were under curfew overnight, including Place de la République and Les Halles in Paris, and parts of central Lyon. Lille and Nice were among the cities to impose curfews for minors. The unrest comes at a particularly fragile moment for France, where public anger over living costs and deteriorating services is colliding with political instability and a fiscal crisis that threatens to turn into a debt crisis as government borrowing costs rise to the highest level in decades. The country faces a divided parliament with no majority and presidential elections in April 2027. In a statement on Tuesday, Lecornu said local officials would impose new curfews where required. Meanwhile, criticism is mounting over President Emmanuel Macron's decision to embark on a three-day tour of the Middle East as France suffers its most severe riots in many years. Riots followed weeks of demonstrations over the country's education system , the cost of living and other issues. While hundreds of thousands of people marched peacefully, pockets of violence erupted, shocking the country, as protesters smashed shopfronts and set Limoges Town Hall on fire. Political commentator Christophe Barbier on radio station RTL said on Monday there was "no longer a pilot in the plane." At the same time, newspaper La Dépêche du Midi wrote in a scathing editorial that Macron had "to see if the misery of a reviled president is less painful in the Persian Gulf sun" as France "sinks deeper into crisis." Macron said on Sunday he was looking to address high fuel prices and secure French energy supplies through the trip to Kuwait, the UAE, Bahrain and Qatar, while strengthening defense and security cooperation. There is also public anger over claims that police lost control of the situation at the weekend as disorder and looting escalated. Police were earlier this month accused of excessive force in their response to student protests, after a 15-year-old ​boy's hand was blown off by a stun grenade. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez' offered to quit his post on Monday after claiming responsibility for what unfolded. Macron declined his resignation, saying immediate leadership of law enforcement was needed. "The lack of enforcement means that more than 3,000 shops have been sacked, and for the economy today we awake with a feeling that the state cannot do the basic duty that it is supposed to do, and this is now creating somehow lack of trust," Fabrice Le Saché, vice president of business group MEDEF, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Tuesday. "This is dangerous because we have been used to... riots in our country — remember the Yellow Vests and other movements — but this one has passed, I think, the level of the previous ones, and we cannot continue to keep going with that same type of situation every time we have social unrest," Le Saché said. French businesses have one of the highest tax burdens in the euro area but now feel they cannot receive basic security in return, he added. Lecornu said Monday that a support fund would be established for damaged or looted businesses, and that the government would talk with insurers to speed up assessments. "The scale of the damage suggests this weekend's riots could ultimately prove more costly than the unrest that followed the death of Nahel Merzouk in 2023," which generated around 1 billion euros ($1.12 billion) in insured losses, Jess Middleton, senior Europe analyst at risk intelligence firm Verisk Maplecroft, said by email.

events.title: Apple unveils the 2026 Designers of Tomorrow
events.summary: Store Mac iPad iPhone Watch Vision AirPods TV & Home Entertainment Accessories Support Text of this article October 20, 2026 UPDATE Apple unveils the 2026 Designers of Tomorrow Curated by Rodman Primack, the exhibition celebrates next-generation designers and how they integrated Apple products into their creative processes Apple’s Designers of Tomorrow showcase, in collaboration with Design Miami, returns for a second year to spotlight the best in emerging talent, this time focusing on the theme of presence. Exploring what still holds the public’s attention amid the hurried pace of the modern world, designers Salem S. Charabi, Isabel Rower, Yoonjeong Lee, and Parafernalia (Genki Matsumura and Sebastián Zorrilla) crafted original works that invite reflection and aim to shift perspectives, engage the senses, and kindle curiosity. “The theme was born from an honest recognition of just how busy our lives have become,” says Rodman Primack, the program’s curator and former longtime creative director of Design Miami. “In answering it, our designers demonstrate the power of objects to shape our physical environments and transform the human experiences that are possible within them.” This year’s participants were handpicked by a jury of global design voices — including Alexandra Cunningham Cameron, Fabien Cappello, Jennifer Dunlop Fletcher, Minjae Kim, Hun Chung Lee, Marion Mailaender, Nifemi Marcus-Bello, Jennifer Roberts, and Apple’s Molly Anderson — for their storytelling, material innovation, and craft. Their work also highlights Apple’s dynamic role in the creative process, empowering designers at every level to capture, refine, and share their ideas with the world. “Apple products continue to emerge as a through line so many extraordinary designers share, spanning disciplines, cultures, and processes,” explains Primack. “It’s a testament to how seamlessly these products and tools can integrate into any workflow.” Ahead of the exhibition, which opens today at Hôtel de Maisons in Paris, the featured designers discussed their final pieces and the tools they used to bring them to life. Salem S. Charabi Egyptian Danish architect Salem S. Charabi blends old-world practices and the latest digital tools to create timeless pieces, and his Designers of Tomorrow project, The Eminence of Light , is no exception. “Light is something we’re all instinctively drawn to, dating back to our earliest fires,” Charabi notes. “A lantern felt like the perfect encapsulation of this idea — a reflection of our capacity to light up the world.” Charabi constructed the lantern’s veil from banana paper, applying Japanese methods to Egyptian palms. A delicate skeleton of meticulously stacked date palm fronds provides a satisfying contrast to the limestone base, which carries the traces of its own formation in its grooves. “Each strand is an octagon in profile — just 3 millimeters wide, split by hand, and carefully drilled,” Charabi explains. “The ends are then sharpened with a chisel to interlock.” Both the lamp and the audience’s attention are suspended by the same tension. The resulting piece feels at once deeply natural and finely engineered. “For this project, every component had to be mapped out in detail,” Charabi says. “I sketched and did all the 3D modeling on my MacBook Pro. It was a complex process getting everything to fit just right — from the carving of the stone and the paper molds, down to the delicate base.” Isabel Rower By blending familiar forms with the unexpected, Brooklyn-based designer Isabel Rower cultivates presence and transforms everyday objects into active sensory experiences. “The surface functions as a site for curiosity for me,” explains Rower. “People don’t always know what my pieces are made of, even as they’re touching them. It’s captivating when something that isn’t readily understood takes the form of a familiar object, like a table or teapot. It generates a kind of friction that brings you into immediate awareness of the objects we use every day.” This intrigue is captured by her piece Padded Chair 1860 , whose dramatic proportions draw on 18th- and 19th-century papier-mâché furniture and objets d’art. Its high-gloss finish stands in sharp contrast to the beaded fringe lining the seat. “The ceramic beads make a sound when brushed, drawing attention to both the material and its form, turning the unconscious act of sitting down into a mindful encounter,” Rower says. Apple is a fixture throughout her creative process. “I use iPhone to capture quick thoughts and document my process, AirPods Pro to listen to music, and MacBook Pro to build my personal visual archive,” says Rower. “I’ll also use Keynote to juxtapose ideas and explore the relationship between images and text.” Yoonjeong Lee For Seoul-based designer Yoonjeong Lee, presence begins with quiet discovery. Through material transformation, she repositions overlooked background objects as central subjects. Her piece New Form showcases a trio of worn-down pencils that have been given new life as nails. “I wanted to express this year’s theme through something small that we could all recognize — a shared experience,” Lee explains. “This story doesn’t carry some grand narrative. Instead, it takes a second look at the familiar to help you rediscover that which has been quietly forgotten.” The base of the piece doubles as a wooden table and lamp. Sheets of paper serve as a lampshade, softly diffusing the light below, while the pencils hold them firmly in place. Applying her signature technique of building volume through repetition, Lee stacked roughly 5,000 thin sheets of veneer to construct the wooden base. Lee’s focus on overlooked structural elements extends to her workflow, where she credits iCloud, AirDrop, and Notes for keeping her process seamless. “I often use iPad Pro and Apple Pencil to create a sketch and jot down quick thoughts, but it’s how my devices connect to each other that makes them, and all their flexible features, truly useful,” she explains. Parafernalia Founded by Genki Matsumura and Sebastián Zorrilla, Parafernalia is a design studio that spans from Monterrey to Mexico City. The duo’s creative process is driven by constant dialogue, questioning, and iteration, often powered by FaceTime. “For us, presence can take many forms,” says Matsumura. “We experience it with ourselves, with our surroundings, and with others. Our piece explores how all these expressions can coexist within a single object.” Their piece MonoAmbiente 1 considers presence as both a personal relationship with one’s surroundings and a collective act. When closed, its acid-etched stainless steel surface forms a vast landscape. Its dual state invites the observer not only to examine it but to experience it. Once expanded, it reveals stools and a table, turning a distant scene into an intimate setting where two people can converse, play chess, or share a drink.

events.title: The manosphere stars who helped Trump win are losing their shine
events.summary: The manosphere stars who helped mobilize young men for Donald Trump in 2024 are losing their shine with that very audience. Why it matters: Trump and Republicans rode a wave of cultural cachet to reach young male voters. Now, the president and some of his most influential online allies are showing signs of losing their grip on that audience ahead of the 2026 midterms . Driving the news: New polling from the Democratic project Speaking With American Men suggests some of the most prominent influencers during Trump's 2024 campaign have lost their luster with young male voters, per Puck News , Joe Rogan's favorable rating among young men dropped from 11 points, while Elon Musk's popularity dropped 14 points and Tucker Carlson lost 12 points. Andrew Tate, who was arrested on sex trafficking and rape charges, had "a -30 net approval rating," per Puck. Between the lines: Economic pressures and the Iran war have become major concerns for young men heading into the midterms, Puck reported. Those issues have caused tension between Trump and the influential voices who bolstered his last campaign. State of play: Young men are turning on politicians, podcasters and influencers, many of whom may have influenced recent political outcomes. They're becoming more skeptical and turning their backs on politicians, especially Trump. The 2026 Young American Men Survey from Cygnal similarly found that among 18- to 30-year-old American men, Trump, Vance and the Republican Party all were viewed unfavorably. Trump's numbers among young voters dropped precipitously. Marquette Law School national polling shows that Trump's approval dropped from 40% in January 2025 to 19% in April 2026, before rebounding to 28% in June. The law school hasn't polled on the question since then. Yes, but: Young men aren't especially enthusiastic about Democrats, either. Former President Barack Obama, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), and NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani were the only Democrats showing upticks in favorability ratings, per Puck. Context: Several prominent manosphere personalities have been critical of Trump in his second term, particularly on the Iran war and the Epstein files release. Rogan , like many MAGA influencers, has criticized the war and the Trump administration's handling of the Epstein files. Tucker Carlson has chastised Trump over many issues, including his partnership with Israel in going to war. Vice President Vance has even admitted the White House "screwed up" on its communications about the Epstein files. Reality check: Researchers question how influential podcasters and personalities actually were in 2024. A September working paper from the NYU Center for Social Media, AI and Politics found that podcast exposure did not necessarily cause Trump's gains among young men. Researchers, who reviewed 36,659 podcast episodes from 2024 alongside two survey datasets, found podcasts explained only a small portion of the widening youth gender gap. The other side: Influencers still have enormous reach among young voters. A survey from Morning Consult published on Oct. 16 found that nearly two-thirds of Gen Z adults say they get news from creators, while 62% trust creator recommendations. Business Insider reports that one in four U.S. adults feel influencer content has affected their voting decisions. Separate Marquette polling found that 54% of adults who consumed podcasts for political news approved of Trump's job performance in June, compared with 38% of adults overall. The bottom line: The manosphere's biggest personalities still have sway, but the direction of the country isn't helping them — or Trump — with young men.

events.title: Union attacks NatWest plans to get workers back to the office
events.summary: The Unite union has hit out at a plan by NatWest to reduce the rights of 30,000 of its employees to work from home. NatWest says it is moving to a hybrid approach where workers will be required to attend the office at least two days a week, from February. The bank says this is still very competitive with the rest of the finance industry, and exceptions will be made for colleagues who require additional flexibility. But Unite said NatWest's decision was "out of touch with the realities facing its workforce", with many facing higher travel and childcare costs. Firms have been gradually drawing people back into the office since working from home became the norm for some office workers during the Covid pandemic. In January last year, Amazon required staff to return to the office five days a week after they had been working two days at home. Other firms such as Boots and JP Morgan have brought in policies requiring head office staff to be in every day. But Barclays faced a backlash from staff last month over plans to require workers to go to the office three days a week. It brought in a longer transition period in response to staff and union complaints. Unite said NatWest was abolishing its "remote first" employment category, which allows 13,497 workers to attend the office around twice a month, and requiring 17,272 hybrid workers to increase their office attendance. The union says that many of the affected workers are lower-paid grades, and the new requirements will increase cost-of-living pressures, while disrupting the arrangements of disabled workers and carers. In a statement, Unite general secretary Sharon Graham called NatWest's move a "kick in the teeth" for its workers. "Thousands of workers face higher travel and childcare costs and disruption to caring responsibilities," she said "For NatWest to impose these changes while reneging on existing agreements shows complete contempt for its workforce." Graham called on NatWest to "ditch these proposals and engage properly with its workers". A NatWest spokesman said: "Flexible working remains an important part of how we work but we've also learned more about the value that spending time together brings for our colleagues and customers - helping teams collaborate, share ideas, build relationships and learn from one another. "That's why we're introducing a more consistent approach across the bank, with colleagues expected to spend at least two days a week in the office, depending on the needs of their role and business area. "We recognise this will be a change for some colleagues and we're giving them time to plan ahead and will support them through the transition." events.title: Google Cloud outage hits UK banks
events.summary: Online services for a number of U.K. banks in and around London are being disrupted by a Google Cloud outage LONDON -- Online services for a number of U.K. banks in and around London were disrupted by a Google Cloud outage Tuesday. The cloud outages began just after 2 a.m. eastern, or 6:08 a.m. GMT. The center of the outage is London, but the impact can extend outside of the U.K. if apps in other countries rely on London-based infrastructure. “Our engineering team continues to investigate the issue,” Google Cloud said early Tuesday. It said that it was starting to see a recovery of services. U.K. banks that reported disruptions include Lloyds, Halifax, HSBC and Revolut. “We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services," Revolut said in an email. "We can confirm that all our customers’ money and data are safe. We’ve been working to fix the issue since it was identified this morning and apologise to anyone affected and for any inconvenience caused.” Shark kills woman swimming off South Africa's Eastern Cape, beaches closed Prince Harry reveals reason he wanted to move back to England South Korea to withdraw some Kyiv embassy staff as row over POW transfer deepens Lloyds said its app is again operational. “We understand the root issues have been resolved, so we expect all our services to be back to normal soon,” a Lloyds spokesperson said in an email.
