events.title: A concrete vision: Saint-Gobain and Microsoft Discovery build for the future
events.summary: PARIS — Saint-Gobain’s business is construction materials. It got its start in 1665, when King Louis XIV charged the company with making the mirrors for his lavish new palace in Versailles. And he needed a lot of mirrors. The idea was to break the monopoly that glass-making power Venice had at the time, cutting costs and improving efficiency. These days, Saint-Gobain has 161,000 employees in 81 countries making construction materials — glass is still important, but there’s also gypsum for plaster board, insulation and concrete admixtures and cement additives. These last elements — products for cement and concrete — represent one of the company’s most important product groups, and like glass in 1665, one of the most challenging. Cement production uses a lot of energy, and accounts for around 7% of annual CO2 emissions globally. Saint-Gobain is looking for chemical elements that could reduce those carbon emissions and improve the strength of cement. “It would have taken our researchers a year to create the knowledge base. Using AI, it took us a couple of hours.” Mojdeh Rastgoo-Lemaitre, a digital acceleration program manager at Saint-Gobain, said that using Microsoft Discovery saved months of time for researchers working to improve an additive for cement. Photo by Chris Welsch for Microsoft. So, when the company’s researchers collaborated with engineers from Microsoft earlier this year in using Microsoft Discovery , a new AI-powered agentic platform for scientists and engineers, to find solutions, the results stunned them. “We actually gathered 62,000 patents and 44,000 abstracts,” says Mojdeh Rastgoo-Lemaitre, a digital acceleration program manager overseeing the project to find lower-carbon, less expensive options. “Without using this technology, it would have taken our researchers a year to create the knowledge base. Using AI, it took us a couple of hours.” With a broad smile, she says Microsoft Discovery helped the team to narrow the data, analyze some novel possibilities in the chemistry involved and come up with several hypotheses about new ingredients for cement additives worth testing in about six weeks. A breakthrough in how research is done “So, yes, the researchers are very happy with Discovery,” Rastgoo-Lemaitre says. “It’s a great tool to help them have new ideas, and to go faster.” Saint-Gobain was one of Microsoft’s first clients to use Discovery in private release in March of this year, and teams from both companies worked on fine-tuning the platform. The team from Microsoft was from a new operating business called the Microsoft Frontier Company, which places Microsoft engineers inside companies like Saint-Gobain to deliver solutions using AI applications and tools like Microsoft Discovery. Discovery lets scientists orchestrate AI agents to search literature, connect information, generate hypotheses, design experiments and run analyses. “The construction industry, from production to running, is 40% of the world’s carbon footprint,” Ursula Soritsch-Renier, chief digital and information officer at Saint-Gobain says. “We’re not going to stop constructing, but we can make change, and who is better placed to do that than us?” She says Saint-Gobain is embracing technology as a means to cut waste, reduce energy use and be more efficient. The efforts to decarbonize the making of cement is just one illustration, she says. “You don’t just push technology for the sake of technology. You need to always understand the ‘why’ and the ‘what for’.” Ursula Soritsch-Reiner, chief digital and information officer, at Saint-Gobain’s headquarters in Paris. Photo by Chris Welsch for Microsoft. Technology that creates real-world impact For example, Saint-Gobain has changed the way it delivers plaster board to construction sites. Before, it came in a standard size, and workers cut the board to fit the rooms being built. But the leftovers just went to the dump. “We have now a cut-to-order system,” Soritsch-Renier says. “So, we get the building information model, we optimize the cuts, then nothing goes to the landfill.” She says the new system improved time-to-installation by 30%. “In construction, time is money,” she says. “And the environment wins because in the end it is less raw material and less energy. And that’s thanks to the digital tools we’re using.” Microsoft has been a key partner, Soritsch-Renier says, and the framework agreement the two companies signed in July will benefit both companies by accelerating the search for sustainable construction materials and processes. “You don’t just push technology for the sake of technology,” she says. “You need to always understand the ‘why’ and the ‘what for.’ And with that understanding you develop and you evolve and you push things forward with new tools, like with the research platform.” Saint-Gobain’s efforts to embrace cutting-edge technology took another step at the beginning of September, when it appointed Annica Hagen to a newly created role as the company’s first chief artificial intelligence officer. She will work with Soritsch-Renier to define how AI can support the Saint-Gobain Group’s strategic plan. “It’s important not to talk about AI as a means to an end,” Hagen says. “It’s an enablement to get where we want to go. My main task is to enable growth — and how can we use AI to enable that? Now is the time to shape the future.” Annica Hagen is the new (and first) chief artificial intelligence officer at Saint-Gobain. Photo by Chris Welsch for Microsoft. An exciting time to be an applied scientist Rastgoo-Lemaitre says the teams at Saint-Gobain’s Innovation Hub Europe in the Parisian suburb of Aubervilliers were already thinking about other projects where they could apply Discovery, but that research and development on the cement additives would continue. Saint-Gobain already has a cement-additive called EnviroAdd that reduces the need for clinker in cement by about 20%. Clinker is the ingredient in cement that binds, and it’s made by super-heating limestone, which is where the production of CO2 is most significant. By searching across domains outside of the construction industry, Rastgoo-Lemaitre says, the scientists using Discovery were able to find some molecules they otherwise would not have considered. The idea is to create a new chemical additive that could further reduce the need for clinker in cement while making it stronger. “They are right now testing those molecules for the behaviors and chemistry they are looking for,” she says. If the potential bears up under scrutiny, the next steps would be passing the potential solution to the development team, which would test the additive in physical conditions. A new era of discovery at Saint-Gobain “Every day that I’m using AI today, I think, if I had only had this my life would have been so much easier, and I could have done so much more.” Silvia Mariani is the managing director of the Saint-Gobain Innovation Hub Europe in Aubervilliers, France.

events.title: Advancing digital sovereignty with greater control and choice
events.summary: Oct 20, 2026 | Douglas Phillips - President and Chief Technology Officer, Microsoft Specialized Clouds Across my conversations with leaders in government, critical infrastructure and regulated industries, one priority consistently rises to the top: putting technology to work on their most important systems while maintaining the control those systems require. This challenge is becoming more important as advanced cloud and AI capabilities move into public services, regulated processes and essential operations. Organizations are considering more than where data resides. They also seek to understand who can access and operate their systems, how sensitive digital assets remain protected, which technology dependencies matter most and whether critical services can continue as regulatory, geopolitical, security or network conditions change. Digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control and security over the technology they depend on, while continuing to innovate. Last year, we introduced Microsoft Sovereign Cloud to give customers more choice in how they address these requirements. Since then, we have continued to turn our commitments into practical capabilities across public cloud and customer-operated environments, while expanding how we enable partners to address sovereignty requirements in their local markets. Today, we are sharing the next stage of that work. A continuum of control, built around the workload Our approach to digital sovereignty starts with the workload. Each workload carries different requirements for data, operations, technology dependencies, continuity and risk. Microsoft Sovereign Cloud is designed to make it easier for organizations to apply the appropriate level of control to each workload without forcing every application into the same deployment model. Those needs can vary widely across organizations. A public-facing digital service may benefit from the scale and pace of innovation in the public cloud. A system supporting essential operations may need to continue running locally if connectivity is disrupted. An AI workload handling highly sensitive data may require models, data and processing to remain within a customer-controlled environment. Microsoft Sovereign Cloud is designed around this workload-based approach, providing a continuum of management, control and options across Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud and the Sovereign Partner Ecosystem. Organizations can apply the level of control appropriate to each workload while maintaining a consistent approach to governance and operations across their digital estate. Sovereign Public Cloud adds capabilities for workloads that require greater control and transparency while continuing to benefit from the scale and innovation of Azure. Sovereign Private Cloud extends cloud capabilities into customer-operated environments, including connected and disconnected operations. The Sovereign Partner Ecosystem broadens the continuum through independently operated environments, specialized partners, locally relevant expertise and technologies that support customers’ sovereignty requirements. These are not isolated destinations. Customers can combine public cloud, private cloud and partner capabilities across their digital estate, applying different levels of control to different workloads as their operating needs evolve. Making control more visible in Sovereign Public Cloud For many workloads, the public cloud provides a combination of scale, innovation, integrated security and compliance. Organizations can benefit from these capabilities while applying additional sovereignty controls for residency, confidentiality, operator access, policy and continuity. Our work in Sovereign Public Cloud makes these controls easier to understand, apply and demonstrate. Sovereign Control Panel , entering public preview at Microsoft Ignite, brings these signals together in a unified Azure portal experience. It helps organizations understand their sovereignty posture, apply and manage controls, identify gaps and risks and take action to address them. It also supports business continuity readiness by helping customers understand workload dependencies and assess portability across operating environments when required. This visibility complements controls across the operator-access lifecycle. Just-in-time Access and Customer Lockbox give customers additional control over access to their environments. For customers in the European Union (EU) and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), we are rolling out Data Guardian , which adds European-resident oversight by a trusted EU partner for qualifying Microsoft engineer remote access to in-scope production systems. Production Touch Ledger , also launched with phased rollout in the EU and EFTA, creates tamper-evident records of that access and the actions performed. Azure Key Vault Managed Hardware Security Module (HSM) already gives customers dedicated, single-tenant protection and control over the encryption keys used by supported Azure services. Last year, we committed to extending that control beyond Microsoft infrastructure. External key management with Azure Managed HSM is now generally available, allowing customers to keep the root encryption key in hardware they own and operate on-premises or through a trusted third party. This gives organizations another option for workloads that require physical control of key hardware outside Microsoft infrastructure. Azure confidential computing helps protect supported data while it is processed in a hardware-based and attested trusted execution environment. We are also increasing transparency into the technologies that underpin that trust. Azure Confidential Clean Rooms , now in limited preview, applies confidential computing to approved multiparty collaboration, allowing participants to analyze shared sensitive data while limiting broader exposure of the underlying information. Together, these capabilities provide additional technical and operational controls that can support a broader digital sovereignty strategy aligned to an organization’s legal, policy, security, resilience and business requirements. Designing for resilience and operational independence For some workloads, digital sovereignty also means maintaining critical operations as connectivity, geopolitical and operating conditions change. Resilience must be designed from the start so essential workloads can continue operating through disruption. To help customers prepare for these scenarios, we are publishing new sovereign business continuity guidance and architecture patterns . These resources help organizations translate resilience requirements into architectures they can plan, implement and test before they are needed. For many workloads, the scale and geographic reach of the public cloud provide a strong foundation for resilience across locations and operating conditions.

events.title: Monetary policy could turn accommodative as AI productivity gains take hold: MAS chief economist
events.summary: While AI-related investments are driving economic growth, the technology has yet to deliver significant productivity improvements across the wider economy, says MAS chief economist Edward Robinson. MAS chief economist Edward Robinson said central banks should stay restrictive for now, as AI investment is boosting demand but has not yet lifted economy-wide productivity. He warned that misreading the shift could raise inflation risks, after MAS tightened policy in April and July 2026 before holding rates in October. Robinson said AI is helping Asia, especially electronics exports, and could lift productivity by up to 0.6 percentage point a year if adoption, skills and infrastructure improve. SINGAPORE – Central banks may be able to ease monetary policy once artificial intelligence delivers widespread productivity gains, but they should keep policy appropriately restrictive for now as the AI investment boom fuels demand, said Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) chief economist Edward Robinson on Oct 20. While AI-related investments are driving economic growth, the technology has yet to deliver significant productivity improvements across the wider economy, he said. Speaking at the Beijing Financial Street Forum, Robinson cautioned that misjudging this transition could carry risks, calling for a gradual, data-dependent approach to monetary policy. MAS tightened monetary policy in April and July 2026 amid rising inflation risks, before leaving its policy settings unchanged in October. In its latest monetary policy statement on Oct 14, the central bank warned that domestic inflation could remain elevated if the AI-related boom generated broader economic spillovers and pushed up unit labour costs. Still, Robinson noted that the AI boom has been particularly beneficial for Asia, with AI-driven electronics accounting for more than 70 per cent of the region’s export growth this year. Beyond manufacturing, Asian economies – including China – are also making progress in developing AI technologies, ranging from advanced chips to large language models. However, Robinson, who is also MAS deputy managing director for economic policy, said growth in industries producing AI-related technologies has largely been driven by increased investment and more intensive use of existing resources, rather than improvements in efficiency. New data centres are being built, advanced equipment is being used more intensively, and workers and machines are effectively “working harder”, rather than “working smarter”, he noted. “AI is diffusing across the wider economy faster than the personal computer and the internet did,” he said. “While early evidence points to efficiency gains in specific applications, it remains too soon to identify a decisive economy-wide step-up in productivity.” Nevertheless, Robinson pointed to the potential for substantial gains over time, drawing parallels with the introduction of electricity a century ago. The productivity benefits of electrification became substantial only after factories and workflows were redesigned around the technology, he said. Similarly, AI could require widespread adoption, investments in skills and infrastructure, and changes to how organisations operate before its full economic benefits emerge, he added. With sufficiently broad adoption and appropriate investment, AI could raise total factor productivity growth by up to 0.6 percentage point annually, Robinson said, pointing to estimates from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. “This could meaningfully offset the negative effects from demographic ageing and other structural headwinds in Asia,” he noted. events.title: The AI boom doesn’t answer to the Fed
events.summary: Liz’s view One rule of investing is “don’t fight the Fed.” Playing the contrarian to the Federal Reserve’s plans to stimulate or dampen the economy only ends badly. But Big Tech is not run by rule-followers. AI giants have been almost willfully indifferent to the rising cost of money. Rates go higher, and they borrow more. It’s a problem for the Federal Reserve, which is trying to tamp down inflation that, as Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee told us last week , is “jumping out of its lane” — spreading from AI-linked sectors into unrelated parts of the economy. The Fed’s main lever, at least so far, isn’t working. Mark Zuckerberg and Dario Amodei aren’t giddy consumers whose spending cools when borrowing gets expensive. They see themselves as great men of history, securing super intelligence for the West and ushering in an age of intergalactic abundance. They also believe customer spending on AI has only just begun, and so the coming revenue can justify their investments. That kind of existential drive can’t be discouraged by an extra 75 basis points of bond interest. Both the AI companies and the Fed are desperate for goodwill and credibility. If mortgages cost 15% and hyperscalers are still spending like there’s no tomorrow, people are going to be very mad at both of them. Notable Speaking at the IMF annual meeting in Bangkok last week, Warsh recognized that AI investment was creating a “shock” on prices, but reiterated his conviction that the technology would bring wealth and productivity in future.

events.title: Qatar is ramping up liquefied natural gas exports as prices surge
events.summary: There are more signs that Qatar is ramping up liquefied natural gas exports as prices surge and inventories dwindle ahead of the Northern Hemisphere winter. One tanker is now sailing toward Poland through the Red Sea, according to Bloomberg, and at least 20 more shipments have passed through the Strait of Hormuz to other destinations since early September. The gas could help halt the surge in consumer prices and slow the decline of Qatar’s $200 billion economy, which the IMF expects to contract by 15.6% this year. It’s unclear how the LNG is getting out: Qatar’s prime minister said last month that buyers had negotiated passage with Iran for the few cargoes that made it through during the first six months of the war. But Doha also seems to have adopted the “Hormuz shuttle” strategy Gulf crude exporters are using. Tracing the journey of Al Rayyan, one of Qatar’s oldest LNG tankers, Bloomberg tracked the vessel transferring its cargo to another ship in the Gulf of Oman before returning to Ras Laffan to reload. LNG ship-to-ship transfers are more complex than oil transfers, requiring cryogenic hoses to handle gas chilled to minus 162 C (minus 260 F). The effort is paying off, however: QatarEnergy restored LNG exports in September to about a third of prewar levels, Bloomberg reported. — Mohammed Sergie

events.title: Airlines shun reopened Riyadh airport after last week’s attacks
events.summary: Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport officially reopened on Sunday, but most scheduled flights have been canceled so far this week. Saudi authorities require airlines to get prior permission for every flight , according to a NOTAM issued over the weekend, while US and European regulators are warning carriers about the kingdom’s airspace. Lufthansa has suspended flights until Nov. 18, Cathay Pacific until the end of January, and Delta has pushed back the launch of its Atlanta route to March 2027. Attacks on Riyadh’s airport damaged six aircraft with a combined insured value of about $375 million, The Wall Street Journal reported, prompting Saudi carriers to evacuate aircraft worth up to $4 billion from the city. Many travelers are now driving to Bahrain, Qatar, and the UAE to catch commercial flights, while the wealthy are paying a premium of more than 50% compared to prewar rates to fly private out of al-Qassim airport, an almost four hour drive north of Riyadh, according to the Financial Times. — Ed Clowes

events.title: Trump isn't out to hurt Ukraine, Rubio tells Zelensky
events.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in a phone call Tuesday that President Trump hasn't issued any kind of order to harm Ukraine. Why it matters: The call was an effort to prevent the crisis between the U.S. and Ukraine from escalating further — and to push back on Ukrainian accusations that Trump is trying to coerce Zelensky into making concessions to Russia. The 45-minute call took place several hours ahead of a new round of peace talks with White House envoy Steve Witkoff aimed at reaching a unified position with European allies on an updated peace proposal to present to Russian President Vladimir Putin. Driving the news: The crisis broke out 10 days ago when Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia at the same time his envoys were in negotiations with Ukrainian officials in Miami. Zelensky on Monday lobbied a bipartisan group of senators to press the Trump administration to remove what he says are restrictions on intelligence sharing and weapons supplies. Behind the scenes: Rubio told reporters on Tuesday that he clarified to Zelensky that the Pentagon hasn't changed anything when it comes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine, weapons sales or restrictions on the use of the Starshield satellite system. "No change was ordered. It is not true that we restricted it," Rubio said. Rubio acknowledged to Zelensky that there could be a delay in sending Patriot interceptors that have already been paid for by NATO countries. But the reason, he said, is that the U.S. needs to make sure it has enough to protect its own military bases around the world. "Nothing is being deliberately denied. We balance between our obligations to partners and our own needs," he said. "There hasn't been a deliberate political directive to harm Ukraine." Rubio also asserted that the several cases in which Ukraine didn't get advance warning of Russian ballistic missile attacks were a result of technical failures, not a U.S. order. What he's saying: "No doubt there are tensions," he said. "That is why we had the call. The president is frustrated. The president is responding to the insinuation that he is doing things to deliberately harm Ukraine, which is not fair and not true." Rubio said Trump is "angry and frustrated" about the lack of progress in peace talks between Russia and Ukraine after two years of efforts. The other side: Zelensky wrote on X after the call that he is "grateful" for Rubio's "readiness to help and his clear position." He said Ukraine needs ballistic missile interceptors and early warnings to protect Ukrainian citizens and stressed that "the situation with Starlink and Starshield needs to be restored." State of play: Witkoff arrived in Oslo on Tuesday for talks with Zelensky and European leaders. The talks there are expected to include Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, President of Finland Alexander Stubb, representatives of the E4 nations (the U.K., France, Germany and Poland) and officials from the EU and NATO. Following Oslo, Witkoff plans to travel to Russia to meet with Putin and present ideas developed in consultation with Ukrainian and European leaders.

Text of this article October 20, 2026 PRESS RELEASE Apple announces new American Manufacturing Program partners for iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro From U.S. titanium to advanced camera technology, American suppliers are producing key components in the latest iPhone lineup CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today announced new and expanded partnerships with American companies that are supplying critical materials and components for iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro. Through its American Manufacturing Program (AMP), Apple is partnering with Perryman Company, a Pennsylvania-based titanium producer, to supply titanium for Apple products, including iPhone Duo. Apple is also expanding its partnership with Qnity Electronics, headquartered in Delaware, to produce technology for the new variable aperture in the iPhone 18 Pro camera system — the most advanced Apple has ever made. Apple works with suppliers in all 50 states and supports more than 450,000 American jobs. Last year, the company deepened that commitment by launching AMP, aimed at bringing even more advanced manufacturing and critical component production to the United States as part of Apple’s $600 billion, four-year commitment to U.S. manufacturing and innovation. “We’re thrilled to expand our work with companies producing advanced materials and components for our newest iPhone lineup right here in America,” said Sabih Khan, Apple’s chief operating officer. “American ingenuity is vital to all our products, from the titanium crafted for iPhone Duo to breakthrough camera innovations in iPhone 18 Pro. We’re proud to work with Perryman and Qnity Electronics to continue expanding our American Manufacturing Program and support U.S. jobs.” The grade 5 titanium enclosure on iPhone Duo is exceptionally strong, providing amazing durability to the first foldable iPhone. Apple will commit up to $100 million over the next three years with Perryman, a family-owned business and a global leader in manufacturing specialty titanium products. At its site in Houston, Pennsylvania, Perryman melts, forges, and rolls titanium with a minimum of 80 percent recycled content for iPhone Duo. Apple is also expanding its partnership with Qnity Electronics to build key camera technology for iPhone 18 Pro in the U.S. Qnity, which joined the American Manufacturing Program in March, will produce advanced films essential to the new variable aperture camera system on iPhone 18 Pro. Variable aperture is at the heart of the new 48MP Fusion Main camera, which enables incredible light and depth control. It’s powered by on-device intelligence that automatically lets in more light for darker settings and helps get sharper detail in brighter ones. Nearly 100 components in iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro — from wireless chips to the silicon that powers key functions across the devices — are produced by American companies and drawn from suppliers in more than a dozen states. That footprint continues to grow, empowering partners across the country to bring new capabilities online: Broadcom is expanding and modernizing its Fort Collins, Colorado, facility under a $1.5 billion capital investment announced in July, producing advanced radio frequency components for a wide range of Apple products. The multiyear agreement will produce more than 15 billion U.S.-made chips. Corning , an Apple partner since the original iPhone in 2007, produces specialty glass for Apple in Harrodsburg, Kentucky, including Ceramic Shield. By the end of 2026, all of the cover glass for iPhone — including iPhone Duo — and Apple Watch sold worldwide will be produced at this facility. Coherent continues building on its multiyear agreement with Apple, supplying new vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser technology from its Sherman, Texas, facility. This technology enables Face ID and other key features across iPhone and iPad, including the redesigned, even more useful Dynamic Island on iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. TSMC ’s Arizona fab continues to scale its production of advanced chips used across a range of Apple products, including iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch — producing more than 100 million chips for Apple in 2026. Construction on the north campus is progressing as Apple’s partnership with TSMC in Arizona grows. events.title: Two decades ago, he asked, ‘What’s the matter with Kansas?’ Now he’s back to look at the 70-year con of ‘creativity’ and ‘innovation’
events.summary: “Look at this sweatshirt,” Thomas Frank says in a video interview from his study in Bethesda, Md. He pulls at his maroon hoodie, which he’d just picked up from a thrift store the other day. The badge on his chest reads, “Innovation Fitness.” “These words are everywhere now,” he says with his ever-present smile and laugh. “It’s total saturation.” Frank has spent three decades arguing that Americans misread and misunderstand their own economy, perhaps most famously in his 2004 modern classic, What’s the Matter with Kansas? , which followed his evolution from college Republican to something else and probed why so many people from his native Kansas City area voted against what he understood as their class interests. His latest, The Creativity Con: How Innovation Became America’s Biggest Racket , takes aim at a staple of business journalism: the idea of “innovation” as something fundamental to American business. Frank is gracious toward Fortune , which publishes America’s Most Innovative Companies, runs the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum and Workplace Innovation Summit, and hosts a “Leaders in Innovation” series. “You guys have been very critical of all the stuff you ordinarily cover,” he says. He recalls that The Baffler, the journal he cofounded in 1988, kept a stack of old Fortune issues in its office. “We had this huge box of back issues,” he says, recalling the great painted Art Deco artwork that Fortune was known for in the 1930s and ’40s. “We used to just sit there in the office and pore over it.” Much of Frank’s book is about the cult of innovation and creativity that dates back to the postwar years. Much of the modern concept traces back to, of all things, the mind of an adman straight out of Madison Avenue: Alex Osborn, the “O” in BBDO. Among other things, Osborn popularized the term “brainstorm,” which once meant a mental seizure of sorts but which Osborn turned into a militaristic business term, as in storming an idea with your brains. Frank spent a week in Buffalo, looking through an archive of Osborn’s papers. He says Osborn and his colleagues collected everything that used the word “creativity” in the 1950s and ’60s to document the progress of their pet idea. “The word I use in the book is ‘ideology,’” Frank says, adding that he hopes that doesn’t sound too “political and really heavy-handed.” He describes the ideology: “This is how history works; this is how a country prospers … We’ve been saying that since the 1950s.” The problem is that it just “hasn’t really worked out,” Frank says in chipper but mournful fashion, pointing out that Osborn, “no fan of the New Deal,” pushed the ideology toward considering blue-collar workers as uncreative. “It has hurt us. It’s hurt us really bad.” Now Frank says AI has made his argument harder for white-collar workers to ignore. This is the point where the creativity gospel turns on the people who preach it the most. It’s “sort of an unspoken strain in all of the talk about AI,” he says. Just as “innovation” came for the working class and the Rust Belt as automation and outsourcing devastated communities like his hometown, Kansas City, AI now threatens the same displacement for the supposed creative class. “I have a lot of fears about it, too,” Frank says. “I’m right in the crosshairs … Nobody gives a damn about the creative class and their innovation districts anymore.” Frank’s own use of AI is mixed. He says it has “revolutionized” archival work, recalling that when he wrote The Conquest of Cool in the 1990s, he sat in a library paging through old issues of Life , Fortune’ s former Time Inc. stablemate. Now the whole run is searchable; he can even count how often a word appears. But he notes that he recently asked an LLM about a song lyric stuck in his head, and it confidently and wrongly told him it was from The Great Gatsby . When he pushed back, it said, “You are absolutely right,” before offering another wrong answer. Frank’s deeper complaint is that AI won’t be revolutionary enough: It will replicate the fatal flaw of journalism in treating authority’s misleading answers as truth. He calls the way LLMs work as dangerous: “Do the experts say it? Well, then that’s the truth.” The problem, he adds, is that “expertise evolves constantly.” People want “the correct answer with a capital C,” he says, “and I feel like that’s one of the dangers of AI.” It “reproduces orthodoxy.” “In some ways,” Frank says, “it’s easier to get your hands on the truth than ever before.” But in other ways, “we’re in this world of clouds and mystification and orthodoxy that you can’t question or touch … It’s going both directions at the same time.” He says he hopes that “digging” for the truth doesn’t disappear in the mixture. Perhaps it’s no surprise Frank’s criticism has an antiestablishment flavor. He has often cited punk rock as an inspiration for his work in The Baffler . An early journalistic coup was when Frank exposed the New York Times ’ Style section had printed slang from Seattle’s grunge scene that Sub Pop employee Megan Jasper had made up. (The invented slang included “wack slacks” for old, torn jeans, and “swingin’ on the flippity-flop” for hanging out.) Punk, he argues, is a perfect example of true innovation, unlike the supposed innovation of the Osbornian fashion. “People talk about Paris in the ’20s or these moments of medieval Florence. The only one that’s happened in my lifetime was the punk rock explosion.” Describing it as “totally unauthorized,” he says it’s “not the sort of creative thing that anybody would have celebrated at the time.” A lot of punk rockers were “unemployed people, working-class people; they did something really amazing. We haven’t seen an explosion of creativity like that in a long time.” This is a very Gen X kind of attitude, I had to point out, which Frank mostly dismisses. “In America, we like to talk about generations, but we hate to talk about social class,” which is something he considers “really obviously the motor behind everything.” At the same time, he says younger people struggle to picture the economy he grew up in. His father was an engineer for General Motors, and all of their neighbors also worked on the GM assembly line. “We all lived in the same kind of houses,” he says. “The idea that blue-collar and white-collar would basically have the same standard of living … at the time, that was a cliché. Everyone said that.” Frank recalls The Baffler ’s first anthology, Commodify Your Dissent , published in 1997, which carried the subtitle “The Business of Culture in the New Gilded Age.” That was a bit early, he says, laughing. “You don’t get a prize for being right about these things.” Does he advise Fortune readers and AI users to listen to more punk rock? “Exactly. Think for yourself. Do the research and read this book.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Taobao invests $19 million in Singapore promotions for 11.11 sale launching Oct 20
events.summary: Chinese e-commerce giant Taobao is partnering Pursuit Of Jade star Zhang Linghe to promote its annual 11.11 sale. Taobao is spending 100 million yuan (S$19 million) on Singapore’s 11.11 sale, with free shipping vouchers, public transport ads and shopping vouchers to grow its market share. The company has widened free shipping, added air express delivery and PayNow, and says Singapore is a key hub for Chinese brands entering South-east Asia. Taobao is using AI tools and local recommendations to stand out from rivals like Pinduoduo, while English AI features are due next year and Alibaba faces profit pressure. HONG KONG – Chinese e-commerce giant Taobao is investing 100 million yuan (S$19 million) in Singapore’s promotions for its 11.11 Singles’ Day sale , which kicked off on Oct 20. The e-commerce company’s biggest sale of the year – which runs till Nov 13 – is part of Taobao’s efforts to expand its presence here. The 100 million yuan includes free shipping vouchers, physical advertising on public transport in Singapore, and shopping vouchers for customers, said Cora Cai, Taobao’s Singapore country head, at a press conference on Oct 16 in Hong Kong. The physical advertisements in Singapore include about 200 big screens in the Central Business District and residential areas, with spending double that of 2025’s 11.11 season, Cai said. This is part of Taobao’s continued investment in the Singapore market and its overall expansion into foreign markets, Cai said. Since introducing free shipping with $0 minimum spend in August 2026, Taobao has expanded eligible products across fashion apparel, sports and outdoors, and maternity and baby products categories, with the majority of trending fashion apparel now eligible for free shipping. Taobao has also introduced air express delivery, allowing users to upgrade eligible parcels to air shipping for as little as $1, to receive their purchases as quickly as in five days. The e-commerce platform also started accepting payments via PayNow in October. “Singapore is one of the countries we’re expanding in, as the appetite for Chinese brands is high in Singapore,” said Cai. “Singapore has become a hub for Chinese brands to go overseas in South-east Asia – they often pick Singapore as their first stop in the region.” She said 70% of Singaporean online shoppers buy clothing from Taobao, while furniture is emerging as the fastest-growing category among Singaporean home buyers. Taobao faces fierce competition from other Chinese e-commerce platforms, such as Pinduoduo, which competes on price by offering heavily discounted products. Cai said that Taobao intends to differentiate itself through its large variety of products and its technical capabilities to help consumers find what they want. “Consumers nowadays don’t buy an item just because it’s cheap; they buy it because they actually need it,” she said. “We aim to upgrade our overall shopping guide capabilities, so consumers can find what they want faster. Simultaneously, through AI and curation, we ensure that products genuinely suited for the local market are visible.” The app’s new AI features include a localised recommendation algorithm and enhanced AI shopping assistants, said Ye Tian, general manager of Taobao Tmall Overseas. Currently, many of these advanced AI tools are optimised only in the Chinese version of the app. AI functions in other languages, including English, are in the pipeline over the next year, as the platform targets broader demographics across the Asia-Pacific region, said Taobao. Taobao declined to comment on how much it invested in its latest AI upgrades. Its parent company, Alibaba Group, on Aug 20 reported higher revenue in its most recent quarter, boosted by the global artificial intelligence frenzy driving demand for its products. However, net profit plunged 76 per cent year on year to 10.5 billion yuan, reflecting the impact of large strategic investments and economic pressure in its home market.

events.title: TSH Resources yet to respond to SGX’s haze queries; First Resources pledges cooperation
events.summary: Agribusiness companies have come under increasing scrutiny over their potential links to the transboundary haze. SINGAPORE – Plantation company TSH Resources has yet to respond publicly to queries from the Singapore Exchange (SGX) over fires in Indonesia amid growing attention on agribusiness firms’ operations as transboundary haze affects the region. The company, which has a primary listing on Bursa Malaysia and a secondary listing in Singapore, had not published a response as at 6pm on Oct 20. It also did not respond to queries from The Straits Times. In response to ST's queries, a spokesperson for Singapore Exchange Regulation said it was engaging TSH Resources to seek information on the impact of the fires on its operations, and would require the company to disclose any material information. Under SGX's regulatory framework, companies with secondary listings in Singapore are required to simultaneously publish on the SGX website any announcements made in their home markets. Unlike companies primarily listed in Singapore, those with secondary listings generally follow the rules of their home exchanges, although SGX may impose additional requirements. A spokesperson for Bursa Malaysia told ST on Oct 20 that it was aware of the issue and monitoring developments closely. The spokesperson did not confirm whether Bursa had queried TSH Resources, but said it would engage relevant parties where there were valid and verifiable grounds to do so. Recent bourse filings, including one on Oct 20, showed that TSH Resources had been buying back its own shares. TSH Resources was among seven listed companies named by Senior Minister K. Shanmugam during a media doorstop on Oct 19 as having received queries from SGX. He said companies could not just rely solely on statements about their fire prevention policies. The Government would ask for the full facts from companies, seeking evidence on where the fires started, who owned the affected land, and what steps were taken to contain them. In response to his remarks, First Resources said on Oct 20 that it welcomed a thorough, evidence-based examination of the ongoing fires and haze situation, and reiterated that it strictly enforces a longstanding zero-burning policy across its operations. It said it is confident that an objective review of the available evidence would show that it does not clear land using fire, either directly or indirectly. It added that it was open to constructive suggestions from regulators, customers, investors, civil society organisations and other industry stakeholders on strengthening fire prevention and management. Other companies including Golden Agri-Resources, Indofood Agri, Kencana Agri, Wilmar and Bumitama Agri had not published additional statements, after responding to SGX’s queries last week. The Indonesia Stock Exchange has also queried listed companies over the fires and haze, prompting disclosures on their fire prevention measures and the impact on their operations. Most of the companies said the fires had not materially affected their operations or financial performance. Among those who have responded were Astra Agro Lestari, PP London Sumatra Indonesia (LSIP) and Salim Ivomas Pratama, which have ownership links to Singapore-listed companies. Astra Agro Lestari said in an Oct 16 disclosure that fire mitigation protocols were in place across its concessions. But the company acknowledged that its subsidiary, Subur Agro Makmur, located in South Kalimantan, had been affected by forest and land fires. The company, which is controlled by Astra International, a subsidiary of Singapore-listed Jardine Cycle & Carriage, said the fires had not resulted in any operational shutdowns or materially affected its production targets or financial performance. It also noted that the fires had been extinguished . Astra Agro Lestari also noted that employees at Subur Agro Makmur were being questioned by the law enforcement authorities, although the company said it had not received any “administrative sanctions” over the incident. Meanwhile, LSIP said on Oct 15 that it was monitoring its operating areas in Sumatra and Kalimantan, with no unplanned shutdowns or material asset write-downs arising from forest fires. It added that it strictly enforced a zero-burning policy and used mechanical methods to clear unproductive plantation areas. LSIP is majority-owned by fellow Indonesia-listed plantation company Salim Ivomas Pratama, which is in turn controlled by Singapore-listed Indofood Agri. In a separate disclosure on Oct 15, Salim Ivomas Pratama said it strictly enforced a zero-burning policy and used mechanical methods to clear unproductive plantation areas. The company said its plantations were also equipped with firefighting vehicles and equipment, while designated employees underwent regular training in fire prevention and emergency response. It added that it had not experienced any material business interruptions or adverse operational impacts from the fires.

events.title: Jobless rate falls but small firms cut back hiring
events.summary: The UK's unemployment rate has dropped to its lowest for more than year, but job vacancies have continued to fall as smaller businesses cut back on recruitment, official figures indicate. The jobless rate fell to 4.7% in the three months to August, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said, the lowest since July last year. However, vacancies fell by 21,000 in the three months to September to 691,000, with the ONS saying small firms were citing labour costs as a key factor in scaling back hiring. The figures are the last official snapshot of the jobs market before the Budget, and analysts said they indicated the jobs market was showing signs of recovery despite the weakness in hiring. ONS deputy director of labour market statistics, David Freeman, said the labour market remained "broadly flat", with the latest data showing the employment rate edging up and "a small drop in unemployment". "The number of workers on payroll remains slightly down over the same period, though data for the most recent month suggests that might be starting to level off," he said. "The number of vacancies has seen its largest fall since the start of the year, concentrated mainly within smaller businesses, which cite increased labour costs as a key factor." Energy costs have risen since the Iran war began, and companies have also said that increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made it more expensive to employ staff. The number of job vacancies fell to its lowest level in more than five years, the figures indicated, with the largest decrease in construction jobs. Average earnings excluding bonuses rose 3.7% in the three months to August, up from 3.5% last month. Taking inflation into account, wages grew 0.8% in real terms. Pat McFadden, the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, said the figures "show the resilience of our labour market" with the UK's employment rate "now the third highest in the G7, despite a backdrop of global uncertainty". However, he said that "too many young people still find themselves locked out of employment". The government is working with industry "to bring young people back into the labour market and prevent them from drifting into the welfare system", he added. But Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said on X , external that "businesses can't afford to hire". "This is what happens when you attack employers, tax jobs, and put up red tape," he said. The latest ONS figures showed the unemployment rate for those aged 16 to 24 was 15.6% in the June to August quarter. While that was down from 16.4% in the March to May period, it was still higher than the rate of 14.6% seen in the June-to-August period last year. Separate ONS figures have indicated that nearly one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" On Monday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham warned the UK faces an "economic catastrophe and moral failure" due to high levels of youth unemployment. Ashley Webb, senior UK economist for Capital Economics, said the fall in the unemployment rate was "unexpected", and that it suggests the labour market "continues to recover". But "with businesses' energy costs likely to fall only slowly, we still think hiring will stay subdued," he said. Louise Murphy, senior economist at the Resolution Foundation, said the labour market "has performed poorly in recent years as the number of jobs has fallen and pay growth weakened". But she added that the UK's "recent bout of economic resilience may finally be creating some green shoots", pointing to "rising employment levels and private sector wage growth stabilising". The quality of ONS statistics has been criticised in recent years, with a review last year finding "deep seated" issues with the body . The Labour Force Survey, which it uses to report payroll and employment figures, has suffered from low response rates. In an update on Tuesday, the ONS said that response levels had improved, but that "some volatility" remained in the statistics. Have you been affected by the issues raised in this story? events.title: For investors, the Iran war redefined energy security
events.summary: Nearly eight months of war in Iran have produced one of the most severe energy shocks in decades, exposing a sharp divide between the countries that absorbed it with surprising ease and those forced into painful tradeoffs. Resilience, it turns out, comes less from any single technology or policy than from systems-level thinking, long-term investment, and deliberate planning. The countries that coped best were not always those with the most energy resources. They were the ones that had built flexibility, redundancy, and alternative pathways into their energy systems. China drew on strategic reserves, alternative pipeline imports, and fuel switching. The US benefited from record domestic oil and gas production, regional storage and solar to improve summer grid stability, and secure North American supply chains. Highly electrified countries such as Norway relied on hydropower, heat pumps, EVs, and infrastructure located far from the conflict zone. Emerging markets fared worse. Bangladesh and Pakistan imposed electricity restrictions and other demand-reduction measures. Wealthier economies across Europe and Asia largely avoided shortages only by paying sharply higher prices for LNG and other fuels. The dividing line ran not between producers and consumers, but between countries with options and countries without them. Three lessons stand out for governments and investors: Domestic electrons are safer electrons. The principle is straightforward: The shorter and more secure the energy chain, the fewer vulnerabilities a country carries into a crisis. Energy that is produced, generated, or stored at home is often more reliable than energy that must travel through vulnerable supply chains and geopolitical chokepoints. Few countries can achieve outright energy independence, but all of them can reduce their exposure to single points of failure. Solar and storage have scaled quickly in recent years on cost and technical readiness alone. Some producers will expand oil and gas output as demand shifts away from the Middle East to places with safer access to global trade routes. The Iran war is also unlocking public and private money for nuclear and geothermal energy. Nuclear deserves renewed attention as both an energy and national security asset, since reactors provide reliable electricity largely insulated from short-term geopolitical shocks. Small modular reactors could go further, supplying dependable power close to military installations, advanced manufacturing facilities, and AI data centers. Meanwhile, breakthroughs in deep drilling and new enhanced geothermal systems could vastly expand access to around-the-clock power beyond “traditional geothermal regions.” Electrification is now as much a security strategy as a climate strategy. Every domestically produced electron reduces exposure to disruptions in global fuel markets. That shifts the burden onto the grid. The challenge is no longer simply generating enough power. It is building the systems required to deliver that power where and when it is needed. The US electric grid is one of the largest on Earth, and it is aging rapidly. Some 70% of transmission lines are more than 25 years old, and the average large power transformer has been in service for nearly four decades. Demand for transformers has surged, yet the US has only one domestic producer of the specialized electrical steel needed for transformer cores. In 2025, 80% of power transformer supply and 50% of the distribution supply parts came from abroad. The American workforce is thinning too. The power sector will need more than 500,000 additional workers by 2030, just as hundreds of thousands of existing energy sector employees retire. Permitting compounds the problem: Major US infrastructure projects can take four to five years to secure approvals, delaying as much as $1.5 trillion in investment. As energy supply struggles to keep pace with demand, those delays have drawn political attention and, finally, action, including significant legislation passed at the state level and a new bipartisan permitting reform bill proposed in the Senate. The countries that cope best with the next crisis will not necessarily be those that build the most infrastructure. They will be the ones that make the best use of what they already have. Not every energy security challenge can wait a decade for a new power plant, transmission corridor, or major industrial project. In the US, with its aging grid infrastructure and rapidly growing power demand, that constraint bites. But many of the answers already exist: Long-duration batteries can store electricity during periods of surplus and release it when shortages emerge. Grid-enhancing technologies can raise transmission capacity, ease congestion, and improve the efficiency of existing assets. Smart-grid software and demand-management tools can shift consumption away from periods of peak stress without new steel in the ground. Every crisis is said to carry opportunity. The lesson from 2026 is that the most successful energy systems of the next decade will not merely generate more power. They will store it better, move it more efficiently, and protect it more successfully.

events.title: £30 rise in payments for crisis-hit households
events.summary: Sheffield City Council's crisis resilience fund can be used to pay for essentials such as utilities Crisis payments for people in Sheffield who are facing severe financial difficulties have been raised by £30. Single person households which qualify for help from Sheffield City Council's crisis and resilience fund will now be entitled to a one-off payment of £95, up from £65 previously. Meanwhile, two-person households can apply for a payment of £110, while homes with three or four people are entitled to £120 if they qualify and households with five or more people can get £130, the authority confirmed. Announcing the change, councillor Elle Dodd, chair of the authority's finance and performance policy committee, said life was "difficult and expensive" for "too many people" in Sheffield. The fund can be used to help people buy essentials such as food, toiletries and utilities, the council's website stated. The increase was put in place after a cost-of-living review conducted by the committee, which is made up of a group of Sheffield councillors. The review found almost 50,000 households in Sheffield were struggling to make ends meet and could not pay their bills . At least 7,000 crisis grants, totalling nearly £600,000, have already been awarded by the council since April. Dodd said: "Behind every statistic is someone making impossible decisions, feeling stressed and looking for a little breathing room. "We are determined to tackle the root causes of poverty, and to provide immediate support to those who need it. "We are keeping tackling poverty and the cost of living firmly on the agenda." events.title: DIY repair clubs are helping Americans save money and fight big tech
events.summary: US community repair clinics teach people how to fix their belongings, pushing back against throwaway culture O n a recent Monday night, a volunteer-run workspace bustled with dozens of fixers in Brooklyn, New York . Some tinkered with sewing machines while others soldered circuit boards at a workbench. Caleb Young, a co-founder of the Brooklyn Spark space, fit a DIY suction device on to the handle of a Dyson vacuum cleaner. “It’s in our culture to throw things away, but sometimes the fix is easier than you’d think,” Young said. The Fixit Clinic is open every Monday night to walk-ins. Anyone with a broken item they’d like to fix – from torn clothes to malfunctioning electronic devices – can drop by during open hours and get the repair help and tools they need. It’s a way for people to push back against tech companies, making their phones and gadgets deliberately unrepairable so they buy newer devices while creating large amounts of e-waste . The clinics also foster community: once people learn to repair their possessions, many get addicted and like helping others, Young said. “We like to tell them, ‘Why not take a few seconds to try and open something up?’” he said. “It’s broken anyway.” The Brooklyn clinic is part of a nationwide network offering community repair. Peter Mui, who founded the first Fixit Clinic in Berkeley, California, in 2009, said that he has seen the number of clinics explode during the past few years; at least 2,000 have been hosted across the country. “We’re offering these workshops in libraries, at colleges and in public spaces where fixers and community members can come together,” Mui said. Similar, unaffiliated clinics have seen success, too. The community-run Repair cafe , originally founded in Amsterdam, now has about 250 US locations. Neighborhood repair events at local community centers are also popping up around the country. Policy proposals have even matched this grassroots demand. Since 2012, 24 states have successfully passed some form of right-to-repair legislation, mandating that manufacturers make their products repair-friendly instead of destined for the landfill. This year, 57 right-to-repair bills have been introduced in 22 states that would make machines such as phones, wheelchairs and construction equipment easier to repair. Members of Congress have also introduced a bipartisan federal automotive right-to-repair bill, called the Repair Act , but it has yet to be brought to a full House vote. Mui attributes the growing interest to people questioning the environmental and economic costs of our consumer culture. “So much of our capitalist system is tied up in our endless consumption,” he said. “But if we come together to take agency and empowerment over the things we own, we can build a more sustainable future.” Starting a bottom-up repair culture The first modern right-to-repair state law was passed in 2012, when Massachusetts granted car owners the right to fix their cars at independent service shops. Congress passed a bill in 2014 that legalized “phone unlocking”, which allowed consumers to change their cell service carrier without buying a new phone. Farmers and states have also filed lawsuits against the agricultural equipment manufacturer John Deere over repair restrictions to their equipment, resulting in settlements with the company . Right to repair reached a new level of public consciousness in 2024 when customers across the country were upset over broken McFlurry machines. The Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) protected the software on these machines, meaning only their manufacturer, Taylor, could fix them. After petitions from consumers and consumer advocacy groups, the US copyright office granted a copyright exemption that would allow third-party repairs on McFlurry machines. Nathan Proctor, the senior director of the Right to Repair campaign at the Public Interest Research Group, said that corporations’ responses to right-to-repair laws have ranged from compliance to active resistance. For example, Apple has gradually made some parts and manuals available for repair, while the automotive industry has fought back against right-to-repair laws. “Some companies are hostile and refuse to provide repair materials, while others have made national policies to sell spare parts,” he said. But the growing grassroots movement of community repair brings Proctor hope. “We need to both change the law and build out a culture of repair,” Proctor said. “To see these community events start up with no institutional backing – that’s a signal that something about repair is clicking with people.” Educating the next generation of fixers At San Jose State University in California , the Fixit Clinic student organization was recently voted the most influential club on campus. The student-led group holds monthly clinics for fellow students and community members at libraries around the city.

events.title: Thames Water creditors secure former Labour minister to drive rescue deal
events.summary: Stricken UK water supplier lines up John Hutton as independent chair designate if takeover goes ahead The group of Thames Water creditors pursuing a £10bn rescue deal for Britain’s largest water supplier has lined up a former senior Labour minister to chair the company, as it tries to win over the government. The creditor consortium, called London & Valley Water, said on Tuesday that Lord John Hutton had been selected as independent chair designate of the Thames Water board, if the consortium’s deal is approved. Creditors have been locked in talks with ministers and regulators for months over the future ownership of the debt-laden water company, which has 16 million customers in the south of England. Andy Burnham has told officials to rip up their plans for how to fix Thames and present him with more radical options for the stricken company, the Guardian reported this week . Before he became prime minister, he said he would nationalise Thames. The company has been battling to stave off bankruptcy for years and is running out of cash. It recently asked its creditors for an additional £2.4bn . The creditor group said Hutton would be supported by Mike McTighe, a telecoms and turnaround specialist, who is leading Thames’s overhaul. McTighe had been lined up as the new chair in August to replace the incumbent Sir Adrian Montague, if the creditors’ takeover is approved by the government. McTighe has now been appointed vice-chair designate and is expected to work closely with the management team. Hutton served in Tony Blair’s and Gordon Brown’s governments as work and pensions secretary, business secretary and defence secretary and has experience ‌across public policy, energy and infrastructure. He has chaired the Nuclear Industry Association, Energy UK, and manufacturing association Make UK. Other roles include chairing the Association of Infrastructure Investors and London Luton Airport, and serving as non-executive director of Scottish Power Energy Networks. Hutton said: “I am looking forward to being part of the new leadership at Thames Water and helping get this hugely important business into a better place. “People living in London and the Thames Valley have the right to expect the highest possible standards of customer service and proper environmental stewardship from their water company, and that will be our focus as we look to the future.”

events.title: Oil prices hit five-month high as Houthi escalation worsens supply and inflation fears
events.summary: Oil prices hit a five-month high on Tuesday after the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen continued attacking Saudi Arabia, further stoking concerns over supply and higher inflation that could prompt interest rate increases. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, was trading 1.52 per cent higher at $111.30 per barrel at 2.27pm UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, climbed 2.30 per cent to $100.80 a barrel. Crude prices were last at these levels in mid-May. On Friday, Brent hit $110 for the first time since May, while WTI topped $100 for the first time in a month. The Houthis claimed responsibility for renewed strikes on ⁠Saudi energy, airport and military targets ⁠on Monday, escalating tension in the region and bringing down stock markets in the Gulf. The rebels claimed to have carried out six attacks on the kingdom, which included strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, a military airbase near Abha International Airport, a naval task-force camp and a Saudi radar in Bir Askar. With the US-Iran conflict continuing, crude supplies from the Middle East remain choked, prompting moves to ensure adequate supplies globally. The International Energy Agency last week said it had agreed to release more than 20 million barrels of diesel to the market amid a surge in diesel prices. Gulf oil producers, meanwhile, have pushed tanker transfers as far as India’s coast and slashed prices to keep crude flowing to Asia, as the makeshift export network around the Strait of Hormuz buckles under congestion and persistent attacks . The fighting has kept energy prices elevated, nudging inflation upwards and, in turn, raising the probability of another interest rate increase by the US Federal Reserve, which is scheduled to meet next week. Analysts are now expecting a second straight raise as Fed officials seek to tame inflation. "Brent crude hovering near five-month highs following geopolitical tensions in the Middle East has reignited fears of sticky inflation," analysts at US energy company Duncan Oil said. "Surging energy costs have led investors to believe the Fed will keep interest rates higher for longer to tame inflation." Ship movements in the Strait of Hormuz, which before the war made up a fifth of the world's energy exports, remain under pressure. events.title: Tesla’s Roadster represents a feat, and a defeat
events.summary: Andy’s view The new Tesla Roadster is science fiction: It can zoom into the air, perform barrel rolls, and then plop down softly using cold-gas rocket thrusters. Unveiled last week at a rocket facility in Texas, the Roadster is a triumph of engineering — an exquisite toy for the super-rich, if it ever reaches production (the disclaimers on the advance orders suggest CEO Elon Musk himself has doubts). Yet, paradoxically, it also represents a defeat: The Roadster isn’t a vehicle that will turn the tables on China, outcompeting the likes of BYD in the consumer market. Instead, it represents the future in another way, one in which China owns global mass manufacturing not just in cars but everything else — machine tools, pharmaceuticals, ships. As low-priced Chinese exports swamp global markets, politicians from Washington to Brussels to Berlin diagnose the problem largely as one of Chinese overproduction, and are putting up trade barriers to protect their domestic industries. The EU and China, for example, recently agreed to set quotas with tariffs for Chinese hybrid cars, and are considering similar restrictions on other industrial categories. But this misses the broader challenge. China’s surging shipments are much more than just surplus production, the difference between what comes out of Chinese factories and what can be sold domestically in a sagging economy. They are a deliberate strategy, clearly stated in the country’s five-year industrial plans and, ultimately, represent China’s quest for national power. The implication for Western industry leaders is existential: They can either climb the technological ladder into increasingly rarefied niches — like Tesla, with its Roadster — or risk being destroyed by Chinese rivals, as is currently happening to Volkswagen in China, still its largest single market. In fact, influential Chinese strategists don’t recognize the concept of overproduction at all. Lu Feng, a professor at Peking University’s School of Government, sees a showdown on the way between China’s “industrial socialism” and the US’ “financial capitalism” — and he warns that caving to foreign pressure to curb “overproduction” would be “ tying our own hands .” In this way of thinking, since China’s desire for power is limitless, there can be no question of producing too much. Kyle Chan, a researcher specializing in China’s industrial policies at the Brookings Institution, labels Lu’s brand of economic nationalism, “industrial maximalism.” Perhaps, then, we should call the Roadster a prime example of its opposite: “industrial minimalism.” Among leading global automakers, Tesla had the best chance of owning the future of mobility. Indeed, its Shanghai gigafactory, built in 2019, and the local supply chains it developed were a catalyst for the entire Chinese EV industry. But Musk is now clear-eyed about the competition he helped spawn. Without trade barriers, he warned in 2024, China would “pretty much demolish most other car companies in the world.” Musk is now betting Tesla’s future on becoming a robot maker. But he’ll run into the same issues in that sector, too. The challenge from China is systemic, not industry specific. The country’s industrial machine is set up to commoditize products through overwhelming economies of scale, to bring down prices, and conquer global markets — regardless of financial return. This is not about profit maximization. It’s about power maximization. Writing in The Guardian, the tech reporter Chang Che, who recently visited 11 Chinese robot makers across five cities, sees a future where the US leverages its advanced research capabilities to try to build the ultimate robotic machine — one that can “mow your lawn, walk your dog, and babysit your children” — while China cranks out functioning robots for each of those tasks at a fraction of the price . Already, China accounts for 60% of all the world’s new factory robots. It also has the capacity to supply 100% of global demand for EVs. Michael Dunne, the author of the forthcoming , told The Wall Street Journal that what remains for Western carmakers “ is to move up or get pushed out. ” The Tesla Roadster is, quite literally, aiming for the skies. Other carmakers will have to make a similar vertical ascent, or bite the dust. Notable Zeroing in on the term “ scenario innovation ,” a recent Sinocities article explained China’s state-sponsored process of opening up real spaces, like roads and factories, so that companies can test new technologies in real-world settings.

events.title: 'I'm fed up of swiping': The singles choosing dating events over apps
events.summary: Olivia says she chose to attend this dating event because she has "app fatigue" Checking in at a dating event in a bar in Guildford, Olivia Miller-Davis is understandably apprehensive. Even bringing a friend with her doesn't remove the awkwardness at the start of the night. "It's always nerve-wracking when you're meeting new people," the 28-year-old admits before downloading an app that will match her to other daters based on their star signs. This is speed dating 2026-style and Olivia, like many people we speak to, is here because she's fed up of "endlessly swiping" or as some describe it "app fatigue". She says she hates judging people with "really limited information and just a couple of pictures" because she doesn't feel she can "really fully commit" with so little to go on. According to a recent study from online regulator Ofcom 11% of adults use dating sites but it suggests the time we spend on them is dropping, from a peak of almost four hours a month in 2023, down to three hours last year. Edward believes apps are designed so you don't actually find "the one" Olivia's first match on the night is Edward and he agrees that recent dating trends leave him feeling cold. "I mean, they're designed so that you don't find 'the one', because they want you to come back and use the app forever. They don't want you to get married from the app." The event is organised by Love at First Sign, a dating company that uses an app to match people based on astrological connection, but most people are just using it as an icebreaker. Director of events Lissy Cleminson says the way people date is changing and a big factor is more home working since Covid, which means people do not meet in offices or on the commute. "The little meet-cutes don't happen so much when you're at home with your shirt up top and your pyjamas down bottom," she jokes. As you may expect at a dating event many of the singles told us they were keen for that in-real-life or IRL experience. There are a lot of #SingleTok and #Singlelife accounts on TikTok and Instagram reviewing dating events. Candice Gallagher runs an account called @Candilicious and recently went to 10 different dating events in 10 weeks. She describes herself as an entrepreneur and thinks in business terms dating events deliver "much greater return on investment". The 40-year-old says all too often dating online can lead to "chat graveyards" with very limited conversation. "At a dating event, everyone is single, everyone's ready to mingle, and your chances of having a good conversation are much greater." Dating events provide a better "return on investment" than apps, says Candice Gallagher Many people at the event in Guildford agreed dating events were better value for money because "you get to meet a range of people" in person for a similar cost to one date from an app. These events typically cost around £15 to £30 and often include a drink and activity or icebreaking gimmick, in this case an app that is used throughout the night. Olivia believes money plays a big factor in dating. "I wasn't working for a bit because I changed careers and because of that I put dating on hold." Olivia remembers thinking it "couldn't be a priority" and feeling she needed to wait until she was "earning enough" before dating again. She is not alone in finding dating expensive. More than a quarter of daters surveyed by Barclays suggested rising costs had changed how they date. And a couple of recent studies suggest the monthly cost of dating - from apps to entertainment and clothes - can add up to around £130. Many people at the event in Guildford agreed dating events were better value for money Those running apps are quick to point out online is still a big part in the way people meet. New research from Match Group, which owns Tinder and Hinge, suggests that out of those who had ever had a romantic relationship, about 21% of baby boomers surveyed met their most recent partner at a pub, bar or club. The survey of 3,007 single people also suggests that of those who had ever had a relationship, 20% met their most recent partner on a dating app and 20% met through friends. Chine Mmegwa, head of strategy, corporate development and operations at Match Group, says Tinder has made tweaks to its service in the past year to win back younger daters. As well as helping users find out more about each other in advance of dates, through interactive music and astrology features, it has introduced "double date mode" for friends who want to date together. And Tinder is doing more to encourage people to connect IRL, she says. "They want to be in person. You've seen us launch events across the US and now the UK. We are bringing IRL experiences into the app. "What we're doing is putting IRL into our experience. And so we are bringing that gap to what they're looking for in person, using the apps." In Guildford, Olivia says her night was a success because she met some men she might want to go on a first date with.

events.title: HKMA to swap jobs of 2 deputy heads as part of succession planning: sources
events.summary: Deputy chief executives Darryl Chan and Howard Lee will take over each other’s roles next month The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) will reshuffle the roles of two deputy chief executives next month as part of the de facto central bank’s succession planning strategy, two sources with knowledge of the matter told the South China Morning Post. Darryl Chan Wai-man will take over as CEO of HKMA’s Exchange Fund Investment Office from November 9, where he will manage the HK$4.46 trillion (US$568 billion) Exchange Fund – the war chest used to defend Hong Kong’s local currency, according to one source. Chan would replace fellow HKMA deputy chief executive Howard Lee Tat-chi in the position, with Lee assuming Chan’s current role in monetary management on the same date, the source said.
