events.title: Europe to see 'biggest-ever' increase in air fares next year, Ryanair chief says
events.summary: Ryanair Holdings chief executive Michael O’Leary has forecast a record increase in European air fares next year as the Middle East war continues to push up oil prices , forcing airlines to pass on their fuel costs to consumers. Ticket prices are set to increase by as much as 20 per cent next year, Mr O’Leary told a news conference in Brussels on Tuesday. As a result, airline margins will be squeezed because even the jump in fuel surcharges won’t make up for the higher oil bill, he said. “You’re going to see the biggest increase in airfares, I would say in history, in Europe in the next 12 months,” Mr O’Leary said. “The question is, will that increase in airfares be enough to cover the dramatically higher oil bills? I don’t think it will be.” The comments by the head of Europe’s largest budget carrier add to the more pessimistic outlook for the aviation industry, which has been forced to contend with a dramatic rise in costs even as travellers continue to splurge on air tickets. Mr O’Leary said most European airlines, including his own, lack significant hedging next year to protect against higher oil prices. In addition, there’s less capacity in the market as some airlines struggle, while higher taxes are further dimming the picture for the industry. “We’re 85 per cent unhedged next year, and most of the other European airlines are in a similar position,” he said. Ryanair's shares dropped as much as 2.1 per cent, bringing the decline to 25 per cent for the year. At that rate, that would be the worst annual stock return since 2018. The chief executive used his news conference to dish out against regulation in markets such as France and Belgium, where Ryanair will reduce its footprint in response to higher taxes. He repeated that the European aviation industry will continue to consolidate as weaker players struggle to survive in a high-cost environment. Air Baltic and Spain’s Volotea are the latest European carriers to undergo restructuring as higher costs take their toll. Last week, Deutsche Lufthansa won the race against Air France-KLM to acquire a stake in Portugal’s state-owned TAP. Meanwhile, US private equity firm Apollo Global Management is laying out the framework to take over EasyJet. Airlines across the world have suffered from soaring jet fuel costs since the Iran war began in late February. Ryanair’s most recent earnings in July showed the conflict hit its profit and caused later bookings amid concern about jet-fuel supply availability. Mr O’Leary said separately that he aims to receive the first delivery of the carrier’s Boeing Max 10 aircraft in January, with about 16 more expected up to April.

events.title: Netflix hunts for its next big hit after US$135b stock market wipe-out
events.summary: Netflix is among the top 10 worst performers in the technology-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index. Netflix is under pressure after losing more than US$135 billion (S$173 billion) in market value in 2026, as weak engagement and fewer hit shows hurt growth. It is changing its content team, cutting about 1,000 jobs, and may focus on “more premium, conversation-driving originals” and higher 2027 spending. Investors will watch the Oct 20 earnings call for signs of recovery, but analysts say proof of better engagement and ad growth is still needed. NEW YORK – Netflix needs to prove that it can produce hit movies and TV series again to stop a slide that has erased more than US$135 billion (S$173 billion) in market value in 2026. The streaming giant reports earnings after the close on Oct 20, and investors will likely be more attuned to what content executives say is coming over the next six months than to the company’s third-quarter numbers. The stock is down 26% in 2026, putting Netflix among the 10 worst performers in the technology-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index and on track for its worst year since 2022, and it is coming off a 14% decline in September. The reason is no secret to anyone following the company: User engagement has stalled owing to a lack of popular content despite heavy spending driven by a crowded, competitive entertainment landscape. Netflix won the fewest Emmy Awards in a decade in 2026, and the company is not growing fast enough , according to co-chief executive officer Ted Sarandos. “The content’s getting very expensive, and there are just still too many players,” said Ken Mahoney of Mahoney Asset Management. “I think there are so many better tech stories out there than Netflix that have sticky customers.” Netflix is taking steps to improve its content and raise its audience numbers. On Oct 19, it announced that the head of its film division, Dan Lin, was leaving, and last week replaced its chief content officer, Bela Bajaria, with Peter Rice, the former chairman of Walt Disney Television. The company also plans to cut about 1,000 positions in various departments globally in a bid to reduce costs. For investors, however, the issue is that this earnings report will not reflect those moves. And even if executives give a solid revenue outlook, it is unlikely to quell the debate around engagement, according to Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Geetha Raganathan. “A stronger (fourth-quarter) slate could revive viewing and ads, but investors will want proof that engagement can improve without derailing margin expansion,” she wrote in an Oct 19 note. The addition of Rice signals a potential pivot towards “more premium, conversation-driving originals and higher 2027 content spending”, she added. Analysts following the company expect it to report a 12% rise in revenue in the third quarter to US$12.9 billion, and a 39% jump in earnings to 82 US cents a share, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Its gross margin is expected to be 51%, down slightly from the second quarter. Wall Street remains generally bullish on the stock, with an average price target of about US$92 suggesting a 32% rise over the next 12 months. And while sentiment has weakened, with two analysts putting sell-equivalent ratings on the shares in September, bulls see a vibe shift coming. “While total viewing is still weak, quality has improved as reflected in hour/top-10 title and the number of sequels is increasing” through the end of 2026, Oppenheimer analysts led by Jason Helfstein wrote in an Oct 14 note. Three months of US price increases and one month of higher ad rates should give revenue a boost, and the recent headcount reductions will allow for more spending on marketing or content or provide upside to margins, they added. Management may offer some indications for what it expects in 2027, but the company is unlikely to offer thorough guidance, according to Mark Mahaney of Evercore ISI. He was particularly enthusiastic about Netflix’s recent release of East Of Eden. “East Of Eden looks very promising to us,” Mahaney wrote in a note to clients on Oct 16. “Steinbeck is BACK!” Ad revenue may be more important to investors than audience engagement, according to Wedbush’s Alicia Reese, who says the segment is on track to double to roughly US$3 billion in 2026. “Netflix is actively making changes that should address both its engagement issues and shift dollars from heavy infrastructure to more focused content spend,” Reese wrote in an Oct 16 note. One argument for buying the stock would be valuation, considering it is priced at less than 19 times earnings projected over the next 12 months, the lowest valuation since 2022 and a steep discount to its 10-year average of 49. That helps explain why KeyBanc Capital Markets analyst Justin Patterson believes the Netflix bear case is already priced into the share price. “The bear case on slowing engagement and more modest margin expansion is arguably priced in,” he wrote in an Oct 12 note.

events.title: Today in Paris, we announced new capabilities across Microsoft Sovereign Cloud, expanding choice and control for organizations running their most sensitive workloads across public and private cloud, and our growing partner ecosystem.
events.summary: Today in Paris, we announced new capabilities across Microsoft Sovereign Cloud, expanding choice and control for organizations running their most sensitive workloads across public and private cloud, and our growing partner ecosystem. https://lnkd.in/gDjmHetu Intriguing to hear what Microsoft is defining as sovereignty. My understanding of EU digital sovereignty is that we want independence from manufacturers who retain control of how we use their products/services. If your vendor can shut down your service — by definition — your use is not Sovereign. After reading the article I noticed one potential challenge here is vendor lock in. Even if organizations gain more control over where their data lives and how workloads operate, how easy is it to move away from the Microsoft ecosystem entirely without major costs or disruption? True digital sovereignty should include not just control, but the freedom to switch providers when needed. What are your thoughts? The fundamental contradiction remains very visible. The US cloud act legally compels American service providers to produce data upon request, meaning absolute digital sovereignty via a US corporation is an ongoing legal impossibility. The proposed solutions in the blog expose the technical limits of this approach, why ? Operating an Azure local environment on disconnected private hardware is simply traditional onpremise hosting reliant on a proprietary software stack. A company might own the physical servers & sever the network cables, but they are still running a closed source system. True digital sovereignty requires the ability to audit the technology independently. Local security agencies are legally prohibited from inspecting the compiled binaries of Microsoft software. They cannot verify the underlying mechanics and/or write their own internal security modifications. The organisation remains permanently dependent on a foreign software supply chain. EU public institutions are actively shifting toward open source platforms & domestic providers specifically to escape this type of extraterritorial legislation. Rebranding disconnected virtualization as a new product does not alter the underlying jurisdictional reality. Sovereignty isn’t about where the servers sit, it’s about which law applies to them. In June 2025, Microsoft France’s legal director told the French Senate under oath he could not guarantee that French data would never be handed to US authorities. The CLOUD Act still applies, and will always. A sovereign cloud under US jurisdiction should be an oxymoron. Europe doesn’t need sovereignty under licence What would be the key outcomes and business values it brings for MS cloud user Satya Nadella Great to see digital sovereignty evolving beyond data residency toward a more comprehensive approach to control, resilience, and operational independence. As AI agents become more deeply integrated into enterprise workflows talking from the first hand experience, questions around where they run, what data they can access, what actions they’re authorized to take, and how those actions are governed become increasingly important. The workload-based approach is particularly compelling: combining cloud innovation with the right level of control, security, and resilience for each workload. Trustworthy agentic AI requires not just intelligence, but also clear boundaries, governance, and operational accountability. Mehr Optionen bedeuten für stark regulierte Sektoren leider nicht automatisch mehr Kontrolle. In der Praxis verlagert die wachsende Feature-Vielfalt das Problem oft nur auf die Compliance-Ebene, weil technische Souveränität ohne echte operative Unabhängigkeit die Auditoren am Ende selten überzeugt. Does Microsoft have a road map for CADA compliance offerings, by 2028/2029? @Satya Nadella , Have you offlate noticed declined in usage of Microsoft edge, when we open the browser it gets overloaded with all content, eats up memory and is making even normal browser usage impossible. Pls reduce AI pushes amd widgets on the page. Where do we see the YIMBA zealots making their voices heard for data centers to be built in France? Unless the data centers are in place then you can’t have geographically restricted data sources and solutions. events.title: Chancellor rejects calls to raise Capital Gains Tax in Budget
events.summary: Chancellor John Healey says he wants to avoid an investor exodus from the UK Chancellor John Healey has dismissed calls from some Labour MPs to increase Capital Gains Tax (CGT). Cabinet ministers Wes Streeting and Louise Haigh both previously voiced support for raising CGT before Andy Burnham became prime minister in July. Ahead of next week's Budget, as first reported by the Times , external , Healey is minded not to increase CGT - which is imposed on the profit people make when they sell an asset that has increased in value, such as shares in a company or properties which are not primary residences. The move followed warnings that it could end up costing the government money if wealthy people leave the country or defer selling off assets. If you pay income tax at the basic rate then CGT is charged at 18%. For higher and additional rate income tax payers, the CGT rate is 24%. Last year, HMRC estimated , external that lifting the lower rate of CGT by 1% could raise £5m by 2028-9 but increasing the higher rate of CGT by 10% would reduce the Treasury's receipts by £3.6bn in 2028-9. The amount raised could be reduced if people adapt their behaviour to the tax rise, for example by moving abroad or deciding not to sell a property. The chancellor gave an indication of his approach last month in a speech when he spoke about the importance of businesses and self-employed people making profits. "I want to see this country as a country of wealth creation. I want our government decisions and policies to raise the levels of confidence, and investment, and profit in British business," Healey said. Burnham has faced warnings against lifting CGT. His former adviser and Goldman Sachs Chief Economist Lord Jim O'Neill suggested it would send "the wrong message to business". But influential Labour figures had pushed for equalising CGT and income tax, with the former generally attracting a lower tax rate. Louise Haigh, a key ally of the prime minister, had suggested capital gains should go up to be closer to income tax, before she became Burnham's first secretary of state. In an article for the Renewal journal, , external Haigh argued that raising CGT would "shift the taxation burden away from punishing work, and towards unproductive capital accumulation which does little to grow the everyday economy". She said this could be accompanied by measures to ensure that "genuine investment returns are not penalised". Defence Secretary Wes Streeting called for a "wealth tax that works" in May, shortly after resigning as a minister in former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's government. He had argued that equalising CGT with income tax would address an unfair system that was "penalising work". Healey had already ruled out levelling the two tax rates, according to a report in the Financial Times last week , external . Asked about the government's plans for CGT on BBC Breakfast, Communities Secretary Angela Rayner would not speculate on the Budget. Pressed over whether rejecting calls to increase the tax was a win for the rich, she said the government had already taken steps to give people "breathing space" and help with the cost of living. It comes after senior banking executives told the BBC they expect Healey to raise taxes on the sector. UK banks have been reporting bumper profits, leading to calls from unions for higher taxes. Healey is due to set out his tax and spending plans at his first Budget on 28 October, against the backdrop of the US-Iran war which has led to rising prices. The chancellor is under pressure to find measures to ease the cost of living and fund an increase for defence at his spending review next year. The chancellor's options for raising money are limited as Labour's 2024 manifesto pledged not to increase income tax, National Insurance and VAT, the three big revenue raisers. The government is also restricted in how much it can borrow due to its self-imposed rules on debt. What is the Budget and what could be in it? Published 17 hours ago Labour will not have the courage to cut spending, says Badenoch Published 11 hours ago Banks expect to be hit with higher taxes in Budget Published 4 days ago In a pre-Budget speech on Tuesday, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch urged the government to cut spending and reduce its borrowing. She said the prime minister and the chancellor should "live within our means" and pointed to her party's plan to save £70bn in cuts, including to welfare and overseas development aid. Badenoch told an audience in central London that Labour would not "find the courage" to cut spending. She said the chancellor wanted to deliver a "nothing to see here Budget" but added: "Britain cannot afford to do as little as possible." The Liberal Democrats have said the government could raise £14bn partly by introducing a windfall tax on the profits of banks. The party's deputy leader Daisy Cooper said the money could go towards cutting fuel duty, rail and bus fares and VAT for hospitality businesses.

events.title: Free trade agreements may be out of fashion, but APEC can further existing deals: Jeffrey Siow
events.summary: Second Minister for Finance Jeffrey Siow said on Oct 20 that APEC can build on existing regional trade agreements such as the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership. Singapore urges APEC to build on existing regional deals like RCEP and CPTPP to keep trade open, as free trade agreements may have fallen out of fashion. Jeffrey Siow said regional cooperation could include digital partnerships, such as ASEAN’s DEFA. Siow spoke at the APEC finance ministers' meeting in Hong Kong. SINGAPORE – Countries should continue to pursue economic openness and collaboration through forums and platforms like the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) grouping, even as the global consensus that has sustained openness has weakened, said Second Minister for Finance Jeffrey Siow. Speaking at the APEC finance ministers’ meeting in Hong Kong on Oct 20, he noted that inking free trade agreements may no longer be in trend. This comes as strategic competition is increasingly driving countries to impose trade restrictions and distribute industrial subsidies to protect their critical sectors and secure supply chains. Against this backdrop, Siow said: “We need more forums and platforms like APEC for economies to come together, build common ground, and advance cooperation. “Free trade agreements may have fallen out of fashion, but we can build on existing regional trade agreements such as the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP).” The ASEAN-led RCEP is the world’s largest free trade agreement, comprising around 30% of global gross domestic product and around a third of the world’s population. It involves 15 countries, namely Indonesia, Singapore, Brunei, Cambodia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Thailand, Vietnam, Australia, China, Japan, South Korea and New Zealand. Meanwhile, the CPTPP is a free trade agreement among 12 countries: Japan, Australia, New Zealand , Singapore, Brunei, Canada, Chile, Malaysia, Mexico, Peru, the United Kingdom and Vietnam. Siow added that like-minded countries can work together to advance topical interests through plurilateral arrangements involving more than two parties but fewer states than multilateral agreements. He cited digital economy agreements including ASEAN’s landmark Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA) , that is expected to be formally signed in November to lay the groundwork for closer digital integration across South-east Asia. He also mentioned Green Economy Agreements, which Singapore has advocated to accelerate its transition towards a green and sustainable future. He also named the Future of Investment and Trade Partnership, known as FIT-P, as an example of flexible cooperation between like-minded countries. The grouping of 20 small and medium-sized, trade-dependent economies allows some of them to move on initiatives “while the door remains open for others to join later”, he said. For instance, 10 FIT-P members endorsed a joint declaration on strengthening the rules-based trading system on March 16, before three more members joined at a later date. Siow also said that open economic cooperation must come with domestic support, as the benefits of globalisation, which have been enormous on aggregate, have not always been evenly shared. “Workers and industries have borne the costs of rapid technological change. The advent of artificial intelligence will add to these pressures,” he added. At a session on the global and regional outlook at the APEC meeting, Siow said that while the global economy has remained resilient amid the ongoing Middle East conflict, growth has been unevenly distributed and heavily dependent on AI investment. He said: “If the productivity gains from AI fall short of expectations, financial markets could experience a correction, and economies could find ourselves exposed to bigger risks.” Siow added that for growth to be sustained, AI investments must be translated into wider productivity improvements and good job opportunities. This is a focus of Singapore’s Economic Strategy Review, Siow said, where the country is growing industries generating high-value jobs which are assisted by technology. He said semiconductor firms like Micron and GlobalFoundries are expanding their operations in the Republic, with new roles in engineering and operations tapping AI, robotics and smart manufacturing technologies. Singapore’s workforce is also being equipped with future-ready skills. In accountancy , for instance, AI is being used to analyse large volumes of financial transactions, identify anomalies, and prepare detailed reports. “But accountants must still interpret the findings, exercise professional judgment and advise businesses,” Siow said. “ Singapore has launched a programme to help accountants develop the skills to work effectively with AI.

events.title: ‘For Panama, it is life or death’: how drought is choking the canal that feeds a nation
events.summary: Failed rains and a dire El Niño threaten the waterway that sustains the country, with farmers selling cattle to survive T he cattle should be ambling, grazing contentedly, through Robert Delgado’s fields. Instead, the animals slump in the shade, tongues lolling, in futile attempts to avoid the blistering heat. Soon it will matter little whether their appetite returns, for there will be no grass left to graze. In Azuero, an agricultural region in Panama ’s Arco Seco (Dry Arc), the summer is generally relentless and unforgiving. But this year, the crucial rainy season that precedes it – typically from May to December – has brought little rain to parched fields. The watering holes, streams and rivers that farmers rely on have not been replenished, and pastures – the vital source of animal feed during the dry months – have not regenerated themselves. Delgado’s milk production has fallen by half. As the dry season approaches, he is selling off cattle for fear of what is to come. He says: “I and other producers have had to slaughter or sell animals of high genetic value simply to avoid the heartbreaking prospect of watching them die of thirst or starvation. The lack of water has greatly affected us, and it is going to continue to do so.” Panama is gripped by a water crisis. A rainy season punctuated by drought, exacerbated by the climate crisis, has ravaged large swathes of the country. El Niño threatens to continue the havoc. In August, the government declared a national state of emergency that will remain in place until June 2027. Authorities forecast rainfall deficits of more than 50% in some regions until December. “The situation is dramatic,” says Panama’s environment minister, Juan Navarro. “Climate change has undoubtedly increased the frequency and also the gravity of El Niño, as well as other climate extremes; we used to get an El Niño every 10 or 20 years. The last, in 2023, cost the Panama canal almost a billion dollars in revenue.” And this latest El Niño, Navarro says, citing scientists, is pointing towards being the worst in history . He says: “We are already starting to feel the impact, but we have seen nothing yet. For Panama, this is life or death. The canal is life and death for our economy, and for our drinking water supply.” Panama’s economy relies heavily on the Panama canal – and the canal is acutely vulnerable to the climate crisis. The 50-mile (80km) waterway linking the Atlantic and Pacific oceans, through which about 5% of global maritime trade flows , accounts for up to 7.7% of Panama’s GDP . The freshwater lakes that supply the canal’s locks, Gatún and Alajuela, also provide drinking water for about 2 million people – nearly half of Panama’s population . A sizeable chunk of the country’s hydroelectricity generation also depends on the watershed. In September, low water levels twice triggered restrictions on daily vessel transits. While some have been lifted, officials are braced for worse when the El Niño-intensified dry season begins in December. The government is funnelling $80m (£60m) towards “resilience actions” to prepare for El Niño, Navarro says. In the long term, it is investing about $1.5bn in a reservoir on the Indio River intended to supply Lake Gatún and meet demand for the next five decades. The new reservoir is, in Navarro’s words, “the most important investment we are making – Indio is the ultimate bet on resilience”. Yet the project has not come without controversy and fierce resistance. Damming the Indio River will flood the lands of 550 families in 38 rural communities , about 2,500 people in total, who live in the basin. Cropland will be swept away, graves exhumed and reburied elsewhere, and whole communities – homes, schools, churches – will be dismantled. In response, people have held street protests, taken legal action and set up blockades. Yet the project is steaming ahead; authorities forecast completion in two to three years. “For us, this isn’t merely a matter of changing homes,” says Florentino Chirú, vice-president of the Coordinadora Campesina por la Vida Contra los Embalses (Peasant Coordinating Committee for Life Against Dams). “It means leaving behind the history of entire generations. Furthermore, we would lose fertile land.” According to Chirú, farmers rely on small-scale livestock farming for their livelihoods, meaning they would lose their only means of feeding themselves and generating income. “The impact would be absolutely devastating. There are no words to describe it. I’ve lived on this land for 63 years; my whole life is here,” he says. “If we were to be displaced, well, this is our life insurance. We would be left with nothing.” Get a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development team The Panama Canal Authority says the resettlement will include compensation for homes, land, crops and livelihoods, along with support to restore families’ income sources.

events.title: 'Gulf security is our security', says former UK defence secretary
events.summary: Britain should do more to help its allies in the Gulf, including considering strikes on the Houthis , because Washington's priorities have changed and its partners must now stand together, former UK defence secretary Michael Fallon has told The National . The US , he said, is “shifting its priorities to homeland defence, to the Indo-Pacific. And therefore, it means that in terms of Washington, perhaps Europe and the Middle East count for less than they used to”. That shift is structural, not a passing mood. “We've also seen a change in the United States,” Sir Michael said, recalling a country that “helped us win two world wars in Europe”. With the Gulf and Europe pushed down Washington's list of priorities, the burden falls on the allies. “I think we should be doing more,” he said. “These are our partners and friends, and we should be helping more.” For Britain, that means being ready to act against the Houthis . “That means, if necessary, we should be prepared to consider strikes as we did two years ago” he said, alongside the US and other European nations, as in the joint US-UK air campaign against Houthi targets that began in January 2024. Sir Michael, who served as the defence secretary from 2014 to 2017 under prime ministers David Cameron and Theresa May, was speaking in Dubai on the sidelines of the inaugural Middle East chapter of Signum Global Advisors, chaired by Charles Myers and launched by Raha Moradi, where he took part in a closed-door, onstage discussion. Sir Michael was careful with his words about the White House. Asked whether US President Donald Trump was an unreliable, unpredictable partner for the Gulf and Europe, he pointed to Moscow instead. “The most unreliable person clearly is President [Vladimir] Putin.” It is, to borrow the Irish, a mé féin foreign policy in Washington: me, myself and I. For America's allies, the old guarantees are no longer a given. However, he was clear that the ground had moved. “You have an unpredictable element now,” he said. “Policy shifts suddenly.” 'Gulf security is our security' “Gulf security is our security,” Sir Michael said. “It's our economic security. It's our energy security.” The trade and energy flowing through the region, he said, fed straight into the British economy and inflation, “and in the end, affects interest rates back in the UK”. “So we have a huge interest, as well as friendships and historical ties,” he said. The pressure on those ties is rising. Since July, the Houthis have been in direct conflict with Saudi Arabia , declaring a naval blockade of the kingdom and attacking Saudi tankers in the Red Sea, while threatening to close the Bab Al Mandeb strait, the southern gateway to the Suez Canal. The Strait of Hormuz has already been disrupted by the US-Israel war with Iran. Britain has stepped up, but only so far. In April, the RAF deployed its Rapid Sentry air-defence system to Kuwait. Last month, in the first substantial foreign policy decision of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government, London agreed to a Saudi request for an RAF Voyager tanker to keep the kingdom's Typhoon jets in the air for longer. Ministers described it as a strictly defensive, “time-limited commitment”. “Well, we've responded to Kuwait's call for assistance,” Sir Michael said. “The Saudis asked us for help.” The most obvious step, he said, is to make sure the Houthis cannot disrupt the Bab Al Mandeb strait in the way Hormuz has been disrupted, which means tackling Houthi strikes “at source”. Asked whether strikes would be a big step for Mr Burnham, he said: “It would be, and clearly, they've considered it.” Labour has been reluctant before. In February, under Keir Starmer, the government initially refused to let the US use British bases, including Diego Garcia, for strikes on Iran, before reversing course. Sir Michael said the government had now “reversed that decision and said they can use Diego Garcia, but I think we should be doing more than that”. Gulf states, he said, are “with us, by the way, in the long-term battle against international terrorism ”, as they were in the international coalition against ISIS. Europe's turn to do more The same logic applies in Europe, where, Sir Michael said, the continent had been too slow to carry its share of the pressure on Moscow. He called Washington's diesel deal with Russia a misstep. This month, the US Treasury waived sanctions on Russian diesel sales until April 2027, and on Friday, Mr Trump signed an executive order pausing new Russia sanctions passed by Congress. “I'm afraid it's a miscalculation,” Sir Michael said. The volumes are too small to bring down diesel prices in the US and the deal is unlikely to move a ceasefire any further forward, he said. Mr Putin, he argued, would read it as weakness. “He's given up nothing in return,” he said. Russia has kept up its attacks on Ukraine 's civilian infrastructure, he added, and “he hasn't come to change any of his negotiating position about the future of Ukraine”. Asked whether it undermines sanctions as a weapon globally, he said it does. “You're either all in on sanctions or you're not.” Mr Trump, he conceded, has a point: “Where Trump is right, that our sanctions haven't been fully applied.” Europe has been far too slow to cut its dependence on Russian oil and gas, to police the shadow fleet and to use sanctioned Russian assets to help Ukraine, Sir Michael said. “Europe keeps passing new packages of sanctions, which rather casts doubt on the previous packages.” The EU adopted its 22nd package on October 12, the largest single round of listings yet at 1,569 individuals and entities. Brussels is already drafting a 23rd. Yet EU countries still bought €817 million ($917 million) of Russian pipeline gas and €615 million of Russian LNG in September. Pressure on Kyiv The stakes are highest in Ukraine . “I believe steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate,” President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Bloomberg this week. “I am not saying that this is the goal our partners are pursuing. I don't want to think that our American partners believe the war” against Russia “could be ended sooner at Ukraine's expense. But that's how it looks.” A capitulation would not only encourage Mr Putin, Sir Michael said. It would put Russia's near neighbours “in the firing line, whether it's Moldova, the rest of Georgia, even the Baltic states, even though they're part of Nato ”. Moscow regards those countries as its “near abroad”, he said, “and they will be much more exposed. But it will also send a signal right round the world to other countries that want to extend their borders”. “China, of course, has ambitions to bring Taiwan formally back inside China, to extend its influence across the South China Sea.” The idea that might makes right, Sir Michael warned, “is very dangerous for the international community”. events.title: Billionaire Mukesh Ambani launches India’s biggest-ever IPO
events.summary: Low-cost broadband provider Jio Platforms aims for £81bn valuation when it floats on the stock market on Wednesday India’s second-richest man, Mukesh Ambani, is launching what could be the country’s biggest-ever initial public offering (IPO), despite a stock market downturn. Mumbai-based Jio Platforms, a telecoms company backed by Meta Platforms and Google, is hoping to raise up to 302bn rupees (£2.4bn) and is targeting a 10.3tn rupees valuation when it floats on the stock market from Wednesday. Set up a decade ago as a subsidiary of Ambani’s conglomerate Reliance Industries, and led by Akash Ambani, the oldest son of patriarch Mukesh, Jio offers low-cost broadband to millions of Indians. Jio secured 212 anchor investors on Monday before its blockbuster IPO. They include some of the world’s largest fund managers, such as: BlackRock; Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund; the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority; Fidelity Investments; Schroders; JP Morgan Asset Management; Franklin Templeton; Invesco; and Prudential. On Wednesday, shares will be offered to retail investors, and the IPO is set to close on Friday. Reliance Industries said in a stock exchange filing last week that Jio had set a price range of 1,065 rupees to 1,119 rupees a share for its maiden share sale, offering up to 270m new shares. The family-owned conglomerate has been encouraging its 400,000-plus employees to buy shares, offering them a discount of 54 rupees a share. At the top end of the price range, Jio would be worth 10.3tn rupees, which would make it India’s fourth-largest company, behind its parent Reliance Industries, Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank. It would be more than twice as much as the 4.9tn-rupee valuation in 2020, when Meta and Google invested in the company. However, the top valuation is far below initial expectations of more than £110bn when the telecoms group posted a draft prospectus in the summer. It comes amid a broader stock market slowdown in India, with the blue chip Nifty 5o index down more than 12% this year. Niha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern India Jio launched its telecoms services in September 2016. It gained 16 million subscribers in the first month, and topped 100 million subscribers within 170 days, according to Reliance Industries. It is credited with making mobile internet more affordable, by triggering a price war. The company intends to expand further into artificial intelligence, cloud computing and digital infrastructure. Isha Ambani, who sits on Jio’s board as a director, told investors last week that the business idea was spawned by the poor connectivity she and her brother Akash faced when they returned to India on a break from studying in the US in about 2009-10. She struggled to submit a college assignment online because the internet was not working. “What followed was a conversation about why should India be left behind,” she said. “Akash firmly believed that the answer and solution to this was creating a digital technology platform company.”

events.title: Singapore-based semiconductor firm Mi Material to expand into US, Malaysia in $215m IPO
events.summary: Mi Material CEO Kevin Tan said that the company will focus on maintaining healthy earnings post-IPO, as it looks to grow its specialty alloy business to support the semiconductor industry. Mi Material launched a $215m SGX IPO offering 77.5 million shares at $1.80 each. Trading on the mainboard is expected to start on Oct 28. The Singapore-based firm is a top-two global solder sphere supplier, with 24% of the 2025 serviceable market. FY2025 revenue was US$65.3 million and net profit was US$10 million. Most IPO funds will build a US R&D centre, with more work in Singapore, Taiwan and Malaysia. Chief executive Kevin Tan said growth stays strong, with 28% CAGR and a focus on earnings. SINGAPORE – The future of chip manufacturing lies in producing customised chips with specialised materials that improve reliability and heat management, and Mi Material sees enormous potential as a major supplier in this sector ahead of its listing on the Singapore Exchange. The Singapore-based semiconductor materials firm is looking to raise $215 million through its mainboard share offering, including $139.5 million from the initial public offering (IPO) launched on Oct 19 and $75.5 million from the placements to cornerstone investors. The offer of 77.5 million shares at $1.80 per share comprises a public offer of 6.2 million shares here and 71.3 million shares offered to institutional and overseas investors. OCBC is the issue manager, and serves as joint bookrunner and underwriter with CGS International. A separate cornerstone tranche of 41.9 million shares has also garnered interest from seven fund managers, which will account for the remainder of the funds raised. These include three under the Equity Market Development Programme – Amova Asset Management, Fullerton Fund Management and Manulife Investment Management (Singapore). Mi Material’s public offer closes at noon on Oct 26, and its shares are expected to commence trading on Oct 28 at 2pm. The solder sphere supplier is one of the two largest in the world, accounting for 24% of the global serviceable market in 2025. Solder spheres are tiny spherical pellets that connect semiconductor chips to circuit boards and packaging in mobile and wearable devices, and in more demanding applications in data centres, edge AI and renewable energy. Mi Material’s parent company, Bursa-listed Mi Technovation, builds die-sorting and inspection machines for outsourced semiconductor assembly and test companies (OSAT) that handle the final post-fabrication stages of chip-making. The materials business began as Taiwanese firm Accurus in 1998 before it was acquired by German chemicals giant Henkel in 2006. Following a management buyout in 2010, the firm pivoted to its current business of patented solder sphere manufacturing, which Mi Technovation subsequently took over in 2021. Mi Material’s total revenue for FY2025 was US$65.3 million, with net profit at US$10 million. Three of its largest customers – which are end-market chip designers in the premium consumer electronics, AI application-specific integrated circuits, and high-bandwidth memory sectors – made up 50% of its revenue in the financial year ended Dec 31, 2025. Meanwhile, its top five direct customers, including OSAT and fabrication companies, contributed around 46% of its revenue. Chief executive Kevin Tan said at a media briefing on Oct 19 that the company has seen its compound annual growth rate (CAGR) rise to around 28% over the last three years, which is rare for a company that has been established for close to three decades. “Bear in mind that we are not a vanilla IPO where we started from a start-up – in those cases, a few hundred per cent increase is very normal. But we are already the top two in the world for this technology, and to grow at 28% CAGR is actually a very difficult thing.” The company has two facilities in Tainan, Taiwan, and Ningbo, China, and its third facility in Senai, Malaysia, is close to completion, with trial production runs under way . It is expected to have seven production lines by next year. Most of the IPO’s $168.2 million proceeds will be invested in a research and development centre in the US, which will also serve as a demonstration platform for Mi Material’s US-based clients. The company will also set up an R&D laboratory in Singapore, bringing it closer to its clients’ regional headquarters, and upgrade its existing facility in Taiwan. Asked whether the lacklustre performance of recent IPOs on the SGX was a concern, Tan said the company’s priority is to ensure healthy earnings. “No matter what we tell the investors about the equity story, at the end of the day, we must be able to recognise it in terms of earnings,” he said, adding that higher earnings will naturally convince the market about its business performance and sustainability.

events.title: Google cloud failure hits millions as UK courts and banks knocked offline
events.summary: Services restored for most users, but power fault stalled hearings and left Revolut, Lloyds and HSBC customers unable to pay or move money An outage at Google’s cloud services in the UK has caused widespread disruption, hitting courts and leaving millions of customers unable to access or send cash at banks including Lloyds, HSBC and Revolut . Google blamed a “power event” for the failure at its London-based Cloud computing operations on Tuesday, which affected its “europe-west2-b zone”. The US tech company said services were starting to come back online as of 1pm London time, and were back online for most customers by 3pm, but not before critical financial transactions and legal proceedings were disrupted. That included the video system used by defendants, lawyers and other parties to attend court hearings remotely across England and Wales, which failed to work throughout the morning. The issue was believed to have delayed several hearings, as the system is often used for defendants who are in custody but need to attend court. Meanwhile, bank customers at high street lenders and leading digital bank Revolut were left in limbo as services including card payments, cash withdrawals and transfers were disrupted. By 5pm most Revolut services were still marked on its website as having problems, with only six out of 27 services listed, including support chat and internal transfers, said to be working. The City regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority, confirmed it was in touch with Google and seeking more information about the outage. The Bank of England’s Prudential Regulation Authority is also understood to be speaking with the tech firm. Halifax, owned by Lloyds Bank, said on X that some of its customers had been unable to log in via the app and online. Revolut said its app was down because of a “service disruption” affecting several services, but insisted that customers’ funds and data were safe. The outage was affecting new and current customers, hitting its sign-up, sign-in, card payment, transfer, ATM withdrawal and cryptocurrency services. In a statement, Revolut said: “We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services. We can confirm that all our customers’ money and data are safe. We’ve been working to fix the issue since it was identified this morning and apologise to anyone affected and for any inconvenience caused.” A spokesperson for Lloyds originally said that customers were having issues with “certain online services” on Tuesday morning but that they were aware of “similar issues affecting other organisations”. By the afternoon, the banking group issued an update saying: “We understand the root issues have been resolved, so we expect to [have] all our services back to normal soon.” HSBC customers had also been complaining online that they were struggling to access their accounts. A spokesperson for the bank said: “Our services have returned to normal following earlier access issues. We continue to monitor the situation closely and thank customers for their patience.” This outage will be the first major test for the FCA and the Bank of England since the City watchdogs were handed powers to regulate Google and other rival services that have been supplying “critical” cloud services to UK financial firms this summer. Their response is already facing scrutiny by the influential Treasury committee of MPs, whose chair Meg Hillier wrote to the regulators asking for details about how they reacted and a sense of the total impact on the UK financial system. Hillier has asked for an initial response by 4 November. The property portal Rightmove was also reportedly affected by the Google cloud outage, and NewsThump, the satire and spoof news website, was struggling to load. Reports suggested Royal Mail and DPD had also suffered disruption. Google said: “We will publish an analysis of this incident once we have completed our internal investigation. We thank you for your patience while we’re working on resolving the issue.” An FCA spokesperson said: “We are aware of the incident affecting services provided by Google and are engaging with them and affected firms to understand the impact. “People need to be able to access their money and make payments, so we expect firms to fix issues quickly, keep their customers informed and ensure no one is left out of pocket.”

events.title: Are you a first-time buyer in England? Would the government’s Your First Home scheme help you?
events.summary: We would like to speak to people in England who are planning to buy a new-build flat or house as their first home Last month, the government announced plans for Your First Home (YFH) , a scheme which aims to give a helping hand to first-time buyers who do not have the luxury of being able to call on the “bank of mum and dad”. YFH applies to England only and is just for prospective first-time buyers looking to buy a new-build flat or house. It is intended to help buyers who have a regular income but have been unable to save for a large deposit or don’t have financial support from their family. Those taking part in the new scheme will be offered a government-backed equity loan worth 20% of the purchase price. Meanwhile, the minimum deposit the buyer will have to put down will be just 2.5%. That means the buyer will only need to take out a standard mortgage for 77.5% of the property’s value. Because the equity loan part will initially be interest-free, the government says participants “could save hundreds of pounds per month” compared with the standard 95% mortgage popular with many first-time buyers. More details of the scheme will be announced at the budget on 28 October. We would like to speak to first-time buyers in England . Would this new scheme help you get on the property ladder, and do you think you would apply for it (if eligible)? We would also need a photograph of you to accompany our piece. events.title: Europe has few alternatives to counter China other than costly protectionism
events.summary: The Scene Pascal Lamy negotiated China’s accession to the WTO in 2001 on behalf of the EU. A decade later, in a speech in Shanghai, Europe’s former trade commissioner lauded what he called a “win-win” outcome. But like a growing number of current and former European leaders, he’s grown alarmed as China’s trade surplus with the EU has ballooned. Lamy, now with the Jacques Delors Institute, was one of the authors of a recent policy paper that called for restrictions on Chinese exports using a quota system — an idea that the EU has now embraced. Q&A Andy Browne: Is the EU-China trade war now off? Pascal Lamy: I interpret the recent deal on hybrid cars’ export restraints as a first step in the right direction. I think the European side will consider this as a down payment. In my view, we need further steps to seriously address this rocketing Chinese trade surplus with Europe. So is this a tactical concession by China or a strategic shift? Both interpretations are possible. But from the EU side, this will not be seen as sufficient. Is the car deal a model for other sectors? Yes, indeed, although voluntary export restraints raise a series of technical issues. It’s certainly easier for hybrid cars than it is for chemicals or pharmaceuticals. And, of course, when you look at the numbers you need quite a lot more given the [EU’s] €350 billion annual trade deficit with China. You once called China’s WTO accession a “win-win.” Recently, you said that “China is killing open global trade.” What changed? I changed my mind because China changed. None of us predicted the speed of economic growth in China. A lot of people now say ‘you made a mistake by not forecasting that China would become an enormous elephant.’ My usual answer is: Who said that at the time? Give me some evidence that we had a choice between those who said ‘be careful’ and those who said ‘that’s a great idea.’ [Former Chinese Premier] Zhu Rongji thought that the Chinese miracle was a clever mix of Chinese characteristics and good old Western liberal capitalist market recipes. This is not the view of Xi Jinping. He believes that the incredible economic success of the past 20 years is due to the fact that China is led by the Chinese Communist Party. Also, the state-owned sector is larger today than it was in 2010. What’s changed, too, is that China no longer plays the game of comparative advantage, which is the ideological basis of the World Trade Organization. If you are better — cost and quality wise — than I am at everything, where’s the comparative advantage? Isn’t a big part of the problem that China now out-competes Europe? I’m not saying that all of China’s comparative advantage is, let’s say, WTO illegitimate. There is their education system, their engineers, their planning system, and the size of their market. But there’s another part which is not in line with an open rules-based trading system. By the way, what’s also changed is that a lot of markets that were open to China — the US, Turkey, Japan — have taken protectionist measures. China’s exports are now going to Europe, the only large and deep market that is still wide open. Germany and France have proposed a “kill switch” that could shut China out of European markets completely. Is that a good idea? I disagree with that formula. It’s like the US using Section 301 to determine whether a trade partner is playing fair or not. The Jacques Delors Institute has proposed a WTO compatible quota system with in-quota tariffs and out-of-quota tariffs. That’s a big difference — it’s predictable, rules-based, with benchmarks and numbers, and everyone understands clearly how the system works. There is no unilateral determination except for the size of the quota. China also has a ‘kill switch’ — rare earths. Can Europe really afford to risk a trade war? China’s rare earth dominance is time-limited. The US, EU, and Japan have started working on alternatives. If you over-use market dominance, markets adjust, and there’s a big price incentive to innovate. Tariffs raise prices. Are European consumers ready to pay a premium? Some prices will be higher, yes. Protection is costly. But what’s the alternative? You have to choose between that and industry closures, social problems, and the growth of extremism on the right and left of European politics. Can China be persuaded to compromise? I’ve been trying to convince my Chinese friends that they should care about this. We have to convince them that if the people who will govern Europe are the products of industrial and social shocks that China is creating, they will be much tougher with China than we, traditional center left or center right, are.

events.title: AI takes on great experiment in self-rule
events.summary: Slowly but surely, the leading AI companies are creating a national self-governing structure to oversee their technology and its societal impact. With the federal government largely hands-off, Anthropic, OpenAI and others are self-regulating their technology and now setting up their own plans to redistribute their wealth. Why it matters: Not since the age of the robber barons have America's industrial titans wielded such sweeping power to shape society — and decide how their private fortunes should serve the public good. In the modern era, Washington has largely exercised those powers through regulation, taxation and public spending. The big picture: President Trump has no interest in new regulations. Instead, he has blessed a basic framework for the AI companies to regulate themselves — and potentially each other — outside of formal government monitoring. Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Elon Musk's XSI, Meta and Nvidia are working on different versions of this. This is all voluntary and rests on the public trusting companies the size of industrialized nations to responsibly police themselves. These companies are in a frantic race to create human-surpassing superintelligence. All are pressing ahead, even as their leaders — particularly at Anthropic — warn of potentially catastrophic risks and profound economic disruption. At the same time, some AI leaders are promising to direct a portion of their vast wealth to benefit those outside their companies. Zoom in: At least three competing visions are emerging for sharing the spoils of the AI boom, each with a different answer to who should control the wealth. Anthropic: The company. On the eve of its blockbuster IPO, Anthropic pledged 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund that could grow into one of the largest philanthropic institutions in history. At a hypothetical $2 trillion valuation, its stake would be worth $100 billion — more than the Gates Foundation's current endowment. Including earlier founder and employee pledges, roughly 20% of Anthropic's shares are earmarked for the public good. Musk: The people. Musk responded to Anthropic's announcement by urging the company to give shares "directly to the public." On Monday, Musk pledged to give every American child a share of SpaceX next year — a staggering $10.5 billion giveaway at current prices. Musk called it the "first of many," though he offered no details on how the unprecedented distribution would work. OpenAI: The government. CEO Sam Altman has floated giving the U.S. government a 5% stake in OpenAI through a sovereign wealth fund — potentially handing Washington a multibillion-dollar interest in one of the world's most powerful AI companies. Altman envisions an Alaska-style fund that could distribute the industry's investment returns directly to Americans, though the plan remains preliminary and would likely require congressional approval. Reality check: The numbers are staggering. So are the assumptions about future wealth, billionaire follow-through and the public's willingness to trust its benefactors. Bill Gates and Warren Buffett launched the Giving Pledge in 2010, a voluntary promise by billionaires — including Musk — to give away most of their fortunes. Gates built a philanthropic empire, only to become a lightning rod for conspiracy theories. Anthropic's ambitions depend on extraordinary growth projections — its own employees envision 17% GDP growth in 2030 — while Musk has a history of making spectacular promises that fail to materialize. Anthropic's roots in effective altruism , a philosophy deeply distrusted by the Trump administration and its allies, also raise a more fundamental question: Who gets to define the public good? Between the lines: No industry requirements or consensus exist on how best to redistribute their expected wealth. But Trump Accounts — which allow families, businesses and individuals to invest in tax-advantaged funds for children — are emerging as a favorite vehicle for free-market AI leaders. Billionaire investor Brad Gerstner, a driving force behind the program, is championing a vision of broad-based ownership in which ordinary Americans share directly in the economic upside of the AI revolution. SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell and her husband in July pledged roughly $320 million in company shares to 2 million children through Trump Accounts — a potential blueprint for distributing an even larger slice of Musk's fortune. What to watch: The Trump administration hasn't fully relinquished its regulatory authority, potentially complicating the emerging experiment in AI self-governance. After Anthropic disclosed that its AI had submitted a false homicide tip to Philadelphia police and improperly interacted with government websites, the White House declared that AI companies must report security incidents and remedy any harm. "This notification and remediation process is not optional," Trump's Super Intelligence Force warned — a striking assertion of federal authority just weeks after the president blessed a voluntary system of industry oversight. Axios' Zachary Basu and Bradley Olson contributed reporting.

events.title: Why Democrats are pushing their donors to care more about state legislative races
events.summary: The News YOUNGSTOWN, Ohio — John Boccieri’s tour through northeast Ohio politics is a microcosm of the Democratic Party’s decline, especially in state legislatures. In 2008, Boccieri left his seat in the Ohio state Senate to flip a Republican-held House seat. He lost it in the 2010 GOP wave, which gave the party control over redistricting and put his old district out of reach. Democrats appointed him to a safe state House seat in 2015, though he left it to run for state Senate in 2018. But he lost that race, and went back to work as a pilot. This year, Boccieri decided to try again for a seat in the state house. He bet that Republicans’ winning streak couldn’t survive a second Trump midterm, with Vivek Ramaswamy leading their Ohio ticket. “The seat that I’m running in is still gerrymandered,” he told Semafor last week. “But we need someone who’s going to help Amy Acton, when she’s the governor, to push back on unregulated, unchecked data centers, and make sure that the state house corruption ends.” Boccieri now exemplifies a new trend in Democratic politics: In the final weeks before the midterms, the party is trying to convince its donors that a “blue wave” could spread even farther — if their money isn’t all spent on a handful of House and Senate races. “Democrats are always in this spot of this ‘coulda, woulda, shoulda’ with state legislatures,” said Leslie Martes, the CEO of Forward Majority, a nonprofit that spends on Democratic state legislative campaigns. The group has warned donors that Republicans are still ahead in both parties’ top target races at the state level. “There’s this idea that these top-of-the-ticket candidates are going to lift the whole ticket, but that’s not the case,” Martes explained. “I worked in North Carolina in 2008, when Barack Obama was winning the state, and we didn’t pick up a single seat in Raleigh. There’s a lot of work to increase the name ID of our candidates at the state legislative level.” The fight to control state legislatures intensified last year, after President Donald Trump urged Republicans to draw new congressional maps in the states they control that eliminate as many Democratic House seats as possible. Strategists in both parties said that this redistricting scramble has changed how donors are being approached for state legislative races — rarely the first places where the largest political funders send their cash. Mason Di Palma, a spokesman for the Republican State Leadership Committee, said that his group began warning donors that Democrats could force their own gerrymanders if they swept state-level races in 2026. In practice, that meant that if Democrats could expand their control in Minnesota, capture Wisconsin’s Assembly, and flip Pennsylvania’s state Senate, they would gain the power to delete GOP districts in each state. “If Dems get trifectas, what will stop them from redrawing maps?” said Di Palma. “Your dollar goes further in state legislative races.” Both parties have stepped up their recruiting for downballot races, with Democrats benefiting from an overall confidence that they’d make gains in the midterms. In Wisconsin they spotted a chance for their first trifecta since 2010 thanks to new maps; in Pennsylvania, the popularity of Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro was already helping them inch toward Senate control. Know More Redistricting is reshaping the political outlook in many states, with the possibilities for partisan control divided into three categories. First, there are states where neither party thinks that they can break the governing trifecta: Republicans are at no risk in Arkansas, Tennessee, or Indiana; Democrats are not worried about losing either the governor’s office or the state legislature in New York, Illinois, and California. The dead zone includes places where state legislative elections are held in off-years: Louisiana, Mississippi, New Jersey, and Virginia. The next crop of states with marquee legislative fights this cycle feature one party that’s trying to break a governing trifecta, or at least end a supermajority that makes it easier for the party in power to force new maps through. This group includes Nebraska, where Republicans in the “unicam” have been a vote away from eliminating the presidential electoral vote for Omaha’s 2nd Congressional District. Ohio, where Democrats don’t think they can flip the state legislature, is also in this batch — it could still make Acton governor and elect enough legislators to sustain her vetoes. “I’m very excited that we may break the supermajority in this election,” Acton told Semafor last week. Finally, there are states where one party could win a trifecta, sometimes in places where they’d have the ability to draw new maps in 2027. Wisconsin and Pennsylvania top that list for Democrats. It also includes Arizona, where the party is a few seats away from control — and where Republicans have said they’d use a trifecta of their own to revisit the state’s redistricting commission. The total money heading into state legislative campaigns pales in comparison to what Republicans have spent to hold Texas’ Senate seat. But the States Project — which, like Forward Majority, was created to help Democrats win more legislatures — announced a $100 million haul last month; the RSLC is looking at spending “north of $52 million” on its targets. In key states, Democrats say that they remain outgunned; in Wisconsin, local GOP donors have helped swing-seat Republicans in the Assembly spend $11.3 million, compared with $7.6 million for Democrats. “The right wing has been at this for more than 50 years,” said Mandara Meyers, the States Project’s executive director. “They have entrenched advantages and GOP megadonors are still pouring millions into individual races.” David’s view The story of modern state legislature battles is a Republican breakthrough in 2010, followed by 16 years of Democrats trying to claw back whatever they could. They started with lawsuits and ballot measures; in Michigan, Virginia, and Colorado, they created less partisan redistricting processes that kept both states competitive, not slanted toward one party. Trump’s national redistricting push quickly changed their strategy, and the threat of new maps every two years helped both parties raise more money for 2026. Forward Majority’s ask for a final $2-5 million to avoid being outspent came after Republican donors to the party’s other PACs funded the key GOP state legislative campaigns. There’s table talk about whether Trump’s low approval ratings can hurt his party as much as Obama hurt his party’s in 2010. The spending picture is completely different now: Democratic donors pledged never to neglect state-level races again, and Republican donors never stopped investing in them. Democrats are still not sure whether they can break through in the sorts of non-urban, non-suburban areas where Republicans have been drawing maps for 10 years, confident that these voters are permanently realigned. events.title: Empathy divides Americans by religion, with white evangelicals standing apart
events.summary: Data: PRRI, 2026 American Values Survey ; Chart: Russell Contreras/Axios White evangelical Protestants are the only major religious group in which a majority says empathy can become dangerous when it leads people away from a society guided by God's truth, according to a new survey . Why it matters : The survey lands amid a quiet civil war within American Christianity over who deserves empathy. Conservatives ranging from evangelical pastors to Elon Musk have framed empathy as a vulnerability in debates over immigration , racial justice and LGBTQ+ rights . In a February 2025 interview with Joe Rogan, Musk called empathy "the fundamental weakness of Western civilization," while acknowledging its potential good and warning against its weaponization. By the numbers: The annual American Values Survey from the nonpartisan Public Religion Research Institute (PRRI) released Tuesday found that 42% of white evangelical Protestants agreed that empathy is a foundational moral value that helps build a healthy society. Separately, 54% agreed that empathy can become dangerous when it leads people away from a society guided by God's truth. In every other religious group, PRRI found that at least 66% agreed with the foundational-value statement, including 73% of white mainline Protestants and Hispanic Catholics. Empathy's foundational value was endorsed by 83% of religiously unaffiliated Americans, 80% of respondents grouped under other non-Christian religions, 77% of Jewish Americans and 65% of Latter-day Saints. The intrigue: The survey found a 30-point partisan gap: 84% of Democrats agreed with the foundational-value statement, compared with 54% of Republicans. Independents were at 70%. White evangelicals stand out among religious groups, but PRRI reports religious and partisan results separately. The survey doesn't establish how much white evangelicals contribute to the Republican-Democratic gap. Zoom in: The divide also tracks with PRRI's Christian nationalism measure. Among people PRRI classifies as Christian nationalism adherents, 38% agreed that empathy is foundational, compared with 94% of rejecters. PRRI classifies respondents as Christian nationalist adherents or sympathizers based on support for a U.S. government and laws grounded in Christianity and the view that Christians should exercise dominion over society. Six in 10 adherents agreed that empathy can become dangerous, compared with 6% of rejecters. What they're saying: "As Christian nationalist leaders attack the sentiment of empathy, a disturbing 'empathy gap' has opened, separating Republicans and white evangelicals from most other Americans," PRRI President and Founder Robert P. Jones said in a statement. Jones said the findings raise questions about the moral foundations that let people from different backgrounds share a democracy. Methodology: PRRI conducted the American Values Survey online Aug. 20–Sept. 7, 2026, among 5,200 adults in Ipsos' KnowledgePanel and 339 additional adults recruited through opt-in panels to increase sample sizes in smaller states. The survey covered adults ages 18 and older in all 50 states and the District of Columbia. The margin of sampling error is ±1.6 percentage points at the 95% confidence level for results based on the entire sample.

events.title: Republicans see shrinking boost from redistricting
events.summary: House Republicans are quietly scaling back hopes for the 10-seat boost they sought from redistricting nationwide, amid a souring political climate and polls showing a collapse in GOP support among Latino voters in Texas and Florida . Why it matters: On their down days, Republicans privately worry that the great redistricting war of 2026 will net them only one seat nationwide, according to top GOP strategists. Zoom out: At the beginning of the cycle, Republicans viewed redistricting like an umbrella in a storm: It could keep their House majority dry in a light drizzle — but in a political hurricane, it wouldn't be enough. They're not second-guessing the redistricting strategy, even as they wince at the price tag. According to AdImpact, Republicans have spent $133 million on TV ads trying to win in 15 redrawn districts that were supposed to be easy pickings. Still, they no longer talk seriously about redistricting saving their House majority, as they did a year ago — before the Iran war helped boost inflation and sink President Trump's approval ratings. By the numbers: Early this summer, Republicans believed they had created 16 more GOP-friendly seats: five in Texas , four in Florida , two in Ohio and one each in Alabama , Louisiana , Missouri , North Carolina and Tennessee . But since then, courts tossed a Missouri map and the political environment has darkened, with Democrats holding an 8-percentage-point lead in new Washington Post-ABC polling . GOP support has eroded particularly among Latino voters , raising Republican fears of losing seats their mapmakers counted on after Trump nearly won the Hispanic vote outright in 2024. "Texas, I'd be surprised if we got all five," Rep. Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) told Axios this month. "Florida, I'd be shocked if we got all four." The other side: Then factor in California , where Gov. Gavin Newsom, eager to show his party he was willing to fight back, engineered a new map with four more solidly Democratic seats — and one slightly more competitive seat. Democrats are supremely confident they can win all five — and their main super PAC has already stopped super PAC spending in one. Zoom in: So, two weeks before the Nov. 3 election, Republicans are squinting at the map and expecting to win 7 to 12 of the 15 remaining seats they redistricted. The breakdown: GOP strategists privately think Republicans can still win 2 to 4 of the 5 seats that were redrawn in Texas, and 2 (maybe 3) of the 4 new seats in Florida. They could go 0 for 2 in the redrawn seats in Ohio. The revamped seat in North Carolina is a jump ball. They're banking on winning all three new seats in Tennessee, Alabama and Louisiana. Under their most pessimistic calculations, Republicans worry their mid-cycle redistricting wave could yield just 7 new seats in red states. But then factor in Newsom's countermove in California, which put Democrats in a strong position to flip 5 seats. And in Utah, a judge forced the state to redraw its districts, obliterating a GOP-friendly seat — and creating a Democratic-leaning one in the Salt Lake City area. So as it stands now, a worst-case scenario for the GOP's final score after all that redistricting: Republicans gain 7 seats and Democrats gain 6. A year of nationwide redistricting to net one Republican seat. The details: Republicans are confident about three pickups in Southern states, where the Supreme Court's Voting Rights Act decision allowed GOP legislatures to redraw maps. They have already conceded one redrawn seat in Ohio as part of their midterm triage . Then there's Texas. Republicans are truly confident about just two of the five seats they redrew: The 9th District in the Houston area and the 32nd District in the Dallas area. The main Republican House super PAC has pulled out of Texas' 28th District in South Texas, essentially conceding the seat held by Rep. Henry Cuellar (D). It was rejiggered from a district that Trump won by 7.3 points in 2024 to one he would have won by 10.4 points. In Texas' 34th District , which touches the Rio Grande Valley and was similarly redrawn to include more Republicans, parties are spending roughly $18 million on TV ads. Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez had a small lead over Republican Eric Flores in the latest NYT/Sienna poll . And in Texas' 35th District in Central Texas, which went from one that Kamala Harris won by 33.7 points to one that Trump would have won by 10.4 points, both parties have spent close to $6 million, according to AdImpact. It's too close to call. The bottom line: In a true blue wave, Republicans could lose seats Trump won by double digits. But in that scenario, Republicans would be unlikely to blame their losses on redistricting. They'd point the finger at Trump.

events.title: Three returning Democratic committee leaders still behind on dues
events.summary: Rep. Maxine Waters, D-Calif., is one of three House Democrats who have yet to pay their DCCC dues in full despite plans to return to top committee jobs next year, according to a draft of the DCCC’s September dues report seen by Semafor. The document, which is not final, only reflects dues paid through last month; Waters has paid $450,000 in dues to date, or about two-thirds of her goal, rather than the report’s $200,000, a person familiar told Semafor, which will be reflected in the DCCC’s October dues report. Other committee ranking members lagging on the goal, according to the September draft: The top Democrats on the House Administration and Ethics committees — Reps. Joe Morelle of New York and Mark Desaulnier of California, respectively. Outgoing ranking members Angie Craig of Minnesota and Nydia Velázquez of New York are also behind, though retiring members and frontliners generally don’t pay dues in full. A person familiar with DeSaulnier’s thinking said he always paid his dues in full and intends to continue to do so. House Democrats are considering rules changes to mandate dues payments to serve on committees like Appropriations and Financial Services. The clashes over dues are a perennial issue among House Democrats that has animated previous challenges to gavels, but they’ve taken on increased importance as Democrats try to flip the House. And with House races becoming more expensive, some in the party think the dues issue will resonate with the caucus. Virginia Rep. Bobby Scott, the top Education and Workforce Committee Democrat who is facing a competitive race, has paid his dues in full.

events.title: The budget deficit swells, while the cost of debt rises
events.summary: Data: Office of Management and Budget via Fred , U.S. Treasury; Note: 2026 GDP estimated using extrapolated Q3 growth via CFRB; Chart: Emily Peck/Axios The U.S. budget deficit is ballooning, reaching $2 trillion this fiscal year, according to the latest figures. Why it matters: That's the largest deficit since 2021, when the U.S. was climbing out of the pandemic recession. The deficit is being driven in part by the cost of servicing the nation's enormous debt at a time when interest rates are rising due, in part, to the inflationary impact of the Iran war. By the numbers: The federal government paid out $1.052 trillion in net interest on its outstanding debt — all those Treasury notes and bonds we keep writing about — for the 2026 fiscal year, which ended Sept. 30, according to the Treasury data. That's more than what was spent on defense, and was the country's third-biggest outlay after Social Security ($1.67 trillion) and Medicare ($1.07 trillion). Stunning stat: Federal net interest costs in 2026 are estimated at 3.3% of GDP, which would be a record high, according to an estimate from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. Between the lines: This is the price tag for years of borrowing at much higher interest rates — a sort of new normal since inflation started rising in 2021. Rising interest costs add to the deficit, driving still more borrowing and putting additional pressure on the federal budget. The intrigue: The last time interest costs approached these levels was when President George H.W. Bush was in office. At the time, the administration negotiated a bipartisan deficit reduction package that raised taxes, breaking President Bush's infamous "Read my lips, no new taxes" pledge and arguably led to him losing re-election. Still, in the 1990s, the Clinton administration and Congress worked to balance the budget through tax increases and spending cuts. What to watch: There's little appetite for that kind of work from either party, but the so-called bond vigilantes might still press for it.

events.title: Israelis lose faith in elections ahead of vote
events.summary: The US isn’t the only country struggling with a slice of the electorate that lacks confidence in its domestic elections. Ahead of an Oct. 27 vote that will decide Israel’s future leadership, Israelis’ confidence in their elections sits at an eight-year low, according to new Gallup polling that found 56% have faith in the integrity of the vote. That’s down from a high of 71% in 2023, following the Oct. 7 attacks by Hamas. There’s a huge confidence chasm between those who approve of the country’s leadership under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and those who don’t — just 37% of the latter have faith in the vote. President Donald Trump has endorsed Netanyahu in his reelection bid (though his vice president, notably, has not ), but fewer Israelis are pleased with him: Sixty-two percent of Israelis now say they currently approve of US leadership, down 14 points from last year. — Morgan Chalfant
