events.title: Anthropic’s leaked AI bill sparks backlash
events.summary: The News The debate around the contours of an acceptable federal AI safety bill shifted again after a draft of a proposal Anthropic has been pitching to lawmakers on Capitol Hill leaked late last week. Anthropic, long seen as the safety-promoting frontier lab, found itself on the defensive, with one of its top lobbyists posting about tweaks it plans to make to the draft that more accurately reflect the dizzying pace of AI progress and the company’s stance on pre-empting state laws. That draft bill is a legislative version of an AI safety framework the company has been pitching for months, a company spokesperson told Semafor. However, AI safety advocates are arguing it doesn’t go nearly far enough, unfairly pre-empts state laws, and accepts too much possible risk. OpenAI quickly saw an opportunity to distinguish itself from its rival, with Chief Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane writing in a post Monday implicitly directed at Anthropic: “Policy decisions must ultimately be made through our democratic processes with our elected officials leading. … No one company (including OpenAI) should write the rules alone for a technology with such profound implications for our economy, society and national security.” Ashley’s view Over the past few years, Anthropic has embraced regulation in a way that other AI companies haven’t. As the frightening possibilities of its advanced AI have emerged — and as its fight with the US government has brewed — the company has started to seek regulation through methods that have promoted heated debate within the federal government (like pitching the terms that would allow officials to block the release of certain models). OpenAI has generally been a savvier, subtler Washington player, wanting to be seen as ready to endorse compromise federal AI bills written by lawmakers, as it pursues a strategy across the states of encouraging similar frameworks it finds acceptable.

events.title: The most awkward Senate delegation ever?
events.summary: If Sherrod Brown wins his Senate race, Ohio’s delegation will be the most awkward in the chamber next Congress. Brown would have to serve with Republican Bernie Moreno, who defeated Brown in 2024 — and would likely become the leading tactician in charge of toppling the Democrat again in 2028. That’s thanks to a quirk in the Senate cycle math: Brown would have to run again for his seat in two years, against a National Republican Senatorial Committee that Moreno is likely to take over for the 2028 campaign. Moreno told Semafor that the theoretical matchup “won’t happen,” predicting that incumbent GOP Sen. Jon Husted will win. But he joked it would be “tempting” to defeat Brown again: “Sherrod Brown should just get a job.” Brown and Moreno never spoke after Moreno’s 2024 win, according to a person familiar with the matter. They also never debated. The Brown campaign declined to comment. A Brown-Moreno delegation would be even more dramatic than the 2024 rivalry between then-Sen. Jon Tester, D-Mont., and then-NRSC Chair Steve Daines, who successfully unseated him.

events.title: Why US investors are snapping up Germany's famed Mittelstand
events.summary: Increasing amounts of US capital are flowing into Germany's traditional industrial firms and family-owned businesses. As many business owners struggle to find successors, more companies are becoming acquisition targets. What do the long-established German companies Birkenstock, Viessmann, Linde and ebm-papst have in common? All have fallen into American hands. Traditional German family-owned businesses and small-to-medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) have become increasingly attractive to US companies and investors. Last year, US investors were involved in 76 acquisitions and investments in German industrial and manufacturing companies, according to an analysis by financial data provider PitchBook. The transactions were valued at about $29.5 billion (€26.3 billion) in 2025, nearly double the 2022 total. As of August 19, 2026, the figure stood at $23.9 billion. No successor, but an investor instead "From what we are seeing in the market, the interest from US investors in German companies is definitely still there," said Samar-Ahmad Albrecht-Mahmood of Veracity Capital Investments, which advises companies looking to invest in Germany. German companies, particularly those in the industrial and manufacturing sector, remain attractive, "because many of them are highly specialized, have strong customer relationships and very good technical know-how," he told DW. "In many cases, these are businesses that have built up a strong position in their niche over decades." At the same time, many German business owners are reaching an age where they are thinking about selling their business, Albrecht-Mahmood underscored, pointing out that "there is often no successor within the family." "This brings companies onto the market that might not have been available for sale a few years ago," he said. Notable takeovers this year include ebm-papst, the Mulfingen-based manufacturer of electric motors and fans, which was bought by US company Madison Air for $5.4 billion in August. In June, the long-established Augsburg-based company Everllence, formerly MAN Energy Solutions, was sold to Bain Capital, with the US investment firm acquiring a 51% stake in the company. Fewer acquisitions, but more investments According to Die Deutsche Wirtschaft (DDW), a German business information network focused on the Mittelstand (medium-sized and family-owned companies), no country owns more German firms than the United States . Of the total 7,861 companies identified in the database "German Companies Under Foreign Ownership," 1,750 are currently held by US investors. Young startups — Germany's next tech champions? PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), one of the world's leading auditing and consultancy organizations, also underscored the growing US investor interest in acquiring German companies. In a report, titled Destination Germany, PwC said that while the number of acquisitions and equity investments has not increased, the financial volume of the deals has jumped. The report highlighted, in particular, the acquisition of BASF Coatings by the US investment firm Carlyle, in partnership with the Qatar Investment Authority (QIA), for around €7.7 billion. The deal was struck on October 26, 2025, and closed on June 30 of this year. According to a recent survey by the American Chamber of Commerce in Germany, about 62% of the US companies active in the country are expecting business conditions to improve over the next three to four years. Meanwhile, some 52% of them are planning to expand their operations in Germany, up from 49% in 2024. Where are all of Germany's inventors? At first glance, however, the increase in US acquisitions and equity investments does not seem to align with the decline in US investment flows to Germany last year. According to the Bundesbank, significantly less investment capital flowed from the US to Germany in 2025 than in the previous year. While foreign direct investment in Germany has risen overall — from €57.4 billion in 2024 to a total of €86.1 billion last year — investment from the US amounted to only €11.8 billion, nearly 44% less than in 2024. In contrast, investment from the United Kingdom rose to around €26 billion. "I would say the trend is continuing, although perhaps not simply in terms of higher deal numbers every year," Albrecht-Mahmood said. "The general interest in good German industrial companies, especially strong Mittelstand businesses, remains high." Relatively low valuations also play a role, the expert argued. "Compared to the US, we still see situations where German companies are valued more moderately, particularly in the SME segment. This can make acquisitions quite attractive for international buyers." This article was originally written in German. events.title: Excessive wealth, extreme emissions – and ecocide: what I learned at Europe’s big superyacht show
events.summary: These yachts are highly popular with the ‘super-bourgeoisie’ – and getting bigger. Can anything be done to stop them destroying our seas? W ho knew? Apparently everyone did, apart from me: you don’t wear shoes on a superyacht. Now, about to step on to my first teak deck at the Monaco Yacht Show, I’ve got to take my trainers off, and I’m having a sock panic. Have they got holes? Do they even match? Do they smell? To be honest, I’ve come dressed all wrong for Europe’s big annual superyacht trade exhibition. The code for men seems to be crisp and tucked in, blazers and chinos, navy and white, sculpted hair and designer sunnies. (I went colourful, loose, casual). For women, it’s something like Riviera elegance. Everyone – whether they’re Italian, French, English, German, American, exhibitors, buyers, brokers, charterers – seems to know each other. The international superyacht community seems to be a close-knit one, and I’m not part of it. Yet. For now, though, I’m boarding my first vessel: a relatively modest Zeelander 8 – 23.9 metres (79ft) long, built in the Netherlands. It has a rather retro look about it, with pleasing curves and a rear end not unlike a Porsche’s. I could imagine James Bond at the wheel. It’s fast too, reaching 40 knots (46mph); I could be in Saint-Tropez in a little over an hour. Downstairs there’s a huge owner’s cabin, plus a couple of double guest cabins, all en suite, with lots of nice details, such as a cream-coloured leather floor. In the less opulent crew quarters, there’s room for two or three. How much does it cost? This one is not actually for sale – some of the boats here are, others are for charter, some just for show. But I could order one just like it, it would take a year and a half to build and cost me about €9.5m (£8m). Tempting, certainly, but I need to see a few more before rushing into anything. I can’t help noticing that, compared with some of the others packed into Port Hercules, the Zeelander 8 is a bit … well, small. Is it even a superyacht? There seems to be some debate about how long a yacht has to be to be super – some say 24 metres, others 30. No question about this one – a Fast50, made by Italian builders Baglietto, with room for 12 guests and a crew of nine. It’s not as fast as the Dutch one, despite the name. Its four engines take it to 30 knots, but that’s actually very quick for a 50 metre boat. Perhaps more importantly, its gross tonnage, referring to internal volume, is 499; a sub-500GT yacht isn’t subject to the more stringent safety and environmental rules under the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) that yachts over 500GT are, so they require less frequent surveys and have fewer restrictions on crew size and certification. My favourite features are the large “beach club” (the open deck at the back) and the Jacuzzi right up at the pointy end. Imagine it: sitting with a glass of fizz, in the bubbles, at 30 knots, Céline Dion blasting out … where do I sign? Oh, again. Not for sale. The first Fast50, fresh from the shipyard, is already sold, but they won’t tell me how much for or who to (superyacht owners can be quite shy). The search continues. The trouble with superyachting, I’m finding here in Monaco, is that you think you’ve found the perfect vessel, and then you look over there and there’s a bigger, better one. It’s not just me – this is reflected in the Global Order Book, published by Boat International, which tracks construction projects. The 2026 GOB counts the number of yachts over 24 metres under construction globally at 1,093. In 2016, it counted 755 vessels under construction. This year’s figure is actually down 3.95% from last year, but that’s balanced by an increase in average length and gross tonnage. In other words, a few fewer, but they’re getting bigger. New prefixes are required, “mega” and “giga”, but for simplicity’s sake we’ll stick with superyacht. Here at MYS 2026 there are 118 superyachts, with a combined length of 5,508 metres, and a value of €4.5bn. Despite the sock shame, I’m beginning to feel more comfortable. Most people are friendly. It’s a lovely day on the Côte d’Azur – I’m offered ice-cream, branded fans and straw hats. It’s not just the yachts, there are stands for everything connected. Would I like to come to a wine tasting later “exploring superyacht wine trends”? Of course I would. Am I interested in yachting in Saudi Arabia? Hmmm, maybe next year. There are loads of toys on show – jetskis, eFoils, even submersibles. And if you’re still finding life at sea boring, there’s a portable golf simulator, with cameras and sensors, plus a screen, with hundreds of real courses programmed into it. So after dropping anchor off St Barts you can play a round at St Andrews. It costs €170,000 (£143,000).

events.title: "Power is probably the forever bottleneck": Grid delays threaten the AI race.
events.summary: Silicon Valley moves fast and breaks things, but the U.S. electrical grid moves slowly and requires permits. The explosive growth of AI is colliding with the glacial pace of building out new power infrastructure, prompting a new warning from Goldman Sachs that energy bottlenecks are set to stall the AI race. Why it matters : Amid a wave of anxiety from Wall Street about the debt-fueled AI buildout, Goldman points to power as the biggest risk to trillions in spending in a new report shared exclusively with Axios. Driving the news: Goldman expects global data center power demand to surge 170% between 2025 and 2030, with more than 60% of that growth coming from the U.S., according to the report . "Power is probably the forever bottleneck," Jason Tofsky, Goldman's global head of digital infrastructure investment banking, noted in the report. The bank estimates roughly $7.6 trillion in capital spending between 2026 and 2031 across computing, data centers and power infrastructure. Zoom in: The physical infrastructure needed to support AI is moving far more slowly than the technology itself. The U.S. has roughly 2,600 gigawatts of proposed power generation and storage projects awaiting grid connections, more than twice the grid's existing installed capacity, though many projects may never materialize. The median time from an application for a grid connection to commercial operation is roughly five years. Between the lines: The so-called AI race, which has long been defined by advances in frontier AI models, is really about who can get their hands on enough power, Goldman argues. That could mean a longer, less predictable buildout, delayed financial returns and greater risks for companies investing heavily before securing power. Follow the money: The massive expansion is being financed with debt, raising the stakes if construction timelines slip. Goldman projects $420 billion in global hyperscaler debt issuance in 2027, up more than 60% from its 2026 estimate. Debt is expected to finance roughly 35% of hyperscaler capital expenditures next year. And hyperscalers account for just 40% of AI ecosystem credit fundraising, underscoring how widely the borrowing extends. The intrigue: Since January, 86 projects have been canceled or significantly delayed, including 76 directly linked to local opposition, according to Goldman. Put together, this paints a picture of extended delays. Yes, but : Slower deployment could also help prevent over-investment by giving actual demand time to catch up with spending. Meanwhile: The boom is transforming utilities from traditionally slow-growing businesses into major beneficiaries of AI investment. Utility capital plans are expected to reach $1.3 trillion between 2026 and 2030. Tech giants are considering arrangements to directly fund the power generation, transmission lines and electrical infrastructure their data centers require. The bottom line: If you build AI systems, users will come, but they can only stay if there's enough power to go around.

events.title: I let agents plan a WNBA Finals trip (but kept my wallet to myself)
events.summary: Let's call it the Battle of the Bots, part 1: I decided to put two of the newest personal AI agents, OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse , through their paces, with the WNBA Finals providing a natural testing ground. Why it matters: AI companies are racing to create the digital assistant we turn to for everything from shopping to travel planning. But there's still a gap between what these agents can do and what I'm comfortable letting them do. They also need to pass what we'll call "The Human Benchmark" : that is, can they do something as fast, or as well, as a human? The answer is ... not quite yet, but the capabilities are still impressive. The big picture: For the test, I asked each assistant to plan a fantasy trip to Atlanta to see my beloved Golden State Valkyries, organize a purple-themed brunch watch party and create souvenir programs. I also had them help me shop for Valkyries merch, which eventually turned into a side quest for WNBA basketball cards. The cost: Muse is free for most uses, with optional $20 and $100 monthly subscriptions. Dots requires a ChatGPT Pro subscription, starting at $100 monthly, or access through a business or enterprise plan. More on Dots . Where they shined: Both agents were surprisingly good at handling complicated, multistep assignments. When I asked them to find flights and tickets for Game 3 in Atlanta, both caught that the game had been moved up a day and that tickets weren't yet on sale to the general public. The available seats were being offered through the resale market, likely at inflated prices. Both found good flight options. Muse opened a browser and let me enter my information to try to sign up for a ticket presale. Dots, meanwhile, flagged a scheduling conflict with an enrollment fair, which it gleaned from my AI-assisted effort to keep tabs on the joys of finding the right high school in San Francisco. Where they were creative, but imperfect: Both agents could turn broad instructions into surprisingly elaborate finished products, though neither was quite ready to replace a human editor. For my purple-themed brunch, Muse designed a colorful 10-page recipe booklet featuring ube waffles and lavender-honey butter. Dots produced a more practical eight-page packet with detailed cooking instructions and attention to dietary preferences. Muse's shopping list called for 12 eggs, while its recipes required 13. Both agents also designed invitations that needed aesthetic and language edits before I'd send them to friends. Both menus were far more elaborate than anything I'd actually make for a basketball watch party. Left to my own devices, I'd probably just buy some purple-frosted donuts. Another creative test: I asked both agents to create a 1980s-style WNBA Finals souvenir program, then later to turn my photos from Game 1 into a keepsake. Dots' 38-page vintage program was more visually engaging, with player photos, graphics and extensive statistics. Muse's 35-page version was less attractive but had some fun touches, including a fictional computer ad and an advertisement for my imaginary brunch. Both programs contained questionable statistics. Muse later sent an unsolicited update correcting several factual errors. For the photo program, Dots delivered a 12-page version in just 47 seconds, while Muse took considerably longer. It did, however, suggest an interesting photo spread highlighting different generations of Valkyries fans. Where they struggled: Actually doing things. I asked both agents to help me buy Valkyries merchandise, eventually settling on WNBA trading cards. Both helped compare options and prices. I chose Target, where my store credit card offered a 5% discount and free shipping. Muse attempted to complete the purchase but got stuck at Target's sign-in page. Dots instead directed me to the Target app, where my account and payment information were already saved. Dots' less automated approach turned out to be faster, even though both services support purchases with user approval. The trust problem: Both agents could have done more if I'd been willing to give them greater access to my accounts and wallet. I'm not yet comfortable authorizing purchases of hundreds or thousands of dollars, or at a point of trusting them enough for consequential decisions. The bottom line: For me, the sweet spot for these agents is doing the research and legwork while leaving me to make the final decisions. P.S.: I couldn't actually make the Atlanta trip or host the brunch because of other commitments. But I did end up buying three boxes of WNBA basketball cards. You know, for research.

events.title: How Trump’s FBI Purge Saved Lindsey Graham and James Clyburn From a Bribery Investigation
events.summary: Beatrice Caciotti for ProPublica. Source images: Getty Images, Hawaii News Now, South Carolina Department of Transportation. On March 3, 2020, Sen. Lindsey Graham walked into a private dining room at Charlie Palmer Steak in Washington, D.C. Graham’s time was expensive. He was meeting with two executives and a lobbyist from a Hawaiian naval defense contractor called Navatek. And he had required them to commit to $40,000 in campaign contributions for a 45-minute meeting. Navatek’s CEO, Martin Kao, was confident that was all the time he needed. “Shoot all he has to really do is stop by and say ‘yes,’” Kao wrote to a Navatek lobbyist and a fellow executive the day before, in an email seen by ProPublica. “That should only take a minute and he’s on his way. We don’t need to pretend we give a shit about each other.” At the dinner, Graham ate little and talked a lot. But Kao got the “yes” he was hoping for: Graham agreed to steer a $10 million government contract Navatek’s way in his native South Carolina, Kao later recounted to the FBI. In exchange, he said, Graham asked Kao to pledge a total of $100,000 to his reelection campaign. “Paper Trail” Podcast Hear the reporters discuss their reporting on the FBI on ”Paper Trail.” In early 2025, the FBI opened a sweeping investigation into bribery on Capitol Hill with Graham’s steakhouse dinner at the center. Kao confessed to federal agents that his business model consisted of bribing public officials in exchange for government contracts, and that the research Navatek was providing to the government was often worthless. The scheme involved some of the most powerful figures in Congress, he said — in both parties. In South Carolina, Kao told agents, Navatek made a campaign cash-for-contracts deal not only with Graham, but also with the state’s top Democrat, Rep. James Clyburn, and another influential Republican, Rep. Joe Wilson. Kao told agents that Graham in particular left little room for ambiguity: “This is how much I want, and how much I am going to give you,” Kao remembered Graham saying, according to notes one agent took during their debrief in late 2024. Kao’s admissions would constitute a vast criminal bribery scheme if they could be proved in court — a challenge, given recent Supreme Court rulings that have made it more difficult to win corruption cases. Kao himself posed another hurdle. He was facing prison for fraud and campaign finance violations and was speaking to the FBI in the hopes of reducing his sentence. But the FBI agents who took Kao’s confession — two experienced anti-corruption investigators — could see that much of it lined up with a trove of records they had seized from Navatek. They forged ahead. The FBI took the formal step of naming two former Navatek executives who had worked with Kao as subjects of a bribery investigation. The agency did not designate Graham, Clyburn and Wilson that way, but the agents were actively investigating their interactions with Kao. The agents indicated to their superiors that the lawmakers could become subjects in the future, according to records viewed by ProPublica. The details of this investigation have not previously been reported. President Donald Trump returned to the White House and almost immediately gutted the specialized FBI and Department of Justice teams dedicated to taking on public corruption — an act of revenge for having previously investigated him. The two experienced agents on the case were swept up in the purge, and the career prosecutor assisting them quit after Trump appointees forbade the DOJ’s anti-corruption section from filing any new cases . Today, there is no one left to look into Kao’s explosive allegations, as the Trump administration has abandoned any pretense of prosecuting public corruption. The case is dead. ProPublica has unearthed the investigation by reviewing thousands of pages of legal documents, internal company emails, evidence the FBI used to vet Kao’s claims and dozens of interviews with people who saw how Navatek operated, including an eyewitness to Graham and Kao’s secret steakhouse dinner. This story is part of a series based on our reporting. Last month, ProPublica reported that the FBI had probed the conduct of Maine Sen. Susan Collins, who steered millions in government funding toward Navatek while Kao gave her illegal campaign donations. Collins denied wrongdoing and dismissed Kao as a “convicted liar.” Kao is indeed the only person involved to serve prison time. He pleaded guilty to making illegal campaign donations and a loan fraud scheme in 2022. In 2025, he was sentenced to 87 months in prison. Graham died at 71 earlier this year. His sister, Darline Graham, who was appointed to fill his seat, retained most of his senior staff, including those who dealt with Navatek. She even took up some of his committee assignments, including appropriations. Darline Graham is running for a full term in office this November. Clyburn, 86, is one of the most powerful Democrats in Washington. He is widely credited with tipping the scales for Joe Biden during the 2020 Democratic presidential primary. Wilson remains influential on national defense spending from his senior perch on the Armed Services Committee. James Clyburn, left, and Lindsey Graham speak during an event at the White House to celebrate the 2023-24 University of South Carolina Gamecocks NCAA women’s basketball championship team. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images “Whatever a donor may think or say, a donation would never cause Congressman Clyburn to increase his support for the donor’s request,” Jami LaRue, Clyburn’s communications director, wrote in response to detailed questions. “The Congressman has always striven to assist the University of South Carolina and all of the colleges and universities in his district when called upon to further their important missions. The crimes and lies of an imprisoned fraudster will not cause the Congressman to waver in his support for these fine institutions.” David Snider, Wilson’s communications director, did not address a detailed list of questions sent by ProPublica. “Congressman Wilson does and has always abided by campaign donation regulations set forth by the Federal Election Commission,” Snider said in an email. In an emailed statement, Taylor Reidy, who was Lindsey Graham’s communications director and now holds the same post for his sister, wrote that “any allegations of quid-pro-quo behavior or wrongdoing by the late Senator Lindsey Graham or his staff are simply false.” She said the accusations were the “ravings of a convicted felon” and that her office was never contacted by the FBI about the matter. After Kao’s arrest, they disgorged his donations, she added. The two executives who were subjects of the FBI investigation, Duke Hartman and Joshua Knight, were never charged. Hartman, the other executive at the dinner meeting with Graham, is now the CEO of a new naval research company called Integer Technologies that he co-founded with Knigh

events.title: Burnham vows end to 'rip-off parking charges' under new rules
events.summary: Drivers will be given the right to challenge "rip-off" private parking charges and more grace when using private providers under new rules set out by Andy Burnham. The prime minister announced the changes after concerns were raised that penalties issued by private providers were too harsh and left motorists unfairly punished. The new rules include a cancellation of charges for honest mistakes such as stopping to check directions and for non-payment due to broken ticket machines. Drivers will also get a 10-minute window to leave a car park without facing a penalty. Motoring groups welcomed the changes, but said more needed to be done to stop charges when the driver had done nothing wrong. Private car parks are different to council-owned car parks and streets, but more tickets at private sites are now being issued than ever recorded. According to RAC analysis of government data, some 17 million private parking tickets were issued in 2025-26, a 17% increase from a year earlier. With each charge worth up to £100, the data suggests drivers could collectively face private parking charges worth more than £4.6m each day. In one case, a woman was taken to court in a £1,906 claim after taking longer than five minutes to pay at a car park in Derby . The charge was eventually dropped . "Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your number plate wrong shouldn't end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat," said Burnham. He added that such charges left "people feeling ripped off and out of pocket". A guaranteed five-minute period to decide whether to park A 10-minute window to leave without facing a penalty Cancellation of charges for issues drivers can't control, such as vehicle breakdowns in car parks Cancellation of charges for honest mistakes such as stopping to check directions, as well as for medical emergencies or broken ticket machines Maximum charges of £20 on appeal for slip-ups such as forgetting a parking permit, entering the wrong vehicle registration, or forgetting to confirm the registration in the machine when parking A freeze on the maximum parking charge at £100, which is the same limit as the current private parking Code of Practice The new code will apply in England, Scotland and Wales. Operators who do not comply risk losing access to DVLA data, making it more difficult to pursue the car's owner even if they do issue a charge. 'I got fined £11k over a five-minute parking rule' Published 1 August 2024 Firm told to pay £10,240 in five-minute parking row Published 5 April 2025 The government's Private Parking Code of Practice has been seven years in the making. In 2019, an act of Parliament was passed to create a code but the code was withdrawn in 2022, due to "resistance from the private parking industry", according to the RAC. The current industry Code of Practice, created by the British Parking Association and the International Parking Community, was introduced in 2024 and updated last year after a review . Angela Rayner, the Communities and Housing Secretary, told BBC Breakfast that parking "shouldn't be a way of making money". Asked if the changes were an admission that motorists have been "ripped off" by parking companies for years, she said: "We're calling time on it. They have regulated themselves and they have their appeals process but we're giving it more meat now." She said the current level of fine was a "proportionate response to when people don't follow the rules". Derek Millard-Smith from the British Parking Association said the group welcomed the changes as it would "increase trust" and said "detterents work" when it came to questions over the cost of fines. "We know dog fouling, rail fare dodging, littering - all those levels are around £100 or more because that is a level that is deemed sufficient to change behaviours." Both the AA and the RAC said the new code was a good first step but did not go far enough. The AA said some drivers pay up even if they have done nothing wrong, just to avoid the hassle and over fears of legal action being taken against them. "There is still a huge amount of work to do, such as tackling the scourge of debt recovery fees," added Jack Cousens, head of roads policy at the AA. "Ultimately, we need to stop charges being issued in the first place, especially where the driver has done nothing wrong." The RAC's head of policy, Simon Williams, called for the banning of debt recovery fees and said the current industry-run appeals bodies should be replaced by a single independent one. The government said it would be consulting on the issue of debt recovery fees, as well as other recommendations from the Competition and Markets Authority. events.title: Surprise drop in UK unemployment to 4.7% as John Healey’s first budget looms
events.summary: Latest ONS data presents mixed picture amid slump in job vacancies and analysts warning labour market is ‘running on idle’ Healey to reject calls to raise CGT in budget Unemployment in the UK has fallen unexpectedly in the final snapshot of the jobs market before John Healey’s first budget next week. The jobless rate fell to 4.7% in the three months to August, from 4.9%, according to the Office for National Statistics . City economists had forecast a rise to 5%. In a further boost to the chancellor, the figures also showed that the number of payrolled employees rose by 13,000 between August and September, to 30.3 million. However, a slump in the number of job vacancies illustrated what some economists said was an economy moving sideways. After hitting a peak of 1.3m in the period after the pandemic, vacancies fell by 21,000 to 691,000 in the three months to September, the lowest since 2021 during the Covid pandemic. Ben Harrison, director of the Work Foundation thinktank at Lancaster University, said the fall in unemployment “should not make the government complacent ahead of next week’s budget”. He said: “The UK is still amid a jobs drought with vacancies at their lowest for over 12 years outside of the pandemic.” Vacancies fell particularly sharply across the construction sector, suggesting Britain’s builders cut back on hiring last summer. Data on wage growth was mixed. Stripping out bonuses, average pay growth rose to 3.7% from 3.6%. However, when bonuses are included the rate fell to 3.7% from 3.9%, indicating that only a few workers received bonuses. Wage growth in the UK remains above inflation, which was 3.1% in August and is expected to rise to 3.4% when figures for September are published on Wednesday. The Bank of England is widely expected to raise interest rates in response to higher prices at next month’s meeting of the monetary policy committee (MPC). The pound rose against the dollar after the labour market figures were released, by about half a cent to $1.3352, as investors bet on the increased likelihood of a rate rise from 3.75% as early as next month. Members of the MPC are split on the need for further increases in the cost of borrowing with some, including the Columbia University professor Alan Taylor, arguing that the committee needs to wait several months to see whether costs and wages continue to rise. Financial markets expect interest rates to rise to between 4.75% and 5% by the middle of next year, although the consultancy Capital Economics said recent improvements in the labour market were modest and the central bank would probably cap interest rates at 4.25%. Ellie Henderson, an economist at Investec, said lower unemployment and higher wages would make a majority of the MPC nervous about leaving interest rates on hold. “The MPC will collectively decide to increase the Bank rate by 0.25 percentage points at the next meeting in November, framing it as a ‘risk management’ move, in case the data were to turn or energy prices move even higher,” she said. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “Sterling markets seem to agree, with the pound strengthening on the numbers, gaining modestly against both the US dollar and the euro.” Suren Thiru, the chief economist at the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales, described the labour market as “running on idle” with employers limiting recruitment and pay awards “in response to surging cost pressures and pre-budget policy uncertainty”. He said: “The continued fall in vacancies is a flashing red warning light for the labour market, suggesting that a damaging side-effect of this year’s AI-fuelled economic growth has been weaker hiring demand, compounded by elevated employment costs.” The ONS estimated there were 715,000 unemployed young people aged 16 to 24, down by 28,000 on the quarter. Harrison of the Work Foundation welcomed the drop, but said ministers should be more focused on the number of jobless young people remaining at 54,000 higher than 12 months ago. The secretary of state for work and pensions, Pat McFadden, said: “Today’s figures show the resilience of our labour market with unemployment falling and the UK’s employment rate now the third highest in the G7, despite a backdrop of global uncertainty.” But he conceded that many young people needed support to enter the labour market. “That’s why we are working with industry, to bring young people back into the labour market and prevent them from drifting into the welfare system.” UK unemployment and employment statistics Unemployment and employment statistics

events.title: What is the Budget and what could be in it?
events.summary: Chancellor John Healey will set out Labour's tax and spending plans when he delivers his first Budget on 28 October. He has refused to rule out tax increases after acknowledging government borrowing costs are at "historic highs". But the government's room for manoeuvre on tax is limited. Before the 2024 general election, Labour promised not to increase three big revenue earners for the government: income tax, National Insurance and VAT. In his statement, delivered to MPs in the House of Commons, Healey will set out how the government plans to raise or lower taxes. Alongside the Budget, the Treasury will publish details about the measures and their costs. The independent Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), which monitors government spending, will also publish an assessment of the health of the UK economy and a forecast of what it thinks will happen in the future. The run-up to the Budget typically generates speculation about what might be in it, which the government is trying to keep to a minimum this year. Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham face a difficult balancing act, trying to offer more support to households and meet commitments on defence spending, while also sticking to Labour's manifesto commitments on tax and the government's self-imposed fiscal rules. The previous chancellor, Rachel Reeves, set out two main rules, which the new leadership has vowed to follow. These are: Not to borrow to fund day-to-day public spending by the end of this parliament To get government debt falling as a share of national income by the end of this parliament In March, the OBR calculated that the first rule would be met with a gap - or headroom - of £23.6bn. However, this headroom is expected to have shrunk. Analysts are divided on how much it may have fallen by. While a rise in government borrowing costs will increase debt interest payments, higher inflation could push up tax revenues. KPMG believes the government's buffer could have fallen to £12bn, but the Institute for Fiscal Studies estimates it could be £20bn. There has been speculation over what specific measures will be announced in the Budget. Bank bosses have told the BBC they expect Healey to raise taxes on the sector . UK banks have been reporting bumper profits, leading to calls from unions for higher taxes. The Treasury has options: it could raise a 3% surcharge on profits which was lowered from 8% under the previous Conservative government, or it could raise the bank levy that is based on the size of their balance sheets. Further details on the Your First Home scheme, aimed at helping first-time buyers in England to purchase a property, are expected to be announced in the Budget. The scheme will allow people to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It would provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase. There had been speculation that Capital Gains Tax (CGT) - which is imposed on the profit people make when they sell an asset that has increased in value - could be changed, through either higher rates or by removing or amending exemptions. However, this has now been ruled out . The Times has reported , external that online retail giants such as Amazon and eBay are expected to be made responsible for collecting tax owed by traders using their platforms. The paper said the money raised is expected to be used by the government to cut business rates for High Street shops, by raising the threshold at which small companies start paying rates from £12,000 to £18,000. Fuel duty was frozen under the Conservatives in March 2022 and Sir Keir Starmer's government continued the freeze, deciding in May to push back a planned 3p increase in September until the end of this year. Healey told the BBC in late September that the time and place for dealing with rising petrol and diesel costs was the Budget, but would not give details on whether the freeze would be extended again. Household energy bills are set to see their biggest rise in four years in January, with a typical annual bill forecast to jump by £276 . There has been speculation , external that Healey is planning energy bill help for households on certain benefits. The High Value Council Tax Surcharge - dubbed the mansion tax - was announced in last year's Budget and will apply to properties in England valued above £2m from April 2028. There had been speculation that the government was considering extending it to properties worth more than £1.5m. However, reports now suggest , external Healey has ruled this out. In the first three months of the year, the UK's economy grew by 0.6%, while in the April-to-June quarter it grew by 0.5%. The most recent data showed the economy grew by 0.1% in August after growth of 0.4% in July, with both figures stronger than expected. Analysts say the UK economy is proving resilient in the face of energy price shocks caused by the US-Israel war with Iran.

events.title: A modest increase in bank taxes is not the end of the world for lenders | Nils Pratley
events.summary: A modest increase in bank taxes is not the end of the world for lenders As long as Healey doesn’t go overboard, a small turn on surcharge dial will not seriously undermine flow of capital E veryone is familiar with the banks’ plea: raising taxes on them amounts to taxing the nation’s growth. If you increase how much banks pay, goes the argument, less interest will be paid on deposits and loans will cost slightly more, meaning we’ll all be worse off eventually. In terms of economic theory, it’s coherent, it should be said: in an ideal world, a chancellor would strive to lower costs of capital at every opportunity. In the real world, however, John Healey faces multiple competing demands, even from within a business lobby that extends well beyond the banks. As this newspaper revealed last week , the chancellor is likely to increase bank taxes in his budget next week. In the current climate of trying to “stay the course” on the fiscal rules by finding some money from somewhere, tapping the banks is a reasonable policy. Or, at least, better than most alternatives. First, today’s conditions for banks are plainly gentle: defaults are historically low and interest rates are high. Banks’ returns on tangible equity – a better guide to how they are doing than pure profitability – are heading towards 20%. Most non-financial firms would love such a number. Provided Healey doesn’t go overboard, the flow of capital is not going to be seriously undermined when the starting point for banks’ returns is so good. Second, all the indications suggest Healey will indeed opt only for tweaks. If the mechanism is the surcharge that banks pay on top of corporation tax at 25%, then an increase to 8%, from 3%, would amount to £2bn-ish extra from across the sector. He may not even go that far. Analysts at UBS calculate that a doubling of the surcharge to 6% would reduce UK banks’ profits only by about 2% on average, with a roughly 3%-4% impact for the domestic-focused banks, meaning NatWest and Lloyds. That cannot be called a violent change in the operating climate, or a devastating blow for the shareholders or the equity-incentivised executives. Dividends or share buybacks may be trimmed a bit, but the share prices for both banks are up by a fifth in the past year. Third, we’ll have to wait to see whether any move by Healey is part of a wider financial services package that could include bank-pleasing elements. There’s always scope for another hack at the thicket of regulations, for instance. Or help on capital buffers. And, if Healey is really as pro-growth as he claims, he’d consider this column’s perennial pre-budget suggestion to scrap or cut stamp duty on shares – a move that would seriously improve UK companies’ cost of capital (see Tax Policy Associates’ paper ) and do wonders for banks’ wealth-management divisions. The point is that a small turn on the surcharge dial is better than other ways of extracting the odd billion or two for the banks. A windfall tax would be too arbitrary. Changing the way banks’ deposits are remunerated at the Bank of England would look like interference in the central bank’s independence. The surcharge is a well-understood mechanism. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning None of which, one suspects, will stop the howls of complaints from banks, or halt the grumbles about the loss of competitiveness versus other financial centres. But an extra £2bn, or less, from the financial services sector simply doesn’t sound like a gamechanger if Healey acts as expected. Even JP Morgan’s Jamie Dimon, who likes to play politics at budget-time with his proposed new London headquarters , might reflect that some other European capitals – Paris, say – don’t look like a bed of roses.

events.title: Landholders and politicians push for tougher laws on renewable energy developments
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Landholders push for more regulations amid renewables rollout Glenn Franz and his parents own a property next to Wambo Wind Farm. ( ABC Southern Qld: Brandon Long ) About 12 community action groups have come together to discuss the challenges landholders face amid growth in the renewable energy sector. The group is calling for a minimum 3-kilometre setback from residences and up-front decommissioning bonds. Regional Voices Queensland will continue advocating for better protections for those impacted by renewable energy projects. A coalition of rural community groups is demanding tougher laws governing renewable energy developments, including mandatory turbine setbacks, stricter decommissioning rules and stronger protections for neighbouring landholders. Regional Voices Queensland (RVQ), a loose alliance of about 12 community action groups representing communities affected by renewable energy projects across the state, brought landholders, farming industry representatives and politicians together for its first major meeting today at the Franz family farm beside the Wambo Wind Farm at Diamondy, 280 kilometres north-west of Brisbane. The meeting, co-organised by Member for Maranoa David Littleproud, focused on reforms to planning laws, with more than 70 participants travelling from communities including the Southern Downs and other parts of regional Queensland. Regional Voices Queensland members are demanding tougher laws governing renewable energy developments. ( ABC Southern Qld: Brandon Long ) RVQ chair and Property Rights Australia board member, Jim Willmott, described the alliance as a "supergroup" formed after community organisations dealing with individual projects identified common concerns. Queensland's wind farm code has not allowed developers to comply simply by meeting a specified separation distance since 2024. Projects must meet all of the code's performance outcomes, including noise criteria at neighbouring dwellings. David Littleproud says affected landholders wanted clarity around the issue. ( ABC Southern Qld: Brandon Long ) Mr Littleproud said affected landholders were seeking practical safeguards rather than opposing renewable energy outright. "They're not asking for anything irrational," he said. "They're actually being quite considered and it's coming from a lived experience." Farm co-owner Glenn Franz, who does not host the turbines, said the experience of living beside the wind farm had highlighted gaps in existing protections, particularly around visual amenity and the financial risks associated with dismantling turbines at the end of their operational lives. "We've got 13 wind turbines surrounding us within a 3km zone," Mr Franz said. "There's got to be safeguards for the future. "It'd be nice to have the security up front, not as a pay-as-you-go-down-the-track sort of scheme." Karl Stefanovic interviewed landholders at the meeting. ( ABC Southern Qld: Brandon Long ) The Wambo Wind Farm, a joint venture between state-owned Stanwell and energy infrastructure group Cubico, received planning approval in 2020. Mr Franz said while the project was well advanced, other communities were at the start of the process and could learn from the Diamondy community's experience. Anna Lethbridge and Brendan Taylor from AgForce attended the meeting. ( ABC Southern Qld: Brandon Long ) AgForce policy adviser Anna Lethbridge said safeguards needed to extend beyond project hosts to neighbouring producers, including protections against contamination and impacts on agricultural accreditation. "From an AgForce perspective, we're not opposed to renewables," Ms Lethbridge said. Queensland regulates wind farm developments through its planning and environmental assessment framework, including State Code 23 and applicable approval conditions. Since 2025, new wind farm applications must undergo impact assessment and provide financial security for decommissioning. However, RVQ is concerned the wording is vague and could still leave landholders or taxpayers liable. Developers must now also negotiate a community benefit agreement with the relevant council before lodging an application.

events.title: Zuckerberg spent years building on Apple’s terms. His $100-billion-plus AI bet is about owning everything
events.summary: Mark Zuckerberg says he knew he was taking an enormous risk when he green-lit Meta’s AI build-out—a commitment he pegged at as much as $200 billion—before there was any proof it would work. “We’re going to write this check for, like, I don’t know, like $100 billion, $200 billion,” Zuckerberg said on a recent episode of Cheeky Pint , the podcast hosted by Stripe cofounder John Collison. “I’m like, ‘Alex, are you sure this is going to work?’” Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, appeared alongside Zuckerberg and said decisions of that size get made “long before there’s proof points around whether or not even the thing is working.” He added: “It’s like the opposite of ‘lean startup.’” The episode was released Oct. 12, the same day Meta launched Muse Wonder , the first frontier-class model from the superintelligence lab Wang leads . Meta has guided for as much as $145 billion in capital expenditures this year , much of it on AI infrastructure. Much of that money is going toward what Zuckerberg describes as a “full-stack” operation. “Meta is a full-stack tech company,” he said. “We build our own data centers; we build our own chips; we build our own low-level infrastructure.” Lessons from the smartphone wars Zuckerberg’s push to own the full stack may stem from his nearly two-decade rivalry with Apple and Google, which control the world’s dominant smartphone platforms. Facebook’s iPhone app launched in July 2008, followed by an Android app in September 2009 . Its mobile years that followed were marked by friction with the platform owners, some of it self-inflicted. Zuckerberg repeatedly sought work-arounds to the limits those platforms imposed. In 2013, Facebook pushed updates to its Android app outside the Google Play store, prompting Google to ban the practice . In 2019, Apple shut down a Facebook “Research” app that paid users, including teens, up to $20 a month for sweeping access to their phone data. The biggest blow came in 2021, when Apple began letting iPhone users block apps from tracking them —a change Meta later said would cost it about $10 billion in 2022 alone. Zuckerberg has said that experience shapes his approach to AI. “One of my formative experiences has been building our services constrained by what Apple will let us build on their platforms,” he wrote in a 2024 post on Meta’s website . Speaking with Collison, Zuckerberg said owning the stack is “less about wanting to own a platform for its own sake. It’s about being able to build the best things.” The cost of going it alone Unlike Amazon , Microsoft , and Google, Meta doesn’t run a cloud business that rents its data centers to outside customers, so it shoulders those costs itself. Zuckerberg said a one-gigawatt AI data center costs $50 billion to $60 billion to build and roughly $15 billion a year to operate. Meta’s Hyperion campus in Louisiana is designed to scale to five gigawatts. That could change. In July, Bloomberg reported that Meta is building a cloud business to sell AI computing power and is also weighing selling raw computing capacity. Weeks later, Zuckerberg confirmed the cloud plans on Meta’s earnings call. On Cheeky Pint , he framed all that compute as a hedge. “If … the cost is whatever, $15 billion a gigawatt, we could get, like, a lot more for that,” Zuckerberg said. “So I think that you, in order for it not to work out, it’s not just that we have to fail, AI overall has to fail.” The bet on agentic commerce Meta’s full-stack ambitions don’t stop at data centers. Zuckerberg and Wang want Muse Wonder and the more powerful Muse Wonder Full to drive Muse, Meta’s personal AI agent , which can act on people’s behalf. “The best personal agent should feel like a team of experts in your corner,” Wang said. “Your legal team, and your finance team, and your medical team.” Wang said he uses Muse to “source increasingly obscure teas from increasingly obscure vendors of tea.” Zuckerberg said he set up an Instacart account specifically for Muse, which orders ingredients for weekend baking projects with his 3-year-old daughter. He went from using Instacart maybe twice a year to “once or twice a week.” That vision of full-fledged agentic commerce could, paradoxically, disrupt Meta’s main profit engine. Advertising made up about 98% of Meta’s revenue last quarter, and eMarketer projects the company’s worldwide ad revenue will reach $243.46 billion this year, surpassing Google’s for the first time . Meta’s future business model But if AI agents compare prices, check delivery dates, read reviews, and ultimately make purchase decisions, who are the ads for? Collison raised a version of that question on the podcast, suggesting that a business that “only succeeds by overcharging consumers” would rationally want to keep agents out. Zuckerberg countered that few businesses have tried to block agents and that those that do are likely to lose out. “We have way more businesses that are calling us asking to integrate deeply,” he said. He argued agents could grow commerce overall: “Is the total addressable market for all of commerce just increasing dramatically?” Zuckerberg also sketched how Meta could make money beyond ads. “Subscriptions is going to be a big one,” he said. Muse is free to use, with paid plans at $20 and $100 a month for heavier users. On commerce, he floated taking “a small cut of what you are saving or making for people.” And on Meta’s July earnings call , he pitched business agents as working “just like the ad system”: “We will get paid when we deliver results for those businesses.” What Zuckerberg hasn’t addressed directly, on the podcast or the earnings call, is whether agents will eat into the ad impressions that generate nearly all of Meta’s revenue today. For now, Wall Street isn’t pressing the point. Bank of America analyst Justin Post wrote last week that Meta is “ back on offense with AI ,” naming rising AI spending—not agents—as the top risk. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Cumulative impacts of data centre gas plants overlooked, court hears
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Data centre developer takes Southern Highlands power plant fight to court Gundungurra man Dane Shanahan voiced his opposition to the project during the open-air Land and Environment Court hearing. ( ABC Illawarra: Penny Burfitt ) Nakar Property is appealing in the Land and Environment Court after its application to build a 16-megawatt gas-fired power plant in the Southern Highlands was refused. Community members urged the court to consider all three of the power plants proposed for the site. Lawyers for the applicant and the council will present evidence in coming days. A court has heard the "cumulative impacts" of a series of gas plants proposed to run data centres in the Southern Highlands are being ignored as a result of fragmented planning decisions. Seven community members gave evidence at the site of the development in Moss Vale on Tuesday morning, kicking off a three-day hearing in the Land and Environment Court. The court is considering developer Nakar Property's appeal of a refusal by Wingecarribee Shire Council for one of its projects on the site. The application was for a 16-megawatt gas-fired power plant and battery storage system to power data centres. Separately, the developer has secured approval for another gas-fired plant on the site, a 14MW facility, and is seeking state government approval for a third, 673MW plant. More than 100 community members gathered on the site ahead of the Land and Environment Court hearing. ( ABC Illawarra: Penny Burfitt ) A crowd of more than 100 community members, Land and Environment Court Commissioner Nicola Targett, and representatives for the council and the applicant gathered in an open field in Moss Vale for the first day of the hearing. The first community member to address the court was Dane Shanahan, who introduced himself by his Gundungurra name, Mullyang. The emerging knowledge-holder for the region's traditional landowners told the court his name meant "eagle" and, as he outlined his community's concerns about the project, two wedge-tailed eagles appeared in the sky above the open-air court. After the proceedings, Mr Shanahan described the appearance of the birds as an "ancestral presence". He was one of several speakers to urge the commissioner to consider the application for the 16MW facility in the broader context of the development. "Each piece is being presented as small — each piece is being assessed on its own and no-one is looking at the whole," Mr Shanahan told the court. The court is only assessing the appeal lodged by Nakar Property for the 16MW facility and battery, but Gabby Kent, who lives 1 kilometre from the proposed site, agreed with Mr Shanahan's argument. "The planning processes may be separate, but the cumulative impacts to my family … and my community are not," she said. Will McCarthy says the project needs to be looked at as a whole. ( ABC Illawarra: Penny Burfitt ) Will McCarthy, whose home overlooks the development, echoed those sentiments. "At some point the planning system needs to stand back at look at the development as a whole," he told the commissioner. The court heard the applicant had submitted an amended plan for the development to speakers and parties ahead of the hearing. That submission included changes such as painting exhaust stacks green to address visual amenity, and adding some onsite solar power generation. Mr Shanahan told the court no Gundungurra people had been consulted as part of the development application's Aboriginal Heritage Assessment, despite the cultural significance of a waterway that would be cut off by the project. "It is as significant to the Gundungurra as Genesis is to Christians," he said. "The applicant has proposed to reshape an ancestral waterway without asking the people [whether] it will scar." The power plant and battery would provide power to data centres on Cloud Carrier's Moss Vale site. ( Supplied: Cloud Carrier ) Jacqueline Duc raised concerns about the health impacts of pollutants, telling the court carcinogens from gas power-plants had been linked to lung and childhood cancers. She also raised concerns about the project being located within the Sydney water catchment, saying its tributaries eventually flowed into Warragamba Dam, which supplied 80 per cent of the city's drinking water. The applicant's lawyer, James Smith, did not question any of the community speakers. The court will hear from the applicant's attorney and the council's representative, Michael Staunton, in coming days.

events.title: Gulf states to boost diesel shipments to struggling France
events.summary: The UAE, Saudi Arabia and Bahrain are to sell France the equivalent of 10 per cent of its usual diesel consumption in the coming weeks, French government sources said, as President Emmanuel Macron continued his tour of the Gulf. The aim is reduce European energy prices, which have drawn protests and public anger in France and elsewhere. “The greater the quantity, the lower the price. It’s quite simple,” an adviser to French President Emmanuel Macron said. A large part of the deal was negotiated by Mr Macron during a tour of the Gulf that started with visits to Kuwait and the UAE on Monday. He visited Bahrain on Tuesday, before travelling on to Qatar. France previously obtained guarantees from Saudi Arabia to sell the country 95,000 tonnes of diesel in October and November, bringing the total to 190,000 tonnes over the two months. In addition, the UAE and Bahrain are in the coming weeks expected to separately sell 100,000 tonnes of diesel to France for an unknown duration. “These are political commitments obtained from countries in the region because they know us and they know we are reliable – because we have been there during every critical moment, notably by deploying air defence capabilities,” the adviser said. Sales are to go through French energy company TotalEnergies, whose chief executive, Patrick Pouyanne, has accompanied Mr Macron on his Gulf tour. “Our mission is primarily to secure supplies because there is a risk. We have a diesel deficit, as we are a major importer,” Mr Pouyanne said. “We are in contact with [...] national companies and we are going to sign a contract specifically for France. The commitment in Saudi Arabia is to ensure that supplies continue beyond November.” The announcement is a political win for Mr Macron, who is under pressure in France, which is in the grip of large-scale protests over a cost-of-living crisis. Some demonstrations have turned violent. Authorities have imposed a curfew in central Paris and other parts of the country. European diesel is currently trading at almost $200 a barrel amid the war in Iran and Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. That compares with about $80 at the start of 2026, with refined products rallying much harder than crude prices this year. AI and tech deals During Mr Macron's stop in the UAE on Monday, France and the UAE signed deals in energy, artificial intelligence and advanced technology as the countries strengthen investment and economic ties. The preliminary agreements were signed in the presence of Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, and Mr Macron in the UAE capital. Three agreements focused on AI and advanced technology were signed with French start-up AMI Labs to strengthen research and technological co-operation and explore new applications across several fields, Abu Dhabi Media office reported. Emmanuel Macron visits UAE on Gulf tour – in pictures The deals cover Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, Abu Dhabi’s G42 and computing company Analog. MBZUAI is to focus on strengthening co-operation with AMI Labs in AI research and development, while G42 aims to establish a framework for strategic co-operation in cloud computing infrastructure and AI models. Analog’s deal with AMI Labs is related to exploring opportunities to integrate AI models into robotics and physical AI applications and opening new avenues for developing intelligent systems and expanding their use in industrial and technology sectors. AI is a cornerstone of French-Emirati relations. During a visit by Sheikh Mohamed to France in February 2025, the UAE announced that billions of euros was to be investment in an AI campus and date centre project near Paris. The UAE and France will also boost co-operation in the energy sector, with Adnoc Gas and Schneider Electric signing an initial pact to assess advanced technology and opportunities for operational improvements to help enhance efficiency and improve the performance of energy systems. Adnoc Refining and Technip Energies also signed two contracts relating to a refining capacity enhancement project and a sustainable aviation fuel project. “These agreements demonstrate both countries’ commitment to broadening economic and investment co-operation, strengthening integration between their industrial, technological and research capabilities, and opening new avenues for public-private partnerships to support the development of innovative and sustainable solutions in shared priority sectors,” Abu Dhabi Media office said.

events.title: WA woman's 'harrowing' ordeal stranded in Bali hospital after fall
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts WA woman stranded in Bali hospital after horror fall while on holiday Estelle Ravenscroft is being treated at a hospital in Bali after having a fall. ( Supplied: Marilyn Jones ) A 79-year-old woman is in a Bali hospital in a serious condition after breaking multiple bones when she fell at a restaurant. Estelle Ravenscroft's family are fundraising to bring her home because she is not covered by insurance. The Insurance Council of Australia is urging travellers to persist in efforts to obtain insurance before heading overseas. A West Australian grandmother is facing a potential bill of $100,000 to return home to Australia after falling down stairs at a Bali restaurant. Estelle Ravenscroft, 79, and her husband Keith remain in Bali, where Ms Ravenscroft is in the intensive care unit at a local hospital. Ms Ravenscroft broke both her legs in the fall. The harrowing ordeal has been exacerbated by mounting medical expenses as Ms Ravenscroft is not covered by insurance. Mr Ravenscroft said it was difficult to obtain travel insurance, because of their age. Indonesia is not among the 11 countries with which Australia has a reciprocal arrangement for publicly-funded emergency care. Ms Ravenscroft's family said the 79-year-old had gone for lunch at a restaurant and fallen down the stairs, which had no rails. Speaking this morning, Mr Ravenscroft said his wife had pulled through after a nine-hour operation at a local hospital. "She's sitting up now, but there are some difficulties breathing, and issues with transfusions, but she's pulled through the operation OK, which is really fantastic." Estelle Ravenscroft broke multiple bones when she fell at a restaurant. ( Supplied: Leonie Walsh ) The couple's family has appealed to the community for help with expenses through an online fundraising website. Mr Ravenscroft said travel insurance was increasingly difficult to obtain as people aged. "When you get a certain age, you'll find having the insurances that you think you can have, are not available," he said. "I'd prefer not to go into that, because I'm here at the moment to make sure that my wife is OK. I want to get her home. The family wants to get her home." Ms Ravenscroft's sister Marilyn Jones said the family was grateful for the support offered by the WA community. Estelle Ravenscroft was on holiday with her husband in Bali when she fell at a restaurant. ( Supplied: Marilyn Jones ) "The amount daily is climbing," she said. Ms Jones said she was aware of commentary around the couple's lack of adequate travel insurance. "It's pulled us down terribly," she said. "There are some not very nice people out there, but there are also some wonderful people out there. National Seniors Australia chief executive Chris Grice urged older Australians to investigate all options for travel insurance before travelling overseas. ''So I just feel so badly for someone who is caught in a foreign land, who perhaps can't get home because of the costs involved." He said he was aware of seniors who struggled to get travel insurance as they aged, but urged people to persist. "It depends on age and existing conditions," he said. "It doesn't mean they can't get cover. It all depends on how they are being treated." He said people needed to try and speak directly to an insurer, rather than apply online, if they had concerns. An Insurance Council of Australia spokesperson said its thoughts were with the Ravenscrofts and acknowledged the strain many households were under. "While cost of living is putting pressure on household budgets, a single overseas medical emergency, evacuation, or trip cancellation can cost far more than the premium of even a comprehensive policy," she said.

events.title: Do not be distracted by global crises. Nature cannot wait for a better year – we must act now | Steven Guilbeault
events.summary: Do not be distracted by other global crises. Nature cannot wait for a better year – we must act now In 2022, I helped push through the international agreement to protect biodiversity. Wars and economic pressures can make nature seem like a ‘nice-to-have’. But it is a critical asset, and Cop17 must deliver real action W hen I was five, property developers came to cut down the woods behind my home in La Tuque, Quebec. My mother encouraged me to climb one of the trees in protest, then told the developers, straight-faced, that there was nothing she could do when they asked her to get me down. A few days later, the tree was cut down anyway. I thought about that tree in the early hours of a freezing Montreal morning in December 2022, as the gavel came down on a global agreement between nearly 200 countries to halt and reverse the loss of nature by 2030. I thought about how important nature is for our health, our food security and our economies, but also how much passion there is around protecting it, and how it has the power to inspire people all around the world. Despite differences in national circumstances, interests, and levels of responsibility, what we agreed to do really did, and still does, have the power to create longer term stability for billions of people across borders. We agreed to protect 30% of the world’s land and oceans and channel $200bn (£150bn) a year into nature. We admitted that far more money was flowing into destroying nature than protecting it, committing to address $500bn of subsidies currently contributing to the problem. Nearly four years later, the reality is that we are not delivering on those promises. The context has changed. War, extreme weather and homes swept away or burned to the ground are becoming the norm, and public finances are strained everywhere. Leaders feel pressure to choose between protecting biodiversity, which is perceived as a “nice-to-have”, and policies that look like self-preservation. This is a false dichotomy. Nature is a critical asset for national prosperity and economic security, and the evidence is already there. Farmers in France who have leant on biodiversity instead of chemical fertilisers have seen crops thrive through extreme drought. In Brazil, Indigenous fire brigades have cut blazes by more than 20% in parts of the Cerrado and Amazon, regions vital to the soya and commodity trade with the global north. To the environment ministers preparing for the biodiversity summit starting this week in the Armenian capital, Yerevan, I know what you are about to be told: budgets are tight; there’s a war, an election, a trade dispute. Nature can wait for a better year. But the reality is, there might not be a better year, there is only the one you are in. I and some of the ministerial colleagues that sat beside me in the early hours of that Montreal morning four years ago agree that the ship can be turned around, and it can start with three clear next steps in Yerevan. 1. Stop public finance from backsliding and deliver on your promises In Yerevan, ministers must set out a timetable and interim milestone to deliver on the $30bn public finance promise by 2030, having just fallen shy of the $20bn target by 2025. Overseas development finance dropped 23% last year – the largest drop on record – and it is expected to decline further before the end of 2026. Biodiversity-specific funding within that has fallen 17%. Countries such as the UK are publicly acknowledging that ecosystems such as the Congo basin and the Amazon rainforest are also critical for food security within its own borders. Investing in nature overseas is not charity – it is a sure bet on stable food import costs among other things. 2. Direct finance ministers to address runaway harmful subsidies Finance ministers should meet within the next two years to set out a plan for turning off the tap on subsidies that undermine economic security. We have four years left to start shifting $500bn of harmful subsidies, as this is no longer just an issue only for environment ministries. Harmful subsidies have rocketed to $2.6tn in recent years. Across countries’ biodiversity plans, only 15% had plans to address the gap. The quantity of money spent on destroying nature is 30 times higher than what is going into protecting and restoring it. 3. Close the gap on marine protected areas Ministers must also draw up a plan of action for closing the gap between terrestrial and marine ecosystem protection, building on all the tools that have been used for land, and pushing for progress at the first ever Ocean Cop in New York in January next year. According to national commitments, 27% of terrestrial land is protected, which is something that should be celebrated, while oceans have just 12% similarly covered by protective agreements. Ocean ecosystems are remarkable and humbling places with unfathomable potential.
