events.title: The CO2-absorbing building made of old sinks, windscreens and toilets: Ghent’s £17m design museum is a green marvel
events.summary: Inspired by a gothic cathedral partly built using human bones, this gleaming monument to recycling boasts 82,000 bricks derived from construction waste – following a two-day brick-making festival M useums often try to reflect the world around them, but rarely are they made so literally of their surroundings as the new design museum in Ghent . Rising above the Belgian city’s medieval tiled rooftops like an angular white watchtower, the new building has vacuumed up the city’s condemned concrete frames, windows, car windscreens, sinks and old toilets, and transformed them, phoenix-like, into a gleaming monument to recycling. “There’s nothing new about reuse,” says Andy Groarke, co-founder of Carmody Groarke , the London-based architects who designed the €20m (£17m) project with local firms Atama and Re-st . “We’ve just forgotten how to do it.” He says the team drew inspiration from Ghent’s 16th-century gothic cathedral, Saint Bavo’s, which was partly built using the white limestone blocks of the 10th-century romanesque basilica that had stood on the same site (recent renovations also ghoulishly uncovered walls made of human bones , femurs and tibias apparently having particularly useful structural properties, with crushed skulls for infill). The new design museum doesn’t quite go that far in its nose-to-tail approach, but almost. The toilet cubicles are a smorgasbord of “biomaterials”, each featuring different tiles made of seaweed, flax, wood terrazzo and volcanic ash (you can scan a QR code for more info while you’re sitting on the loo). Some walls are plastered with local clay, while a chunky column in the entrance hall revels in its earthy layers of rubble dug straight from the building site. But the real innovation is the brick , which was specially developed, tested and certified for the project (funded by a grant from Circular Flanders and Sogent, the city’s development agency). Each brick is made of 63% construction waste, sourced from within 8km of the museum, pulverised and compressed with hydrated lime, saving two-thirds of the embodied carbon of a regular fired clay brick. And the lime will continue to absorb CO2 from the atmosphere as it cures over the coming months and years. “We’re not claiming this is a panacea, or a solution to the climate crisis,” says architect Sian Ricketts, Carmody Groarke’s sustainability lead. “But it is a sort of 82,000-brick proof of concept that you can do something different, with the right collaborators and the right clients.” Developed by East Sussex firm Local Works Studio and Brussels group BC Materials , the bricks were made in a former railway depot nearby, with the public invited to mix the ingredients and press their own blocks during a two-day festival of brickmaking. For €10, you can take one home from the museum shop. Public participation extended to defining the very essence of the museum, too. In keeping with Belgium’s democratic traditions, a “citizens’ panel” of 40 people, drawn from a wide variety of Ghent residents, was established to inform what the museum should be. Their 100+ recommendations ranged from incorporating unticketed areas, to being able to see work-in-progress, and having plenty of seating, as well as ensuring that the “chic” building didn’t put people off. The result is as locally sourced and collaboratively created as big civic buildings come. “This expansion and renovation are not about creating more museum,” says the outgoing director, Katrien Laporte, “but about creating more than a museum: a community sense-making museum with real social relevance.” The extension fills a leftover plot on the museum’s site, uniting the galleries that were previously spread between an 18th-century rococo mansion, called the Hotel de Coninck, and a troublesome 1990s addition – designed with a moving glass floor that rarely moved, now thankfully banished. The new building stands with the presence of a grand Ghent house, rising in five large storeys, and turning as it climbs to face the city centre, with big picture windows looking out in different directions on each floor. “We wanted it to feel domestic, industrial and civic at once,” says Groarke. It certainly has a bold presence. Not everyone has welcomed its industrial bulk. Concerns have been raised about how the boxy white mass lumbers into view from the city’s quaint historical centre, and there is something slightly clumsy about the form on the skyline, topped with multiple roofs angled in different directions. Silicone joints between stretches of brick don’t help either, reading as unsightly seams from a distance. The museum defended the height as providing never-before-seen views of the city, and it’s true: when you’re on the top floor – a freely accessible public loft – or the roof terrace below, the panoramic vistas of Ghent’s castle and church spires are a treat. Skyline concerns also fade away as you approach the museum at street level.

events.title: Hiring in the UAE rebounds in third quarter despite uncertainty fuelled by Middle East conflict
events.summary: Hiring in the UAE rebounded in the third quarter of the year to growth of 4 per cent, the highest across the Gulf , as business demand recovers, a report has found. After hiring in the country dropped by 4 per cent in the second quarter, demand recovered from the mid-year slowdown and by September new export business was growing at its fastest pace in almost two years, Cooper Fitch said its third quarter employment index. Companies remain cautious about the year ahead, the report added. Across the Gulf, hiring returned to growth in the third quarter, rising 2 per cent following a 3 per cent decline in the previous quarter. In Saudi Arabia, recruitment rose 1.5 per cent, while Oman recorded 0.5 per cent growth. Hiring, however, fell by 1 per cent in Qatar , 2 per cent in Kuwait and 2 per cent in Bahrain. The Iran war, which began on February 28, has had a significant impact on regional economies, with the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz affecting oil-exporting countries. The International Monetary Fund, in a report this month, projected the UAE 's economy to contract by 3.9 per cent this year before rebounding at a 7.7 per cent growth rate in 2027, as long as shipping routes normalise and the strait reopens. The fund also expects Saudi Arabia 's economy to contract 3.3 per cent this year, while Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar are forecast to see double-digit contractions of 11.3 per cent, 16.7 per cent and 15.6 per cent, respectively, in 2026. Oman is the only Gulf member to see positive economic growth in 2026 at 4.1 per cent. However, all the six states are anticipated to post growth in 2027, the IMF said. The contraction in Gulf hiring "lasted a single quarter and the market is now back within the modest growth range seen through 2025", Cooper Fitch said. "Growth extended across a wider range of functions than in the previous quarter, with paused mandates resuming in sectors such as energy." Sectors hiring Hiring in energy recorded the sharpest increase at 7 per cent across the Gulf in the July-September period. Mandates stalled during the regional tensions returned steadily as conditions eased, the report said. "Clients resumed searches where they left off. In the UAE, growth came from across the energy market, including nuclear and renewables," it added. The delivery of Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 pipeline also supported the sector's growth. "Project directors, commissioning specialists and contracts leaders remained difficult to secure. Candidates with scarce technical skills continued to receive multiple offers, keeping the market firmly in their favour," the report added. Hiring in finance grew 5 per cent, strategy rose 6 per cent – its first increase of 2026, while real estate and software employment was up 4 per cent. Recruitment in sales and marketing rose 3 per cent in the third quarter, "reflecting cautious confidence rather than a broad hiring rebound", while human resources grew 2 per cent, the report said. However, hiring in banking declined 4 per cent, while investment management fell by 5 per cent "after a strong run of hiring earlier in the year, driven by regional platform expansion and fund activity". While hiring picked up in the third quarter, it remained selective, Cooper Fitch said. "Clients focused on advancing active searches and securing specialist capability rather than broad expansion, and several markets and parts of financial services saw lower activity," it said. Looking ahead to the fourth quarter, it remains to be seen whether the improvement can be sustained. "Business demand has provided a firmer base, but costs remain elevated and visibility on trade and shipping is still limited," the report said. "Competition for scarce specialist talent has also intensified, adding pressure on employers seeking to secure critical capability."

events.title: Why have countries been pushing for a vital global climate report to be delayed?
events.summary: Saudi Arabia, Russia and China among those claiming developed countries have skewed findings of IPCC review The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change suspended an important meeting on Friday in Addis Ababa without setting out a firm timetable for its next report. The world’s governments are due to meet in less than a month for the Cop31 climate summit, and this leaves the future of scientific advice to governments on the climate in doubt . The IPCC – the UN-convened body of the world’s leading climate scientists – met for a week but, despite progress in many areas, was unable to come to agreement on the substantive issue of setting a launch date for its next comprehensive assessment of global knowledge of climate science. The seventh assessment report, known as AR7, was expected to be published in 2028, seven years after the last report in 2021 . But some want this timetable to be delayed to 2029, or later. A loose group of governments led by Saudi Arabia, Russia and India, and also including China and Kenya, have raised objections to publishing the report in 2028, arguing that climate science is dominated by developed countries, which they say has skewed its findings. But many scientists, and experts, worry that a delay would prevent AR7 being used to inform the next round of pledges of emissions cuts, due to be discussed by governments at the Cop33 climate summit in late 2028. Under the timetable set out by the 2015 Paris agreement , 2028 is a crucial year as it will be the second “global stocktake” , by which governments’ pledges on emissions are scrutinised to ensure they are in line with the goal of holding temperature rises to 1.5C above preindustrial levels. Saudi Arabia has a long history of obstructing climate action, including seeking to water down previous IPCC reports, and has employees of its oil company and scientists with oil links on the IPCC committees . Would a delay enable more science from developing countries? Most of the science that will be in AR7 has already been published and is now under review. IPCC reports take years to compile, combing nearly every possible source of data, and that is done at an early point in its reporting cycle. Establishing new sources at this late point is more difficult. The IPCC argues that it already takes pains to include scientists from around the world and keeps a critical eye on equity to ensure against developed country bias. Much of the basic science it relies on is based on the global workings of the climate system , and understanding the underlying physics and chemistry, which do not differ from developed to developing countries. Critics also point out that Saudi Arabia, Russia, China and India are all powerful economies with well-established scientific institutions and research bases – if they wanted to produce scientific models themselves, they could have done so by now, or could have provided financial assistance to other developing countries to do so. One possible compromise is for the IPCC to start working now on new ways to bring in more science from the developing world, and undertake a critique of its processes to that end, while keeping to the 2028 timetable for the first part of its four-part report, which deals with the underlying physical science, and allowing the other parts – which cover the impacts of climate breakdown around the world , and solutions to it – to be delayed. What do civil society activists think? They are divided. Some are against a delay and view it as a danger to progress on cutting emissions. Some leading figures support it , arguing that whose research informs the science, and whether scientists from developing countries can participate meaningfully, is as important as speed. Others have issued statements deploring the row while carefully not taking sides. Mohamed Adow, director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank, said: “It is deeply frustrating that governments have failed to agree a way forward. Developing countries must have a meaningful voice in shaping that science, and wealthy nations must provide the funding needed to make that possible. But legitimate concerns about fairness cannot become an excuse for endless delays.” Oscar Soria, director at the Common Initiative group, said: “The failure to agree the timeline is not a procedural detail, it has real consequences.. The answer is not to choose between urgency and equity, but to provide the resources and support needed to achieve both.” A group of 117 scientists, many of them from developing countries, including several from China and one from India, have written an open letter vowing to push ahead with their work . “Our message to governments and to the world is simple: we will keep working,” they wrote. “Equity is built into how our assessment is being drafted. Author teams are working from a far wider evidence base than in AR6.

events.title: ‘No real sense of appeal’: Vinted sellers complain of unfair account ‘bans’
events.summary: Some users claim online marketplace’s automated systems stack odds against them when sales go wrong A fter Catherine Warrilow sold a Zara necklace for £6 on Vinted, she packed it up and posted it off, just as she had done with many things before. Only this time the buyer claimed the parcel arrived empty. Warrilow, 47, from Oxford, provided Vinted with photos and videos of the package, including date-stamped Ring doorbell footage of her leaving the house to post it. But she says the resale platform refunded the buyer and left her out of pocket. “I challenged Vinted on what evidence they had and asked them to supply it, but they simply said ‘based on our evidence’ and ‘our evidence suggests’ and could not explain what that was,” she says. “The photos from the buyer showed that all of the parcel tape I’d used had been removed.” Vinted has become a giant of the secondhand economy. In 2025, users traded €10.8bn (£9.1bn) worth of goods through the platform – a 47% increase on the previous year. It generated €1.1bn in revenue and made a €62m profit. It now operates across 26 markets and has expanded beyond clothes into books, toys, sports goods and collectibles, as well as building its own shipping and payments businesses. It is a success story, but some sellers feel that the odds are stacked against them. Warrilow had used the app for five years, usually selling items her children had outgrown or things she had “fallen out of love with”. After having problems as a buyer, too, she had had enough. In both cases, “small amounts” of money were lost, Warrilow says. “But the principle of the lack of support led me to start a survey.” She did this on the website she set up called Sad Vinted Faces . Within two days, hundreds of people had responded. Since then, she says, more than 6,400 cases have been collected. One of the users who claimed, via Warrilow’s website, that she had had a bad experience, was Maggie, who did not want to give her last name. She says she sold a pair of Birkenstock Boston clogs for £72. When the buyer disputed their authenticity, she provided photographs of the shoes, and a bank statement showing she had bought them from Office. But Vinted decided the shoes were counterfeit, she says. The buyer was refunded and kept them, and Maggie permanently lost her account. “What upset me the most was not just the financial loss, but the feeling that my evidence was never properly considered,” Maggie says. “I had no meaningful opportunity to explain my case, or have it reviewed by a real person.” The consumer expert Martyn James says he has been “flooded” with messages from people who say they were accused of selling counterfeit goods and then had their Vinted accounts, and their money, frozen. “This problem has been bubbling away for a while,” he says. Part of the issue, he says, appears to be the use of automated systems in dealing with disputes. “AI is all well and good as a first line of investigation,” he says. “It is fine to use it to speed things up. But a service cannot exist without the service part, and that has to involve a human being.” He adds: “There seems to be no real sense of appeal. The company is acting as judge and jury, but there is money at play and it is not as straightforward as that.” According to Vinted, all appeals are handled by human reviewers, including Warrilow’s cases. Victoria Chamberlain-Ralphs has built a business selling clothes for clients who do not have time to do it themselves on Vinted. She says her problems started when she was made to convert her account to a “Pro” one, which took her offline for six weeks. “They said that our wardrobe was too big: we have 700 clients, which was, at that time, 18,000 items. They said that they had no capacity to get us back on. “We were emailing constantly, and they said they ‘would get around to it’.” She adds: “I told them I have staff to pay. I have clients asking why their items are not online, and I have a building to pay for.” In three years, Chamberlain-Ralphs says she has had her account shut down about 12 times. “I got banned last Thursday,” she says. “It was a permanent ban due to ‘fraudulent activity’.” She says Vinted gave her no explanation. She had 42 outstanding orders, all of which were cancelled when her account was banned. Five hours later, she says, it was reinstated. “They said it was ‘a false alarm’,” she says. “But that has cost me.” She says her account was also banned in November 2025 after she was accused of selling a fake item of clothing. “I rang one of my clients and got a receipt from Amazon for the trousers I was selling, and proved it was not fake – but they did not remove the ban.” According to Vinted, accounts will be suspended if Pro members repeatedly breach its “catalogue rules,” which prohibit counterfeit and dangerous items, or commercial activity that is not centred on secondhand goods.

events.title: Hollywood AI-listers: is the technology ready to rival flesh-and-blood film stars?
events.summary: Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more . As a freaky Val Kilmer doppelganger stars in a new western and faux starlet Tilly Norwood is set for her feature debut, experts are split on whether mainstream adoption is a long way down the line – or just around the corner ‘D on’t fear the dead – and don’t fear me.” An exact facsimile of a young Val Kilmer , not quite dead and not quite alive, utters that baiting line in the trailer for the new western As Deep as the Grave. Director Coerte Voorhees knows exactly what he is doing – this is an AI-created version of the late actor, approved by his family but bringing with it a heap of controversy about whether such technology could make flesh-and-blood thespians redundant. Not just yet, judging by the extended glimpse of the film released earlier this year : it looks like a thirtysomething Kilmer, if a robot version had been sent back to the 1920s American wilderness by Skynet and, as well as being strangely rigid, had forgotten to download his voice, let alone his signature air of spacey shrewdness. Kilmer’s estate signed off on it, citing his enthusiasm for new technology that expands storytelling, but surely he would have been dismayed by this freaky doppelganger. Many reacted with revulsion to last year’s unveiling of AI “starlet” Tilly Norwood . After her appearance in an introductory “comedy” sketch, Emily Blunt described her as “really, really scary” – underscoring the depth of feeling around the idea of synthetic performers supplanting real ones. What you might call the Norwood injunction – the feeling of a tech-driven agenda imposing something no one asked for – deepened with the announcement the AI-lister will be soon appear in feature-length film Misaligned . Tim Webber, the chief creative officer at British VFX powerhouse Framestore, is sceptical about whether fully AI-generated actors can ever capture the complexity of our inner lives. “AI models are trained on the surface of things – the pixels of internet images, if they’re image models. To get to the level where it’s a human performance, where there’s genuine emotion involved, is a long way further down,” he says. So AI acting, scraping the external texture of past performances, would seem to be the inverse of something like method acting – whose acolytes excavate their internal psyche and emotions in the interests of authenticity. But AI acting is undeniably becoming more realistic. Higgsfield AI – one of many companies currently pushing the possibilities of AI video – recently claimed to have “eliminated” the uncanny valley: that nagging phoneysimilitude effect that has plagued even sophisticated recent CGI reincarnations, such as the de-aged Indiana Jones in The Dial of Destiny . Having released two full-length, entirely AI-generated features this year, Higgsfield’s content lead Adil Alimzhanov is bullish. This new frontier of completely AI-generated films is liberating for artists, he says, and shortcuts laborious Hollywood production structures. The two online-only releases – Hell Grind , a 95-minute action fantasy, and The Cully Hill Boys, a 115-minute Guy Ritchie-esque caper comedy – completed the equivalent of shooting and post-production in a fortnight and a month respectively (not counting time spent on the scripts). Despite actors’ qualms, the future can’t be resisted, says Alimzhanov, 23, who used his own face for Hell Grind’s protagonist. “We can’t fight new tools simply because they transform industries. If you draw a parallel with when cars first came out, if we’d fought that, everybody would still be riding horses today.” Hell Grind and The Cully Hill Boys are essentially extended ads for Higgsfield’s suite of AI content-creation tools. But they show swift progression on the AI acting front. In Hell Grind, released in May, the skate-rat characters only seem to be able to crank out a single emotion per 15-second shot (the limit of the Chinese video-AI model used, Seedance 2.0). The Cully Hill Boys, which came out three months later, is far more engaging, with enough convincing repartee and comic timing to qualify it as quite funny. Its lead trio of grime rappers on the lam are AI-generated likenesses of real-life streetball player Matt Kiatipis, MMA fighter Israel Adesanya and livestreamer N3on – testament to the gen Z, AI-native short-form creators Higgsfield aims to attract. Though there is something quaint about the idea of an “actor” in the age of AI. If bespoke characters can be generated for every film, why have an intermediary play a “role”? Written by a human being, Tim Planagan, The Cully Hill Boys was assembled in 30-second chunks, made possible by this summer’s release of Seedance 2.5. But prompting your way towards something dramatically convincing is labour-intensive.

events.title: Who exactly will be affected by the UK review of benefits for young people?
events.summary: Around one in eight 16- to 24-year-olds are ‘Neet’ – and Alan Milburn is hinting that the overhaul of their support may be controversial With nearly 1 million young people not in education, employment or training (a cohort known as “Neets”), the government and its advisers have signalled that welfare benefits may be cut to fund more job support for them. What may change and who will be affected? Why are politicians talking about Neets? Ministers are expected to make a major policy announcement in November on plans to tackle what has been called a “generational challenge” and a “moral crisis” – the persistent number of young people in the UK who are out of work, not in college or training, or economically inactive . The head of the government-commissioned review of young people and work , Alan Milburn, has been vigorously preparing the ground in media interviews for what he has hinted will be a major – and potentially controversial – overhaul of employment and benefits support for young people. An estimated 960,000 16- to 24-year-olds are currently classified as Neet according to official estimates – around one in eight young people – with this number forecast to rise to 1.25m by the early 2030s. Although the concept of Neets has been around for more than three decades, Milburn has warned the current cohort are different: not simply jobless but estranged from the world of work. Some 45% of 24-year-old Neets have never had a job. He says urgent action is needed to prevent this group becoming a “lost generation”. It is partly the labour market: fewer entry-level roles and apprenticeships for young people, a decline in “Saturday jobs” that leave them less prepared for work, and in many areas, few decent job opportunities of any kind. It is also about the failure of state institutions – schools, the NHS, the welfare system – to prepare them for work. And, says Milburn, it is crucially about the increasing number of young people with “work-limiting health conditions” who he says have become economically marginalised because of their anxiety, depression or neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism. Milburn says that while the welfare system is not the cause of the Neet crisis, it exacerbates it by failing to provide enough meaningful advice and support to young people, especially those with health conditions. Plenty want to work, but job centre interactions with young people are often limited and “administrative” – paying their cash benefits – rather than providing a springboard for them to participate in work or training. The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) does have two major employment schemes, the Youth Guarantee and Pathways to Work, with budgets of around £6bn over three years, but Milburn is sceptical about their ability to reach Neets. Why does the government say it needs to cut benefits for young people? In theory, ministers could invest in new and improved employment support schemes aimed at Neets without cutting benefits. But they insist benefit savings are needed to fund their vision. They say disability benefit spending on 16- to 24-year-olds – currently £800m a year on universal credit health and £3.2bn on personal independence payment (Pip) – is spiralling out of control. In addition, Milburn is adamant that the design of disability benefits can “trap” young people with incomes of £2,000 a month, while incentivising them not to look for work. For every £1 the DWP spends on employment support for young people, £25 is spent on benefits, says Milburn – a ratio he says must be rebalanced. What benefits will be cut or reformed, how – and who will it affect? Ministers and Milburn alike are tight-lipped about any changes, but they are likely to focus on universal credit health and Pip, and the mood music is they will be radical . There is speculation either or both could be cut entirely or dramatically restricted. Some on the right have called for benefits to be removed for young people with so-called “mild” mental health or autism conditions, though because most young Pip claimants have multiple conditions this is unlikely to save significant amounts. A parallel review of Pip by welfare minister Stephen Timms has ruled out means-testing of Pip. Milburn said young people with complex and enduring disabilities will be exempt from any benefit cuts . What are the risks of cutting disability benefits for young people? Campaigners say better job support is essential – but cutting benefits for a cohort already on low incomes will simply drive up poverty and hardship , making it harder for them to get a job. They argue that in many areas there simply aren’t the jobs or opportunities, however comprehensive the job support. Around a third of the 1 million Neets are not claiming benefits, so in theory any changes won’t affect them. The political risk for ministers is that changes spark a repeat of last year’s backbench rebellion on disability benefit cuts, which forced a humiliating government U-turn.

events.title: Inquiry urges halt to plan to burn Sydney's waste in regional towns
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Energy-from-waste inquiry recommends moratorium on proposed incinerators Topic: Recycling and Waste Management There has been strong opposition in Parkes to a proposed energy-from-waste facility. ( ABC News: Joanna Woodburn ) A NSW parliamentary inquiry into waste-to-energy facilities has handed down 22 recommendations. The committee advised that two incinerator proposals in Parkes and Goulburn should be halted pending an independent review. The NSW government has until early 2027 to respond to the recommendations. A New South Wales parliamentary inquiry into energy-from-waste facilities has recommended that the state government reject plans to burn Sydney's waste in regional communities. The select committee on proposed energy-from-waste technology made 22 recommendations after holding seven hearings across 2025 and 2026. The committee recommended that development applications to build incinerators in Tarago near Goulburn and Parkes be knocked back. The chair of the committee, Nationals MLC Nichole Overall, today told NSW parliament it was clear the technology was not appropriate to be built in the communities. "Given the absence of numerous critical elements, significantly the lack of social licence and community acceptance including from local councils and Aboriginal land councils," Ms Overall said. Nichole Overall chaired the select committee's inquiry into energy-from-waste facilities. ( ABC News: Lisa Glenday ) Environment Protection Authority regulations limit the construction of energy-from-waste facilities to four locations in NSW: Tomago, West Lithgow, Parkes, and the southern Goulburn-Mulwaree precinct. "The government, proponents and advocates state that these facilities are safe wherever they are located," Ms Overall said. Existing landfill capacity in Greater Sydney is expected to be reached by 2030, with advocates for incinerators highlighting the technology as a potential solution. The scoping report for the proposed $1 billion Parkes Energy Recovery facility in the New South Wales central west was published by the NSW Planning Department on Tuesday. A sign shows opposition to the proposed Parkes waste-to-energy facility. ( Supplied: Parkes Clean Future Alliance ) If approved, the site would have capacity to process 732,000 tonnes of waste per annum by thermally treating household and industrial rubbish. Almost all of the waste processed would be transferred by rail from Sydney to the site, before being converted into up to 80 megawatts of base load power daily. If approved, the Parkes Energy Recovery facility would have capacity to process 730,000 tonnes of waste per year. ( Supplied: Parkes Energy Recovery ) Ms Overall said the committee heard from residents in opposition to the development throughout the hearings. "Waste is best managed as close to its source as possible," she said. "Transporting hundreds of thousands of tonnes of metropolitan waste to regional facilities, hundreds of kilometres away adds to cost, emissions and impacts." Parkes resident Erik Lensson welcomed the committee's recommendation for the state government to reject the incinerator proposal. "It is entirely unsuitable," he said. Ed Nicholas says the project is safe and, if approved, will deliver benefits to the region. ( ABC News: Laurence Curson ) In a statement, Parkes Energy Recovery director Ed Nicholas said that while the technology is new to Australia, it has been embraced in developed countries around the world. "It's a pity that the inquiry wasn't able to visit an operating facility as part of their investigation," Mr Nicholas said. "Had they done so, they would have seen for themselves how best-practice facilities, such as the one we are proposing for Parkes, work in both rural and urban areas to strict environmental standards. "We are committed to listening to feedback … and demonstrating the real benefits this project can bring at every stage." Veolia is proposing to build the Woodlawn Advanced Energy Recovery Centre near Tarago. ( Supplied: Veolia ) Veolia is proposing to process 380,000 tonnes of non-recyclable waste from Sydney each year at the company's existing Woodlawn site near Tarago. If approved, it would generate enough electricity for up to 40,000 homes. The proposal is before the NSW Planning Department and is awaiting a response to submissions from Veolia. Veolia have been contacted for comment. The committee received more than 1,400 submissions, the majority in opposition to the technology's development.

( ABC News ) Whyalla's six football clubs are facing an uncertain future in the wake of job losses at the steelworks. Members from the clubs say it is unlikely the Upper Spencer Gulf city will have enough players and volunteers to keep all six clubs, with future mergers possible. More certainty is expected for the town after a decision on a buyer is made. Football in Whyalla is facing an uncertain future as the region grapples with the flow-on effects of mass redundancies at the steelworks, with local clubs concerned a drop in player numbers could lead to their demise. Last month, the state government revealed that the steelworks' blast furnace, which had been shut down for months, would not be restarted and, as a result, the plant's direct workforce to be reduced from 1,700 to 1,200 people . A further 300 contractors were also expected to be impacted, and it is unknown how many workers will chase employment opportunities elsewhere and consequently leave the Upper Spencer Gulf city. Last week, more than 250 workers who accepted redundancies finished up at the steelworks . Roopena Football Club is one of the six which make up the Whyalla Football League, and president Robert Brereton said each club was bracing for player shortages. "I think every club in Whyalla at the moment probably doesn't fully understand what season 2027 is going to look like for them," he said. The blast furnace at the Whyalla steelworks has been shut down, resulting in job losses. ( ABC News: Brant Cumming ) He said it was not just players clubs could lose, but volunteers. "Every one of those teams has a level of volunteer support and we've noticed over the journey that it's difficult to find the volunteers needed to keep all the sports on the park." The steel city's population peaked in the mid-1970s, when about 33,000 people were living in the region, but the latest figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics show it had fallen to about 21,400 in 2021. Greg Flanegan from the North Whyalla Football Club said it was likely the number of clubs in the league needed to reduce. "With the expansion of Whyalla getting so strong we went to six clubs, and Port Augusta and Pirie just stayed the same. I don't know that we'll ever get back to that." Greg Flanegan says Whyalla may need to drop down to four clubs. ( ABC News ) President of the Central Whyalla Football Club, Richard Wallace, said he felt "a little bit nervous" about the future of the league. "In the current form — six teams, and we're one team that's been struggling a little bit, if you lose too many people it's pretty hard to keep your club going so it doesn't look good but we're going to hang in there. Whyalla hangs in," he said. He said amalgamation was not on the table for his club "at the moment", but the concept was "not completely a bad thing", noting clubs like Woodville-West Torrens and the Brisbane Lions had won premierships in the years following mergers. "I'm hopeful for the future of footy, and Whyalla. I've got to be," he said. Richard Wallace says the next couple of years will be tough for Whyalla and its football clubs. ( ABC News ) Mr Brereton said the South Australian National Football League had "basically given clubs two options" if considering mergers. "One is one club consumes the other completely, or both clubs fold and form a new club. And the appetite for either of those two options is not high," he said. "All clubs have struggled a bit with that understanding that potentially in a merger one club disappears and 100 years of history goes with it, or they both lose their 100 years of history and a new club forms and they continue on like that.

events.title: Hegseth makes unannounced trip and other Mideast news
events.summary: U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is in the Middle East U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is in the Middle East. Meanwhile, Israeli police have arrested 10 suspects in a wave of settler violence that targeted a U.S. journalist and European diplomats in the occupied West Bank, and Iran-backed Houthi rebels announced attacks in Yemen and across Saudi Arabia. Here's the latest news from the Middle East on Monday. Read our full coverage here . U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has made an unannounced trip to the Middle East. Hegseth announced on social media late Monday U.S. time that he was in the Middle East visiting troops that were on an unspecified, “historic mission.” However, the post also came several hours after Axios reported that Hegseth was in Israel visiting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. When asked about the visit and the reports, the Pentagon declined to comment. Saudi Arabia has executed a Bangladeshi man and woman after they were convicted of committing “indecent acts” in a mosque in the Muslim holy city of Mecca. Bangladesh said that it wasn't informed before the sentences were carried out and has sought information from Saudi Arabia. The Saudi Interior Ministry said the Bangladeshis were executed because of “the gravity and seriousness of their actions in violating the sanctity of both time and place.” It did not elaborate. Police said 10 suspects were arrested on Monday following violent attacks by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank that prompted heavy criticism of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government. Israeli police didn't identify who attacked the people who had come to support Palestinians during their annual olive harvest. Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine was beaten Friday by a crowd of young male settlers while documenting the scene, leaving her with several broken ribs and vertebrae. Masked settlers also attacked a group of European diplomats on Saturday. Palestinians have been subject to surging attacks, rarely leading to arrests or punishment, rights groups say. Netanyahu’s main rival in the Oct. 27 elections, Gadi Eisenkot, said “a handful of criminals is burning up the last shreds of legitimacy left to the state of Israel.” A money shortage has forced the World Food Program to deny food and cash assistance to 500,000 people in Gaza and 200,000 people in the West Bank, according to its acting director Carl Skau, who urged international donors to provide $450 million to fund hot meals and food parcels for the next six months. Skau said Monday in a video briefing that “life in Gaza remains absolutely brutal” and incredibly dangerous, with U.N. teams recording about 50 attacks per day in the past week, while in the West Bank, he saw burned olive fields, camps and villages. There have been more settler attacks over these first two weeks of the olive harvest than during all of last year, he said. Israel's military said Monday that it would resume coordinating the entry of commercial trucks into Gaza, but warned that future reports of merchants paying taxes to Hamas would lead to their licenses being revoked. The suspension since Wednesday cut off the flow of needed food and goods. COGAT, the Israeli military body that oversees humanitarian affairs in Gaza, cited disagreements between Hamas and the merchants over taxes, and claimed to be communicating a decision made by the merchants. Truckers in Gaza said Israel was using the disagreement as a pretext to fight Hamas’ taxation efforts. They said officials in Gaza called the money a “donation” to pay civil servants rather than a tax. COGAT said Monday that Hamas had withdrawn its demands. Airman killed rappelling from Alamodome's ceiling in Salute to Armed Forces ceremony Iran updates: Trump admin prepares options, including 'mother of all bombs' Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Iran-backed Houthi rebels killed at least 53 soldiers in ballistic missile strikes on a Yemeni military camp on Monday, making it one of the deadliest attacks on the Saudi-backed government’s forces since rebels shattered a 2022 ceasefire in Yemen’s civil war . The strikes on the al-Alam military camp also wounded 200 recruits, the Shabwa provincial government said. The Houthi rebels also claimed Monday to have carried out six military operations targeting oil infrastructure, airports and military sites across Saudi Arabia. Saudi authorities say recent Houthi missile and drone attacks have killed 19 people and injured more than 350 others. The Saudi Civil Defense issued more danger alerts across parts of the kingdom Monday. Three separate Israeli strikes hit Gaza City, killing at least two people, according to Shifa Hospital, and two 17-year-olds were killed in another strike on Khan Younis in southern Gaza, according to Nasser Hospital. The Israeli military said it struck Hamas militants in each of the attacks on Gaza City. It did not comment on the other attack.

events.title: Food aid charity under pressure from fuel costs
events.summary: FareShare South West has its distribution hub in Plymouth Soaring fuel prices are putting extra pressure on efforts to get food to thousands of people in need across Devon and Cornwall, the South West's largest food redistribution charity has warned. FareShare South West said demand for food support had risen by 45% since the Covid-19 pandemic, while the cost of collecting and delivering surplus food had increased sharply. The charity, which redistributes surplus food to about 70 organisations across the region, said it was facing the challenge of meeting growing demand while absorbing higher operating costs. Bosses added they were also concerned about the impact on volunteers and staff, many of whom were paying more to travel to their shifts. FareShare South West is an independent charity that obtains surplus food from food producers, farmers, supermarkets and other businesses before it goes to waste. It relies on a mix of government, corporate and independent funding. Recent increases in wholesale oil prices have contributed to higher fuel costs, making travelling and transporting goods more expensive for charities, businesses and households. Ryan Jackson said costs had "increased significantly" It operates from a distribution hub in Plymouth, where about 80 volunteers and four paid staff help sort, organise and load tonnes of surplus food each week. Much of the food, including fresh fruit, vegetables and dairy products, is distributed to charities and community groups. Hub manager Ryan Jackson said: "With petrol rising by 31% and diesel by 41% in the last six months, our costs have increased significantly and those are costs the charity has had to absorb. "At the same time, the number of charities requesting support from FareShare South West has grown across the region." Jamie Henshaw said there "may come a point" when some volunteer cannot afford to come and help The charity said the rising cost of fuel could also affect the people it relied on to keep the service running. Volunteer Jamie Henshaw said: "Everybody's feeling the pinch, but we love what we do. "Volunteers aren't paid, so this comes out of their own pockets. They're giving their time and goodwill. "There may come a point when some simply can't afford to come to work." A crate of apples is ready to be delivered from FareShare's Distribution hub Jackson said prolonged high fuel prices could create further challenges for the charity. "If fuel prices stay high for a long period, it could affect our ability to recruit and retain volunteers," he said. Despite the additional costs, FareShare South West said it remained committed to meeting growing demand. The charity said it planned to move to a larger hub in Plymouth later this year and create more food collection points across the region. events.title: How is the US economy really doing under President Trump?
events.summary: President Donald Trump has been boasting about the performance of the US economy ahead of the midterm congressional elections, claiming he has boosted incomes, reduced inflation and created jobs. Trump has repeatedly said: "We have the hottest country anywhere in the world." While the overall US economy is faring better than many expected after Trump launched his sweeping "Liberation Day" tariffs in 2025, there's evidence those import taxes and the impact of the US-Israel war with Iran have pushed up inflation, with the harmful effects felt by most American households. The US economy is also being helped by an AI investment boom, and could falter if that spending were to dry up. So how does all this feel for the average American? BBC Verify has looked at whether the evidence supports the president's claims. The overall US economy is growing at a respectable clip by the country's recent historic standards. The latest data shows US GDP , external - which is how economists measure the size of the US economy - currently expanding at an annualised rate of 2.2%. And it has increased by around 3.2% overall since the end of 2024, just before Trump took office for his second term. That is more growth than any other member of the G7 group of leading economies over that period. The US growth rate has been faster than was forecast by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) , external in the immediate wake of Trump's announcement of a swathe of new tariffs on goods coming into the US on 2 April 2025. It downgraded its forecasts at the time, citing the negative impact of Trump's import duties on investment and consumer spending. Though it is important to note that Trump eased the tariffs considerably in the months that followed, reducing the impact that had initially been expected on the economy. The US economy has also been heavily supported in recent years by American technology companies making massive investments in AI, including by constructing data centres around the country. Spending on building data centres , external (excluding the IT hardware to go in them) by US businesses in August 2026 was $5bn, almost double the monthly rate when Trump returned to office. Many American voters wanted to punish Joe Biden in the 2024 presidential election, holding him responsible for the pain caused by a significant spike in prices in the wake of the pandemic. The current rate of US inflation , external is 3.7%. That's still well down on the recent peak rate of 9% under Biden in 2022, but higher than the 3% rate that Donald Trump inherited in January 2025. Economists estimate , external US inflation would have been lower without the new tariffs imposed by Trump since he returned to office. While the impact of the Iran war on global energy prices, with the significant disruption to oil and fuel supplies from the Middle East, has also helped push up US domestic inflation. The price of a gallon of diesel in the US , external - a fuel used not only by drivers but also widely in agriculture and industry - hit a record high of $6.52 in September. The price of some grocery staples , external like beef and coffee have risen since Trump returned to office, though the price of eggs has fallen. And some US retailers have warned , external that rising energy prices caused by the Iran war will make producing food more expensive and raise prices at the till. 3. Household income growth held back Average US household incomes are still rising under Trump. The median income - after adjusting for inflation - rose 2.6% in 2025 to $87,460, the highest on record , external . However, the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP) think tank has estimated the combined effects of the following , external on US households: - The expiry of extra government subsidies that had made health insurance cheaper for millions of Americans - Higher-than-expected price rises during Trump's second term, including those linked to tariffs and the Iran war ITEP's conclusion is that the middle fifth of households are, on average, around $1,700 worse off in 2026 than they would have been, while the poorest fifth are around $750 worse off. The richest 1%, by contrast, are estimated to be an average of $12,560 better off than they woud have been, primarily because of Trump's tax cuts. ITEP's estimates about the impact of tariffs on American households of different income levels are broadly similar to those of the Tax Foundation think tank , external . Trump predicted his tariffs would result in America being "flooded with jobs" , external as manufacturing firms set up new factories on US soil to avoid their products being taxed at the border. Since he returned to the White House, an average of 34,000 jobs have been added to the economy each month. ​​But that is significantly down on the 122,000 jobs added each month in the final year of Biden's presidency , external .

events.title: Don’t be fooled. The AI that was supposed to save us time is doing just the opposite | Gaby Hinsliff
events.summary: The government says it can transform the state with AI, but it is no match for the resulting stream of machine-generated slop. And we all pay the cost Another morning, another avalanche of emails. Even after a guilty cull, my inbox is sitting at well over 7,000, but lately I’ve started subscribing to the Quentin Crisp theory of housework: why bother, when after four years or so you stop noticing the accumulating dust? Empty inboxes just fill up again anyway. In theory, email was supposed to save hours of meetings, phone calls and standing over photocopiers. Instead, we just spend hours deleting stuff people wouldn’t have bothered telling us if it had meant picking up the phone, but which they can now spam to their entire database at the click of a button. The glorious ease and convenience of being able to reach the world in seconds came, we now know, with the inconvenience of them being able to reach you right back. events.title: Spain-Based Startups Advance Regional Innovation With Barcelona Supercomputing Center
events.summary: The Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC) ’s AI Factory Accelerator Programme, now in full operation following a pilot initiative, gives startups access to sovereign compute, technical support and training to support innovation across industries. Many of these companies are also members of the NVIDIA Inception program for cutting-edge startups — and as of today, access to some of the BSC AI Factory services are available through the NVIDIA Inception portal . NVIDIA Inception complements the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme by providing members with training through NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute open courses, business mentoring, venture capital connections and other resources. An upcoming extension of MareNostrum 5 — BSC’s public infrastructure serving scientific and technological innovation, powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing — will deliver supercomputing access through the BSC AI Factory and other AI Factories across Europe. BSC AI Factory is among Europe’s first AI factories and the first in Spain, and has delivered more than 800 services to private and public-sector clients since its April 2025 launch. Three Inception members were recently named the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme’s AI Champions at the pilot initiative’s demo day: Qatium ’s water-network platform — already used by more than 250 utilities in 16 countries — is now in early production with its Neural Water Intelligence technology, powered by proprietary AI models trained on MareNostrum 5. Built on NVIDIA accelerated computing, the NVIDIA cuGraph library, the NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo framework and NVIDIA Nemotron open models, the technology helps water utilities make better operational decisions every day. OneCareAI , a research spin-off from BSC, used NVIDIA NIM microservices to develop technology designed to identify signs of hidden atrial fibrillation — an irregular heart rhythm — in seemingly normal ECGs, helping clinicians identify patients who may be at risk of stroke before one occurs. Avatia built a voice-first, multi-agent system that provides pharmaceutical companies with agentic coworkers that support sales representatives and give doctors transparent, curated information about medicines, ultimately helping the right treatment reach the right patient sooner. The system taps into NVIDIA NIM microservices, the NVIDIA Nemotron 3 open model family and the open source NVIDIA NeMo Curator library. Other BSC AI Factory startups — Agrikola AI , Elna Health , Lokutor , Montevive AI , Oppy , Pack2Earth and Up2Smart — span precision agriculture, medical imaging and knowledge access, speech services, enterprise security, sales intelligence and sustainable packaging. The cohort reflects the breadth of what advanced intelligence can now unlock: preventing strokes, detecting breast cancer subtypes before biopsy, putting medical knowledge at doctors’ fingertips faster, replacing petroleum-based plastic with biobased compostable materials, protecting crops with robots instead of chemicals and more. events.title: Arada enters Saudi Arabia with $3.8bn Riyadh project
events.summary: UAE developer Arada is launching a Dh14 billion ($3.8 billion) residential project in Riyadh and plans to build 100,000 homes in Saudi Arabia over the next three to five years as it expands in the kingdom, its chief executive has said. The company will also launch projects in Jeddah and Makkah as the Saudi market opens for foreign investment. “We have a good pipeline coming, and we will probably announce another project by the end of the year,” Ahmed Alkhoshaibi said. “As a group we plan to have 200,000 homes in the next three to five years, with half of that coming in Saudi Arabia.” Arada is jointly owned by Saudi businessman Prince Khaled bin Alwaleed’s KBW Investments and Sharjah-based Basma Group. Following the Saudi announcement, Arada’s pipeline is valued at Dh185 billion across the UAE, Saudi Arabia, the UK, Australia and Syria, comprising more than 70,000 homes. It has completed 17,000 homes so far. Saudi Arabia, the Arab world’s largest economy, has overhauled its property sector, allowing foreigners to buy in designated zones in Riyadh and Jeddah, while introducing “special requirements” for home ownership in Makkah and Madinah from January. It also introduced land tax rules last year to help free up undeveloped land and spur building activity. Riyadh debut Arada’s debut project will be built in the Al Rimal district in Riyadh's north-eastern growth corridor on a plot covering 2.5 million square metres. Apart from 3,500 villas and town houses, it will also have a school, retail outlets and a community centre, as well as sporting facilities and green areas. The project is inspired by Arada's Masaar, a Dh8 billion woodland community development in Sharjah. Units will be sold for between 1,000 and 1,400 Saudi riyals ($267 and $373) per square foot, with construction starting in mid-2027 and completing in five years time, Mr Alkhoshaibi said. Arada KSA, set up in partnership with Saudi property investor Xtopia, will spearhead its expansion in the kingdom, with Mohammed AlDhabaan, chairman of Xtopia as the new chairman of Arada KSA. Arada KSA has access to a significant 10 million square metre land bank across Saudi Arabia with a collective value of Dh49 billion, spanning key strategic locations including Riyadh, Jeddah and Makkah, it said in a separate announcement. Meeting domestic demand Demand for housing in Saudi Arabia is strong as the government pushes to increase home ownership among Saudis. Demand from expatriates following the opening of the sector to foreign buyers is also supporting the market, he said. “The real demand is by the Saudis who need a home, and this is driven further by the government, [which is] pushing for higher home ownership for the Saudis.” “The government's initiative, which we're trying to support, is that they want to provide 300,000 homes delivered in the next three years.” Saudi Arabia has set a target of raising home ownership rates among locals to 70 per cent by 2030 under the Sakani programme – a joint initiative between the Ministry of Housing and the Real Estate Development Fund. By the end of last year, Saudi citizens owning homes exceeded 66 per cent, with one million beneficiaries of government housing support programmes, the Saudi Press Agency reported in January, citing Minister of Municipalities and Housing Majed Al Hogail. Saudi Arabia’s property market was mixed in the second quarter, with nationwide residential transaction values contracting by 26.9 per cent year-on-year to 37.67 billion riyals and the total deal count falling 14.2 per cent, according to the latest CBRE report. The National Residential Price Index, however, grew 2.6 per cent on an annual basis, supported by a 1.1 per cent rise in apartment prices during the quarter. The Al Rimal project will be funded through a Capital Market Authority-regulated investment structure managed by Al Rajhi Capital, an asset-management firm in the kingdom. “We have partnered with Al Rajhi, who will provide the fund management and will also provide the funding. So there is obviously certain equity we put in, but [the] majority is through the fund and the bank,” Mr Alkhoshaibi said. The company is also entering Syria with plans to build a $7 billion “UAE-style” mixed-use real estate project in Damascus in phases over 10 years. The company's property sales are ranging between Dh400 million and Dh700 million a month despite uncertainty over the Iran war, he added. “The external factors will have an impact, but it will be mitigated or reduced by delivering a great product in a great location at a reasonable price, and that's what we've been doing.”

events.title: Brisbane council to embrace early morning culture with new dawn plan
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Brisbane City Council to develop economic plan to embrace locals' early-morning habits The Brisbane City Council will conduct a survey about residents' early morning habits. ( ABC News: Brian Hurst ) The Brisbane City Council has launched a survey of residents' early-morning behaviours to inform a new Dawn Economy Plan. The council says the plan will help improve park facilities and public transport options as Brisbane leans into its reputation as a city of early risers. The survey will be open until November 22. The Brisbane City Council hopes to take advantage of residents' tendency to wake up early with the development of a new Dawn Plan, set to highlight early-morning economic opportunities. To inform the plan, the council is encouraging locals to take part in a survey about their experiences in Brisbane between 4am and 7am. Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner said the responses would help improve park facilities, pathways and public transport options in the early hours. Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner says Brisbane has a thriving dawn economy. ( ABC News: Lucas Hill ) "The reality is there's a thriving dawn economy at the moment," Cr Schrinner said. "People are voting with their feet. They want to get up early, they want to get out and about, and they want to get active." Analysis by University of Melbourne research fellow Dr Anna Edwards found Brisbane has one of the most active early-morning trading hours in Australia . About 13 per cent of Brisbane cafes are open between 5am and 6am. ( ABC News: Tim Swanston ) The research showed 13 per cent of Brisbane food and drink businesses are open between 5am and 6am, and by 8am, about half are serving customers. Dr Edwards said it was "wonderful" to see the Brisbane City Council "drawing on this strength and building on it". "We do a lot of planning of places by space, but we don't necessarily always think about timing. "Things have shifted quite considerably over the last five to 10 years, and I think we need to be thinking about this, but mornings generally have been quite overlooked." Blaine Swanborough co-owns a cafe in Mitchelton that opens at 6am. ( ABC News ) Blaine Swanborough co-owns a cafe in Mitchelton which opens at 6am, and said the community is often out and about by then. "We really see a drop off in trade later in the mornings as it heats up, especially in summer," Mr Swanborough said. "We really try and make the most of it in the early morning. "Our balance is with staff as well … but we try and find that line of providing what the community wants." The council says survey responses will help improve park facilities, pathways and public transport options. ( ABC News: Giulio Saggin, file photo ) Committee for Brisbane chief executive Jen Williams said the dawn economy plan was about playing to Brisbane's strengths. "For a long time, Brisbane has shied away from acknowledging that it is an early-rising city," Ms Williams said. "Whereas now, we can see with the global wellness movement and a focus on health, that people really do want to embrace the mornings. "The dawn economy doesn't come at the expense of the night-time economy. It is really about building a 24-hour city." Council opposition leader Jared Cassidy said the dawn survey was unnecessary. "It's shocking that our Lord Mayor, who has served in Council for over 20 years, has just realised Brisbane residents start their day early," Cr Cassidy said. "It's simple — we need investment in the infrastructure and services necessary to improve our uniquely Brisbane way of life. "Early morning public transport services and lighting in parks and bikeways to support active travel in the winter months would be a great start." The dawn economy survey will be open until midnight on November 22.

events.title: UAE tax rules: What businesses can claim for employee expenses
events.summary: Giving employees the tools they need to do their jobs effectively is a timeless business requirement. Whether a company has standard lists of equipment and resources for different grades and functions, which it should to make onboarding easier, most businesses could produce such lists without much difficulty. There are, however, tax considerations, particularly corporation tax and VAT . Thankfully, Federal Tax Authority Decision No 17 of 2026 has helpfully brought together answers to many of the questions businesses might have. There are five main sections, starting with transport provided for staff. It's critical that employees are not charged for the service and that transport is provided only between their homes and workplaces. Could there be a collection point for several employees, provided it is a reasonable distance from their homes? I would imagine so. Cash payments instead of transport cannot be offered, and there should be no identifiable non-business benefit. Could one employee who fails either test affect the entire arrangement? The decision says nothing about separating qualifying and non-qualifying cases. Best not be the person who tests the rules. What about pooling transport between two neighbouring companies? If the company providing the service changes according to a weekly schedule, would that complicate matters? A strict interpretation would require whichever company provides the service to invoice its commercial neighbour. I don't see how this can be avoided. Anything more complicated might best be outsourced for simplicity. Next is the provision of food and beverages. This is permissible where employees live so remotely that returning home is impractical. What constitutes remote is not defined, although I would interpret it as being unable to reach home within a reasonable time, given an individual's circumstances. This raises the possibility that only a small proportion of the workforce might qualify. No guidance has been provided on whether a minimum number of employees must meet the conditions. The provision must be linked to an employee's role and circumstances, including their workplace or residence. Suitable facilities should not be available at their accommodation or workplace, nor should local food outlets be reasonably accessible. Again, cash payments instead of food and beverages should not be an option. Moving on to company-provided accommodation, this must be an operational necessity. Perhaps the work site is in the Empty Quarter, 100 miles (160km) from the nearest town. Difficult access could make it reasonable to accommodate employees on or near the site. Accommodation and communication Accommodation should be suitable but not luxurious. No swimming pools, expansive manicured gardens, extensive household staff or additional reception rooms. The rules for onboarding new employees are a little more relaxed. Accommodation can be provided for up to 30 days, and the expense claimed, provided it is not ostentatious. Notably, the decision does not exclude employees who have already been living in the country, regardless of how long they have been here. I recall benefiting from such an arrangement when starting a role in the late 2000s. I believe there were two reasons for it. First, treating new starters differently would have been inconvenient. Second, with international personnel flying in and out of the region, putting everyone in the same hotel helped employees become familiar with the business and encouraged social interaction. Mobile phones are another area where guidance already existed, and the new decision restates and expands on it. Devices must be required for work and used only for business purposes. Each invoice should be reviewed, with personal calls identified and excluded from VAT or corporation tax claims. A company may decide to absorb the non-deductible cost rather than introduce an internal system for recovering personal expenses. Sometimes the administrative cost can outweigh the value of recovering small amounts spent on company assets. The new requirement is for a formal standard operating policy. This must be communicated to everyone affected, reviewed periodically, updated when necessary and demonstrably enforced. For businesses without standard operating procedures, this would be a good place to start. If I could, as an accountant, give human resources departments one task, it would be to map every business process and identify the roles and individuals responsible for each. This would strengthen both control and continuity. I can think of few projects more valuable when reassessing internal efficiency, particularly in an AI-driven world where automation is the mot du jour . Lastly comes parking, which is subject to the same requirements as mobile phones.

( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) The mother of Complainant A in the Alan Jones trial has told a court her son's "mood was different" when he returned home from a trip to the veteran broadcaster's private farm. Complainant A says when he was a 17-year-old schoolboy he was indecently assaulted by Mr Jones at the farm. The 85-year-old has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching related to five male complainants. A mother has told a trial she trusted Alan Jones as a mentor to her son before the broadcaster allegedly indecently assaulted the 17-year-old schoolboy at his private farm. One of Mr Jones's five alleged victims, known as Complainant A, alleges the radio host kissed him, put his tongue in his mouth and touched his buttocks when he visited Mr Jones's property in the Southern Highlands as a 17-year-old schoolboy. The 85-year-old has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexually touching, relating to several alleged incidents against five males between 2003 and 2020. The court previously heard the complainant was 13 years old when he sent a letter to the then-2GB radio host, requesting help for his single mother and their serious financial struggles. Emails read to the court show Mr Jones developed a relationship with the boy over several years, and that the prominent media figure helped wipe $600,000 off the mother's home loan and provided $100,000 to assist with the completion of their home. Mr Jones has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching related to five male complainants. ( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) Giving evidence at the trial on Tuesday, the boy's mother told the court her son met up with Mr Jones on several occasions including for private breakfasts at his Circular Quay apartment and lunch at a pub, but that she was never invited. She recalled when her son was 17 and had been invited by Mr Jones to spend two nights at his Fitzroy Falls farm and that she felt "really comfortable" with him going because she "trusted" the radio host. "[Someone] who saw that my son was intelligent as he is." Mother breaks down reading son's note NSW Sexual Violence Helpline on 1800 424 017 NSW Victims Services on 1800 633 063 Bravehearts (support for child sexual abuse survivors) on 1800 272 831 Child Protection Helpline on 132 111 MARS Australia (for men affected by rape and sexual abuse) on (07) 3857 1222 National Survivors Foundation on 1300 124 433 Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578. The woman told the court that when her son returned home from the trip, "his mood was different" and she "knew straight away something was up". "He wasn't sleeping, he was just staying up," she said. She said her son wrote her a letter 10 days later, saying "something happened at Fitzroy Falls" and that "someone did something they shouldn't have" but did not go into explicit detail. The mother broke down several times in the witness box, including when her son's letter was placed in front of her during her testimony. The woman said after receiving the note she asked her son if he wanted to report what happened to police. "He [my son] said to me that 'I wasn't raped'," she said. Mother tells court of her 'dire' financial situation The mother told the court that, before the alleged assault that she was in a "dire" situation, with a $1.3 million mortgage hanging over her head and the builder of her unfinished home walking off the job. The trial heard the woman's partner had also left the country and would often miss child support payments. The woman said a family friend suggested she reach out to the broadcaster for help because "he's influential and there might be people he knows who can help you". The mother said she provided information to her son to send to Mr Jones, who replied with an email saying, "you sound a special sort of young man," and asking for additional information. "When he [my son] told me that, I was incredibly grateful that someone of his stature was interested in what we were doing because we got such a prompt reply," the mother said. "I was desperate, people who are being served repossession papers are not cruising along in life." Court told Mr Jones put mother in contact with head of major bank The woman told the court that Mr Jones organised for the head of the Commonwealth Bank at the time to call her to understand more about her circumstances and try to find a "manageable" situation for the family.

events.title: Witkoff heads to Oslo, plans Russia trip for peace talks
events.summary: White House envoy Steve Witkoff is traveling to Oslo for talks Tuesday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European leaders, a U.S. official said. The big picture: The talks will bring together Ukraine, European allies and the U.S. as they seek to develop a peace proposal to present to Russia . The Oslo talks are expected to include Zelensky , Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, representatives of the E4 nations (the U.K., France, Germany and Poland) and officials from the EU and NATO. Driving the news: The U.S. official said that following Oslo, Witkoff is also planning to travel to Russia, where he hopes to meet with President Vladimir Putin and present ideas developed in close consultation with Ukraine and European partners. Trump adviser Jared Kushner has the flu and will not attend the Oslo meeting in person, but will participate virtually, the U.S. official said. The planned meetings in Oslo build on the discussions held at Witkoff's Miami-area Shell Bay club , where Zelensky committed to reviewing and advancing a series of proposals aimed at creating a pathway toward a comprehensive and durable peace agreement, the U.S. official added. Zoom in: The U.S. official said American, Ukrainian and European representatives worked together over the past week to develop the proposals. "Steve and Jared also spoke with President Zelensky on Sunday to review progress and discuss next steps," the U.S. official said. The trip is also expected to include efforts to secure the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired American teacher whom the U.S. says has been wrongfully detained in Russia. What's next: The U.S. official said the discussions are focused on two parallel tracks: Securing Ukraine's future: Establishing a sovereign, secure, and prosperous future for Ukraine, including credible security guarantees, European integration, and a comprehensive postwar economic framework that addresses Ukraine's financial needs and creates opportunities for long-term growth and investment. Creating the conditions for a durable peace: Developing a comprehensive proposal to Russia that addresses the issues necessary to end the war, establishes a new and enduring security architecture between Russia and Europe, and explores opportunities for postwar economic cooperation. "President Trump has directed an intensive process to develop a comprehensive peace proposal with Ukraine and Europe, and the next step is to test whether that work can form the basis for serious negotiations with Russia," the U.S. official said. "These discussions remain fluid, and substantial work remains. President Trump's objective is clear: to end the killing, bring the war to a close, and establish the conditions for a lasting peace that benefits Ukraine, Russia, Europe, and the United States."

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Eyre Peninsula water security 'unchanged' despite desal plant delays The Eyre Peninsula Desalination Plant is being built at Billy Lights Point outside Port Lincoln. ( ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton ) SA Water says delays on the Eyre Peninsula Desalination Plant will push the delivery of clean water past its original 2026 deadline. Critics argue the setbacks will result in significant budget and time overruns. SA Water says fresh drinking water will now be available to the region by mid-2027. Work on a desalination plant in regional South Australia has been delayed by six months, past when the region was due to run out of clean drinking water. SA Water has announced construction on the Eyre Peninsula Desalination Plant will be pushed back six months, to mid-2027, due to harder-than-usual granite affecting its underground boring Consumer access to water will be "unchanged". Residents of Port Lincoln and its surrounding areas were told they could run out of clean drinking water by 2026. The 35,000 residents of the Eyre Peninsula draw drinking water from the Uley South Basin, which has been depleting at a rate described as "dire" by the state government. The state government funded the then-$330 million Eyre Peninsula Desalination Plant project, which is now expected to cost approximately $470 million, at the Billy Lights Point coastal reserve. Early works began in February 2025 and it was projected to deliver fresh water by the end of this year. "We're a bit behind where we'd like to be," SA Water sustainable infrastructure general manager Peter Seltsikas said. Peter Seltsikas says tunnelling delays have pushed out the plant's completion date. ( ABC News: Brant Cumming ) "The pipelines are done, the desalination plant is substantially complete. "But the tunnelling delay means the first water day is pushing out to the middle of next year." Mr Seltsikas said higher-than-usual rains this year across the Eyre Peninsula had increased the water levels of the Uley South Basin. "We have enough water this year to continue to supply our customers and when the desalination plant comes next year they'll continue to have secure water." Cost blowouts and security concerns Glen Ingham was the spokesperson for community action group Hands Off Boston Bay, which was opposed to the location of the desalination plant. He said the delays were testing the government's claims the site is the "cheapest and quickest" option. Glen Ingham was the spokesperson for Hands Off Boston Bay. ( ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton ) "Here we are now at the end of 2026 and they're [pushing the end date] to the middle of next year. "I'm certain it will be beyond that and the cost blowout will be huge," he said. In a statement, the state government said the revised budget of the project would be detailed once "contractual processes with delivery partners are complete". Mr Seltsikas said the authority recognised the ongoing need to reduce water being taken from the basin. "So we are very much concerned about water security," he said. The state government said a revised Water Allocation Plan for the Southern Basins meant SA Water could extract water from the Uley South Basin and River Murray to meet consumer demand. SA Water's groundwater allocation will reduce to 3.5 gigalitres per year in 2027-28, as the plant comes online. A spokesperson said "it is not expected that water restrictions will be needed".
